msContents.summary: The gospel narrative in thirteen books composed of lines and half-lines of Virgil, with Ross's printed notes.

editorialDecl.p: Diplomatic transcription of the collection copy: spelling, u/v and i/j, ligatures (æ, œ), abbreviations (q;, tildes) and accents are kept as printed; long s is transcribed s. Printer's misprints are kept as printed and noted. Pages are named by the collation of the copy. The English translation faces the Latin line by line; English may carry a word across a line break where the sense of the pair is kept.

Text establishment: two independent machine readings of every line from the page images, compared letter by letter; every divergence adjudicated against the image; corrections logged in editorial notes (type="editorial").

refsDecl.p: Verses are identified by page (collation name) and line number; each Latin verse has an xml:id, which the English line cites in @corresp.

div.p: VIRGILII EVANGELISANTIS CHRISTIADOS LIBRI XIII. Inflante ALEXANDRO ROSÆO. Roterodami, Sumptibus Arnoldi Leers. 1653.

VIRGILII EVANGELISANTIS CHRISTIADOS LIBRI XIII. In quibus omnia quæ de Domino nostro JESU CHRISTO in utroque Testamento, vel dicta, vel prædicta sunt, altisona Divini Maronis tubâ suavissimè decantantur.
Inflante ALEXANDRO ROSÆO. Arma virumque Maro cecinit, nos acta Deumque; Cedant arma Viri, dum loquor acta Dei. ROTERODAMI. Ex Officinâ ARNOLDI LEERS, 1653.

Ad Illustrissimum Puerum CAROLUM Magnæ Britanniæ Principem. CAROLE, spes Patriæ, Patris justissima cura, Et generate Diis, & geniture Deos. Cui dextram HENRICI Magni, & caput opto JACOBI, Et pectus patrium religione sacrum. Vultus utrum præfert, præfer quoque moribus illum; Vtque refers patrem nomine, mente refer. Et facito mox cùm matura adoleverit ætas, Vt firmes Solymæ mœnia quassa tuæ. Mœnia quæ malesana cohors, inimica quieti, Tentat sacrilega præcipitare manu. Et CHRISTVM venerare, suo qui sanguine nobis Hanc Patriam peperit, totque trophæa tulit, Hostibus ejectis, & de Babylone triumphans; Quæ tibi grandiloquo concinit ore Maro. Hic vatum Princeps te Principe dignus habetur, Castaliæ hic fontes cum pietate bibes.

Hic simul Heroum laudes, & facta parentum, Et quid sit virtus intemerata, leges. Disce puer virtutem ex his, verumque laborem, Vt possis sceptro subdere Regna tuo. Quisquis sanctorum sequitur vestigia Patrum, Hic merito Patriæ dicitur esse Pater. C. T. V. studiosissimus ALEX. ROS.

Præfatio omnibus hoc Carmen lecturis utilis. HEM tibi, Amice Lector, Opus antelucanum, à me, horis hyemalibus matutinis nondum stratis egresso, decantatum; Aurora namque Musis amica, & reliquum diei annique tempus aliis studiis & negotiis impendere soleo. Sub gallicinium Cynthius (cui Gallus sacer est) aurem vellere & admonere solet, ut sub id tempus Dominum meum, cum Petro; quem ille voce tantum ter, ego verò vita & moribus sæpius abnegavi, cantando flerem, & flendo canerem; hanc Provinciam detractare, mihi religio fuit, præsertim Musarum ostiis apertis, & non invita Minerva; Eundem honorem exhibere Christo volenti, quem Homerus Vlyssi & Achilli, Virgilius Æneæ: ad hoc Opus concinnandum linguam

elegi Latinam, dicendi genus poeticum, & phrasin in Virgilianam: linguam praetuli Latinam, utpote omnium suavissimam, tanto aliis linguis elegantia superiorem, quanto olim fuit urbs urbibus eminentior; est etiam lingua communis maxime, & cujus beneficio religionis, civilitatis, legum, morum, disciplinarum, & artium participes sumus; dicendi autem genus elegi poëticum; utpote oratorio pręstantius; hujus enim finis sola est utilitas, illius verò utilitas voluptate conjuncta, & prodesse volunt & delectare Poetae, propterea omne tulit punctum: Deinde, Orator quivis esse potest, Poeta autem nemo, nisi cui à natura speciali quodam privilegio concessum est; nascimur enim Poetae, fimus Oratores: Tertio, efficacia in movendis affectibus longe Oratorem superat Poëta. Quis enim Orator Poëtam æquiparabit in describenda amoris, fortitudinis, doloris, aliarumque aut virtu¬

tum aut passionum vi, nisi Poëtae partes agat, ut saepe Oratores factitare solent. Hinc Poësis à Platone, Aristotele, Plutarcho, aliisque viris sapientibus tantum laudata: hinc Imperatores, Principes, Philosophi, Theologi, Poëtices studium non solum in summo honore habuerunt, sed ipsi quoque in eodem egregiam operam navarunt; Alexander mortuum Homerum, vivo Aristoteli prætulit; pluris apud Heronem Syracusanum fuit Poëta Pindarus, quam Plato Philosophus : Virgilio carmina sua in theatro recitanti, universus populus Romanus perinde ac Imperatori assurrexit; ejusdem diem natalem quotannis celebravit Augustus; Ovidio Getarum gens barbara, splendidum sepulchrum extruxit; soli Poetae digni habiti sunt, qui cum Imperatoribus lauro coronentur; Plato Poëtas ἐρμουνέας & ὑπερέτας Deorum vocat; (in Jone,) Philosophia quæ in formandis moribus versatur, in Poetarum sententiis omnino radices egit;

(Sextus Empiricus l. cont. Mathem. c. 17.) Cùm pater meus daret operam, ut in bonum virum evaderem, omnia Homeri Carmina ediscere coegit, inquit Xenophon sub Niceratis persona. (in Symposio) Philosophari intendentibus non sunt Poemata defugienda, sed in poematibus naviter philosophandum. (Plutarc. de audiend. Poët.) Omnis aetas per poeticam longè perfectius fingitur, quam per exempla Philosophorum: idem quoque ibidem ostendit, civitatum & legislatorum fuisse vetus institutum, fabulas adhibere Poetarum, ad hominum mentes suaviter efficaciterq; movendas. Res sacra Poeta est. neque canere prius potest, quam, Deo * plenus : hinc θεόπνευσοι vates, Poetæ ποφου τὸ πριῆιν, vocantur; est enim Poeta, quasi alter Deus; non solum formam ut natura facit, introducens, sed ipsam quoque materiam sibi creans. Sane Poetæ Philosophorum parentes sunt; & exemplis idem (sed efficacius) docentes, quod illi prae-

ceptis. Longum autem, ut inquit Seneca, iter per praecepta, breve & efficax per exempla. Si autem in hoc ἀμέσω saeculo nobilissimum hoc studium pluris haberetur, minus esset rixarum, & infrugiferarum disputationum, quibus Ecclesiae Christianae tranquillitas toties turbatur; Quod verò ad phrases attinet, elegi Virgilianam, nihil enim illa purius, castius, ornatius; est enim Maro, non solum omnium Poetarum doctissimus, sed modestissimus quoque, & vere virgineus, in cujus divino opere non est ulla vox obscoena; in illo sententiae, numeri, figurae, simplicitas, candor, ornatus, incomparabilia, ut verbis utar * Scaligeri. Quantum sit in eo eruditionis reconditae, docti norunt commentatores; in eo, nec Ethica, nec Politica, nec Oeconomica, nec Astronomica, nec Geographica, nec Theologica desiderantur; ex eo gentium mores, terrarum, ac marium situs, bellorum stratagemata, militare robur, facundiae vires, deorum sa¬

cra ediscuntur: est revera Virgilius omnis eruditionis promptuarium; Spero autem Opus hoc viris doctis & sapientibus non ingratum fore ; Sciolis autem & μινσομοσοις non canit meus Virgilius; ut nec olim Caligulæ; Scio enim esse quosdam adeò stupido & bruto ingenio, ut quibus Divinum Poëtices studium non magis sapiat quam Asinis lyra, aut Suibus amaracus. Sed hos ne in hominum quidem censu reponendos, cum * Scaligero puto: quidam forte stomachabuntur quod prophani Poëtae verbis & phra sibus religionis nostrae mysteria descripserini; quibus respondeo verbis D. Ambrosii: Cùm in fide nihil quod vituperare possunt invenerint, aliquid in sermone reprehendunt; agnoscunt non solum sententias, sed etiam versiculos Poetarum scripturis insertos divinis; unde gigantes, & vallem Ti* 11ieren. tanum Prophetici sermonis series non Damase de refugit, & Esaias Sirenas, &c. dixit: Hæc * Ambrosius, * Hieronymus, quam-

vis alioqui Poëtarum & Philosophorum nimis rigidus censor, concedit. Tamen, ut si quid in aliis utile reperimus, ad nostrum dogma convertamus; si quid verò superfluum de idolis, haec radamus, his calvitium inducamus, haec in unguium morem ferro desecemus; ut Israëlitæ jussi sunt tractare captivam mulierem. Non propter superstitionem prophanorum debemus Musicam fugere, aut literas non discere, quia earum repertorem dicunt esse Mercurium, inquit * D. Augustinus. Liceat ergo mihi cum Hebræis sacrum hoc tabernaculum immundorum animalium pellibus convestire, & cum primis Christianis Christum in idololatrico templo colere, illique aedem profanam consecrare; quamvis non video, quare tam castum & utile Virgilii poëma profanum dici debeat; imo illi potius profani sunt, qui, licet Christiani, impudici amoris illecebras carminibus immodestis doceant. Paulus nihil suae sanctimoniae

amisit, quando vectus fuit in nave idololatrica Castoris & Pollucis; nec Christi nomen profanatur, si in nave Virgiliana vehatur : sed quis audet dicere Maronem, de Christo nullam habuine cognitionem, cùm de eo tam apertè scribat in 4 Ecloga, & in digressu de morte Caesaris, in fine 1 Geor. nemo tam coecus est, quin haec de Christo esse dicta, perspiciat, inquit L. Vives. Sed cur non boni illi viri, qui omnium mortalium purissimi haberi volunt, & qui nisi quod ipsi faciunt, nil rectum putant; cur, inquam, non succensent Apostolis, qui linguis profanarum Gentium Christianam Religionem, & Scripturas per Orbem propagarunt? Quod autem nomina Deorum Gentilium hic usurpamus, sciant nobis tam fas esse vocabula à profano usu ad sacrum transferre, quam olim fuit Hebraeis, ex profana Aegyptiorum supellectile Tabernaculi vasa, & ornamenta con-

flare. Porphyrium male habuit, quod * Origenes omnes Graecorum divitias ad locupletandam Christianam doctrinam contulit. Moyses Disciplinas Aegyptiorum, Daniel Sapientiam Chaldaeorum, & D. Paulus Poetas didicerunt, ut his religionem locupletiorem redderent: quanto Auro, Argento, & veste suffarcinatus, exivit de Aegypto Cyprianus, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, Hilarius, hoc prior Moyses fecerat eruditus omni sapientia Aegyptiorum, inquit Augustinus. Præterea illi nobis verborum sunt Authores, eodem a 40. Augustino teste. Non mirum Julianum Christianis humanarum literarum studiis interdixisse, cùm animadvertisset Ethnicos propriis suis pennis à Christianis configi. Ergo mihi liceat bist. c. 10. Virgiliani Carminis supellectilem pretiosam (quamvis profanam ex illorum Senatusconsulto) ad meliorem usum transferre, & Religionis nostrae gemmam aureo illo annulo includere. Deinde, nomina haec Deorum à

nobis furto ablata sunt. Quis enim Poëtarum, quis Sophistarum, qui non omnino de Prophetarum fonte pota"Avaverit? teste * Tertulliano. Quis nescit nomen Jovis, à Jehova deductum? & Adonis ab Adonai, & Jacchi à Jah, & Vulcani à Tubal Cain, & Musæi à Moyse, & Jani, quo Noachum intelligo, à Jain, Vino; ergo liceat nobis quod nostrum est vindicare, & à possessoribus illis injustis eripere. Tertio: nomine Jovis non intelligebant Poctæ Idolum aliquod, sed verum & supremum Deum; ut ex Virgilianis Epithetis constat; est enim illi Jupiter, hominum rerumque repertor; divûm Pater, atque hominum Rex, qui cœlum tempestatesque serenat; rerum cui summa potestas; qui foedera fulmine sancit; qui nutu tremefacit Olympum; Superi Regnator Olympi: Pater omnipotens, qui res hominumque Deumque, aeternis regit Imperiis; torquet qui Sidera Mundi, Rex Ætheris alti: Scio non defuturos

Momos, qui hunc laborem nostrum tanquam inutilem carpent & damnabunt; sed non me latet facilius esse μωμᾶαξ, quàm μιμῆας, reprehendere, quam apprehendere; quis mortalium αμωμος est, & illi ridiculo Deo non obnoxius? sed tales aut Scioli sunt, aut Sycophantæ, aut Philautæ, qui vel ex ignorantia, vel malevolentia vel nimia sui opinione carpunt ea quae ipsi vel non intelligunt, vel praestare nequeunt. Certè à Judæ Proditoris mente non sunt alieni, qui me calumniabuntur, quod pretiosum hoc Unguentum, cum Magdalena, in Dominum meum effuderim; an mihi non licebit fertis laureis & floribus illius caput ornare, quod pro me spinis perforatum fuit? aut Templum chartaceum, illi fortè gratius Templo marmoreo, extruere, & dedicare, qui pro me sanctissimum corporis sui Templum dissolvit? Christum canere & laudare, est opus beatorum coelitum; est finis creationis & redemptionis

nostrae, ergo mihi sit fas illius laudes hic pro modulo meo balbutire. Non est opus inutile juventutem Christianam, a lectione impudicorum Carminum, ad sacram Historiam, jam doctissimis expressam versibus retrahere. Fastidienti stomacho salubrem Scripturarum cibum, mihi liceat, sapientis Medici instar, suavi condimento gratiorem reddere. Hic enim cum pura Virgiliana phrases, veram pietatem, & Religionis nostrae mysteria à teneris annis imbibent. Plato docet, Legum-latores Poetis uti, ut juvenum animi Carminibus deliniti, legibus obsequantur, nec futurus est hic labor Theologis omnino sterilis; praeter enim Divinas Meditationes, sacram Historiam, & Religionis nostrae arcana, hic aptas similitudines, phrases, & figuras suavissimas, ad exornandas conciones invenient, omnibus sane hoc opus futurum est, & utile & jucundum, nisi qui sint, qui mallent generosum vinum ex vase fi-

ctili, quàm ex aureo poculo bibere. Nulla autem est in hoc Opere (exceptis paucis) linea, in qua non invenies integrum Virgilianum Carmen, vel saltem dimidium, aut phrases illius; more autem poëtico fictiones. quasdam, sed pias, & Religioni consonas immiscui, ne versifex tantum esse videar; quod autem Scriptura fictionibus delectetur, testantur tot parabolæ & Apologi per sacram paginam sparsi; ubi autem suspicabar scrupulum aliquem Lectorem malè habiturum, adjeci marginalem notam sensus mei interpretem: qui plures desiderat, consulat priorem editionem. Vale Lector, & his mecum fruere; tibique exopto tantam in legendo, quantam ego in fingendo voluptatem habui.

IN hoc Opere, in quo sacros Scriptores civitate donavi, & Virgilium ex Romano Christianum, & ex Advena feci Proselytam: Sub nomine Sionis & Solyma describitur Ecclesiae Christi status, ab initio mundi, usque ad Domini in coelos elevationem. Variè illam oppugnat & persequitur Rex Pluto seu Satan; qui nullum non movet lapidem, ut Regnum suum Ecclesia subversâ in terris stabiliat, sed frustra semper enim Christus viros virtute & miraculis praestantes praemisit, qui Solymam à Satanae malitia & conatibus tuerentur; Tandem ipse venit, qui doctrina, virtute, miraculis, & morte, Regnum Babylonum evertit; Ecclesiam stabilivit; de Plutone & malorum Spirituum conciliabulo triumphavit.

Admonitio ad Lectorem. IN angustiore margine, l significat librum; E, Eclogam; G, Georgicorum librum; AE, Aeneadum: Ubi verò figura solitaria ponitur, absque adjectione alicujus literae, ibi liber Aeneados significatur.

Pluto animadvertens Solymæ fundamenta ab Abelo jacta, invidia stimulat Cainum Babylonis fundatorem, ut fratrem (quod illius sacrificium Deo acceptum fuit) interimeret; quo occiso, Deus alios excitat qui Solymam ædificent, nempe Sethum, Enosh, Kenam, Malaleël, Iared, Henocum, qui ad Paradisum fuit raptus; Methusalem, Noachum, cujus temporibus, instigante Plutone, Sethi posteri matrimonia contrahunt cum filiabus Caini; ex quibus procreantur Gigantes, quorum sceleribus provocatus Deus diluvium immisit, quo homines pecudesque perierunt, exceptis paucis in Arca servatis; cùm autem Noachus ex columbâ intellexisset siccatam rursus terram, Arcâ egreditur, victimam offert: varia præcepta filiis dat, quos agriculturam docet; cum illis Deus fœdus pepigit; sed senex vino captus, à filio Cham deridetur: interea Pluto, ut rursus Solymæ ædificationem impediret, omnes ad extructionem turris Babel hortatur; quos Deus iratus dispersit, & loquelam confundit; Abramum ex Chaldæa ad extruendam Solymam evocat; illi Christus promittitur, & Canaan; Lothum captivum liberat. Describitur terra, bellum, & excidium Sodomitarum: quæ de Abele, Noacho, Abramo, &c. dicuntur, Christo applicantur.

Per Plutonem intelligo Diabolum, qui τὴν πλούτου δόσιν, divitiarum largitor videri vult, & talis creditur à cultoribus suis: vel quia divitiae è terrae visceribus, haud procul ab ejus regno eruuntur, vel διὰ τὸ πλουτεῖν τοῖς νεκροῖς, omnes enim mortuorum impiorum animae, ad eum descendunt.

div.note: Per Parcas hic non intelligo vel ipsum Deum, vel inevitabilem necessitatem, vel tria tempora, praesens, praeteritum, & futurum, vel pariendi tempora, unde Nona, Decima, Morta, ut videre est in A. Gellio l.3. c.16. Arist. de mundo, Theod. &c. ad Graec. infid. ser.6. vel denique cum Poetis, Iovis scribas; sed Prophetas intelligo, Sp. Sancti amanuenses, qui notitiam rerum praeteritarum, praesentium, & futurarum habuerunt; qui nulli parcunt in denunciandis Dei judiciis: μοῖραι sunt, id est, sors & portio Domini; eadem significatione κλῆροι Sacerdotes vocantur.

Diabolus Draco & Serpens vocatur: hac forma apparuit Evae: sub hac forma cultus apud Gentes. Aesculapio, Mercurio, Minervae consecratur Serpens: horti Hesperidum custos in locis sacris pingi solitus, inter sidera relatus: & quibus non honoribus cultus fuit Daemon sub forma & nomine serpentis, hinc dii gentium serpentinis pedibus picti.

Per Mare mundum intelligo turbidum & amarum, periculis plenum, & monstris refertum. Mare est alternis aestibus reciprocum, modo allevans nos subitis incrementis, modò majoribus damnis deserens, assidueque jactans, &c. Seneca consol. ad Polyb. cap. 28.

div.p: Mortuo Abrahamo, in filium Isaac Palæstinos concitat Pluto, qui invidia puteos ejus obturant pulvere, ut ab ædificatione Solymæ deterreant; sed Deus ei apparens promissa olim Abramo renovat, gemellos dat qui in utero matris luctando præsignabant dissidium quod inter ipsos, & eorum posteros futurum erat; nam Jacobum minorem odio assiduo insequutus est Esau, quare suasu matris Jacob ad Labanum se recipit, illique 26 annis inservit; Deus autem sæpius illum consolatur, promittitque Christum ex eo venturum, & Babylonem eversurum; ostendit illi scalam super qua Angeli ascendebant & descendebant; exercitus Angelicus ad illum tuendum mittitur; cum Christo sub forma Angeli luctatur, victorque evadit, sed poplite ab Angelo percusso claudicavit; & Pluto in magnum discrimen Jacobum & filios conjicit ob raptam Dinam Jacobi filiam; inde ut senem luctu necaret, omnes fratres in Josephum quem pater præ reliquis diligebat, concitat; in puteum puerum demittunt, Judas illum vendit, qui tandem magnus in aula Pharonis evasit ob somniorum interpretationem; pater conspecta tunica hædina sanguine tincta occisum credidit, quare diu Josephum luget; filios in Ægyptum frumentatum mittit, quos Joseph tandem in gratiam recepit. Pluto interea in Jobum sævit, cujus historia describitur; omniaque Christo applicantur.

div.note: Eumenides hic masculini generis facio, eadem licentia qua Virgilius Venerem & Alecto Deos vocat : Descendo ac ducente Deo, Aen. 2. Nec dextra erranti Deus abfuit, id est, Alecto. Aen.7. Scivit enim doctissimus Poeta, Venerem esse semen genitalis, quod est potentia, tam mas, quam foemina. Et cum Alecto sit spiritus malus, non decuit ille semper foemineo sexui alligari, licet hoc Poetae alii faciunt; forte quia maligni spiritus hunc Sexum saepius assumunt quam virilem: Aen. 3. sunt illis virginei vultus. Sic Aen. 7. Alecto in vultus sese transformat miles. & fit Calybe Junonis avis anus, &c. Hic autem per Eumenides intelligo Cacodaemones; ut enim illae, sic hi sunt Dei Ministri, &c. Scelerum vindices, malorum hominum tortores; noctis & tenebrarum filii: sunt etiam aeri-vagi : vocantur etiam angues & canes, in abysso habitant. Tisiphone a τίσις ultio, & Φόνος caedes, μεγαίρειν invidere, Ἄληκτος nunquam cessans, sunt nomini Diabolis aptissima, illi enim nunquam cessant ultione, & caedibus, & invidia, genus humanum infestare.

div.note: Adorare — whether from the word Ador, the grain destined for sacrifices; or from ores, “mouths” [sic] (hence "to adore the people" in Apuleius l. 2. is to address them); or from orare, as in Aen. 10., "I, Turnus, willingly entreat you," that is, I earnestly entreat you. It was performed in various ways: 1. by kissing one's own hand, Job. 21. 27.; 2. another's hand; 3. by bending the knee; 4. by stretching out the hands; 5. by veiling the head, and heads before the altars: "we are veiled with a Phrygian robe," Aen. 2.; 6. by sitting — so Pythagoras taught: let them sit when adoring; 7. by prostrating the body on the ground: thus the Persians adored their kings. In marriage, to adore one's wife is to kiss her, etc.

div.p: Jacobo & Josepho mortuis, Satan ab Israëlitis alienat Pharonis animum, quibus gravia pensa imponit; sed Deus populi sui misertus, Moysen, ad Regem cum mandatis mittit, ut Solymæos ex servitute, variis editis signis & miraculis liberet; tandem Ægypto, multis cladibus affecta, Rege, dum Israëlitas insequitur, in mari submerso, Israëlitæ incolumes transeunt; qui instigante Plutone, in varia peccata incidunt, & in se Dei iram provocant. Lex promulgatur, Manna pluit, nubes interdiu, ignis noctu, viam per desertum monstrat, in quo ob peccata annos 40 errarunt: tria millia hominum ob idololatriam occisa; tabernaculum exstruitur, Pontificis indumenta describuntur. Core cum sociis murmurant & conspirant in Moysen; igniti serpentes mittuntur: Moyses in Pisgah moritur, populus duce Josua transit Jordanum. Describitur terra Chanaan, ubi varia bella inter Solymæos & terræ Incolas. Tandem Josua victor evasit, & Chananaeos subjugavit; cui vita functo, sequuti sunt Judices, qui Solymæam Plutonis invidia sæpe ab hostibus oppressum liberarunt. Gedeon stratagemate hostes in fugam conjicit. Jephthe victor domum rediens, filiam immolat. Describitur Ecclesiæ fœlicitas; & ad Christum fit omnium harum historiarum applicatio.

div.p: Juvenis Sampson dum uxorem peteret, leonem in viâ occidit, in cujus cadavere inter redeundum alvearium repperit. Hic Judex factus, Philistarum frumentum incendit, qui suasu Plutonis in eum conspirant, & ligant; ille autem ruptis vinculis, mille hostes Asini maxillâ sternit, & portas Gazæ aufert; postea blanditiis Dalilæ allectus, illi robur suum prodidit, & capillos amisit; & sic in hostium potestatem devenit, qui oculis effossis, in pistrinum dant. Dum verò postea Dagonis sacra peragunt, Sampsonem in templum ludibrii gratiâ introduci jubent, qui columnæ totis viribus (quæ jam cùm capillis creverant) incumbens, templum diruit, hostesque omnes & seipsum illa ruina obruit. Dagonis solemnitas describitur; Eli, qui Sampsoni successit, audita clade Israëlitarum & filiorum morte, subito expirat; sequitur Samuel, qui Saulum in Regem ungit, petente populo: Saulus filium habuit Jonathan, Davidi charissimum, qui Philistas in fugam conjecit: David autem Goliah Philistærum ducem, qui ipsum ad monomachiam provocaverat, lapillo sternit, & hostes fugat; postea Saulus Davidem veritus regnum affectare insensus servat, & necare statuit, sed frustra; semper enim incolumis evasit; interea Saulus sollicitus de belli eventu inter ipsum & Philistas, consulit Sagam, quæ ostendit illi Samuelis spectrum, ex quo didicit se ipsum cum filiis in prælio casurum; quod sequenti die contigit. David autem solus regno potitus, hostes undique domuit, multas urbes deditione cœpit: sed domesticis seditionibus vexatus est, præcipuè Absalonis, quem Joab occidit. Senio tandem confectus rex, Salomonem successorem designat, qui Templum, cujus magnificentia hic describitur, condidit, & pacem coluit; quæ omnia in Christum quadrant.

div.note: Crater vasis genus poculo capacius, cujus usus fuit solum in libationibus & solennioribus epulis: est etiam vas in quo cibus coquitur, vel mensae apponitur: terra rubens crater, pocula fagus erant. Ovid. 5. fest.

Non est dubitandum plurima dona fuisse exhibita Salomoni, inter quae coronas fuisse aureas verisimile; nam mos fuit Regibus pretiosas offerre coronas, teste Plinio de Claudio lib. 33. cap. 3. coronis aureis ornabatur facies Templi, 1. Mach. 4. 57. seu coronis insculptis lapidibus, & contectis laminis aureis.
Non solum tapetibus abundavit, sed vestibus etiam polymitis & variegatis; & variis picturis florum & animalium ornatis, qualis fuit vestis palmata & paludamentum apud Romanos.

div.note: Hic marmor Parium pro praestantissimo: sic Lycias sagittas, sumo namque speciem pro genere.

Domum Regis templo fuisse conjunctum, colligitur ex versu 9. lib. 1. Reg. c. 7. ubi extenditur usque ad atrium Templi majus, seu exterius. Domus autem Regis, domus saltus Libani, & domus Reginae, non fuerunt tria aedificia, sed unum in tres partes distinctum, ut probat Pineda de rebus Salom. lib. 5. cap. 5. Hic loca erant designata ad jus dicendum, ad convivia, ad arma custodienda: basilica erat magna & pulchra, &c. quam ad causas forenses agitandas, & lites decernendas condidit, &c. In ejus medio aedes quadrata, &c. in ea tribunal magnificum, ubi Rex jura reddebat. Joseph. antiq. lib. 8. cap. 2.

div.note: Ad majorem magnificentiam probabile est, Salomonem habuisse omnia vestium genera, quae res Aegyptia byssus vel sericus bombyx suppeditare, aut Tyrus, Sydon, Seres, aliaeque provinciae peregrinae exhibere potuerunt.

Laena vestis genus, quo Flamines uti solebant inter sacrificandum. Cicer. de claris orat. Chlamys autem vestis militaris pallio brevior; ipse agmine Pallas in medio chlamyde, & pictis conspectus in armis. Virgil. Aeneid. 8.
Ob vestes pictas & variegatas olim celebres fuere Babylon & Aegyptus. Haec ibi Memphitis tellus dat munera; victa est pectine Niliaco jam Babylonis acus. Martial.
Cum tot uxores & concubinas habuerit, Aegyptias, Tyrias, Sidonas, luxui & lautis vestibus conficiendis intentas: sine dubio delicatissimas illi vestes suppeditarunt.

div.p: Regina Saba Judæam ingressa, Oratores Solymam cum muneribus ad Salomonem mittit: qui cognita ex iis adventus Reginæ causa, ut nempe sapientiam suam audiret, & aulæ magnificentiam videret; Reginæ cum ingenti pompâ obviam fit, quam benigne hospitio excepit, eique aulæ suæ splendorem, & urbis varia monumenta ostendit: illa autem admirata tantam sapientiam & gloriam, domum revertitur: Regnum Salomonis cum Christi regno comparatur: Christiani ad pacem inter se, & bellum cum Turca exstimulantur. Salomone mortuo, regnum ipsius dividitur sub filio Roboam; & Solymam expugnat Rex Aegypti. Abias filius Roboami, Jeroboam bello vicit; Abiæ verò filius Asa, Aethiopes superavit. Jehosophat cum Achab à Syriis superatur, classis quam in Indiam missurus erat, submersa est. Precibus hostes devicit. Jehoram Idololatra fratres occidit; Achasiam Jebu peremit; Athalia regnum invadit; Achasiæ, Amasiæ, Vzziæ, Jothami, Achasi, Ezechiæ, Manassæ, Josiæ, Joasi, Joacimi, Joacin, & Sedechiæ vitæ breviter describuntur. Judith Holofernem somno vivoque obrutum, obtruncat, & patriam obsessam liberat. Chaldæi Solymam expugnant, & funditus cum Templo evertunt: Judæi autem captivi Babylonem ducuntur, ubi 70 annos manserunt; quo tempore Prophetas Deus ad illos misit, qui de Christo liberatore vaticinantur.

div.note: Hic Joacimus tradidit se obsessum Nabuchadnozari sub finem regni sui anni tertii, vel initium quarti: datis obsidibus (inter quos Daniel & tres pueri) & parte vasorum templi. Dan.1. tributarius in regno suo relinquitur: sed deficiens ad Aegypti Regem à Babyloniis iterum captus est, & an. 11. regni moritur.
Hic Joacin, seu Jechonias, regni mense tertio cum matre se Chaldaeis dedidit, & cum totâ sobole Babylonem ductus, initium dedit captivitati 70 annorum.
Zedechia fuit filius Josiae, patruus Jechoniae, 2. Reg. cap.24. at phrasi Hebraeâ frater dicitur, 2. Chron. 36. 10.

Hic Genebrardum sequor, qui ad tempus Nabuchadnozar hanc historiam refert. Ann. regni 13, misit Holofernem in Judaeam & Samariam. An. verò 19. reliquias Judaeorum Babylonem transtulit. Antea quoque dispersi erant Judaei sub Sennacherib, de quâ dispersione loquitur Achior cap. 5. libri Judith: & fortasse Isaias cap. 1. Alii hanc historiam ad Cambysis vel Assueri tempora referunt, sed nunquam erant Persarum Reges Nabuchadnozar vocati. Genebr. Chron. lib. 2.

div.note: Usque ad magni Constantini tempora.

div.p: Exactis 70 annis captivitatis Babylonicæ, & concessa Judæis in patriam redeundi venia, rursus extruitur Templum cum urbe, frustra moras injiciente Satana; & quamvis Judæi tempore captivitatis, & post reditum domum, partim domesticis dissidiis, partim, ab extremis hostibus in extremum discrimen sæpe adducti sunt: Deus tamen memor cœlestis Solymæ seu Ecclesiæ, varios populi sui desensores & vindices excitavit: nempe Hester, Alexandrum Macedonem, Ptolomæum Philadelphum, Mathiam, cum filiis Juda, Jonathan, Simone Hircano, qui typi fuerunt Christi cœlestis Solymæ propugnatoris: sed cùm Deus provocatus esset sceleribus Aristobuli regis & successorum ejus, permisit Judæam in Romanorum potestatem venire: Babylonis namque imperium jam Romam translatum fuit, ubi variis Pluto afficitur honoribus, ejusque regnum longe lateque propagatur: Solyma in servitutem redacta, extincta Macchabæorum familia, & Davidis stirpe sublata, Idumæis regibus subjicitur Judæa: interea Christus tam diu exspectatus & toties promissus, ex Spiritu Sancto concipitur, nunciante Angelo: variisque prodigiis antecedentibus, nascitur ex Maria Virgine. Digressio fit in laudes Christi: ostenditurque illum esse solum Deum Judæorum & Gentium: Græcorum vanitas in multiplicandis diis arguitur: Judæi ut Christum Ducem & Pastorem agnoscant, admonentur atque exhortantur.

div.p: Hoc Libro continentur vaticinia de Christi nativitate, vitâ, miraculis, morte, resurrectione, ascensione, &c. deque amplitudine, potentiâ, & splendore coelestis Solymæ, id est, Ecclesiæ & Regni Christi. Ubi arreptâ occasione sit digressio in laudes Regum Jacobi & Caroli nutritiorum Ecclesiæ parentum. Ubi etiam invehitur Virgilius in sacrilegos Solymæ expilatores, qui rapaci hoc sæculo, Ecclesiæ bona, furore nefario perciti, uncis manibus diripuerunt.

div.note: Lucretius, Virgilius, aliique Poetae, supremum Deum aethera vocant; & quem Plato à cursu Θεὸν, hunc Aristoteles à sempiterno cursu αἰθέρα nominavit, non autem ab ardore, ut Cicero. Hic igitur Christo non attribuo cum Marcionitis aetherium corpus, sed aetherium Patrem cum Ecclesia.

div.p: Christi nativitatem Angeli pastoribus nunciant, qui ut jussi Bethlemum ad puerum contendunt; octavo die Christus circumciditur. Interea nova Stella Magos ex Persia Hierosolymam ducit: Herodes autem ex rumore novi Regis nati turbatus, pueros Bethlemiticos per satellites occidit, Josephus verò & Magi in somno ab Angelo moniti, fugerunt; ille cum puero & matre in Ægyptum; hi per aliam viam in patriam. Postquam Christum adorâssent, Simeon eum Sacerdoti oblatum ulnis amplexus est. Duodecimum agens annum inter Doctores in templo à parentibus inventus fuit, cum quibus privatam vitam egit, donec anno ætatis suæ exacto trigesimo, à Johanne baptisatus in Jordane fuit. Johannis solitaria & frugalis vivendi ratio commendatur. Christum jejunantem variis tentationibus invadit Pluto ; quo victo & fugato, domino ministerium suum praebuerunt Angeli; duodecim tenuis fortunæ socios elegit Christus: describitur conditio Regni Christi: bellum inter Christianos detestatur Poëta, & varias intexit divinas & pias meditationes.

div.p: Postquam 12 ministros in unum convocasset Christus, variis documentis & præceptis instruit, adversus hostium malitiam animat: describitur Divini Verbi potentiâ in ore Apostolorum, quo regnum Plutonis corruit. Christus in nuptiis Cana Galilææ aquam in vinum vertit; postea flagello mercatores è Templo ejecit; Evangelium prædicat, & omnes morborum species curat. Cum Samaritana ad puteum Divinum colloquium habet; cùm autem undique confluentes turbæ illum premerent, Petri naviculam ascendit, & ex ea populum docuit, doctrinam verò miranda piscium captura confirmavit: viduæ unicum filium defunctum resuscitat. Dum verò in navi dormiret, excitatâ tempestate Pluto illum cum sociis submergere tentat; sed è somno experrectus, objurgatis ventis procellam sedat. Ex duobus Gadarenis juvenibus Dæmones ejecit, qui porcorum gregem aquis immerserunt. Hæmorrhoissam contactu vestis sanat. Filiam Jairi mortuam vivificat. Magdalenam lachrymantem à Dæmonibus liberat. Reguli filium absens sanat. In Patria docens, in vitæ discrimen adducitur: Baptista incarceratur, & decollatur. Describitur Herodis convivium, & res gestæ Herodis magni obiter decantantur.

div.p: Christus auditâ Johannis nece, ex Galilæâ in desertum secessit, ubi populi turbam ingentem miraculose pavit: Super mare ambulat, & Petrum pene immersum, liberat: Populum docet & sanat; motus Chananitidis precibus, & fide filiam ipsius sanitati restituit. 38 annos morbo laborantem ad Bethesdam quendam, ad valetudinem reduxit: & hydropicum curat. Pharisæi invidia moti, satellites quosdam miserunt ad capiendum Christum, qui ipsi verbis Christi capti, re infectâ, redierunt: Postea à furente plebe saxis impetitur. In monte Thabor transfiguratur: descendens a monte, puerum à Daemone liberat; & Apostolos objurgat. Capernaum ingressus, tributum solvit, pecunia in ore piscis reperta. Dum docet in Templo, iterum lapidatur, sed se subduxit & Bethaniam pervenit, ubi Lazarum suscitat jam mor¬

div.p: Finita cœna, Christus cum Apostolis in hortum Gethsemani secessit, ubi precantem & sanguine sudantem, Angelus solatur; exhibetque poculum lethali vino plenum, quod ipse Pater cœlestis miscuit: Poëticè describitur poculum ab Angelis fabricatum; in cujus oris, Christi, Apostolorum, multorumque Christianorum martyria cælantur: Describitur Christi passio in horto, quem Judas ibidem, comitante sceleratorum militum cohorte, osculo prodidit, verùm omnes ad Christi vocem in terram ceciderunt; tandem

div.p: Christus cruci affixus inter duos fures elevatur; titulus superscribitur: alter latronum ridet, alter Christum fatetur & orat, cui Paradisus promittitur. Dumque Christus pro inimicis orat, matrem graviter dolentem conspicit, eamque Johanni commendat. Describitur miraculosa Solis Eclypsis, & Judæorum cæcitas; tandem Dominus dolores innumeros & non dicendos passus, exspiravit; tremit terra, rumpuntur saxa, sepulchra recluduntur: velum Templi, quod hic describitur, discerptum est. Centurio his prodigiis motus, Christum Dei Filium agnoscit; dumque latronum crura franguntur, lancea Christi latus confoditur, ex quo sanguis & aqua fluxit. Describitur Christi descensus ad inferos, & ejusdem sepultura; nec non Josephi, Nicodemi, & Matrum pietas; Virginisque Mariæ acerbissimi dolores. Christus tertiâ die, territis custodibus terræ motu, resurrexit. Angeli mulieribus, illæ Apostolis resurrectionem nunciant. Petrus & Johannes ad sepulchrum currunt. Vigiles autem pecunia corrupti, mendacium spargunt, Discipulos nempe Dominum furto abstulisse: Judæorum malitia in Christum describitur. Magdalena adstat sepulchro plorans,

div.p: Christus in cœlum ascensurus, varia præcepta dat Apostolis, quibus benedicit, & Petro Ecclesiæ suæ curam credit. Deus Pater convocato Angelorum concilio, de Christi Filii in cœlos elevatione mentem suam aperit, cui Angeli ascenserunt omnes, & Christo ascendenti ministerium præbuerunt. Poëticè sub formâ magnifici Palatii describitur cœlestis gloria. Dum verò Apostoli Christum ascendentem, oculorum acie curiosius sequuntur, à duobus Angelis de ipsius reditu docentur. Describitur ultimum judicium, & Christi redeuntis gloria: Interea Apostoli Hierosolymam redeunt, ubi in superiore cœnaculo dum unanimes orationi incumbunt, Spiritus Sanctus specie ignitarum linguarum in eos descendit. Hic varia mysteria, & meditationes interseruntur. Christiani ad pacem mutuam rursus exhortantur, & ad bellum Turcis inferendum.

div.note: Hic per Astra Titania non intelligo Solem, de quo in sequenti versu, sed minores Stellas: & sic (puto) intelligendus est Virgilium Aen. lib. 6. cùm ait, Spiritum alere Titania astra, id est, Solem fovere luce suâ Stellas. Est enim Sol anima & mens mundi, ut Macrobius ostendit ex Poëtis & Philosophis. Soli nomina omnium Deorum conveniunt. Sol etiam Spiritus à Salomone vocatur, Eccles 17. Falluntur ergo Virgilii Interpretes (si ipse non fallor) qui per Astra Titania Solem intelligunt.

div.note: Deus est ubique, sedes tamen ejus in Oriente locatur, et in loco honoratiore: Ergo Christus qui Oriens ab alto dicitur, Luc. 1. in Oriente collocatur; illinc Christum rediturum speramus. In Oriente pedes Christi steterunt, Zach. 14. nempe in monte Olivarum. Ex Oriente, scilicet ex Paradiso ejecti sumus; ad Orientem oramus: Orientem Templa nostra respiciunt. Vide Justinum Martyr. ad Orthodox. q. 118. Tertull. in Apolog. Origin. Homil. 5. in Num. Athanas. de Necess. quaest. q. 14. Basil. de Spir. Sanct. cap. 27. &c. Et 70 Interpretes, ad Orientem, Psal. 68. 36. Sicut fulgur exit ab Oriente, sic erit adventus Filii hominis, Matth. 24. 27.

div.note: Vitta ornabantur olim Sepulchra, Cadavera, Sacerdotes, victimae mulieres, Sponsae, Athletae, Victores, Principes, &c. His Vitta pro Diademate sumitur, nihil enim aliud fuit veterum Diadema, quam Vitta, Fascia, vel Taenia: haec namque indifferenter usurpari apud Authores video Diadema à διαδέω, revincio. Pompejus Diademate vulnus circumligavit: imposita capiti vincla veneranda gere. Sen. in Thyest. intelligit Diadema. * Paean Carmen est victoriae, ut ex Aeschylo docet Servius.

Jupiter quasi juvans Pater, seu potius Jovae Pater, à voce Jehova, ut Adonis ab Adonai. Sapientiores Ethnici eundem supremum agnoverunt Deum, quem nos: hunc Jovem nominarunt, cujus nos progenies sumus: ut ex Arato probat D. Paulus. Nec minus licet nobis hunc appellare Jovem quàm Θεόν, aut νοῦν, aut λόγον, aut πνεῦμα: quae voces sunt Ethnicae. Ζεὺς πρῶτος γίνετο, Ζεὺς ὕστατος ἀρχικέραυνος, &c. Vide Orphei Carmen de Jove.

div.p: The Christiad of Virgil Evangelizing, in Thirteen Books. With Alexander Ross blowing [the pipe]. Rotterdam, at the expense of Arnold Leers, 1653.

THE CHRISTIAD OF VIRGIL EVANGELIZING, IN THIRTEEN BOOKS. In which all that has been said or foretold of our Lord Jesus Christ in either Testament is most sweetly sung upon the resounding trumpet of the divine Maro.

[The trumpet] blown by ALEXANDER ROSS. Maro sang of arms and the man; we sing of deeds and God. Let the arms of the man give way, while I recount the deeds of God. Rotterdam. From the workshop of Arnold Leers, 1653.

To the Most Illustrious Boy CHARLES, Prince of Great Britain. CHARLES, hope of your country, your father's most rightful care, born of gods and destined to beget gods: for you I wish the right hand of Henry the Great, the head of James, and your father's heart, hallowed by religion. Whichever of the two your face displays, display him also in your character; and, as you reproduce your father in name, reproduce him in mind. And see to it, as soon as your years have ripened, that you strengthen the battered walls of your Jerusalem: walls which a frenzied band, hostile to peace, attempts to cast down with sacrilegious hand. Revere also Christ, who by his own blood won this fatherland for us and carried off so many trophies, having driven out his enemies and triumphed over Babylon: these deeds Maro sings to you in a grandiloquent voice. Here the prince of poets is accounted worthy of you, a prince; here you will drink from Castalia's springs together with piety.

Here too you will read the praises of heroes and the deeds of your forebears, and what unblemished virtue is. Learn virtue, boy, from these, and true toil, that you may be able to bring kingdoms under your sceptre. Whoever follows the footsteps of the holy Fathers is rightly said to be the Father of his country.
Your Highness's most devoted servant, ALEXANDER ROSS.

A Preface Useful to All Who Will Read This Poem.
Here for you, dear reader, is a work composed before dawn, sung by me during the winter morning hours before I had yet left my bed; for Dawn is friendly to the Muses, and I am accustomed to devote the remaining time of the day and year to other studies and business. At cockcrow Cynthius (to whom the cock is sacred) is wont to tug at my ear and urge me, at that hour, to weep with Peter for my Lord while singing, and to sing while weeping—my Lord whom Peter denied only three times in word, but whom I have denied more often in life and conduct. I scrupled to refuse this commission, especially with the doors of the Muses open and Minerva not unwilling. Wishing to render to Christ the same honor that Homer rendered to Ulysses and Achilles, and Virgil to Aeneas, for the composition of this work I chose the language…

…the Latin tongue, the poetic kind of speech, and Virgilian phrasing. I preferred the Latin tongue as the sweetest of all, and as far superior to other tongues in elegance as the City was once more eminent than other cities; it is besides the most widely shared language, and it is by its good offices that we have our part in religion, civility, laws, manners, the disciplines and the arts. The poetic kind of speech I chose as being more excellent than the oratorical; for the end of oratory is usefulness alone, whereas that of poetry is usefulness joined with pleasure, and poets aim both to profit and to delight, and on that account the poet has carried every vote. Next, anyone at all can be an orator, but no one can be a poet unless nature has granted it to him by some special privilege: poets we are born, orators we are made. Thirdly, in effectiveness at moving the affections the poet far surpasses the orator. For what orator will match a poet in setting out the force of love, of courage, of grief, and of the other virtues…

…or by the force of the passions, unless he plays the poet's part, as orators have often been in the habit of doing? Hence poetry has been so greatly praised by Plato, by Aristotle, by Plutarch, and by other wise men; hence emperors, princes, philosophers and theologians have not only held the study of poetry in the highest honour, but have themselves also spent excellent labour upon it. Alexander preferred Homer dead to Aristotle alive; with Hiero of Syracuse the poet Pindar counted for more than the philosopher Plato; when Virgil recited his verses in the theatre, the whole Roman people rose to its feet before him just as it would before the emperor; Augustus kept Virgil's birthday every year; the barbarous nation of the Getae raised a splendid tomb for Ovid; poets alone have been thought worthy to be crowned with laurel alongside emperors; Plato (in the Ion) calls poets the interpreters and the servants of the gods; and the philosophy which is concerned with the shaping of manners has struck its roots wholly in the sayings of the poets.

(Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, ch. 17.) 'When my father was striving to make me turn out a good man, he compelled me to learn all the poems of Homer by heart,' says Xenophon in the person of Niceratus (in the Symposium). Those intending to philosophize must not flee from poems, but must philosophize vigorously within poems (Plutarch, On Listening to the Poets). Every age is shaped far more perfectly through poetry than through the examples of philosophers: in the same work he also shows that it was an ancient practice of states and lawgivers to employ the fables of poets to move human minds pleasantly and effectively. The poet is a sacred being, and cannot sing until he is filled with God *; hence bards are called θεόπνευστοι, 'god-breathed,' and poets take their name from τὸ ποιεῖν, 'to make.' For the poet is like a second God, not only introducing form as nature does, but also creating the very matter for himself. Indeed, poets are the parents of philosophers, teaching through examples—and more effectively—the same things that the latter teach through pre—

—cepts. The road, as Seneca says, is long through precepts, but short and effective through examples. If in this uncultured age this most noble study were more highly valued, there would be fewer quarrels and fruitless disputes by which the tranquillity of the Christian Church is so often disturbed. As for phrasing, I chose Virgilian style, for nothing is purer, more chaste, or more ornate; Maro is not only the most learned of all poets but also the most modest and truly maiden-like, in whose divine work there is no obscene word; in him the sentiments, rhythms, figures, simplicity, brilliance, and ornamentation are, to use the words of Scaliger, incomparable. How much recondite learning there is in him the learned commentators know; in him neither Ethics, nor Politics, nor Economics, nor Astronomy, nor Geography, nor Theology is lacking; from him [one learns] the customs of nations, the lay of lands and seas, the stratagems of wars, military strength, the powers of eloquence, the gods' sa—

sacred things are learned by heart; Virgil is truly a storehouse of all learning. I hope, moreover, that this work will not be unwelcome to learned and wise men. But my Virgil does not sing for smatterers and haters of the Muses, any more than he did for Caligula of old. For I know that some are of such dull and brutish disposition that the divine study of poetry has no more savour for them than a lyre has for asses or marjoram for swine. But I think, with Scaliger, that such men should not even be numbered among human beings. Some may perhaps take offence because I have described the mysteries of our religion in the words and phrases of a profane poet. To them I reply in the words of St Ambrose: "When they can find nothing in the faith to blame, they find fault with something in its language; they recognise not only the thoughts of the poets, but even their lines inserted into the divine Scriptures. Hence the course of prophetic discourse does not shrink from giants and the valley of the Titans, and Isaiah spoke of Sirens, and so forth" (On the Faith 3.1). Thus Ambrose. Jerome (Letter to Damasus, On the Prodigal Son), although—

—though otherwise too strict a critic of poets and philosophers, concedes this. 'Nevertheless, if we find anything useful in others, let us convert it to our own teaching; if anything superfluous about idols, let us shave it off, let us make it bald, let us cut it away with iron like fingernails, as the Israelites were commanded to treat a captive woman.' 'We should not flee from music on account of the superstition of the pagans, nor refrain from learning letters because they say Mercury was their inventor,' says St Augustine. Let me therefore be permitted, like the Hebrews, to cover this holy tabernacle with the skins of unclean animals, and, like the earliest Christians, to worship Christ in an idolatrous temple and consecrate a profane building to him—although I do not see why so chaste and useful a poem as Virgil's ought to be called profane; rather, those people are themselves profane who, though Christians, teach the enticements of unchaste love in immodest verses. Paul [lost] nothing of his holiness—

—when he sailed in the idolatrous ship of Castor and Pollux; nor is the name of Christ profaned if it is carried in the Virgilian vessel. But who dares say that Maro had no knowledge of Christ, when he writes of him so openly in the Fourth Eclogue and in the digression on the death of Caesar at the end of Georgics 1? 'No one is so blind as not to see that these things were said about Christ,' says Ludovico Vives. But why do those fine fellows—who wish to be regarded as the purest of all mortals and who think nothing right except what they themselves do—why, I ask, do they not reproach the Apostles, who propagated the Christian religion and the Scriptures throughout the world in the languages of profane nations? As for our use here of the names of the pagan gods, let them know that it is as lawful for us to transfer words from profane use to sacred as it once was for the Hebrews to fashion the vessels and ornaments of the Tabernacle from the profane furnishings of the Egyptians—

Porphyry was vexed that Origen brought all the riches of the Greeks to enrich Christian doctrine. Moses learned the disciplines of the Egyptians, Daniel the wisdom of the Chaldaeans, and St Paul the poets, so as to make religion richer by their means: 'laden with how much gold, silver, and raiment did Cyprian, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary come out of Egypt! Before them Moses had done the same, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,' says Augustine. Moreover, they are the originators of our very words, as the same Augustine attests. It is no wonder that Julian forbade Christians the study of humane letters, when he had perceived that the pagans were being transfixed with their own feathers by Christians. Therefore let me be permitted to transfer the precious furnishings of Virgilian song—profane though they be by the decree of those senators—to a better use, and to set the jewel of our religion in that golden ring. Furthermore, these names of the gods were—

...were stolen from us. For what poet, what sophist has not drunk at all from the fountain of the Prophets? Tertullian is witness. Who does not know that the name of Jove is derived from Jehovah, Adonis from Adonai, Iacchus from Jah, Vulcan from Tubal Cain, Musaeus from Moses, and Janus—by whom I mean Noah—from Jain, meaning wine? Let us therefore reclaim what is ours and wrest it from those unjust possessors. Thirdly, by the name of Jove the poets meant not any idol but the true and supreme God, as is evident from the Virgilian epithets. For in Virgil Jupiter is "the creator of men and things"; "father of the gods and king of men, who clears the sky and calms the storms"; "he who holds supreme power over all things"; "he who ratifies treaties with the thunderbolt"; "he who makes Olympus tremble with a nod"; "ruler of high Olympus"; "almighty Father, who governs the affairs of men and gods with eternal dominion"; "he who turns the stars of the world"; and "king of heaven on high." I know that there will be no lack of Momuses,

Momuses, who will carp at this labor of ours as useless and condemn it; but I am well aware that it is easier to find fault than to imitate, to censure than to comprehend. What mortal is without fault and not exposed to that god of ridicule? Such men, however, are either smatterers, slanderers, or self-lovers: out of ignorance, malice, or excessive self-regard, they carp at things which they themselves either do not understand or are incapable of accomplishing. Certainly those who will vilify me because, with Magdalene, I have poured this precious ointment upon my Lord are not far removed from the disposition of Judas the Betrayer. Shall I not be permitted to adorn with laurel garlands and flowers the head that for my sake was pierced with thorns? Or to build and dedicate a paper temple—perhaps more pleasing to him than a marble temple—to him who for my sake dissolved the most holy temple of his own body? To sing of and praise Christ is the work of the blessed inhabitants of heaven; it is the purpose of our creation and redemption.

…of our redemption. Therefore, let it be lawful for me here to stammer out his praises according to my modest ability. It is no useless undertaking to draw Christian youth away from reading indecent poems and back to sacred history, now expressed in the most learned verse. Like a wise physician, let me make the wholesome food of the Scriptures more agreeable to a squeamish stomach by means of a pleasant seasoning. For here, together with pure Virgilian diction, they will imbibe true piety and the mysteries of our religion from their earliest years. Plato teaches (Laws 2) that lawgivers should employ poets, so that the minds of the young, charmed by songs, may obey the laws. Nor will this labour be altogether fruitless for theologians; for besides divine meditations, sacred history, and the mysteries of our religion, they will find here apt comparisons, turns of phrase, and most pleasing figures with which to embellish sermons. Indeed, this work will be both useful and delightful to everyone, unless there are some who would rather drink fine wine from an earthenware vessel than from a golden cup.

…than to drink it from a golden cup. But in this work there is, with few exceptions, no line in which you will not find an entire Virgilian verse, or at least half a verse, or phrases of his. Moreover, after the manner of poets, I have intermingled certain fictions—pious ones, however, and consonant with religion—lest I should seem to be merely a versifier. That Scripture delights in fictions is attested by the many parables and fables scattered throughout the sacred page. Wherever, however, I suspected that some scruple might trouble the reader, I added a marginal note interpreting my meaning; whoever desires more such notes should consult the earlier edition. Farewell, reader, and enjoy these things with me; I wish you as much pleasure in reading as I had in inventing them.

Sennacherib. Sennacherib's army, book 5. Argumentum.

In this Work, in which I have granted citizenship to the sacred Writers and made Virgil from a Roman into a Christian and from a stranger into a proselyte: Under the names of Sion and Solyma is described the state of the Church of Christ, from the beginning of the world to the Lord's ascension into heaven. King Pluto, or Satan, attacks and persecutes her in various ways; he leaves no stone unturned to establish his own kingdom on earth by overthrowing the Church, but always in vain, for Christ has always sent ahead men outstanding in virtue and miracles to defend Solyma from Satan's malice and schemes. At last he himself came, who by his teaching, virtue, miracles, and death overthrew the Kingdom of Babylon, established the Church, and triumphed over Pluto and the council of evil Spirits.

Notice to the Reader. In the narrower margin, L signifies a book; E, an Eclogue; G, a book of the Georgics; and AE, a book of the Aeneid. Wherever, however, a numeral is placed by itself, without the addition of any letter, a book of the Aeneid is meant.

Pluto, observing that the foundations of Solyma had been laid by Abel, incites Cain, the founder of Babylon, through envy to kill his brother because Abel's sacrifice had been accepted by God. After Abel is killed, God raises up others to build Solyma, namely Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, who was carried off to Paradise, Methuselah, and Noah. In Noah's time, at Pluto's instigation, Seth's descendants marry the daughters of Cain; from them the Giants are begotten. Provoked by their crimes, God sends a flood in which human beings and beasts perish, except for the few preserved in the Ark. When Noah learns from the dove that the earth has become dry again, he leaves the Ark and offers a sacrifice. He gives his sons various commandments and teaches them agriculture; God makes a covenant with them. But the old man, overcome by wine, is mocked by his son Ham. Meanwhile Pluto, in order to hinder the building of Solyma once again, urges everyone to construct the tower of Babel; God angrily disperses them and confounds their speech. He summons Abram from Chaldaea to build Solyma; Christ and Canaan are promised to Abram, and Abram frees the captive Lot. The land, the war, and the destruction of the Sodomites are described. What is said about Abel, Noah, Abram, and the others is applied to Christ.

lg.l: I [am] he who once, on a slender reed, tuned
a song, and, having gone out from Egypt through inhospitable crags,
and through the empty dwellings of the Arabs and their vacant realms
I led the sons of Abraham onward; but now the awe-inspiring
deeds of Christ, and God, I sing — he who first from heaven's shores
descended into the womb of the joyful Virgin, and the world
of the lands he visited as an exile, and came to the Canaanite
shores, after being much tossed about both on land and on the deep,
by the force of those above, on account of cruel Pluto's unforgetting wrath;
he also suffered much on the mountain, until he could found the city.
For he sank down upon the wood, and spoke his last words,
and poured out his holy life together with much blood,
and dared to make his way into the depths of blackening Avernus,
but at last returned victorious to his native shores?
And he overthrew the gods of Latium, and the whole Latin race,
and the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
Muse, rehearse to me the causes — what divine power was wronged,
or, grieving over what, did the King of the gods himself compel
a man renowned for piety to pass through so many reversals and face so many toils?

div.note: Horrentia. In Virgil horrentia and horrenda often signify things worthy of reverence and fear: thus "the awe-inspiring Sibyl," Aen. 6; "awe-inspiring through religious sanctity," Aen.; and "the awe-inspiring maiden," Aen. 11. Christ's works, however, were truly dreadful to the Devil and the wicked.
He was an exile of his own will, not under compulsion; for us, not for himself.
Alto, by a Hebrew idiom; for among them a lake is called a sea.
By "the gods above" I mean the rulers, the priests, the scribes, and the like.

By Pluto I understand the Devil, who wishes to be seen as τὴν πλούτου δόσιν, the bestower of riches, and is believed to be such by his worshippers: either because riches are dug out of the bowels of the earth, not far from his kingdom, or διὰ τὸ πλουτεῖν τοῖς νεκροῖς, because he is rich in the dead; for all the souls of the wicked dead go down to him.

This city which Christ founded is the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which throughout this work is called Sion and Solyma. Two loves made two cities, &c. Aug. de Civitate Dei, lib. 14. cap. ult. & lib. 15. in exordio.
He overthrew idolatrous Rome according to the Sibylline oracle, ρώμη μὲν ῥύμη ἔσεται καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος, &c.—Rome shall become a street, and Delos shall become obscure.

lg.l: impelled [him]? Or does the mind of heaven blaze with such great wrath?
Surely in the supreme begetter of gods and men
no wrath forgives; no pain burns in [his] bones:
in Christ there was no appearance of crime or of guile;
but all the guilt was ours; He neither dared
nor could commit any wickedness; never did there fall from his lips
any falsehood, nor could he give way to any fault;
because of the guilt and madness of Adam alone as he fell
he bore these things; he loved an unfaithful friend too well.
There was an ancient city of famous name; that city
Nimrod, the father of Ninus, founded, and with a high
rampart of walls Semiramis girded it about, the wife
of Ninus; then she added bridges and fortifications,
a warrior; she was not, with Minerva's distaff or work-baskets,
accustomed to womanly handiwork, but a maiden [trained] to endure
hard fighting, and to outstrip the winds with the running of her feet.
This city was rich in resources and fiercely devoted to war;
which Pluto is said, above all other lands, this one alone
to have cherished, the rest set behind; here was his altar,
here was his worship; that this should be the kingdom over the nations, Dis
(if somehow the fates allow) even then strives for this and cherishes it;
but indeed that an offspring was descended from Jewish blood
he had heard, one that would one day overturn the Stygian strongholds:
hence a people ruling far and wide, and mighty in the word

div.note: Although God is the mind or soul of the world, the world is nevertheless not an animal, as the Platonists and Stoics would have it: for he is an assisting form, not an informing one, since he is not a part of it, nor an imperfect substance.
This city is Babylon, by which I mean Satan's kingdom. The Devil is the ruler of that city which, in a mystical sense, is Babylon, etc. Augustine, book 2, Against the Letter of Parmenian.
Nimrod is thought to be the same as Belus.

lg.l: would come to destroy hell—thus the Fates ordained.
Fearing this, and by no means forgetful of the wars of old, since once
he had waged war against Isaac’s descendants on behalf of his dear friends;
nor even yet had the cause of his wrath and his fierce anguish
fallen from his mind; there remains, stored deep in his heart,
the judgment pronounced by the King of Heaven concerning the seed
of the woman — namely, that it should crush the serpent's head
and set beneath its feet the raging evil of the dragon.
Inflamed still further by these things, those tossed over the whole sea—
Christ and his companions, and, on land, seeking the furthest reaches—
he kept far from Jerusalem, and for many years,
through various slaughters, through so many perils,
appeasing their enemies with blood, and making offering with their lives,
they wandered, driven about every land and sea;
so vast a task it was to found the people of Jerusalem!
And now be present, and together run through the task begun,
O glory! O [thou] deservedly the greatest part of our fame,
O Christ, God; and, flying over the sea, give sails to one who seeks them;
grant an easy course and favor these bold undertakings,
so that I may now bear your miracles throughout the whole world,

div.note: By the Fates I do not here understand God himself, nor inevitable necessity, nor the three times — present, past, and future — nor the seasons of childbirth, whence Nona, Decima, Morta, as may be seen in A. Gellius l. 3. c. 16., Aristotle de mundo, Theodoret &c. ad Graec. infid. ser. 6.; nor, finally, the scribes of Jove, as the poets have it. Rather I understand the Prophets, the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, who had knowledge of things past, present, and to come, and who spare no man in denouncing the judgments of God. They are μοῖραι, that is, the lot and portion of the Lord; in the same sense priests are called κλῆροι.

The Devil is called Dragon and Serpent: in this shape he appeared to Eve, and under this shape he was worshipped among the nations. The serpent is consecrated to Aesculapius, to Mercury, to Minerva; as guardian of the garden of the Hesperides it was regularly painted in holy places, and was set among the stars. With what honours was the demon not worshipped under the form and name of a serpent! Hence the gods of the nations are painted with serpents' feet.

lg.l: wonders alone worthy of the Sophoclean buskin.
I do not wish to encompass everything in my verses,
not [even] if I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths
[and] an iron voice; but I shall trace the main outlines of events;
and, going back to the world's first beginning, I shall set forth
the ambushes of Satan, his frauds and dreadful wars
against Christ and Christ's servants; whom he himself, before
came down from heaven, sent ahead into the world
to found the longed-for citadels, and the dwellings of Zion,
and to raise the stronghold, and roll the stones up with their hands:
all of whom he hunts with the sword or wears down with guile.
Therefore the works hang unfinished, and the massive battlements
of the walls, and the framework raised level with heaven.
Nor can the towers once begun rise up, until
the long-awaited founder of Jerusalem's citadel himself
has come and built the walls with his unconquered right hand:
walls which neither human force nor the gate of Hell can conquer,
nor will they be able to tear them down with hard iron.
Scarcely out of sight of their happy homeland,
sorrowful, they were spreading sail and churning up the salt foam with the bronze [prow],
those earliest fathers, who through the malice of treacherous Hell
[were] driven out of their homeland, and tossed on the vast flood,
unsure where the fates are carrying them, where it may be granted to come to rest;
when Pluto, nursing the everlasting wound beneath his breast,
rouses up Aeolian storms with treacherous mind;
and he scattered their ships and upheaved the seas with winds.

div.note: Cothurnus is here taken not for the tragic actor's boot, nor for the hunter's — the former was high and built up with cork, the latter flat and low — nor for tragedy, but for the lofty manner of speaking.

By the sea I understand the world: turbid and bitter, full of dangers and crowded with monsters. The sea runs back and forth with alternating tides, now raising us with sudden swells, now deserting us to greater losses, and tossing us without cease, &c. Seneca consol. ad Polyb. cap. 28.

lg.l: Namely, that he may sink righteous Abel beneath the deep,
whom he believes to be the leader who will found Jerusalem’s
promised [walls], and lay Babylon low from her lofty summit.
He therefore, rolling up from their lowest depths huge waves
of his wrath, drives Abel onto the Syrtes,
and dashes him upon the shoals and plunges him in bitter death,
so that he might divert Jerusalem’s kingdom toward the Stygian citadels.
Cain worked the soil with bulls and entrusted pure
seed to the furrows; but Abel, a shepherd,
drove wool-bearing sheep and shaggy she-goats.
While these two, with altars set up, pay their vows in due order,
the elder brought the firstfruits of the crops and cakes to the altars;
but the latter, slaughtering fat beasts duly consecrated
over the flame, offered pleasing sacrifices.
But behold, frequent lightning bolts fell from a clear sky;
with flickering flames, the altar was seized by
fire sent down from heaven’s ethereal Olympus,
which with soft touch was licking Abel's offering.
The young man recognized the omen and suddenly raised both
palms to heaven and worshiped the divine power.
Cain, his mind enraged, could not bear the sight.
Nor could the ruler of the Stygian waters bear it—he who is wont to bring
scourges, death-dealing torches, and poison into homes,
through envy, and to arm beloved brothers for battle:
he breathes a bloodthirsty spirit into him and urges Cain
forthwith to strip his brother's body of its light.
But as he burned, cares and wrath were seething him,
loosed out of the pools of Cocytus and the Stygian marsh:
Without delay, violating every sacred duty and casting the laws aside,
he secretly struck down his unsuspecting brother with a sword in the field
the impious one; for the wound lodged beneath the breast, and
closed the passage of the voice and, with blood, the frail life.
He hoped that he could cover the body with earth and hide
so great a crime in pits; but he who knows all things—
what things are, what things have been, and what events soon to come are being drawn onward—
the cruel altars, and the breast pierced through with iron,
he laid bare, and uncovered all the hidden crime of the house.
But he, out of his mind, with the furies of his crimes driving him,
and unknown, destitute, wanders over the wastes of the earth:
as once a top, spinning under the twisted lash,
which boys in a wide ring, about the empty halls,
intent upon their game, keep driving: it, urged on by the thong,
is carried through curving courses: the unknowing crowd stands amazed,
and the boyish band marvels at the whirling boxwood;
the blows give it life; no slower in his running than that top
is he driven through crags and woods; and in his panic there pursue him
the Furies, armed with torches and with black serpents.
Again and again there meets him the image of his own brother,
sorrowful, and it lifts up a face pale in strange fashion;
demanding with a mighty cry that the murderer be punished.
And because the earth has drunk a brother's blood,
it bears burrs and caltrops, and among the shining tilled fields
a rough wood creeps up, and sluggish in the ploughlands bristles
the thistle; with barren oats, the farmers are disappointed by
the crop they awaited; indeed, bare rock lies everywhere,

div.note: That the slaying of Abel was bloody, God indicates in these words: the voice of thy brother's blood, &c.; so Christ, Matth. 24. 35.
So Josephus thinks — namely, that Cain hid his brother's body. Antiq. l. 8.

lg.l: and the marsh overspreads the pastures with slimy rush.
Not otherwise Christ (because with the highest honour
God cherished) — out of envy and with a cruel death they were killing him,
his Jewish brethren, a race always unjust toward the Lord,
and hostile in its hatreds, never glutted and never at rest.
For these, driven from their homeland and having suffered so many horrors in slaughter,
the whole world is closed to them because of this slaughter.
With these thorns too the sacred page bristles,
and burs and thistles are there, together with the rough thicket.
But after the king of hell destroyed Abel with death,
who had already founded walls hallowed with blood;
the Almighty, lest the works begun should lie broken off,
sent other craftsmen to build the walls:
Seth, who the twofold catastrophe and the sorrowful ruins
of the world set down on twin pillars; Enosh —
He first taught mortals duly to pray.
Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared; then he sent Enoch,
[whom] he caught up on high to the pleasant green meadows of Paradise:
The long-lived stretch out their palms in vain toward the stars,
the forefathers, and the baying of dogs rages into the winds;
and the avenging Furies howled from their lowest abodes,
resentful in their wrath; Pluto roars with bloodied mouth,
[that] a mortal has climbed to the place from which he himself is banished.
And although the fathers had no hope of seeing their ancient homeland,
nevertheless, from this they dared to hope for eternal salvation
and to place greater trust amid their afflicted circumstances;
namely, that after they leave this hated light and human company,
a secluded grove and thickets rustling among the woods
they will at last arrive, and all will possess the glad fields,
where, beneath the wavering shadows stirred by the West Winds,
Comely Enoch rings out with unceasing song
beside the sacred springs, where soft marjoram
breathes on him with its blossoms and enfolds him in sweet shade.
These dwellings—and here the rewards due to merit—Christ
promised to those who shall gird the city with walls,
and who shall dwell in the citadels and lofty roofs of Zion.
After him long-lived Methuselah is sent; he
begot Janus, second in worth to none of the men of old;
for a hundred and twice ten years [Janus] instructs
the world, tottering under the monstrous weight of its crimes —
Janus [does so], by teaching the causes and the signs of the flood.
For Pluto, perceiving that he opposes himself in vain to the raised
ramparts of the walls, and that he cannot, by open
force, turn Jerusalem aside, assails her with silent deceits,
[offering] eternal peace (with this name he cloaks [his] deceit),
and moreover, with feigning heart, the marriage torches
he holds out, namely that daughters from the stock of Cain
may be joined to offspring begotten from Seth’s lineage;
thus he longs to mingle the peoples, and the traitor [wills] one
city, [which] he promised to those who will gird [it] with walls,
namely, that Babylon might hold Zion down under her sway;
and so he takes them by his wiles, and deceives with poison
the wretched sons of Seth; a mighty heat rages in their bones
after they have drunk in with their eyes girls of surpassing beauty;
caught by sweet enticements and by shameful desire,
they rush into frenzy and fire: love is the same for all.

div.note: didascal. mult. [Didascalia multiplex]

lg.l: From these were begotten giants of vast bulk,
Aetnaean brothers, raising their lofty heads to heaven.
What forms of wickedness and what monstrous horrors shall I recount—
the foul couplings, the slaughters, and the savage deeds
of these Cyclopes, which, roused by just anger,
the Almighty washed away and sank beneath the middle of the sea.
Such marriages and such wedding rites are celebrated by
the noble race of Seth and the savage stock of Cain.
So this, of course, is the peace that the king of Avernus holds out:
that fathers-in-law and sons-in-law may unite at the cost of their kin,
and that the Cain-born maidens may be dowered with destruction,
which gave over to death every race of beasts, every race of men.
Therefore Noah, great in righteousness and in piety,
[raising] a work the size of a mountain by the divine art of the Godhead,
building it, framed its ribs together of sawn fir,
Hither the race of birds and of cattle, every kind of wild beast,
and eight human beings (the rest the whirlpool devours in the sea)
he enclosed deep within its hollow side; and the chambers,
vast chambers, together with its belly, he filled with food and drink.
Misshapen she-bears gather, and tawny lions
out of the woods; then the fierce boar, then the deadliest tiger,
and every kind of dog, indeed the fierce breed of wolves as well,
and the long-eared hare, and timid wild asses follow,
and dappled lynxes, and stags unwarlike for battle,
and wool-bearing flocks, and goats that love the heights,
and swift four-footed beasts, and bullocks strong for the plough.
So whatever bird cleaves the light air with its wings
enters — wondrous to tell — the ark by divine prompting;
and high-flying cranes and ravens exulting in their cries;
Sacred hawks, and swans white of body;
the crow which shamelessly calls up rain with full-throated cry:
and the swallow which went circling shrill about the pools;
and, alone upon the rooftops, the owl, with its deathly song
wont to complain, and to draw out long cries into weeping.
Moreover the swift divers fly back from the open sea,
and other birds of the deep, and those which, about the Asian
meadows of Cayster, search among the fresh-water pools.
And the halcyons leave the shores, and the goldfinch the little asses,
and the nightingale her feasts, and the hoarse wood-doves the countryside.
And the turtle-dove has ceased to moan from the airy elm.
Moreover, withdrawing from its feeding-ground in a great column,
the army of ravens has clattered with thick-beating wings.
But neither how many kinds there are, nor what their names may be,
can be reckoned; for it is no use to encompass them by number.
Nor did God will that all these be saved from the waters,
but two of every kind go into the ark;
for the grim boatman takes now these, now those,
but, standing far apart, he keeps others away from the strand.
Scarcely had he shut himself in when, the rains bursting forth, a black
storm rages beyond all custom, and at the thunder there tremble
the heights of the earth, and the plains; there rushes down from the whole sky
a turbid downpour of water, blackest with thick south winds.
Besides, with the barriers burst, Neptune from the deep
is borne headlong in a heaped mass, and over all the plains
he rushes in, and overtops the airy mountains with his flood.

div.note: The acanthis pursues with hatred the asses that devour the flowers of thorn-bushes. Solin. lib. 10. cap. 74.

lg.l: It lays low the fields, lays low the glad crops and the oxen's labours;
and drags the woods down headlong; every kind of wild beast
and flocks, herds, men; and no longer are any
lands in sight, sky on every side, and on every side the sea.
Saved out of the waves [were] these alone, whom the Ark held.
So an Ark — by the Greeks it is called Ecclesia — Christ
built, yet not by human hands, not by masterly skill,
but by his own death and by his mighty word.
And in this wood he hid his friends, shut up within.
While the sheer sea presses down the fields with roaring flood;
while God in his wrath sinks the world beneath the waters.
And as Janus, now the helmsman amid the flood,
every kind of cattle, and every kind of wild beast too,
and men — himself shut in the wood — and the painted birds
carried unharmed over the rocks, over so many blue shallows:
so Christ, fastened to the wood, saved from the underworld
his beloved Jerusalem, and led [her] through the hidden rocks
to the heavenly shore, and sets [her] ashore in the haven on high.
O sprung from the race of the gods, you who from the waves the city of Jerusalem
bring back to us, and preserve [her] everlasting walls;
O awaited one, on the soil of Judaea and in the fields of Zion,
let me have a sure home, let there be a sure rest from toils;
grant that, after long time, I may see my native borders.
Grant [me] at last to overcome all the sea's hardships,
and to endure the world's threats; let every swelling and the rages
of the deep subside, while toward the shores of our sweet homeland
we spread our sails, and run the vast sea in a hollow hull.
After he had borne all the threats both of the sea and of the sky,
Janus, now an old man, driven by so many storms;
At last he sent out from the ship the winged dove,
[bidding her search out] the earth overwhelmed by the floods and by the sky's downfall,
bidding [her] explore it, [to see] whether it begins to lift itself up again
and begins to reveal the mountains and send smoke curling upward.
Long she circles the Ark on weary wings;
nor does she find rest for her feet, for all [the fields], with brimming
the fields swim with brimming ditches, and the rivers, not yet drained,
the rivers; she hides herself again in her familiar cradle.
But after the seventh Dawn had raised life-giving light for mortals
and with her rays had unveiled the world,
he sent the dove out once more through the great void.
Without delay she lifts herself swiftly, and through the air
skims her clear path, and at last settles upon a green tree.
But while Janus scans the sky and follows with his gaze
the dove flapping her wings beneath a cloud,
marking what signs she brings, and where she goes on making for;
behold, with her beak she plucked a green branch from a tree;
and soon the bird, flying, raised herself into the thin air,
and returns, bringing back a branch of the fruitful olive;
she shows that the waters have gone down, and brings back peace.
Here aged Janus first dared to hope for deliverance,
and to put greater trust in his stricken fortunes.
So, when the thickest downpour of divine wrath
has settled upon the world, and beneath the mid-sea has sunk
the human race, lo, a dove has been sent down from heaven,
bearing peace in her mouth and a branch of the long-lived olive.

div.note: Berosus, on the testimony of Josephus, Ant. 1. c. 4., called Noah's ark a ship; while Plutarch, in his book on the comparison of animals, called the ship of Deucalion an ark. And on ancient coins a certain ship was depicted on the side opposite Janus.

lg.l: This is that bough, golden in leaf and pliant stem,
the bough of divine utterance, a great and venerable gift,
which Christ, sent down to us from highest heaven,
brought; but he restored from death the world that had been submerged,
after the first man, already beguiled, had been deceived through death by
King Pluto, who had condemned him to Stygian hell;
But after the seventh Dawn had put the stars to flight,
behold, once more the bird is sent out into the airy breezes,
to search out the sodden lands; she, high upon her wings,
makes for the stars, and was never after given back to Janus' eyes.
From this he understands the earth is dry, and sees that all things
now hold steady under a clear sky: nor do the rivers from their springs
burst forth any longer, swollen by the rain-bringing south winds.
So, after he had appeased with his blood the winds and the showers
of heavenly wrath — Christ — and had put the clouds to flight,
he is borne flying to the stars, and made his way up to the citadels above,
O Father, when you shall have led this soul out of the body's ark
and at your word shall have released its weary limbs,
then grant swift wings to the trembling dove;
grant me to be borne on wings through the empty clouds of heaven,
that with you I may range through the lofty halls of the heavenly Temple.
The year's circle is completed, its months run out,
since the ark, to be tossed about by winds and by waves,
began; but at last to come to rest upon dry land
the Almighty willed, taking pity on Janus from on high;
she came to rest upon the lofty mountains of Ararat;
While the offspring of Janus, unknowing, saw her close to the stars
from the depths of the valleys after these events—the ark
it believed had been snatched aloft to the stars of heaven.
Perhaps it was for this cause that the poets of old sang
because Argo had carried chosen heroes safely across the sea,
that she was set aloft among the stars of heaven.
But the ship of Christ, whose name is now the Church,
after her service is done, will reach her destination and harbors
in heaven one day, when she has escaped the waves of the world
and has borne the leaders of Christ's people to the fields of heaven:
