the almighty Father, to whom belongs the supreme power over all things,
shall take away her mortal form, and shall bid [her]
be a torch of the great upper air, such as Phoebean Apollo [is]
and [his] fostering sister, governing the foaming sea with [her] light.
And now the sea has ceased to be churned with its roaring,
and the true Neptune has driven away the storm that had been unleashed,
with that countenance by which he clears the sky and the tempests;
he drains the gathered moisture as the Zephyrs blow,
and now bids the East Winds refrain from their wintry blasts.
And now once more the flocks have drunk in the light, and the earth-born race
the earth-born race [of men] has again raised its head from the Ark,
and the wild beasts [have been] let loose into the woods, and the stars into the sky;
and heaven's kindness again takes the lands into its care.
The nurturing field brings forth and, in Zephyr’s warming breezes,
the fields open their folds; now the vine-shoot unfurls all
its leaves, and once again the fresh meadows blaze with colors.
And now the old man unbarred the door of the ark, and, himself
worn out with all he has borne, and with a great longing for the land,
went out, and as he stepped forth his first steps faltered;
and his companions at last gain the longed-for shore.

div.note: Not only does a ship aptly represent the Church, tossed about in the world as upon a sea; but of old it was even prescribed that the churches of Christians be built after the fashion of a ship. Clemens l. 2. const. Apost. c. 507.

lg.l: Every kind of bird, livestock, and wild beast comes forth;
the divers fly back to the crags, the swans to the rivers,
the turtle-dove to the woods, the sparrow to deserted roof-tops.
And the Scyllas have made for the upper air on quivering wings,
whom Nisus follows, flying aloft towards the stars.
Now on the shore they spread their wings to the warm sun,
the halcyons beloved of Thetis; now the owl once more plies her late songs;
and the heifer, gazing up at the sky,
looking up [at it], now catches the breezes with open nostrils.
And the ravens, glad with a sweetness beyond their wont,
repeat their clear cries three times from constricted throats,
or four; and the heron flies above the high cloud.
Now the trackless thickets ring with tuneful birds,
and the herds return to mating on their appointed days.
Now the chattering swallow hangs her nest from the beams,
the white bird, hated by long snakes, claps [her wings];
Wild beasts return to their lairs; the she-goats climb the thickets;
the rest of the herds graze through the green grasses.
Janus, having come out and gained the open sky,
first of all builds shrines, and at the altars
seeks peace; he sacrifices chosen two-year-old sheep according to custom.
Soon he began, on the sunny hills, to set vines in rows
and he was then the vintager of the ripe grape;
but after he had gladdened himself with too much wine,
not yet accustomed to mixing Achelous’s waters with the grapes he had lately found:

div.note: Here I use delubrum not to mean a roofed temple, but an open court where water was kept, with which the priests and the sacrificial victims were washed; hence delubrum is said to derive from diluere, "to wash." It is well known that the ancients, long before temples were built, customarily sacrificed in open courts.

lg.l: to mix Achelous’ cups with grapes he had lately discovered: behold, he lies on his back,
conquered in his limbs by the god [of wine], and is stretched out at full length.
But as soon as the boys saw him lying there in sleep,
king Pluto breathes a viper's venom into Ham
so that, laughing, he might show the shameful parts to his brothers
(for the garment, slipped down from his thigh, lay some way off)
which Shem, together with his own brother, veils with a cloak.
So Christ, after he had drained the foaming goblets of the new wine
of the divine wrath, hanging from the stock [of the cross],
lowered his bowed head and sought sleep;
The boys laughed at him both as he hung and as he groaned,
and they laugh as he spews red floods back from his breast.
Then God gives laws to Janus, then upon laws he founded
the world; he forbade brothers to contend in hatred,
or to seize their brothers' goods by ambush, or to carry off plunder.
That they refrain from defiling their hands in a brother's blood;
that their descendants remain under a chaste observance;
that they shun shameful marriage-beds and forbidden unions;
that they not tear the entrails from living animals; that they not feed
on the dark blood of beasts; and now dominion has been
granted over the beasts; for although once on foliage
the fathers were fed, and on a diet of plain grass,
now they may restore the strength of beasts to their limbs.
Moreover, he promises that he will no longer immerse in the sea
the circle of the lands, and every kind of wild beast,
and the human race and the herds and the painted birds.

div.note: I call wine a god in the sense in which the Apostle names the belly a god, Phil. 3. 19. Would that the wine-swillers of our own age were atheists with respect to this god.

lg.l: This covenant Thaumas' daughter confirms with rosy lips:
Iris, that is, dewy, on saffron wings across the sky,
drawing a thousand varied colors against the opposing sun.
But Pluto, not yet sated with the earlier ruin
which he brought on Jerusalem with deadly torches — see,
he pursues the survivors in hatred, and the race still to come;
lest he leave anything untried by which he might utterly overthrow the city
he may overturn, and lay its smoking rooftops level with the ground.
He had heard that from the great line of Shem's descendants
Christ would come, who by a firm covenant would unite
under [one] rule the stock of Jerusalem and the whole race of Japheth,
whom he will govern under equal auspices, and will call allies,
He, so as to subject them all to himself as one common people,
summons [them], and the wretch flings idle reproaches against God;
and he dares call him cruel who, in the vast flood,
while he massed a foul tempest with black rains,
drowned so many beasts and men; he urges that a high
they should build a lofty tower and strive to raise it to heaven,
one that may scorn the sea's waves and the sky's collapse.
Here, he says, shall be the site of the city and a respite from toil;
here let the citadel, here the kingdom be for the nations to come;
Who prevents us from building walls and giving the citizens a city?
O wretched men, rescued from the waters in vain! Is there nowhere
a settled home for you? Shall no walls anywhere be called your own?
Come then, and with me build a lofty tower
near to the stars, and one that may strike Olympus with its summit?
Roused indeed by these words, and driven by frenzy,
they gird themselves to the work; some to draw the furrows:
Others lay foundations; some set about raising enormous masses
of walls; they fit both gates and windows.
These were baking bricks with fire in vast kilns,
these shape [them]; others with windy bellows the air
the air and give it back; that one gathers black bitumen:
Just as bees in early summer, across the flowering fields—
toil keeps them busy under the sun, when they lead out the grown
young of their race, or when the flowing honey
they pack in, and swell the cells with sweet nectar;
or take up the loads of those arriving, or, forming a column,
keep off the drones, that idle herd, from the hives:
the work seethes, and the fragrant honey is redolent of thyme.
Smiling upon them, the maker of men and of things
stands at the summit of heaven, and looks on from a tawny cloud
at the craftsmen pressing on with the work, and uttering empty threats.
No delay: girt with storm-clouds, and in a whirlwind from on high
he comes down from heaven, and pities the vain threats
of the craftsmen, and [pities] that mortals should have such frenzies,
so that they hope they can reach heaven itself.
Therefore he gave them mouths discordant in sound, and all
of them, now differing in language, he scattered to different shores:
Toward Africa, sorrowful Ham, driven from Europe and Asia,
departs, and lives in exile far off on unknown shores,
groaning deeply over his disgrace and the blows of the avenging
Thunderer, and then, left destitute, over the friends he lost,
while, an exile from his homeland, he wanders toward parched Africa
and, gazing back at the tower, he has gone out from his ancestral realms;
nor has he now any hope of seeing his ancient homeland,
nor his dear brothers and the father he longed for.
Now Japheth (so they report) makes for the farthest bounds of Europe.
But Shem settled in the ancestral fields of Asia,
whose offspring pressed on as far as the Dawn and the Indians,
So Babylon lies deserted and has brought ruin upon herself,
and is now a fit house for birds of ill omen,
she whom Pluto once willed to lord it over the nations;
But that mortals should turn the soil with iron
wise Janus ordained: and he first, through skill,
stirred the fields, whetting mortal hearts with cares:
nor did he let his realms lie numb in heavy sloth;
and teaches his offspring to hammer out skills through reflection,
little by little, and should seek in the furrows the blade of corn,
and should strike out the fire hidden in the veins of flint.
Then he taught his sons to put a fence around the standing crop,
to contrive snares for the birds; to burn off the briars;
and to plunge the bleating flock in the wholesome stream.
and to set foot-traps for cranes, and nets for stags,
and to chase long-eared hares and shoot fallow deer,
and to parch the grain in the fire, and to crush it with stone.
And because the earth has now, through the briny moisture
of the Flood, been rendered barren, and is not fertile in cattle,
nor suited to the crop, nor blessed with the gift of Bacchus,
therefore he ordered them to channel slender streams through the fields
and to enrich the bitter soils with rich dung,
and to fling unclean ash over the worn-out fields,
and he taught them to improve wild produce through cultivation,
and to entrust the thriving vine to a shallow furrow.
And when at length the vineyard shall shed its late leaves,
and the cold North Wind shall strip the woods of their glory,
he instructs them to work over, with Saturn’s curved tooth, the vine left behind,
Let him lay hands on the vine, clipping it, and shape what is to be pruned.
I pass over [these things], and leave them to be recounted by others after me.
I pass over [these things].
Meanwhile Shem was laying out the high dwellings of Solyma,
which dread-roaring Eurus had almost submerged beneath Neptune’s waters.
But his descendants, caught by the snares and deceits of Hell—
Namely Arphaxad, then Salah, and Eber the greatest,
from whom the generations after drew their stock, their tongue, and their name;
then Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Nahor, and Terah;
applied themselves less zealously to the task and to the kingdom to come,
forgetful of so great a kingdom and of their own concerns.
Among them the Almighty sees Abram, as he raises anew the dwellings of Babylon,
and thus speaks from heaven on high,
calling him by name: “You are lingering now in Babylon,
laying foundations, and, unaware, a hostile city
you are building—alas, forgetful of your kingdom and your own affairs!
What are you building? or in what hope do you wear away your idle hours in Stygian lands?
You must move from this abode; that land must be sought
which I shall show you; for the great you shall prepare mighty
walls; we shall raise to the stars the descendants who are to come,
and we shall give dominion to the city: and let it not grieve you to leave
fatherland and father, nor to seek out foreign realms.
Or does the glory of such great things not move you at all,
and do you not yourself take up the labour for the sake of your own praise?

div.note: They served other gods, Joshua 24:2. Hence statues began to be made from clay and by the potter's art through the industry of Terah, etc.; on this see Epiphanius, Against Heresies, and Suidas under the entry "Saruch." Augustine thinks otherwise, City of God 16.13. Perhaps the patriarchs were not then as devoted to idolatry as the Chaldeans, yet they were not wholly free from it.

lg.l: Rise quickly, [make for] Jerusalem, and seek out the citadel of Zion.
Thunderstruck by so great a warning, and by the command of the Thunderer,
Abram suddenly abandons the Chaldaean shores;
and he sought out unknown dwellings and foreign fields,
uncertain where the fates are carrying him, where it may be granted to settle;
and at last he passed within the borders of the longed-for land.
Then behold, in the region of the upper air the great king of Olympus
is seated on a gleaming cloud, and thus addresses Abram:
Turn your two eyes hither now, look upon this land,
whether you would [look] to right and left, or toward the sun's rising,
toward the sun's setting: wherever you have looked, all
this land you shall receive; these curving shores shall be held by
posterity destined to come beneath the great vault of heaven.
Here a sure home rises for you, a head over lofty cities.
Mark all the stars gliding in the silent sky,
(for day had withdrawn from heaven, and the fiery stars in night-roaming chariots
were beating upon the spheres of the upper air).
Try, if you can, to count exactly
how many grains of sand on the shore are stirred up by the Zephyr.
Such shall be the offspring which fair Sarah in childbirth,
( barren though she now is ) shall pour forth for you; that greatest one,
the heavenly Christ, born of noble lineage, shall come into the world,
who shall subject Babylon, teeming with empires and raging with arms,
to servitude, and shall rule over the whole world.
Him one day, laden with the spoils of Babylon, into heaven
you shall receive; and he shall be invoked with vows throughout all
the lands over which Phaethon's horses shall breathe their light.

div.note: Here I take right and left poetically, not astronomically; namely, for the north and the south.

lg.l: At these words [his] cares were dispelled, and for a little while
grief driven from his heart; but Pluto flings Abraham into open perils,
that he might drive [him] out of the Canaanite kingdom —
had not the heavenly Father given him strength and courage,
while the Assyrian kings were harrying in war the cities—
five in Palestine—and Lot, his brother's son,
they seize; upon their captive they impose harsh violence and chains.
Not far from Sodom, in the deep valleys, dwelt
Lot; there a savage and unbridled race of men, contemptuous of God,
had founded cities, which the ruler of Olympus
shattered with his thunderbolt, hurling amid the dense clouds flames
of brimstone; the cause which had kindled so great a fire
is plain: namely, wanton Venus stirred an unspeakable flame
within the hard bones of the amorous young men.
Thus God purged the abomination with fire; thus with fire he purged fire.
Alas, how great the forms of crime! What monstrous undertakings
drive wretched mortals on, and provoke heaven?
Ah, how often does he testify with a mighty voice through the air,
the Almighty? How often does it warn us of our crimes—the vast
gate of heaven, thundering, while, dashed against the storm-clouds, there echo back
lightning bolts; nor will the supreme Father's
chiding voice be able to call [us] back, though it threaten again and again.
Does it not come to mind how many kingdoms once paid for their sins,
when the Father in his anger poured the earth out into the waters?
Since that flood, how many did he sink beneath the waters—
vast fields and cities together? How many towers has he laid low with the thunderbolt?
And how many cities did the deep earth, shaken to its foundations and gaping open,
swallow up—cities that now roll about in its lowest depths?
Why should I speak of tempests and raging winds
roused out of Aeolia, or of rains driven from the clouds?
For you all remember it, and you are able to recount it,
Or does no image of so great a terror move you?
nor the world, which is yet destined to perish in cruel destruction?
When the earth shall curtain Olympus itself with smoke,
and shall heave up balls of flame, and lick the stars;
then all the kingdoms of the world, collapsed in flames, shall fall to ruin.
Do you then, O wretched ones, dread Jehovah when he hurls his thunderbolts
not at all? And do blind fires in the clouds
terrify your hearts, and stir up empty rumblings?
Be warned, learn justice, and pay in full the honour due,
O mortals, to him who ratifies covenants with the thunderbolt,
and do not despise the flames of Jehovah and the thunder of Olympus.
It was once a great mother of crops and an exceedingly rich land,
whose golden cultivated fields were watered by
the Jordan, wandering through the plains with its many windings.
But this soil is rich, and glad with sweet moisture,
and the field is thick with grass and fertile in abundance,
and [a land] which once [bore vines] exceedingly strong, and flowing with abundant [wine]
It supplied vines to Bacchus, [a land] fertile in the grape,
which [yielded] such liquor as we pour in libation from bowls and golden vessels.
Now it is a huge lake, a whirlpool with a vast chasm,
which pitchy waters, thickened with black bitumen,
belches up with a groan, and seethes from its lowest depth:
and at times it bursts forth a black cloud to the sky:
over which no flying creatures could with impunity
make their way on wings—such an exhalation, pouring itself from black
jaws, carried itself up to the vaults above.
If by chance any bird flits above the lake,
it drops headlong and leaves its life beneath the high cloud.
This lake, moreover, is not kind even to the fish themselves;
for, swimming in these waters, they commonly die;
hence the Hebrews named the lake “Dead,”
If anyone were to look upon these waters boiling with pitch,
he would swear that the implacable head of the Stygian spring
was here, and the very jaws of rank-smelling Avernus.
Yet here the pleasant River Jordan hides itself.
Here too ashes lie scattered far and wide over the fields,
the remnants of the avenging flame, which the author of the thunderbolt
had sent down upon Sodom (as I said) in a copious shower.
A vast host of flames rushed down from high heaven,
Victorious through the houses and reigning over their lofty rooftops,
Mulciber wrapped the city in flames and hurled a black
with pitchy murk, [sent] a black cloud rolling up to the sky;
so, as the flame overpowered the houses, there fell the proud
towns, and all Gomorrah, levelled to the ground, smoked:
now turned into a dismal lake, and a Stygian marsh
around which black mud and unsightly reeds,
and foul ashes, and barren sands hold sway.
A land unproductive in crops and unsuited to the vine,
unsuitable for livestock and fertile in no kind of tree;
the deceptive apples turn to ash and smoke.
On this plain, which is girt about on every side by mountains
between which [lie] narrow gorges and treacherous approaches
(valleys suited to stratagems and deceptions of war),
the Assyrians were waging war with a dread people.
Here five towns were subject to the Assyrian king
for twice six years: but at last the citizens, raging at unspeakable [wrongs],
shook off the yoke; and they refuse the bridle
to accept any longer, or to obey the tyrant’s command.
Therefore they rushed to arms for liberty.
Those five great cities, with anvils set in place,
renew their weapons: then mighty Admah, and proud Sodom,
and Zeboiim, with Bela, and tower-crowned Gomorrah;
they hollow out safe coverings for their heads, and bend willow
frames for shield-bosses: others [work] bronze cuirasses,
or fashion smooth greaves from pliant silver.
To this the honour of the ploughshare and the sickle, to this all love
of the plough has given way: in their furnaces they forge anew their fathers' swords.
Therefore all Babylonia, rising up in just fury,
demands the rebels for punishment through immediate force of arms;
for whose destruction, in a firm alliance, swear together
the neighbouring nations, and cities, and wealthy kingdoms.
Those who plough your glades, Saranda, who [plough] the rich Syrian
shore, and who drink the waters of the swift Tigris,
and those who till the fertile fields of quivered Persia;
all these, in their tongues, in the fashion of their dress too, and in their arms
came together, each unlike the other; the greatest part scatters bullets
of livid lead, part carries darts,
two apiece in hand; and tawny caps, from a wolf's hide,
it has as covering for the head; the bare sole of the left
foot they have planted on the ground, while a rawhide boot covers the other:
these have curved swords, those have throwing-clubs for weapons;
these fight with the tapering blade, those brandish bristling
javelins in hand, and carry deadly pikes into battle.
This man's broad shoulders a hide, stripped from a fighting
bullock, covers; and his head the gaping jaws
and jowls of a wolf, with its white teeth, have covered.
Bristling with javelins, and in the hide of a Libyan she-bear,
this one strides on exulting; this one a lion's monstrous hide,
unkempt with bristle and gleaming with golden claws,
puts on, and veils his shoulders with a Herculean cloak.
But that one, with a quiver and the covering of a spotted lynx
girded about, walks forward, with attendants accompanying him.
The spoils of a tiger hang from his head down over his back.

div.note: Saranda: so the Euphrates was formerly called, on the testimony of Plutarch in his book on mountains and rivers.

The soldiers of barbarian nations, when about to go forth into battle, used to clothe themselves in the skins of various wild beasts so that they might appear fiercer to their enemies. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 1, chapter 20.

lg.l: And now the huge army of the Persians was drawing near,
and it surmounts the ridge, and comes out from the shadowy woods;
and the columns of the Sodomites pour themselves out from the gates,
and the bronze horns blared in hoarse accord.
Thus each army advanced into the midst of the plain.
From the walls the frightened mothers see from afar the gleaming
arms; they fear the din of men, the sound of trumpets,
and the fields ablaze with javelins held aloft.
Nor are the foes far apart from one another by many paces.
And as soon as the Assyrian the plains smoking with dust
descried far off, and saw the Sodomite columns,
and the Sodomite recognised the fierce Assyrian in arms,
and he heard the approach of footsteps and the snorting of horses:
At once they would enter the fight and attempt battle,
if rosy Phoebus were not now dipping his weary horses in the Iberian
sea and bringing back night as day declined.
They encamp before the city and fortify the walls with a rampart.
When the next bright day, at its first rising, had put the stars to flight,
bringing back kindly light to mortals;
a field for the contest beneath the walls of the great city,
the men of Assyria and Sodom, having measured it out, were preparing it.
The young men stand equipped with steel and ringing bronze
they await the signal; then silence fell upon the field:
the leaders wheel about, and with their shouts the squadrons

div.note: Strabo, in book 16, attests that Sodom was a great city and that its circuit was sixty stadia; in book 3 he also records that it was the chief of cities.

lg.l: goad on, varied in tone; throbbing fear lifts the young men’s exultant
hearts, along with a mad desire for battle.
Then, when the clear trumpet gave its blast, all of them, from their own
stations sprang forward without delay; fierce battle arose.
On every side there is a clash with a terrible roar, and the two
battle lines locked together; the shouting strikes the sky
of the fighters, and the crash of arms, and the groaning of those falling.
Clouds of dust snatch away both sky and ground
from the eyes of the combatants, and [so does] a bristling shower of missiles.
Meanwhile a river of blood runs; the very waters
of Jordan grow warm, and redden with so great a slaughter;
and the black steam of blood flies up into the air; within [the city]
the matrons set the trembling city ablaze with their cries
and pour out prayers; heard by none of the gods,
In fear they redouble their vows and fill heaven with lamentation.
At once there is a running to the walls throughout the whole city.
But at last the youth of Sodom, overwhelmed by missiles,
and able neither to bear such force nor to strive against it,
and outnumbered in the fight, retreats without honor:
some scatter towards the gates, and at a run make for the trusty
walls; part of them, in shameful terror, into wells
tumble down; some hide themselves in caves they know;
others in fear made for the rocks and the mountains near by.
The Assyrians pursue them at speed and with their weapons,
harrying their backs with spears; they give their bodies over to death,
many thousands of men; and [the pursuers] scatter shafts from their right hands;
and they darken the sky: no thicker is the hail through the air
Nor does so great a fall of acorns rain down from the shaken holm-oak.
Limbs strew the whole ground, and members torn away
from those cut down in the fight: just as when, at the first cold,
Eurus bears down upon the woods with wintry blasts;
the leaves strew the ground as the trunk is shaken,
They trample upon the slain, and strip bare the limbs still warm,
the Assyrians [do], and each adorns himself with fresh spoils.
They seize the captives and bind them with heavy chains,
and subject captured Lot to harsh force and bonds.
Meanwhile the Chaldaeans, after their successful exploits, attend to their
bodies, indulge in wine, and, relaxed by sleep,
have lain down; the region lies silent far and wide in the shadow of night.
But indeed, as soon as there glides to Abram's ears
rushing Rumour as messenger, that Lot had been carried off by the soldiery,
and that the citizens of Sodom had either fled, turning their backs,
or had laid down their lives on the very threshold of the gate.
In a frenzy he seized his weapons and called his servants to arms,
and cuts short every delay; then, in the silent night,
he falls upon the enemy buried in sleep and wine,
seeing bodies sprawled about, chariots upreared along the shore;
men lying among the reins and wheels, and arms lying there too,
and wine too; a vast carnage and a panic-stricken uproar
he stirs up, and with his right hand sends countless men down to Tartarus,
and turns the terrified kings to flight; laden
with enormous plunder he returned, and brought Lot back.

div.note: Abram overcame them off their guard, unwary, unarmed in their beds, and useless for fighting through drunkenness. Joseph. antiq. lib. 1. cap. 11.

lg.l: The king of Salem, likewise king of men and priest of Jehovah,
Melchizedek meets the victor, uttering joyful blessings.
He congratulates him on his return, serving out wine and bread,
to whom the victor Abram renders tithes of the spoils.
So, after King Pluto had carried the human race captive down to Orcus
and had exerted all his might and drawn the bonds tight,
Christ, hastening from heaven, came down to the shades.
And he tracks down his own brothers, and through the midst of the enemy
bursts his way, laying low the ranks of Styx with a mighty word,
and with his radiant face he struck terror into the bloodless shades.
But when the shades saw Christ advancing and roaring dreadful threats,
they wheeled about in fear and, falling back,
raised a feeble cry; then, with a suppliant look
and on bended knees they worship the name of Jesus.
He flies on and, the abyss laid open, seizes the black host
and bound [them] behind their backs with a hundred knots of bronze,
he unbarred the jaws of Tartarus, and the doors of Dis,
and the grove growing dark with black dread.
Then he snatched the wretched from death, and broke their chains,
rejoicing, he bore his friends aloft to their homeland.
where the light is everlasting, and life knows no end,
and where there is the ineffable gift of tranquil peace.
Here golden halls gleam with purple gems.
The whole floor sparkles with stars, the proud panelled ceiling
surpasses the flame of Phoebus with flashing radiance.
For no guilty man is it lawful to tread the pure threshold;
but those whose piety and vigorous virtue shine here,
and who possess justice and a mind conscious of what is right,
who also possess age-old faithfulness and a life that knows no deceit;
for these alone is the house of almighty Olympus thrown open.
Here the holy fathers shine, who form the greatest throng:
Here Christ's twelve companions shimmer with light,
among whom Christ himself, most beautiful, blazes out,
just as when the Morning Star, bathed in Ocean's wave,
has lifted up the holy face of heaven; and, dissolving the shadows,
flashes among the night-wandering fires of the stars.
And as the golden Sun blazes among the twelve constellations.
Here too are the pious Prophets, and those who before the walls of lofty
of Jerusalem, fall in battle; and the unmarried maidens,
Mary here, a radiant goddess above the ethereal clouds,
shines in a robe starred with tawny jasper.

div.p: After Abraham's death, Pluto stirs up the Philistines against his son Isaac. Out of envy they stop up his wells with dust, so as to deter him from building Jerusalem; but God appears to him, renews the promises once made to Abraham, and gives him twins, who by struggling in their mother's womb foreshadowed the discord that was to arise between the brothers and between their descendants. For Esau pursued the younger twin, Jacob, with unremitting hatred; therefore, at his mother's urging, Jacob withdraws to Laban and serves him for twenty-six years. God, however, repeatedly comforts him and promises that Christ will descend from him and overthrow Babylon. He shows him a ladder upon which angels were ascending and descending; an angelic host is sent to protect him; he wrestles with Christ in the form of an angel and emerges victorious, but limps after the angel strikes him in the hollow of the knee. Pluto also casts Jacob and his sons into great danger because of the abduction of Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Then, in order to kill the old man through grief, he stirs up all the brothers against Joseph, whom his father loved above the others. They lower the boy into a pit; Judah sells him; and at last, because of his interpretation of dreams, he rises to greatness in Pharaoh's court. On seeing the kidskin coat stained with blood, his father believes him to have been killed and therefore mourns Joseph for a long time. He sends his sons into Egypt to obtain grain, and Joseph eventually receives them into his favor. Meanwhile Pluto rages against Job, whose story is related; and everything is applied to Christ.

lg.l: When Abraham had departed this life, his son Isaac
succeeded, an heir not unworthy of so great a father.
He, harassed by Philistine treachery, through the envy of Orcus
Through envy he suffers exile, for with dust all
the wells that father Abraham dug they silt up,
Thus they also deny foliage to the flock and keep it from the springs.
But God renews for him the promises he had once given to his father,
and with words soothes his grieving heart.
To him his most beautiful wife a twin offspring, at a birth
bore in one and the same [birth]; but—a thing wondrous to tell—
the boys struggle in their mother’s womb.
But when the pregnant mother had brought forth the twins,
Jacob seized hold of the elder brother's heel,
and this indeed was reported to be dreadful and marvellous to see:
for the responses of God, when he was consulted, foretold that he [Jacob] would be famous and fortunate
and that there would be renowned
progeny, which would bring the whole world under its yoke,
and would rule Jerusalem, which was destined to be in everlasting peace.
Hence Esau’s offspring waged continual war against Jacob’s people,
and the King of Erebus goaded Edom on
so that by treachery he might make away with his defenceless brother.
Nor did the wiles of guileful Edom escape the brother.
For when he was coming of age alongside him, being of the same age,
turning over a thousand schemes in his cruel heart, he seeks
to cut short, as soon as he can, the life of his guiltless brother.
Fearing this, Rebecca, that most beautiful mother, urges her son
to hasten his flight and to depart from his native land,
and to bend his steps secretly to her brother Laban.
Jacob did not delay after his dear mother’s counsel;
He obeyed; and at a swift pace pressed on to Haran,
and here, forced to serve under an unjust master,
twice ten years, through the hatred of the ruler of Avernus.
Yet he came away exceedingly rich in cattle and flocks, and
blessed with twelve sons; and to him
the Lord, appearing, soothed his heart with words.
"I pledge all things worthy of your vast undertakings,"
he says, “and, with offspring beyond number, the towers of Sion;
and I promise that Christ shall come from your seed;
who in triumph shall despoil Babylon, and fierce peoples
shall crush, and shall establish customs and walls for men.”
And while, hastening his journey, he bends his course toward Haran,
dread night covers the lands with damp shadows.
And now upon a stone, under the open sky, weary Jacob
was taking sweet sleep. The king of high heaven
showed him a ladder whose top reached all the way to heaven.
Upon it ascend and descend the crowded companies
of the dwellers in heaven; God himself took his stand at the top, and the whole
circle of the lands he looked down upon, and the deep sea.
So God seemed to stand before the eyes of him as he lay
in his sleep, made plain in abundant light — the light in which he
had once offered himself to the sight of Abraham and his faithful descendants,
and shone out through the night in pure radiance.
Then he addressed him thus and dispelled his cares with these words:
“Born of gods, and destined to beget gods; for you, weary as you are, walls
And we promise both a race and a city that shall abide, and
this land on which you lie stretched out; and amid
hard rocks you lie all night on an uncovered bed.
I will not leave you alone in so great a peril,
nor do I refuse to go with you as companion wherever you flee.
Go on, then, and do not abandon the long toil of [your] flight;
and do not yield to hardships, but go against them the more boldly;
for I will give you back unharmed to your homeland, and through many years
the fortune of your house shall stand firm; a great stock of descendants
shall crush nations and number ancestors upon ancestors.
He spoke, and hid himself among the fiery stars of heaven.
But dread broke the young man's sleep, and over his bones and limbs
sweat streamed, bursting out over his whole body.
And now Night, driven onward by the hours, had reached the midpoint of her course.
when the young man is shaken from sleep, just as an early-rising woman,
[on whom it has been laid] to sustain her life by the distaff and by humble craft,
rouses the ash and the sleeping fires,
adding night to her work: and by lamplight she keeps her maidservants busy
at their long stint of wool, so that she may keep chaste the marriage bed
of her husband, and may be able to bring up her little children:
Just so the son of Isaac, no slower at that hour,
rises and gazes at the golden stars of heaven’s temple.
he lifted his palms to heaven, and worships the divine power
of great-souled Jehovah, who presides over the glowing stars.
This place, he says, is the lofty house of the great Thunderer
and it is the gate of heaven. O how worthy of reverence! Behold,
God is here (I had not noticed); God dwells here. Without delay, the stone
on which he had laid his neck while he slept at night
he lifted it from the ground and, as soon as he saw the light begin to dawn,
pouring rich oil over it, he consecrated it to you, Jehovah,
and poured out prayers, and called upon the Lord in his vows:
Almighty Father, if you are moved by any prayers,
look upon us — this alone [we ask] — and if by our devotion we deserve it,
then grant [your] help, Father, and make all this firm,
and go with your servant; cover [my] body with clothing;
Now, I pray, provide an exile with the gifts of grain;
so shall you yourself always be God to me, and your altar
a tender lamb from our sheepfolds shall often stain [with its blood].
And if you accompany me on my journey, while, as an exile,
I leave my native lands, and if you send me back to my own realm,
not only, gracious Father, shall we celebrate your honor
with ancestral songs, and bring platters and sacrificial cakes,
and many a victim shall fall before the altars by our right hand:
but I shall load the threshold with tithes and various gifts;
and let this stone be a witness to the divine presence,
and let the place hold the name of Bethel forever.
This Ladder is Christ, whose origin is heavenly,
and he walks upon the earth and hides his head among the clouds.
He joined heaven and earth by an everlasting covenant.
The great dwellers in heaven glide down from the stars of the upper air,
To us mortals by the power of his blood; and, relying upon the steps of his
merits, we ascend to the stars.
He too is the stone on which we find rest, ailing
mortals, our hearts troubled by manifold cares,
while, driven from our homeland, we plough the vast plain of the sea.
Grant, Christ, that through you I may surmount the heights of heaven;
grant that I may climb, unconquered one, by the steps of your merits:
may it be permitted me to touch the thresholds of the heavenly ones; lead me,
lead [me], O Christ, to the Father; bid [them] part far and wide,
the clouds, that my mind may carry its steps into high heaven;
And when dread night has wrapped me in gloomy shadow,
and sleep shall close my swimming eyes:
may it be permitted me to rest that night with you,
and upon you besides, for you are the stone torn from the mountain
on which we loosen our limbs in calm rest,
we sons of Christ, in the darkness of death and at the setting of the sun.
And now, about to see again his homeland and his father's dwellings,
the son of Isaac sets about his journey with his dear wife,
with his servants, and his children, with the household gods and the great gods.
Behold, radiant troops come to meet him,
of heaven-dwelling youths, whose temples [shoot forth] ruddy flames,

div.note: By Teraphim I understand what Rachel stole. They were called Penates, because they were worshipped in the inner chambers (penetralia) of houses, or because through them we inwardly (penitus) breathe, live, and understand. They were also called the Great Gods; for Apollo, Neptune, Jupiter, Minerva, Juno, Vesta, etc. are called both Penates and Great Gods by the poets. See Macr. Sat. lib. 3. cap. 4. Nat. Com. lib. 4. c. 2. Servius, etc.

lg.l: pour forth joyfully, and their shields send out flashing lightning.
Golden is the hair upon them, and golden the helmet;
they gleam in striped cloaks: then their milk-white necks
are entwined with gold; each of them brandishes two dreadful
weapons in his hand, their bodies covered by long shields.
These God, for Isaac's son, who feared both the wrath and threats
of his own brother, sent down from heaven on high;
and bade them relieve the man with aid, and add strength [to him].
They do just as they were bidden: they guard the unarmed man,
they supply him strength, and fill him with daring spirit;
and admit him to their camp as an ally, and confirm their alliance.
Jacob recognized the princes of heaven and their divine weapons,
the son of Isaac, and their golden locks and flashing eyes;
and gave hope to his wavering mind, and loosed his fear:
This is that vast army of the heavenly ones, this is [the host]
which keeps us safe in our sleep, by night and by day.
These have encircled the walls of Jerusalem with a close-set ring;
these press round about at the gates and at every tower
to lay the enemy low in slaughter, and to girdle the walls with flames,
These guard our cities better against enemies
than can javelins, or those who strive to defend them with stones,
and to ply fire, and to fit arrows to the bowstring.
These are the chariots, these the horses which once upon the mountains
Elisha saw breathing fire from their nostrils;
Then the terrifying flashes, and the din, and the dread,
the prophet perceived, together with wrath and its attendant flames;
and these, gleaming far and wide with snowy brightness,
they glided down from high heaven to serve Christ
while he was passing his life on earth among mortals.
May such companions never be far from me, O greatest of all,
while I live, nor when I leave this light and mankind.
But me, driven by so many waves yet unharmed across the sea,
may they set down on the longed-for shores of the heavenly fatherland.
But because [his] mind, against dangers yet to come, had not yet
of Isaac's son was not yet firm enough against dangers to come, there came a winged armour-bearer,
blazing with a starry shield and heavenly arms,
Striking in countenance, whom the Father sent from on high
to wrestle and to supply the man with strength and courage;
like a heaven-dweller in all things: in voice and complexion,
his golden hair, and his arms fierce with their clangour.
A golden bow rings from his shoulders, and there gleams a golden
helmet; then his saffron cloak and its rustling folds,
of fine linen, he had gathered into a knot with tawny gold,
embroidered with the needle in [his] tunics and the splendid coverings of [his] legs.
He girds himself for the fight; and Jacob's trembling
breast he tries, by wrestling, to harden against wounds.
But lest the fight should seem unequal for Jacob,
weary already, and bearing neither weapons in his hand nor shields,
he laid aside his radiant arms beneath the oak that faced him:
the helmet terrible with its crests and spewing flames,
and the death-bearing sword, the corselet stiff with bronze,
blood-red, huge, as when a dark-blue cloud
kindles with the sun's rays and gleams back far and wide:
Then the smooth greaves of electrum and of gold refined,
and the spear, and the shield's fabric past all telling.
Thus naked he attacks [him] naked, and now from the Ocean night
rushes in, and folds the earth about with dusky wings.
But while he turns the various outcomes over in his heart,
the son of Isaac, fearing his brother, beside the water of the Jabbok,
upon green leafage, and beneath the cold vault of heaven,
lay down, letting his eyes sink in sweet sleep;
But the winged ones enclosed him in a dense ring.
But behold, from the midst, his arms laid by, the wing-bearing captain
advances out of the column; his companions do reverence to him as he goes.
Great is the majesty of his countenance; great beauty flashes from his eyes.
The rays of the golden sun encircle his shining
temples; his hair breathes out a divine fragrance.
This is he, Jesus, the Prince of the heavenly host,
mighty in arms, the master of war, the martial Hero,
whom, as a child of our race and blood, there shall bring forth
a Virgin, when, as the years glide by, the time shall come;
a Virgin who alone has known the travails of Lucina.
Nor shall any child of Jacob’s race raise his Abrahamite
forefathers to such heights of hope; nor shall the land of Judaea ever
boast so greatly of any nursling.
This is the man, this is he whom you hear promised to you again and again,
Judaea; this is the divine offspring; he shall establish the golden
ages—he who shall extend Jerusalem’s dominion beyond the farthest Garamantes,
the land of the Ethiopians and Arabs, and the wastes of the Getae,
as far as the unknown shores of the Indians;
Him many peoples, many who know their own blessings,
and they sought him for themselves and wished to acknowledge him as king;
A nation lying beneath the seven-starred Hyperborean Wain
serves our Lord; Egypt worships him, as does mighty
Lydia; so too the peoples of the Parthians, and the Median Hydaspes,
the unbridled Numidians, the inhospitable Syrtis,
and the Dacian descending from the allied Hister acknowledge him.
Toward the lofty citadels of triumphant Zion he
drives his chariot as victor, marked out by the richest spoils;
he will overthrow cities and the battle lines of his enemies
and the Eumenides themselves, the brood of fire-ruling Avernus;
having avenged the forefathers of Judah, and the profaned temples of Jehovah.
He, when great tumult throws the Christians' cause into confusion,
will steady it by prayer, will lay low the Turks and the rebel Indian,

div.note: Here I make the Eumenides masculine, with the same licence by which Virgil calls Venus and Allecto gods: "I descend, with a god leading," Aen. 2; "Nor was a god absent from the wandering right hand"—that is, Allecto—Aen. 7. For the most learned poet knew that Venus is the seed of generation, which is a power as much male as female. And since Allecto is an evil spirit, it was not fitting for him always to be bound to the female sex, although other poets do this—perhaps because evil spirits assume this sex more often than the male: Aen. 3, "They have maiden faces." Thus, in Aen. 7, Allecto transforms himself into the features of an old woman, and becomes Calybe, Juno's aged [priestess], etc. Here, however, by the Eumenides I mean evil demons; for as the former are, so the latter are ministers of God, avengers of crimes, tormentors of wicked men, sons of night and darkness. They also wander the air; they are also called serpents and dogs, and dwell in the abyss. Tisiphone, from τίσις, "vengeance," and φόνος, "slaughter"; [Megaera, from] μεγαίρειν, "to envy"; and Ἄληκτος, "never ceasing," are names most apt for devils, for they never cease to assail the human race with vengeance, slaughter, and envy.

lg.l: and hangs up captured barbarian arms for the thundering Father.
What a city—Jerusalem—will you behold? What kingdoms will you see arise
under this pious king? With Judah’s forces accompanying him,
to what heights will the Christians’ glory rise through mighty deeds!
This [day] I would keep, were I an exile on the Gaetulian Syrtes,
or caught on the Argolic sea and in the city of Mycenae:
whatever lands that lie beneath the Sun may call me,
I shall always honour, always venerate Jesus:
who by his death earned a heavenly crown on my behalf,
and, victorious, laid the enemy hordes low with a word.
And now he attacks the man, comes upon the fearful one, and
he rouses to the fight; a sudden trembling seizes the limbs
of Abraham’s descendant, and little by little he tries to withdraw from the field
and turn his back in flight; but more fiercely the winged
messenger presses upon him and spurs him on; he also supplies him with strength,
that he may be able to stand up against so great a divine power,
and to bear its force; so, after light was restored to his mind
and the darkness scattered, unarmed he girds himself for the fight.
At once each stood erect on tiptoe,
and, undaunted, raised his arms toward the upper air;
they join hand to hand and challenge each other in combat.
The princes of radiant Olympus turned their eyes,
and laid their weapons down from their shoulders, and lean their shields back
And they fix their spears in the ground; heaven's own fiery
stars are astonished; astonished, veiled in grey-green reed,
was Jabbok, and now went more slowly with his glassy waters;
marvelling at the number of heaven-dwellers, whose mighty throng
fills the banks, while Christ, in the likeness of our [nature],
clothed, exercises his limbs on grassy wrestling grounds.
Now they see heaven and earth, both man and God,
joined with one another in fierce contest; but
for a mortal to hold out against such mighty strength—
who could have done it, if God himself had not given him strength?
And now between them they trade blows with great force.
Here indeed shame and valour are blended into one.
Anger rouses their spirits, labouring breath shakes their limbs;
all that night through they wrestle on the high bank,
and, taking turns, they roll themselves over the whole expanse:
and now this one, now that one lies rolled over in the sand;
and so each exerts his strength with all his care.
Long the struggle hung in doubt; at last the victory passed
to the son of Isaac; but the Angel strikes with a strong blow the sinew
of his knee-hollow; at once he walks with steps that are not even:
yet the hero is neither cast down in spirit nor terrified,
though he leans on a staff as he takes alternating steps;
he holds the winged one fast in his grip, and does not let him go
until he proclaims glad tidings and grants a favourable outcome.
He assents to the supplicant; meanwhile the wheeling day was hastening on,
and with its light now full the day had put night to flight.
In such words the winged Spirit addresses the victor:
"Blessing on your new valour, Jacob; to you the ruler of Olympus"
[He] readily yielded the palm of this contest.
Behold, your unconquered right hand has overcome the mighty God;
do not fear — you shall bridle rebellious men with law.
He spoke, and beating his vast wings with loud clangour
Michael is borne aloft to ethereal Olympus.
Not otherwise had Christ, with the hard stock of Jacob,
wrestled in shifting struggle, until
he succumbed, overcome by great violence and wound upon wound.
Thus the victor willed to give way to the conquered nation,
and to take the bridle, and to obey a bloody law.
But yet this victory of Judah's was an unhappy one;
for with its knee injured the nation wanders with limping steps,
fleeing the face of God, an exile with its kingdoms taken away;
it seeks unknown cities and deserted shores.
But when [the dawn] had lit up the lands with Phoebus' lamp,
and Aurora had driven the dewy shadow from the sky,
speaking words of blessing to his companions, and praying all good fortune [for them],
he raises himself up swiftly, and making his way through the clear air
he took his seat in the longed-for dwellings, in the citadel of heaven.
But Pluto, still unable to bear it, rages monstrously in his Stygian
cave and sends the Furies forth into the air,
Indeed, he tries to convulse the house of aged Jacob with hatred
and to arm the brothers, united in purpose, for battle,
hoping by this means to overthrow the godly people.
For the brothers, a spirited phalanx, kindled with grief
because Shechem had dared to violate Dinah’s chastity—
some draw swords with their hands, while others seize spears,
and one desire holds them all: to settle it with the sword,
to avenge Dinah, and to exact the punishment the crime deserved.
But Simeon, with his brother Levi, in youthful arms
Girded up, they go where the grim Fury drives them,
both distinguished in courage, both in surpassing feats of arms;
and alone they carry out the slaughter, unknown to their father Jacob;
they fall upon the wretched citizens, who groan bitterly,
pinned to their beds, and slowed by the wound lately
taken in the groin, while every male is circumcised
with the broad blade, after the custom of Jacob's people.
the watchmen are cut down, and everywhere the helpless bodies
bodies; King Hamor, who by chance upon high coverlets
was breathing sleep from the fullness of his breast.
Shechem too, and a great nameless throng,
they slay, and in their frenzy lord it over the burning city.
Thus fury, and the mad lust for slaughter,
drove them, ablaze, against the unwary citizens and those lying on their bedding,
for one man's crime and the ravished honour of their sister.
And had Jacob not escaped in good time
to Bethel at Jehovah’s warning, with his bloodstained offspring,
that day would have been the last for the father and his line.
Indeed God's portents stand in the way with terrors of every kind,
lest the neighbouring nations pursue with torch and sword
the sons of Abraham (while they withdraw from the city and make for safety),
distinguished by their spoils and proud of so great a slaughter.
saw [them] glad at such success and high in spirit,
the king of Erebus [saw] the young men; while he tosses on a tide of wrath,
see, with fresh devices he falls upon his exulting enemies:
The father cherished Joseph alone more than all the others;
whom he clothed in a tunic of embroidered stuff.
But while an unlooked-for rest had, as it chanced, through his limbs
crept over him, straightway the gate of sleep was unbarred,
the horn gate, by which an easy passage out is granted to true shades.
Behold, he sees the stars, and you, most brilliant lights
of the world, which lead the gliding year through heaven,
doing him reverence as suppliants; and moreover [he sees] that before him
his brothers' sheaves of wheat had fallen down in the field.
As soon as he had told this vision to his brothers, they all,
indignant with anger, and driven by the goads of black
envy, resolve to consign the innocent man to death.
Afterwards, while he was visiting his brothers the shepherds, they
conspired together to destroy one wretched man.
Long since a wicked plague had crept through their limbs —
envy, which Pluto, sending it forth from the seat of the
dread sisters, bids go through the upper air.
Fearing, that is, that he might found the walls of a city —
Joseph, whom he assails with a thousand wiles and with craft.
But Reuben, whose mind held the better counsel,
forbade [them] to stain their hands with a brother's blood,
and urged rather to let him down into a nearby pit.
Judah frees him from the pit, and sells for silver
the guiltless one; the Midianites buy [him], and him
they lead into the land of Egypt, and to a powerful lord,
to Potiphar, they sell [him].
But the brothers steeped in the blood of a slaughtered kid
the boy's striped tunic, and to their father Jacob

div.note: The gate of horn signifies a body free of foul and gross humours, and as it were translucent; in such a body dreams are true and clear. The ivory gate, on the other hand, denotes a gross body, glutted with surfeit, where dreams are troubled, obscure, and false.

lg.l: They show [it] torn, and red with thick gore.
He, believing his son mangled by a wild beast's tooth,
was stunned, the wretched man, and the warmth suddenly left his bones:
tears poured down his cheeks, and a voice broke from his lips:
Unhappy Joseph, in what region am I to seek you?
I shall see you return no more. Are you he, of my old age
my late repose — could you leave [me] alone,
cruel one? And you, sent into such great dangers—
was your wretched father given no chance to address you one last time?
Alas, in an unknown land, given as prey to dogs or to bears
or to birds, you lie; tigers take possession of your body,
monstrous ones perhaps; your mother did not, at your funeral rites,
lead you forth, nor close your eyes, nor wash your wounds,
covering you with a robe. What land now holds your limbs and severed members
and your mangled corpse? This old age
is the lot due to our [years]. O you, most holy wife,
happy in your death, and not kept back for this grief,
while I, on the contrary, by living on have outlasted my destiny, a survivor,
so that I should be left a father. O three and four times blessed [are those]
to whom, before their fathers' faces, beneath the high walls of their homeland,
it befell them to die; for their lifeless bodies are entrusted to a tomb,
are consigned; but you, dearest son,
will lie naked, Joseph, upon an unknown shore.
But why do I turn over these unwelcome things to no purpose,
or why do I delay? let these be the consolations of my grief,
that I saw the death of my wretched son [to be] not cruel.
Each man's own day stands fixed; the time [of life] is brief and beyond recall,
For all there is [a brief span] of life; the loss of a tomb is light.
Besides, these things do not, without the great will of Jehovah,
come to pass; nay more, the Stygian — and the realms untrodden by the living —
groves shall I behold, and my son beneath deepest Acheron
shall I address again; I do not seek the joys of life,
nor is it right, but [I seek] to carry them down to my son among the lowest shades.
Having said this, with trembling hand he tore his garments,
sprinkled over with dust, and shaggy with horsehair,
and he wept for his son many months together.
Meanwhile [Potiphar] set Joseph over his household, and to him
Potiphar committed the whole care of his servants.
He was of striking appearance, and of comely face;
and by love of him, and by shameful desire, was seized
Potiphar's wife, who night and day pursued
shameful intercourse with the youth, and cast aside her modesty;
But he is moved by no entreaties nor by any bribe
to profane the marriage-torch, or to break the laws of chastity.
his mind stays unmoved, the tears roll down in vain.
So, after [harsh love] had stirred the fire in the wretched woman's bones,
harsh love, Pluto, [taking] a serpent from the Furies’ tresses,
hurls [it], and slips it into her bosom, down to her inmost heart.
It, gliding between her garments and her smooth breast,
winds along with no touch felt, and deceives her in her frenzy,
breathing a viper's spirit into her; for her neck it becomes the twisted
gold, that huge snake; it becomes the band of a long fillet,
and it binds up her hair, and glides slippery over her limbs.

div.note: In much the same way, Philo Judaeus portrays Jacob in mourning.

In agreement with Eugubinus in his Recognition of the Pentateuch, I take this to mean sackcloth. Dust is not mentioned in the text; nevertheless, it was customary in times of great grief to sprinkle oneself with dust.

lg.l: The woman rages, distraught, and in her husband’s presence
accuses the innocent man, as though he had tried to violate the bed
of his absent master; and, holding up the garment torn from
Joseph’s arms, she says: “This treacherous
foreigner, while he was making sport of us—I immediately filled the house
I filled with shouting, and spared neither voice nor anger.
But he in panic fled away, his garment left behind."
By such snares, and by the artifice of his perjured wife,
the tale was believed, and he, caught by her guiles and forced by her tears,
Potiphar curbs the innocent man with chains and prison.
After this, he who presides over the green fields of Egypt
saw in his sleep seven, of surpassing body,
oxen feeding across the meadows, and along the brimming
rivers, where there is moss too, and the greenest grass on the bank;
then as many wasted thin with leanness, and these upon the former
fell in ravening hunger; then he sees in a field
a stalk that bows down with seven heavy ears;
then another; this one put forth seven empty ears,
and suddenly devoured the seven full ears.
At this the king, troubled by the portents, seeks answers from the gods
and sends men to inquire at Phoebus’ oracle.
Alas, the minds of seers are ignorant! Apollo as diviner is of no avail,
nor can the seers, when consulted, give any answers.
Ah, how often has Phoebus’ tripod deceived the wretched
while they seek counsel, and hang upon the prophet's threshold?
They go away uncounselled, and come to hate the prophet of the gods.
But the young Joseph, into whom a great mind and spirit
the almighty Father inspires [him], and opens up what is to come,
he chants truths; he does not commit marks and names
to leaves, which the wind drives on when the hinge is turned,
or which the door scatters as they flutter in the cave; not here
does he chant dread riddles, and bellow back from the cave,
wrapping falsehoods in dark sayings; nor does he enjoy the converse
of false gods: but, by the breath of the true Divinity
addressed, Joseph chanted true oracles.
Driven therefore by this report, the King out of the prison
leads forth the fate-speaking seer. The manacles and the tight
bonds Pharaoh orders to be lifted, and thus speaks with friendly words:
Whoever you are (from now on forget the fathers you have lost)
you shall be ours; and, at my request, learn these truths thoroughly—
what they mean, the dreams that terrify me and hold me in suspense;
tell it yourself, and willingly give voice to it with your own mouth.
For I have gone to seers, and sought oracles with prayers,
reporting the portents of the gods, demanding what their meaning may be,
but Apollo deludes my mind with false replies:
There is no trusting Phoebus, there is no discernment in his seer.
With these words he tells Joseph his two dreams.
But he, with fear laid aside, unfolding the true
meaning, informs [him] that seven years are coming

div.note: Many things are shown by God in sleep; for true dreams are from God. "For the dream too is from Zeus."

The chief gods of the Egyptians were Serapis, Osiris, and Isis: different names of a single divinity. So among the Greeks and Romans: Apollo, Phoebus, Cynthius — yet in both cases the same god, namely the Sun, whose oracles they everywhere consulted. See Macrob. Saturn. l. 1. c. 20. 21.

lg.l: [years] full of the gifts of Ceres, and as many to come
in which Sirius will scorch the thirsting fields,
the grass will wither, and the sickly crop will refuse sustenance;
nor will the Nile hide the land beneath black silt.
The ears of grain and the oxen portend these future events to you.
Therefore, he says, you should gather the grain and store it under cover,
while the yield loads the furrows and overwhelms the granaries,
and, mindful of the famine to come, while the year runs over
with fruit, livestock, and sheaves of grain stalks.
These are the things of which my voice is permitted to warn you.
And after the seer had thus spoken them with friendly lips,
Immediately he is laden with various honours and with gold:
His neck is encircled, and his finger ringed, with gold:
he is clothed in a garment of fine linen and, in the second chariot,
he is borne along as the people roar with acclamations and applause.
Thus the man who until then had long been confined in close fetters
and imprisoned in iron now wields the reins of the kingdom.
Now the stars of heaven, now the Sun, and the sheaves of grain,
with eyes cast down, adore this holy star.
For maddened hunger drove the father and his sons
to seek Egypt and venture into distant lands.
Him whom they once despised they now revere, and all

div.note: Adorare—whether from the word Ador, grain destined for sacrifices; or from ore, "mouth" (hence in Apuleius, book 2, populum adorare means "to address the people"); or from orare, "to entreat," as in Aeneid 10: "I, Turnus, willingly entreat you," that is, "I earnestly entreat you." It was performed in various ways: 1. by kissing one's own hand, Job 21:27; 2. by kissing another's hand; 3. by bending the knee; 4. by extending the hands; 5. by veiling the head—and, before the altars, our heads: "we are veiled in Phrygian raiment," Aeneid 2; 6. by sitting—so Pythagoras taught: when worship is performed, let them sit; 7. by prostrating the body on the ground—thus the Persians worshipped their kings. In marriage, to adore one's wife is to kiss her, and so forth.

lg.l: As suppliants they acknowledge their guilt, and beg for pardon,
Judah above all, with tears for his younger brother
poured out — the brother whom Joseph was then holding in darkness and chains,
because of the cup found in his sack.
He, humble and suppliant, his eyes and his imploring right hand
stretching forth, says: “He has indeed deserved it, and I do not plead against it;”
"use your lot as you will; if any care for a wretched father
can touch you, I beg you, have pity on his old age,
and send the youth back unharmed to his country and his father;
a father whom cares already wear away, and his mind has been troubled
by Joseph's death; lest worse news should wound his ears
and compel him to cut short his bitter life.
For if he does not see him brought back, he will believe he has perished.
Inflict harsh violence and chains upon me instead, as your captive.”
Joseph was weeping, and would not conceal himself
any longer, nor could he bear so great a grief;
but, himself a suppliant, he bowed his heart to brotherly love;
forgetting all their crimes he pardons them, and unasked
he comforts them, pouring out tears between every word,
and repaying his brothers' deeds with deeds their opposite.
For he bestowed various honours on them all, and
weeping, he hung in his father's embrace and about his neck;
whom, conveyed in his own chariot, he escorted to the palace.
Not otherwise does it begrudge Christ the citadels of Jerusalem —
the Jewish nation, today; so once it begrudged the honour
offered from heaven; Judas sold him, and all
the brothers conspired for his destruction; in the tomb's
they hide him in the tomb's hollow; but the supreme Creator of all things
Having brought him out of darkness, he carried him above the golden stars,
golden, and clothed him in a gleaming white mantle of light;
and granted him to recline at the sacred banquets of the gods.
And he makes him master of the storm-clouds and of the tempests.
He, destined to be Judge of all things, from a tawny cloud
shall burst, light and radiant, through the heavenly spheres,
borne on a flaming chariot; then the whole vast world
shall acknowledge him as Lord; nay, Jacob’s own race
shall worship the divine majesty that it now despises and hates.
Job too, of Edomite stock, was founding the lofty walls
of Jerusalem — the man whom the King of greedy Acheron,
implacable, assails unprovoked with the teeth of envy.
Job was a guardian of right, and the single most righteous man
that ever lived, and once the wealthiest in the fields of Ausitis.
Five flocks of bleating sheep were his, and five herds
of cattle came home, and he turned the earth with a hundred ploughs.
This man had seven sons, as many rewards of love;
and three daughters besides, of outstanding beauty of body.
Blessed with such great possessions, he flourished in his ancestral fields,
an old man now, and ruled his own people in tranquil peace.

div.note: "From Abraham he was the fifth, a descendant of Esau." Athanas. in Synop. He was not, therefore, a Hebrew descended from Nahor, as the Hebrews and Jerome on Job would have it: for the land of Uz lies in Idumaea and on the borders of Arabia. Hence Job is called an Arab by Chrysostom. Job's three friends too were his neighbours, and Idumaeans. The land of Uz is called Ausitis by the Seventy. See August. l. 18. de civit. c. 47. Chrysost. Hom. 2. de patient. Job. Origen, Theodoret, etc.
I reduce the seven thousand sheep to five flocks; the three thousand camels, the five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses, to five herds.

lg.l: But suddenly Fortune changed and broke faith
after her own fashion, for she is ever a shifting and changeable thing.
While the brothers joyfully hold their feasts together.
While the husbandmen were breaking up the fields with the hard ploughshare,
while in the empty pastures the donkeys crop the grass,
behold, the hostile Sabaean tribes came,
who are wont to carry off plunder and to live by robbery;
and they drive off all the donkeys after killing their guards,
together with the herds of cattle and the magnificently built bulls.
And they lead away all the heifers of surpassing beauty,
and while the Father, in the midst of the storm-clouds' night, with flashing
thunderbolts [armed], hurls them with his right hand — at which upheaval the vast
earth trembles, and lightning-flashes redouble as the clouds are rent:
the bleating flocks perished, and the keepers of the sheep.
Besides, the savage race of the Chaldaeans, the husbandmen
unwary, secretly overpowers with the sword, and drives off the camels.
Moreover, while opposing winds in a swift whirlwind
clash—Zephyr and Notus, and Eurus rejoicing in his eastern
steeds: upon the lofty roofs, with a dreadful roar,
they bear down together, and from its deepest foundations the whole
house they overturn, and it buries all the children
while they were indulging in wine; and Jobab, with garment torn,
thunderstruck at the fate of his children and the ruin of the house,
disfiguring his grey hair, drenched with filthy dust.
Then with his right hand he cut his hair, and sought the ground,
bowed low, and poured out from his breast such laments:

div.note: Satan mingled himself with this storm.

lg.l: My Mother brought me forth naked into the light of day,
and this same one will receive me on my return and lay me away naked,
enfolding in her quiet lap [my] ashes and bones.
You gave me whatever measure of kingship this is; you gave me the sceptre,
holy Father, and now by right you demand those same things back from me;
you rule the empire of the world with a nod: all things obey
your commands, great King, wherever Phoebus, retracing his course,
looks down upon both Oceans from the summit of Olympus.
Therefore may your great and memorable name live on.
But the ruler of Avernus, not content to have dragged through these punishments
the man outstanding in piety;
While the gods’ high house stands open, and while he himself, aloft
in his starry halls, the begetter of men and of gods
calls together a council of the winged ones within heaven’s
golden thresholds; they assemble in the double-doored halls,
and among them Satan, from the seat of the dread sisters,
appears, bristling, shaking his windy wings.
No monster is more dreadful than he, nor has any fiercer
plague and wrath of God risen from the Stygian waters.
Though he reigns in the blind hall of darkness,
from which he sends fear and a sick man’s grim diseases upon mortals,
and death and cares, and dreadful wars,
yet whenever the King of high heaven gives his assent, from there
he dares to trust himself to the sky on swift-flying wings.

div.note: All this is to be understood by way of anthropopatheia, whereby spiritual things are shadowed forth under things of sense.
Although Satan is not permitted to enter the heaven of the blessed, from which he was cast out, he can nevertheless by God's permission enter the visible and aetherial heavens.

lg.l: He comes to Jove's throne and the threshold of the supreme king,
and loudly accuses Jobab;
and heaps fresh charges upon him, and demands penalties
undeserved: "this man," he says, "reveres you with a feigned heart,
and worships the Thunderer with an insincere mind.
Surely you have ringed him with a rampart and high walls;
but if you were to send upon him some unspeakable disaster and grim
ruin, you will see that he will curse you; therefore,
by your leave, let it be permitted to try Jobab's strength."
He assented, and with his nod sets all Olympus trembling,
the Almighty, and granted leave to ravage Job's body
with an ulcer, and his limbs with burning pustules that made them bristle.
At once Satan comes down from the height of heaven,
behold, on the wing, and is borne earthward in a swift whirlwind.
Just as an arrow driven from the bowstring through a cloud —
armed with the gall of cruel poison, which a Parthian—
a Parthian or Cydonian—hurled, an incurable shaft;
hissing, and [the shaft], unseen, darts across the swift shadows;
Thus did such a king, born of night and sent down from
the ethereal stars, make his way, lashing the air with his wings,
and the plague, whirring, carries itself to and fro before Job's face.
A strange numbness unstrung his limbs with fear,
when from afar he recognized the dreadful whirring and the wings;
and his hair stood on end with horror, and his voice stuck in his throat.
At once the sick man's complexion changes, and ghastly emaciation disfigures his face;

div.note: "...his name before was Jobab," etc. The Seventy Interpreters, at the end of the book of Job. See Theod. q. 91. on Genesis.

lg.l: emaciation disfigures [him]; into his bones immense pain
works its way in; dreadful filth, and an untrimmed beard.
Sudden scabs harden on his languishing body,
and a most loathsome itch assails the whole skin.
But confidence did not fail great-hearted Job;
but he maintains an unconquered spirit within his wasting body,
sitting among the ashes; his limbs reek with corruption,
and he scrapes them with a potsherd. Meanwhile, behold, three rulers—
when they arrived, they beheld, squalid beyond belief,
the man’s face and his body, wasted thin by grim decay—
all let their tears fall, and gave forth a groan;
and they tear the garments from their shoulders and swiftly befoul
their hair, dressed in the customary fashion, with filthy dust.
Then for seven days and nights they kept silence, grieving over
the cruel sufferings and the misfortune of their innocent friend.
But none of them could come any nearer to him
or walk beside him; such a breath from his dark throat
pouring forth, carried itself up to the vaults above.
But those who ought to have come to wretched Job's help,
and to comfort the destitute man, driven by so many bitter blows,
attempt to renew the unspeakable grief of the stricken man:
and with tongues armed with the gall of poison they double
his wounds, and drive clean through his breast with hidden shafts.
And (alas) they leave the blind barbs fixed fast in his veins.

div.note: "My bone hath cleaved to my skin, my flesh being consumed, and there are left only my lips about my teeth." Job 19. 20.
So he himself confesses: "My wife shuddered at my breath," Job 19. vers. 17.

lg.l: While they falsely accuse [him] of crimes, and [say] that, deserving [them],
punishments, had paid [them], they say; yet the noblest hero,
second in valour to none of the fathers of old,
with unconquered strength and mighty courage, endured their wrath,
as well as the arrogance of his companions and their harsh words.
But after he had overcome the empty wranglings of kings
and had borne the proud scorn of his wife, and
the loss of his children, his wealth, and his royal sceptres,
Satan, armed with furies and with black serpents,
he cast beneath his feet; and as rewards for the victor
the almighty Father gives three daughters of surpassing beauty,
whom many eager mothers throughout the neighbouring towns
longed for as daughters-in-law; seven sons he added to him,
and the sons of his sons, and those who shall be born from them.
He doubled the wealth that had been lost, the herds and the flocks,
the silver and the gold, and his years; nor does slow old age
weaken the powers of his mind, or alter its vigour,
and at last, laid to rest, he slept in untroubled peace.
So Christ, by the savage malice of wily Judas
stricken, was dragging out his life in darkness and grief;
Against him the sons of Abraham, thrown into confusion—at once all
Latium, in anxious [uproar], bands together in oath, and the young men rage,
savage; then the Latins, on a false charge of treason,
the innocent man, on an unspeakable accusation, because he taught the truth,
consigned to death. A thousand harsh toils—alas!—
and poverty, and hunger he bore, then the arrogant commands
of his Hebrew wife; not one of his companions dares approach Jesus;
all could bring themselves to leave him alone,
in his final death, and [him] sent into such great perils,
and while the master wrestles with harsh death,
while death devours the mangled corpse, blood and all, and while
his breath makes his sides heave with his final gasps,
and his limbs hung from the wood, pale with gore:
his enemies mock him, and fling ungodly taunts,
nor does anyone pity at all Christ's unjust death.
He, however, bore the whole force of the savage enemy,
and the envy and hatred of men, and the mockery of his kinsmen,
with unconquered strength, and the din of raging Avernus
he set beneath his feet; nay, the thresholds of black Dis
he burst through, and the king who belches out empty flames
he seizes him and locks him in a knot, embracing and clinging fast as he throttles him,
until his eyes are forced from their sockets and his throat is drained dry of blood.
Then the almighty Father doubled his Son's honours
and marked him out with a radiant covering of light.
He himself, his head adorned with leaves of the trimmed olive,
holding the sceptre of the world, and bearing his shining wounds,
in a gleaming chariot of clouds ascends to the stars.
At once the high house is flung open, with its proud doors,
of the heaven-dwellers; Christ enters with many thousands,
bearing great trophies, and triumphing over the enemy and over death.

div.p: With Jacob and Joseph dead, Satan turns Pharaoh's mind against the Israelites, upon whom Pharaoh imposes heavy tasks; but God, taking pity on his people, sends Moses to the king with his commands, so that by performing various signs and miracles he may free the people of Jerusalem from slavery. At last, after Egypt has been afflicted by many plagues and the king has drowned in the sea while pursuing the Israelites, the Israelites cross safely. At Pluto's instigation, they fall into various sins and provoke God's wrath against themselves. The Law is promulgated; manna rains down; a cloud by day and fire by night point out the way through the wilderness, in which they wandered for forty years because of their sins. Three thousand people are slain for idolatry; the tabernacle is erected, and the high priest's garments are described. Korah and his companions murmur and conspire against Moses; fiery serpents are sent. Moses dies on Pisgah, and the people cross the Jordan under Joshua's leadership. The land of Canaan is described, where various wars take place between the people of Jerusalem and the inhabitants of the land. At last Joshua emerges victorious and subdues the Canaanites; after his death come the Judges, who deliver the people of Jerusalem when they are repeatedly oppressed by enemies through Pluto's envy. Gideon puts the enemies to flight by a stratagem. Jephthah, returning home victorious, sacrifices his daughter. The blessedness of the Church is described, and all these narratives are applied to Christ.

lg.l: After Joseph had departed from the world above,
King Pluto stirs up Pharaoh against the offspring of Abraham,
who wears out their backs with burdensome heaps of mire,
and ordered the newly born to be plunged into the river;
hoping thus that he could wipe out the whole nation.
But the father of the gods, pitying [their] unjust lot,
In a green bush belching out light and flames
he appears to Moses, whom, hiding behind the sedges,
the King's daughter found beside the river's banks,
enclosed in a little basket made of soft rushes or bark.
Thermuthis reared the boy in her father's hall.
But when his years had ripened into full growth, Moses,
having slain the Nile-born man, in the lonely mountains his life
passes, and feeds the flocks on the green grass.
Amram begot him, but Korah brought forth Amram,
and Korah had been begotten of the blood of Levi.
God bids this man, Moses, go as an envoy to the king’s lofty walls
and demand peace for the nation
of Abraham’s descendants, oppressed now for so many passing years,
that at last the wretched may be allowed to depart from the kingdom
of Egypt, and to reach the land so often promised.
Moses' pleas availed nothing; the King's violence
grows still greater, and Pluto closes [the King's] gentle ears.
Then the almighty Father, giving the reins to raging wrath,
— dreadful to tell — [made] the waters of the Nile turn black:
he made it so; the stream is turned into foul gore;
and in the palace the futile creatures sang their old lament,
then plagues of every kind make sport [of them]; out of the dust of the earth
creatures wondrous to behold are born in marvelous fashion;
at first without feet, but soon buzzing with wings,
they mingle together, and more and more take to the thin air,
until, like a rain-shower poured out from summer clouds,

div.note: Origen thinks it was a kind of covering formed from the bark of trees. Hom. 2. on Exodus.
Thus Josephus names her, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 5.

lg.l: burst forth, or like arrows from the twanging bowstring,
whenever the nimble Scots begin their first skirmishes.
A storm of flies on dark wings
a fiercer East Wind carried from the eastern waters.
They settle on the plants and defile everything with
their filthy touch; and all the year's hope, entrusted to the earth,
