perishes; the harvests could neither be sown nor rise up.
Then [the plague] gave over to death every kind of herd-beast, every kind of wild beast;
hence calves die everywhere in the lush grass,
and give back their sweet lives at the full mangers.
He sinks down on the grass, luckless and forgetful of his contests —
the horse that once won; he turns away from the springs, and with his hoof the ground
he strikes again and again; the bull, steaming beneath the hard ploughshare,
falls: and from his mouth he vomits blood mingled with foam;
and he raises his last groans; the ploughman goes off in sorrow,
unyoking the bullock that mourns his brother's death,
and he has left the plough standing fixed in the middle of the work.
With the flocks' bleating and frequent lowing, the rivers,
and the parched banks and the sloping hills resound;
and sheep and oxen are slaughtered en masse
in the stalls; the carcasses, fallen apart, lie foul with putrid gore.
Scant ashes, [scattered] with a throw; and of beasts and of men
[break out in] burning pustules, and a foul sweat spread over their stinking
followed upon the limbs; the sacred fire ate away their bodies.
The heavens thundered, and the sky flashes with fire upon fire.
Then bristling hail in abundance, rattling, leaps upon the roofs;
alas, poorly then does the vine-leaf shield the mellow grapes.
Nay more, a measureless column of waters comes down from the sky;
the blackest South Wind darkens sky and earth,
and with a huge downpour the glad crops and the oxen's labours
it washes away; the ditches fill, and the hollow rivers rise
with a roar; and the sea boils with its heaving channels.
And now clouds of locusts are massed together by the East Wind,
and darken the air with their wings — a marvel to behold;
they lay waste leaves and fruits, and the ripened grain,
nor, once the ears are devoured, does anyone set the sickle to them —
[no] farmer; the labours of men and of oxen perish.
Storm-clouds have wrapped the daylight round, and the dank night
has carried off the sky; see, all things bristle with thick darkness.
For three full days, rendered indistinct by blinding gloom,
Egypt lies shrouded, and for as many starless nights.
No one is able to tell day from night in the heavens;
and many portents besides of the disaster to come
strike terror with dreadful warning; then the winged Spirit
cut down with the sword all the firstborn of Egypt.
But the unhappy king, terrified by these prodigies — behold,
he gives way under vast grief; the halls ring again
with dreadful wailing; and the hearts of the people are shaken,
stunned by such great calamities and the ruin of their country.
And much he blames himself, that he did not of his own accord send away
the sons of Abraham. King Pharaoh himself orders them all, with utmost haste—
mothers and men—to depart from the Pharian land.
The people are gathered together for exile, a pitiable throng;
from every side they came together, ready in spirit and in means
for whatever lands Moses might wish to lead them into.
To cut short delay, the tyrant’s cruel hatred
and keen fear drive them all; they snatch things up and rush;
you would see them migrating and rushing out of the whole city;
And just as ants a huge heap of grain,
when they plunder it, mindful of winter, and lay it up under their roof:
the black column moves across the plains, and their plunder through the grass
they carry along a narrow track: some shove the big grains,
straining at them with their shoulders; some marshal the ranks,
and chide every delay: the whole path seethes with the work.
And now, as help for the journey, treasures from the proud enemy
they seize, an untold weight of silver and of gold.
But when they had reached the shore of the Red Sea,
the King repented that he had thus let go unpunished
the offspring of Abraham, and now resolved to exact punishment;
Therefore he orders his companions to take up arms,
so that they may pursue the fugitives with sword and flame; and he himself
calls for horses and arms together, and proudly at a bound
springs into the chariot and plies the reins with his hands.
He shakes his weapons in his hand, and burns hot with sudden hope.
Moses saw them coming from the opposite shore;
the sons of Abraham saw them; and through their inmost bones there ran a cold
trembling.
But when the Lawgiver’s staff struck the liquid plains,
the waves begin to part far and wide,
and Nereus [draws] back, and, sucking in again [the waters] rolled back by his surge,

div.note: Moses stands on the shore, facing the enemy.

lg.l: [The sea] flees the rocks, and leaves the shore behind as the shallows slip away,
where the people might set their steps; and lo, suddenly
the wave, reared up into the likeness of a mountain, towers above,
and took into its vast fold both the people and their leaders,
and set them all ashore on the edge of the further bank;
So us, through the surges of the world, and through the flood of [his] blood,
Jesus sets ashore upon the bank of [our] heavenly homeland.
And now they were all following, with steps on treacherous ground,
the chiefs of Egypt, the king himself, and all the young men:
when suddenly the sea, rushing down with a dreadful roar,
burst upon the land, and flung its wave over the crags,
foaming, and with its swell drenched the furthest sand;
and swept up in its swift surge both chariots and men;
here and there [men] appear swimming in the vast whirlpool,
men’s weapons and cloaks, and Egyptian treasure, [appear] amid the waves.
So at last had escaped all the disasters of Egypt
the offspring of Abraham; and all of them, [away] from the Red shore,
went on keeping even measure, and sang of Jehovah,
with a cloud showing the way by day, and a torch by night.
But although the king of Erebus now occupies the whole world by force
and extends the dominion of the city of Babylon everywhere,
yet, implacable, with ceaseless wrath
he pursues Jerusalem as she wanders among inhospitable rocks.
How often he stirs up the wrath of heaven against the wretched,
while he urges [them] to violate the sacred laws of the Thunderer;
and to rise in unjust frenzy against King Moses?
They had come to the pool which is now called bitter,
For its unmistakable taste furnished proof and twisted the grim faces
of those who tried it with a bitter sensation.
They cry out against Moses; he quickly [tore] a branch from a tree
a green branch, with which he made the waters sweet;
Thus Christ, with true sweetness, moved the souls corrupted by the bitter sin
of the fatal tree.
Then raging hunger drove the sons of Abraham to rise
against Moses once again; he invoked Jehovah in prayer.
At once manna—airy, heavenly gifts—
you pour down from above, O greatest ruler of the gods;
and you send a cloud of birds, and the sounding throng
of the winged host, which darken the sky with their feathers.
Not otherwise did Christ send down from heaven on high
to us the purest honey of the divine word.
Again, while they thirst, they hurl abuse at Moses.
But he draws glassy waters out of the rocks,
and with his rod he was able to furnish fresh streams.
Not otherwise, when it pierced Christ's side and laid it open —
the lance — a stream of sweet water flowed from his breast,
and red drops run down over his whole body.
And now they were drawing near to Sinai, when the Amalekites
sweep their whole battle line against Judah and station it upon the rampart.
That line Moses routed by his prayers, and he takes the spoil,
while he stretches both his palms to the stars of heaven;
so Christ by his death scattered the throngs of hell,
stretching out his two arms upon the tree he had triumphed over.
While Moses ascended the mountain, everything seemed to collapse
amid terrifying thunder; the sky flashes again and again with fire,
and lofty Sinai nods, its summit shaken.
The trumpets sounded; black smoke rises into the air,
the earth trembles, the wild beasts have fled, and mortal hearts
throughout the nations fear has struck down, abased; then suddenly,
while the crowds quake, dreadful decrees through the air
rush down from the mountain with a roar, and fill the assembled ranks.
But while the son of Amram lingers with Jehovah on the mountain,
believing that he had perished, caught up by whirlwind and fire,
the sons of Isaac wished to cast a calf out of gold.
This Satan, the inciter to crimes, urged upon Aaron.
And now a festal day is celebrated, and, joyful, over the grass
they lay their bodies down beneath the branches of a tall tree;
and they load the tables with the feast, and set out the cups.
After hunger was banished by the banquet, and the tables cleared away,
they rise up, and mingled together they roar about the altars —
mothers and men, boys and unwedded girls
their temples wreathed with flowers and with twisted boughs,
and calling upon the ill-starred image of a bullock in their vows;
they perform ungainly dance-steps, and chant songs.
Meanwhile, the king of almighty Olympus addresses the son of Amram,
while he watches the maddened people from a tawny cloud,
commanding him to exact in blood the punishment they deserve
from the deranged people; he swiftly snatched his lightning-like sword
from its sheath and, in a frenzy, charged
Into the midst of the assembly; to him brothers of the blood of Levi
join themselves as allies; and a most wretched slaughter arises.
He lays three thousand men low on the ground, and shatters the calf,
that unspeakable memorial of the crime, and burned [it] with fire.
After this the son of Amram, as he had been commanded, the movable temple
raised up, rich in gifts and in the divine presence of Jehovah.
They gave gifts heavy with gold, and talents of silver,
the people gave Moses a vast quantity of bronze and hyacinth-blue garments;
gems, and fine linen, and wool, and sweet-smelling woods
and fleeces they bring, dyed with Assyrian dye;
and the juice of ambrosia; from goats, others shear
their beards and hoary chins, and their shaggy hair,
for use in the sacred rites and for coverings of the holy tent.
But after Moses had raised up the sanctuary of Jehovah,
the high Priest enters the holy inner chambers;
and, as commanded, he slaughtered fat beasts at the altars.
Before Jehovah, in a pure robe, amid the heavenly beings
he stood, and stretched both palms up to heaven;
a custom which Moses commands to be observed every year.
Upon him a fine linen robe flowed down to the very ankles;

div.note: The Israelites remained two years beside Mount Sinai and the neighbouring places; in which time Moses built the Tabernacle and published the Laws. In Kadesh-Barnea they stayed nineteen years; another nineteen years they wore away, now advancing, now falling back, now straying; until through forty-two encampments or stations they came, after forty years, to the eastern bank of Jordan. See Genebrard. Chron. lib. I.
I mean the Cherubim.

lg.l: Over this, moreover, was a cloak interwoven with fine linen,
hanging down from the shoulders, and softly blushing with hyacinth-purple.
[with] golden bells which would give out a hoarse ringing,
and pomegranates hung from the woven border.
Then he wore an embroidered mantle or robe,
which covering, woven round about with fine linen and gold,
shone from afar. Resplendent with gems and gold,
the breastplate in which he is clad bears the twelve names
of the patriarchs descended from Sarah; and above, on his high shoulders, two
gems shine out, inscribed with the names of kings.
He wears a sash of fine linen, and the huge weight of a belt
which the hand of craftsmen has interwoven with much gold.
For his head he has a covering, namely a gleaming white turban;
a linen headband is fastened beneath with a purple ribbon,
and a golden plate shone upon his consecrated brow,
bearing the name of holy Jehovah—a name that no one
can utter aloud — engraved, the work of the divinely gifted Aholiab;
and the tunics have sleeves, and the mitres have ribbons.
Not otherwise our Christ, a Priest without end,
having entered the inmost places of heaven, vows and prayers

div.note: The peplus, on Donatus' testimony, belonged to the rites of worship among the heathen also; and both men and women had their peploi. So Priam, Iliad 24. The peplus was also a garment embroidered with the needle.

The linen tunic was close-fitting, with tight sleeves; but the hyacinth-blue one had sleeves of the same colour sewn on at the sides. The little cap is bound at the back of the head with a fillet, so that it may not easily slip off the head. Jerome, Epist. 8.

lg.l: he pours them forth continually, and no sacrifice is more pleasing than they.
A snow-white robe of virtues veiled Christ.
When he poured forth his crimson life from his whole body,
he shone richly with dark red and purple.
He stood before the altars, wrapped in a purple robe.
But now he shines beneath a gilded covering of light,
beaming far with the flash of gems; and his own
he bears on his shoulders, cherishes in his bosom, and adorns with a crown
everlasting, such as upon its lofty head is worn by
the very power of priests, of kings, and of prophets.
The pomegranates mark out the nations and the peoples streaming
to Christ past counting; and the little bells [mark] the voice
clear-ringing of heavenly speech, sounding everywhere.
And as the stitched belt is fastened beneath the priest’s belly,
and a clasp bites where his sides meet;
signifying that the high priest must be chaste in every respect,
lest the dreadful lust of Venus
steal through his senses, or stir up fire in his bones —
harsh love — while he kindles the altars with chaste torches:
Thus Christ could succumb to no sin.
But his mind was holy, and in his beautiful body
a pure, heavenly spirit shone; therefore
he fastened golden girdles beneath his gleaming breast.
O Christ, God, Prophet, and King, and great Priest:
protect your servants, O King; glide into their hearts, O Prophet;
pour out prayers for me from your divine mouth, O Priest;
and pay vows to the Father, and the gifts of your merits
bring, you who in a heavenly robe of state and comely girding

div.note: Revel. 1. 13.

lg.l: Wholly you blaze forth, whose priestly fillet gleams with snowy light.
Purify me, and cover me with the covering of [your] long robe;
and set me upon your shoulders; me, with your whole heart,
receive; grant that I pass a chaste life without stain.
Hang the nations from the hem of your tunic, and let them bear
the seeds of righteousness, and be gathered together into one heaven:
that they may worship you with holy meal and a full cup.
And stir up ringings, and shake the cymbals around the tunic;
Cause the sounds of the Word and the clattering bronze instruments to follow.
Meanwhile Moses, following the commands of Jehovah,
sent out scouts, who were to survey the coasts of the land
of promise, and bring back to their comrades an exact report;
what places these were, what men held them, where the nation's walls stood.
But they report that there are hard battles with the people;
that the men are fierce, that there roam upon the high mountains
unspeakable Cyclopes; that throughout these shores dwell men
as glut themselves on human gore and on bloody feasts.
At these words, they all raised groans and prolonged
weeping in vain, and there ran across the lips a shifting
and troubled murmur of Abraham's sons; soon there arose a savage
a riot, and the base crowd rages in its passions;
as when a wave has begun to whiten in the midst of the sea

div.note: Here, with Cornutus and others, I take acerra not to mean a censer but a cup in which wine was offered. By the terms far and acerra, therefore, I understand bread and wine in the Eucharist.

lg.l: farther on, and draws a swelling curve from the deep; and once rolled onward
toward land, it roars mightily through the rocks; no smaller than the very
mountain, it crashes down; but from below the wave seethes up
with its eddies, and flings the black sand high aloft.
Korah with his companions threatens death and instant
destruction upon Moses and upon his brother: but the earth, splitting open,
sucks [them] down to the seats below, and into a vast pit
many of the conspirators, and many [more] were burned up by
the bristling battle line of fire across the broad fields.
And because so often they scorned the holy oracles,
the sons of Abraham were compelled to go through all their misfortunes again,
the wretched men, among the crags; and to turn back once more
through the deserts of the Arabs, and to expose their lives to dangers.
As the months rolled on, thirty-eight great cycles
they completed in wandering over inhospitable rocks,
retracing every tangled path, before the blessed
land's borders they entered, and the fields appointed by fate.
But while the people wander through the parched fields,
and through the Arabs’ settlements, sparsely dotted with dwellings,
they press toward the borders of Canaan, where the cool Jordan, through fields
rich in men, flows in a gentle course;
(I shudder as I tell it) serpents in enormous coils,
past counting, leap out onto the dry ground from the deepest thickets
and from the earth's blind hiding-places: and these, in a long train,
gliding through the grass, make for the people's tents.
Dark-blue markings [ran along] their backs, and a gleam mottled with gold
set their scaly hide ablaze: as, among the clouds, the rainbow
draws a thousand shifting colours when the sun faces it;
And their blazing eyes suffused with blood and fire,
they licked their hissing mouths with flickering tongues:
As many as the waves that roll on the Libyan marble sea
where fierce Orion sinks beneath the wintry waters;
or when the thick ears of corn are scorched beneath the new sun,
whether on the plain of Hermus, or in Lycia's yellowing fields —
[so many] breathe a viperous breath and spread poison
through the veins; the accursed fire was devouring the afflicted limbs.
So many perish by a cruel death, and many
pray for death; it wearies them to gaze upon the vault of heaven.
At once Moses fixes upon an upraised spear,
in the midst of the assembly, a serpent stiff-wrought of bronze,
which, set facing the sun, cast forth a brazen light;
the bronze snake bristles with its markings, spews out flames,
and at the sight of it every plague flees from the body,
and every serpent glides away in winding coil
into the earth's crooked hiding-places, while the people applaud.
Thus Satan once, in the glades of Paradise, a serpent's form
assumed, and infected the first parents with his plague,
coiling his slippery back with breast reared high;
he indeed is able to turn himself into every shape:
into fire, and a horrible wild beast, and a flowing stream:
he becomes a wolf, and of a sudden a bristling boar, and a black tigress,
and a scaly dragon, and a lioness with tawny neck.
He, then, not unmindful of his own art, into a serpent
is turned, and lays aside his own face and his dress;
and, mottled with great markings over his long belly,
he assails the mother, his three-forked tongues flickering from his mouth;
Probing the senses, he drives black venom into the limbs
with hidden bites; and leaves the unseen stings behind,
fixed in the veins; and, having slipped deep into the vitals,
the serpent's maddening evil roams through the whole
human race, and feeds upon its wretched limbs.
But Christ, the bronze serpent suspended from a lofty pole,
casts a terrifying light beneath the clouds;
the hosts of serpents, terrified throughout every land,
scatter, and with trembling step make their way down to Tartarus.
The sight of him was the cure for our madness,
and was an aid than which none was more immediately effective
to take the deadly contagion away from our limbs.
After—through flames and a thousand pursuing weapons,
through seas, through diverse lands and inhospitable rocks—
he had snatched away his companions and recovered them from the enemy’s midst—
Moses, who had at last grasped the borders of fleeing Judaea,
is raised aloft onto Pisgah; from there,
standing far off upon the mountain’s lofty summit, he gazes in wonder at

div.note: Spirits have, properly speaking, neither garment nor face. These things are nevertheless said of them because they often appear in human form and in clothing.

lg.l: the plains and the valleys, the cities and the walls of the land;
so at last he peacefully passed away from the world above.
The almighty Father conceals him in a secret place,
so that no one may see or touch him.
Then Joshua, mighty in arms and commander in war, settles
the people, after long wanderings and through so many perils,
in the dwellings they had longed for. Then Jordan, brimming over, at its topmost
banks foamed; so great a rainstorm had burst from the clouds,
and cold water, melted from the snow-white mountains,
melted, filled far and wide the ditches and the streams.
Here, with twin golden horns and a bull-like face,
he flows through Palestine’s fields with glassy waves—
Jordan, than which no other river, through the rich tilled land,
pours more violently into the purple sea.
And now the priests and the people draw near to the river.
And as soon as they had touched the roaring waters with their feet,
the waves part, and the river, terrified, flows back,
where the people might set their steps in safety; just as once
the wave stood round about, arched into the shape of a mountain,
while Moses, through the midst of the sea and the swelling waves,
made his way and did not wet his swift soles in the sea.
So now the river flees backward away from the sulphurous waves
to its head; a sheer mountain of water rises up in a heaped mass,
leaving the fish stranded and bare, like shipwrecked bodies,

div.note: I mean Lake Asphaltites.

lg.l: in the parched mud: with steps not at all timid the hero,
Joshua brings safely across the river both mothers and men,
and sets them down on a grassy mound and on the high bank,
and soon with great force he overthrows the neighbouring cities.
This is that famous [land], renowned on many shores,
the land of Palestine, promised to the descendants of Abraham;
an ancient land, mighty in arms and in the richness of its soil;
No bulls breathing fire from their nostrils
have ploughed these lands for the sowing of a monstrous serpent’s teeth;
nor has a crop of men bristled with helmets and thick-set spears.
But teeming crops and the gifts of bounteous Bacchus
have filled [it]; olives and glad herds possess [it].
Here clear springs, and meadows for ever green,
are at hand, and quivering brooks that lap the grass.
Sweet honey flows; here milk abounds.
The more the milking-pail shall foam from the drained udder,
the more richly will the streams run from the pressed teats.
Why should I recount to you balsam oozing from fragrant wood,
and the berries of the ever-leafy acanthus?
Or so many outstanding cities, and harbours and lakes,
and rivers gliding beneath ancient walls;
and the Sidonian sea, hissing as its waves flow back;
and the hard veins of iron, and the mines of copper?
Here the water does not bear iron-shod wheels upon its back,
[water] which is now host to broad wagons and before to ships;
Here bronze vessels do not burst apart, nor do garments stiffen
once put on: nor do they hew the liquid wine with axes:
nor has a bristling icicle hardened upon unkempt beards.
Nor, on the other hand, does Sirius here scorch the fields to barrenness,
nor does the grass thirst, dying from the fault of the burning air.
Liber does not begrudge the hills their vine-leaf shade,
nor does a sickly crop ever deny the reapers their food.
But with gentle gusts, and with the warm breezes of the West Wind,
the blessed indulgence of heaven renders this land [a place]
renders [it a land] where the vine-shoot has no fear of the rising south winds,
or of the rain driven from the sky by the great north winds;
nor does he rail at a late summer, and the loitering west winds —
the countryman — nor does he complain of the Cauri that breathe out cold,
for there the Sun with his horses comes upon winter more slowly,
and swiftly drives it beneath the earth, opening
the gates of heaven with summer light, and unbarring the year with horns
of gold, and adorning the meadows with colours.
But here raging tigers are present; and the savage [brood] of lions

div.note: For the healthfulness of its air, the mildness of its sky, and the richness of its soil, this land is celebrated above all other regions of the world by writers sacred as well as profane. See Deut. 8. Plin. Joseph, &c.

Virgil said "gate" in the singular—as in "the gate of heaven thunders"—meaning the air; I say "gates" on account of the three regions of the air, which are freed from clouds and darkness by summer heat and light.

"The white Bull with gilded horns opens the year," says Virgil. I name the Sun in Taurus, and assign him horns on account of his rays: both because he was worshipped in the form of a ram under the name of Jupiter Ammon, on the testimony of Macrob. Sat. lib. I. cap. 21, and because the Sun is the same as Bacchus, who was painted with horns.

lg.l: Nay more, aconite seeds deceive the wretched who gather them;
and the wolf scouts for an ambush around the sheepfolds,
and prowls by night about the flocks: here too many
deaths and havoc misshapen she-bears have dealt.
This [land] a fierce race of men—Gideon and valiant Samson,
and Jephthah, inured to hardship, and Shamgar, and Ehud—
brought forth; this [land] brought forth King David and the thunderbolts of war—
the Maccabees, that is; Solomon, ruling in peace
a people accustomed to war; and you, O greatest Christ,
who often, victorious on the farthest shores of the earth,
keep the unwarlike Turks away from our citadels.
Hail, great mother of crops, land of Canaan,
great in men, once most dear to heaven, but now,
shameless one, you pay the deserved penalty for treachery against the Lord,
mocked, and without honour you lie, struck down in ruin.
But the lord of Dis has raised his head out of black Orcus.
the sons of Abraham building citadels, and settling in the land
of promise, seeing [this], the wicked one roars with rabid wrath:
and that they have found a way through the midst of the battle-lines, and through the midst of the waves,
this he resents as an outrage, and all
the Furies he calls out of Orcus, and arms them with poisons.
Discord goes with [them] as companion, exulting in her twice-rent robe,
whom Bellona follows with kindred scourge;
and against the people of Palestine she hurls herself on Stygian wings,
raging with anger, filling the cities with loud cries.
Rolling a bloodshot gaze, her trembling cheeks suffused with blotches,
flushing red with her heart aflame.
But before these, like the leader of the column, goes black
Envy's plague, wasted away with the utmost emaciation,
feeding madly on her own entrails and her own blood;
and whose old age, overcome by decay and drained of truth, [is]
pale, most foul with the discharge of her belly; she defiles
everything with her unclean touch; beneath her moist
palate her tongue lies black, while he-goats look askance;
she advances, scattering her venom through the towns of Canaan,
and she bids the young men be armed and move out from the gates,
urges the leaders to arms and to destroy with the sword the nation
that has been exiled from its homeland for so many passing years.
And to these Fear, coming on with trembling steps, adds
herself as companion — she from whose whole body sweat has poured,
and whose hair has stood on end, and whose voice has stuck in her throat.
Rumour, an evil swift of foot, and on nimble wings
flying ahead, had gone before the black column of her companions,
terrible; sweeping in her flight at once the fields, at once the seas,
she stirs the neighbouring cities to war with her reports;
[telling] that mobs of robbers, used to living by plunder,
deserters from Egypt, have now beside a fair river
settled there, and whispering this everywhere from mouth to mouth:
as the cold South wind at times murmurs through the woods,
as the troubled sea hisses with its ebbing waves.
Immediately the kings throughout the neighboring towns convene a council
and they were deliberating over the kingdom’s uncertain affairs.
exchanging many thoughts among themselves in varied conversation:
what forces, for so great a war, against such great hosts
would suffice, who [should be] the leaders, which should follow each [of them],
the battle-lines filling the plains, who should guard the walls,
and who should make fast the city's approaches, and take up the towers.
And while the elders were seeking counsel among themselves
as to what they should do, through the Canaanite fields with a great uproar
behold, a messenger comes rushing and fills the cities with panic:
that the Hebrews, drawn up in battle line, were coming down from the River Jordan,
and that armed cavalry were descending across all the plains.
At once their spirits were troubled and the people’s hearts shaken,
and their wrath was roused by no gentle goads.
In alarm they demand weapons in hand; the young men roar for arms;
the neighbouring kings urge one another to arms,
to guard the fatherland, to drive the enemy from their borders;
they exchange pledges of loyalty and unite their allied forces,
and far and wide they empty whole fields of their tillers.
One group prepares to march on foot across the plains; another, towering on tall
horses, storms along dust-covered; all call for arms.
Part burnish smooth shields and gleaming spear-points
with rich fat, and grind their axes on the whetstone.
And now the war-trumpets sound; the watchword goes out as the signal for war.
Here one man, in alarm, takes a helmet from the house; another the snorting
horses drives beneath the yoke; his shield and a breastplate triple-woven with gold
he puts on, and girds himself with his trusty sword.
They drew up the battle-lines; the column of horsemen had gone before;
a storm-cloud of foot follows; and, shield-bearing, over all
the plains the columns are packed close; with sword-points there bristles
an iron harvest, [its points] drawn, and smooth bronze arms gleam,
struck by the sun, and they hurl their light up beneath the clouds:
As many thousands of birds as hide themselves in the woods
when evening, or a wintry rainstorm, drives [them] down from the mountains.
Nor any less meanwhile does the fierce leader, in his fathers' arms,
the son of Nun, whet [his] war-spirit, and rouse himself with wrath,
and, greedy for the fight, he had cased his calves in bronze
on this side and on that, and he hates delay, and brandishes his spear.
And now the leaders of Canaan, and the whole army of foot,
draw on; the horsemen, bristling with bronze, come near,
drawn up in ordered squadrons; throughout the whole air roars
the prancing steed, and fights against the tightened reins,
turned this way and that; then far and wide with spears the iron
field bristles, and the plains blaze with arms held high.
And on the other side too the son of Nun, and the offspring of Jacob,

div.note: Virgil testifies everywhere that arms of bronze were once chiefly in use. So Lucretius, bk. 5: "and the use of bronze was known before that of iron." They worked in bronze too: "with bronze they worked, and black iron there was none," says Hesiod — unless we prefer that the word chalkos should signify iron as well.

lg.l: Facing [one another] they come into view on the field, and their spears, with drawn-back
right hands, they level far out, and they brandish their darts,
and the men's advance and the horses' din blaze up;
and now each side, having advanced within a spear's cast,
had halted; suddenly they break out in a shout, and their snorting
horses they urge on; at once they pour weapons from every side,
thick after the manner of snow, and the sky is overspread with shadow:
as great as the rainstorm that comes from the west with the rain-bringing Kids
lashes the ground, while storm clouds laden with so much hail
plunge down into the shallows, when Jupiter, bristling with south winds,
hurls the watery tempest, and bursts the hollow clouds in the sky.
At once the Canaanite and valiant Judah, their spears opposed,
braced against each other, charge with their spears and are the first to collide
with a huge crash, and the shattered chests of the galloping steeds
they burst, chest against chest; harsh battle rises up.
And just as, in the great upper air, winds at strife
stir up their battles with matched spirit and matched strength,
neither do they themselves yield to one another, nor do the clouds or the sea;

div.note: Not every use of horses was forbidden to the Hebrews, as some would have it, but excessive luxury, in horses as much as in wives, in gold and silver, and the rest: that is, lest they should place their trust in a multitude of horses, as the nations do, having forsaken the true God; lest they should have commerce with the Egyptians, among whom the finest horses were; lest they should grow proud at the number of their horses.

lg.l: Long the battle hung in doubt; standing firm, [the men] strained against all things.
Not otherwise do the Canaanite lines and the lines of Jacob
clash together: foot clings to foot, and man presses close on man.
Then indeed rise the groans of the dying, while in the deep blood
weapons and bodies and, intermingled amid the slaughter of men,
half-dead horses roll about; everywhere black gore
is poured out, and the field is filled with a dreadful roar.
Now grim Mars was making the mourning equal, and their mutual
deaths; alike they fell, and alike they charged on,
victors and vanquished; and flight was known neither to these nor to those.
But amid the slaughter and the falling ranks the captain
Joshua is borne along on his horse, and spurs on the squadrons with his shouts;
now with entreaty, now with bitter words he kindles their courage,
calling each man by name, and restores to the battle those who had been driven back.
Then wrath swells all the more in their discordant hearts,
and the sons of Abraham, rallied once more, mass together at the same place,
Each of the men strives for himself with all the force at his command.
No delay, no rest: in a vast struggle they press on;
and, rushing swiftly forward after hurling their spears from afar,
they plunge into battle with shields and ringing bronze.
The earth gives a groan; then the repeated sword-strokes
they redouble, and the mighty crash of arms fills the sky.
At once the battle line is thrown into confusion, and the tyrants
throw away their shields; in panic flight they turn their backs across the fields.
And the leaders scattered, and the companies left desolate,
make for safety, and turning away drive their horses toward the walls.
The sons of Abraham, as they press on and bring death, no one
has strength to withstand with weapons, or to stand against;
but they carry back slack bows on drooping shoulders.
and the hoofs of the beasts pound the dusty plain in their gallop.
There rolls toward the walls, murky with black gloom,
dust; and from the watchtowers the mothers, beating their breasts,
raise a womanly outcry to the stars of heaven.
Meanwhile the sky begins to churn with a mighty rumbling;
into turmoil; there follows a storm-cloud mingled with hail,
the hail crackles as it bounds across the fields, and with its massive weight
lays the young men low on the ground while they turn their backs across the fields.
The kings, in trembling dread, reach the same cave;
come down; fires flashed, and the sky [was] witness
of divine wrath against the Canaanites; Joshua, [son] of Nun,
meanwhile the victor rages furiously over the whole field,
once his blade has grown warm; indeed, like a black whirlwind he
rages, dealing out death across all the fields.
He tracks the trembling kings through the scattered columns:
these approaches, and now these approaches, and he ranges over the whole
circuit on every side, and tireless brandishes his unerring spear.
On one side the Sun looks on, on the other the maiden daughter of Latona;
nor does the departing Sun double the lengthening shadows,
nor can the evening star come forth while Olympus is unwilling.
Until those whom the cave keeps shut in blind hiding-places
the son of Nun drags out into the midst, who, with his foot on their necks
firmly planted, hangs the kings from a lofty pole.
Straightway a most dreadful message fills the neighbouring cities,
and Rumour brings tremendous turmoil to the people:
that the battle-lines of so many kings are wiped out, that the phalanxes have fallen
the hope of the fatherland, and that the kings have been cut off by an undeserved death;
that the enemy press on in fury, and, with the war going their way,
have seized everything, that terror is now borne to the walls.
The mothers redouble their vows in fear, and nearer to the danger
fear advances, and now the image of War looms larger.
At once, amid fearful tumult, the neighbouring nations banded together,
and they muster legions from every side:
those who fell the lofty ridges of Lebanon, who [hold] the dewy, brook-watered
farmlands of Palestine, and those whom tilled Samaria feeds;
who work Galilee's high hills with the ploughshare;
and those who drink the lake of Merom, and those who beside the great sea
dwell close at hand, and those whom the Jordan, straying in its windings,
washes; and those whom Tiberias waters with its glassy waves—
Tiberias — from every side they run together, weapons snatched up,
untamed farmers, and they bristle with drawn sword-points.
Four and twenty are at hand in flashing arms,
neighbouring kings, whom a vast throng follows.
Others bridle chariots, or with a leap hurl themselves

div.note: "The kings who dwell about Lebanon, &c., and as many of the Canaanites as till the plains, with the Palestinians called in to help, &c." Joseph. antiq. lib. 5. cap. 1.

lg.l: They spring up onto their horses, and blaze with drawn swords.
Nor would anyone [think] that bronze-clad battle lines, out of so great a host,
would think [were] being mingled, but rather that from the deep flood an airy
cloud of hoarse-voiced birds was being driven toward the shores.
Who has power to take in the exact number in verse?
Whoever wishes to know it might as well wish to learn, concerning the Libyan sea,
how many grains of sand are tossed by the West Wind;
or, when the east wind falls more violently upon ships,
know how many Ionian waves come to shore.
And now the whole army was moving over the open plains,
rich in horses, rich in embroidered raiment and in gold,
shields ring, and the earth, startled, quakes at the beat of feet,
but the son of Nun, [gazing] on the plains smoking with dust,
looked out far off, and saw the Canaanite columns,
and he heard the approach of footsteps and the snorting of horses:
all were struck dumb, and a chill shudder ran deep through
their bones, when the sons of Abraham saw a cloud of black dust gathering
and darkness rising over the plains.
With such words the Almighty addresses Joshua:
Do not falter, Leader, in defending my people:
nor [fear] to arm your hands against so many thousands.
Why do you hesitate? now is the time to call for horses, now for chariots;
Do not trust to your feet; with the sword a path must be broken through your foes,
where that densest mass of men presses on.
No divine powers press upon you; you are pressed by a mortal foe—
mortal; you too have both spirits and hands
unprotected; why, inglorious, at the very threshold,
do you give way? why does trembling seize your limbs before the trumpet!
Tomorrow's light — if you do not judge my words idle —
shall behold vast heaps of slaughtered Philistines:
Rise now and, as Dawn comes, be the first to order your comrades to be summoned
to arms; and take the shield left to you by
unconquered Moses, who also edged its rim with gold.
Remember, once the hams of the four-footed beasts are cut, the reins,
and the light chariots, to burn with crackling flames:
Break off every delay, and seize the camp in its confusion.
When he had spoken these words, he mingled himself with a dark cloud.
The leader marvels, yet at the omen he lifts his spirits.
And he, after he had prayed, gazing up at the vaults above,
first proclaims to his comrades that they are to follow the standards
and set their hearts on arms, and make themselves ready for the fight.
Forth comes the legion of Abraham's sons, and in serried
columns they pour from the crowded camp; their brazen arms far off
rang out horribly, on the helmet-peak the crests quiver
blood-red, and the whole sky stands thick with dust.
The captains dart to and fro, resplendent in gold and purple:
and they kindle their comrades' spirits for the battle; at last
the son of Nun, whirling his javelin, sends it flying into the air
as the opening of the fight, and towering he bears himself onto the field.
His comrades take it up with a shout, and follow with a roar
dreadful to hear; with great spirit and strength both
the battle lines clash: across the whole sky sweeps a turbulent
A storm of missiles, and an iron rain, comes rushing down.
They hurl their weapons by hand: just as, beneath dark clouds,
the Strymonian cranes give their signals, and swim across the upper air
with a din, and flee the south winds with a cry that speeds them on.
The hoarse war-horns sound, a mournful cry goes up to heaven
from the young men at war, and from those falling under harsh war,
The Leader himself charges into their midst, and, with the war-god favouring him,
terrible, a savage slaughter without distinction
he stirs up, and flings loose every rein of his wrath;
mowing down with the sword whatever is nearest, and through the broad column
blazing he cuts a path with the steel; then far and wide, with spilled
blood the ground runs wet, and the air hisses with spear-shafts:
just as when flame falls upon a cornfield while the south winds rage,
or a headlong torrent, swollen by a mountain flood,
lays the fields flat, lays flat the glad crops and the oxen's labours,
and drags the woods down headlong.
But such might, and the divine powers set against them, to bear
since the enemy cannot, [they begin] little by little to withdraw from the fight,
and tremble with fear; all put their trust in fleeing feet,
their weapons cast aside. The fiery Leader presses on:
sweeping across the field he gives many brave bodies of men to death;
He sends many men rolling half-dead, or with his chariot the ranks
he tramples down, or hurls the spears he has snatched up at those who flee:
just as when recently, beside the streams of the chill Rhine,
the Goths' war-god clashed upon his shield, and the raging
horses, rousing war, he loosed: they, over the open plain
They outstrip the South Winds and the West Wind; roused by the pounding, there groans
of feet, the earth groans; and all around, the faces of black Dread
and Wrath and Ambush, the Leader's retinue, are driven along.
So Joshua, eager amid the thick of battle, drives his horses
smoking with sweat, he urges them on (a pitiful sight), exulting over the slain
exulting over kings; the swift hoof scatters drops
of blood, and the gore is trodden, mingled with sand.
So, after he had laid low the enemy battle-lines in war,
and had made himself master of the lands and sceptres of so many tyrants
as victor, then he divides the spoil among all his companions;
apportioning it in equitable shares or assigning it by lot;
Just so Christ, through a thousand missiles flying in pursuit,
led us in our wretchedness to the waters of the river of baptism.
And he sets us all down unharmed beyond the stream, on the high
banks of the Promised Land, where cool Tempe
and icy springs, and soft meadows grow green.
Here on the sunny hillsides the grape takes on its colour;
and here the bees are sated with thyme, and the she-goats with foliage,
and the cows, fed on clover, swell their udders;
Junipers too stand there, and shaggy chestnut trees;
everywhere the fruits lie strewn, each beneath its own tree.

div.note: Jesus: that is, Joshua.

By these tropes and figurative expressions I describe the Church and spiritual graces, a mode once familiar to the holy Prophets: "The mountains," Isaiah says, "will sing; the trees will clap; in place of the wild nard a fir will rise, and in place of the nettle a myrtle will grow," ch. 55.

lg.l: How rich in snow-white flocks, how abundant in milk
is this land! How the well-fed bullocks frolic across the meadows!
How the crops here run riot in the fat fields?
The ewe-lambs stray untroubled on the high mountains.
Here the herds never fear great lions,
Nor does the scaly serpent drag enormous coils over the ground, nor with so vast
a sweep coil itself into a spiral.
The wolf is no bane to the stalls, nor shades to the crops,
nor winds to the trees, nor hail to the vines; but here
the grim lioness flees the wolf, and the wolf himself the she-goat.
Nay more, the timid fallow deer and the fleet-running stags,
here they roam both among the dogs and about the houses.
The serpent too has perished, and so has the treacherous poisonous plant.
Here too honey flows, and the rough bramble bears amomum;
the oaks bear golden apples, grapes stand on the briars,
the tamarisks sweat rich amber from their bark.
Here grim winter does not rage, nor with cold does it split
the rocks, nor here are the courses of the waters bridled by ice;
but there is radiant spring, and thickets rustling in the woods,
and fields for ever fragrant with sweet herbs;
and rivers run down between green valleys,
and the thickets always ring with tuneful birds.
Christ will have us dwell in these realms,
once the enemies have been cast out and the abyss conquered.
The battle-lines of the furies rush together, and all of them upon one,
upon one man alone they press with hatreds and with thronging weapons.
But he, undaunted, shakes off all their force with a word,
and rushing through foes, through weapons, lays low the Stygian columns,
and puts them all to flight: as if, gliding through the upper air,
he were harrying the birds of the shore, and the sounding throng
of the winged column — Jove's bird in the open sky.
Then in triumph he sets his foot upon the captive necks of kings,
and after he had divided the kingdom among his exulting companions,
he withdrew from the earth, and fled deep into the clouds.
Now after he had scattered his life into the fleeting breezes,
the leader, son of Nun; Judah’s fairest offspring,
marked out by fame, and likewise by fortunate arms,
succeeded him; with great force he captured Salem, and even the
lord of the Bezekites, and the fierce peoples,
the victor subjected to servitude and now takes possession of their sceptres.
But because the counsels, and the so often repeated commands of the Thunderer,
the sons of Abraham despised, at Satan's urging; Jehovah,
the Father who wields all wars beneath his own divine will,
permitted enemies to harry the new realms with the sword,
and rebels often to bear arms against the offspring of Judah,
and allows the native peoples to remain in their ancestral lands;
but when they had grown sick of their crimes too, and the mighty Lord
they humbly prevail upon with their prayers, and seek pardon;
God arms leaders outstanding in valour against their enemies,
supplies them with strength, and fills them with daring courage:
lest Babylon exult too much, while she cuts down his friends
Heaven’s mighty power tests them with afflictions, and to the underworld
thrusts down those whom he wills, above the fiery stars of the world,
to raise up and to settle in a portion of the heavenly kingdom.
Here is the home, here the fatherland which Christ appoints for those
who, fighting for Jerusalem their fatherland, suffered wounds.
The homeland crushed by war, the leader renowned in arms
Othniel avenges; Ehud, most confident,
succeeded him; he, with a blade hidden beneath his garment,
pierces that notable man, Eglon, between the flank and the groin;
He, vomiting rivers of blood, falls, and the bloody
he bites the ground, and dying he writhes upon his own wound.
Following him, Shamgar summons the hardy countrymen together;
They arrive unexpectedly: one armed with a charred firebrand,
another with a heavy knotted club; whatever each man found
as he rummaged, anger makes a weapon of it; in rustic combat
and with cudgels and fire-hardened stakes they rout the enemy.
The leader himself sent Philistines down to the underworld,
six hundred [of them] with an ox-goad; then follows the prophetess Deborah,
under whose command Jabin’s vast army
is wiped out; the leader fell by a woman's weapons,
Sisera, whom Jael pinned fast with a sharp spike,
his brain pierced through; the iron passes through both temples;
After her Gideon, using not arms but stratagems,
overwhelms the enemy off their guard and at rest in sleep;
He took three hundred young men; these, with sounding bronze
[and] with earthen jars,
past the middle of the night he led up against the enemy's camp.
Then suddenly the trumpets sounded, and the broken pitchers
revealed an unhoped-for light;
The Midianite soldiery, frenzied, seized its weapons, but there was too little reason in taking up arms:
for they turn their own strength against their own vitals;
and, while a sudden uproar threw them into confusion, they dealt one another
wounds, and there arises a most wretched slaughter
of men defending themselves with arms and rushing into arms.
Others, thrown into disorder, flee in shameful panic;
Gideon, pursuing these men with speed and spear alike,
tramples them down and hurls snatched-up spears at the fugitives.
Then wrath swells all the more in their discordant hearts,
and now the sons of Abraham, gathered together, mass in the same place,
and dare to engage hand-to-hand and advance farther.
They laid low the chieftains Oreb and Zeeb, and of the two
they cut off the heads, and carry them dripping with blood
aloft on uplifted spears, a marvel to behold.
After him Tola rules his people in peace; Jair
succeeds him; Jephthah, a most valiant hero, follows Jair—
who broke his country’s repose and roused its sluggish
men to arms as their leader, together with ranks now unaccustomed to triumphs;
columns; he who with his right hand had piled up so many heaps of carnage;
but he sacrificed his own daughter at his ancestral altars,

div.note: Here I pass over Abimelech, because he was a bastard and is called a tyrant, whose rule was over the Shechemites alone, not over all Israel.

lg.l: Thus sealing his vow with blood, and with a maiden slain;
unhappy [man] — however later generations report those events —
love of his vow prevailed, and the boundless craving for praise.
For while among her companion nymphs the soft fleeces
she cards, richly dyed with the colour of shellfish,
and the maiden solaces her long toil with song;
a messenger arriving brings back word that the enemy have fallen,
and that her father is returning, accompanied by a great triumph.
At once she flings aside, spindles and all, her soft allotted wool,
the unhappy maiden, and bends her steps to meet her father;
and, knowing nothing, she plies the dances and beats the timbrels.
As soon as her father sees her coming, beside himself,
he stiffened, and with trembling hand tore his garments.
“Ah! Why, daughter, do you destroy wretched me—and yourself?” he said.
There fell from my mouth an irrevocable vow, namely
that if Victory should favor us in our battle,
I would sacrifice whatever should first meet me: but you
are the one to meet us, but, alas, under no happy
auspices! Daughter, I shall look upon a cruel death,
and I shall stain a father's hands in my child's blood;
or shall I be forced to turn the merciless blade against my own flesh?
With a groan the dutiful maiden received her father's words,
her burning cheeks bathed and streaming with tears:
“There is no delay on my account, Father,” she said; “pay to the Thunderer
your vows, and do not for a daughter's sake break your promises and your pledged faith.
And since by God's power the victory has fallen [to us]
for us, and you have snatched trophies from a strong enemy;
slay me, and send the sacred blood flowing from my throat.
But come — since they are pressed hard by bitter fates —
one thing I beg: let it be allowed [me], two months together,
in the lonely mountains to weep for my barren youth,
which knows neither sweet children nor the rewards of love;
I ask for a respite for myself and my sister-nymphs,
until my own fortune teach me, wretched as I am, by grief;
This last favour I beg; have pity on one who prays,
and when you have granted it to me, I shall leave it heaped up by my death.
In such words she was praying, and such tears, most wretched,
the maiden poured out; but her father, both weeping and groaning,
lightly kissed his daughter, and to her as she asked leave
gave assent, that she should pass the months on the high mountains.
Ah, unhappy maiden, now you wander in the mountains
among bristling thickets and the lairs of wild beasts,
you whom no cities receive into their houses, nor within their walls;
among boars you stay unafraid, and among lions;
but at home you are not safe, you whom for the altar
a cruel father destines, surpassing lions in savagery.
Ismarus, or Rhodope, bore him among their crags —
who defiled a father's right hand with his daughter's death.
And now the unspeakable day was at hand, now the rites are made ready,
the salted meal, and the fillets about the temples:
the maiden took her stand before the altar, and, her trembling cheeks
suffused with blotches, and pale with the death to come;
and when she [beheld] the salvers, the bowls, and the cruel axes
She looked upon [them], lingering a little in tears and in thought,
and, about to die, addresses her wretched parents one last time:
Dear father, and you, O sweetest mother, who
you bore me, hateful to the fates — whose milky
breasts we often, as an infant, drained dry with tender lips;
once the authors of my blood, be now the authors of my death.
With the sword break off, as soon as may be, this hated light:
and take back this wretched breath which we drew from you.
For long—if anything at all is long for mortals—
have we lived, and with our blood glory will come to us,
a glory which no later age will ever leave unspoken.
Heaven-dwelling companions, whom from the very beginning of life
I have had as guardians, while the fates and God allowed,
receive this soul, and release me from these cares:
I have lived, and I have run the course that nature had given,
and now my noble shade will pass beneath the earth.
I have seen the enemy destroyed, and the rods of office recovered,
my homeland rescued from slavery, and my parent returned;
happy, ah too happy, if only the threshold
of the house I had not touched, and had taken myself outside the dwelling.
But the mother, frenzied and raving, tore away her robes
and her golden hair, and beats her breast with her fists,
and, having torn her trembling cheeks: “Alas, in my old age you alone are
my hope, she says, and my rest, my only delight,
and the only one on whom the whole house leans and rests;
are you to be torn from me by an untimely death? shall the blood
of [my] innocent daughter stain the cruel altars?
What am I saying, or where am I? what madness turns my mind?
Unhappy mother, now the impious deeds come home to you.
You will see your daughter sinking and spewing warm blood
from her mouth, and you will close her dying eyes.
Was it you, then, pitiable Iphis, whom—when she came rejoicing—
fortune begrudged me, so that you should not see our
joys, nor enjoy, maiden, your father's trophies?
Is this our homecoming, and the triumphs we looked for?
Is this that great faith of yours, father, crueller than bears?
Ah, if there is any pity, if you can be bent by any prayers,
spare your own offspring; have mercy on the innocent girl;
and do not slaughter all our hope with bloodstained hands.
But if there is no way to escape an unspeakable death:
if neither our love, nor the right hand once pledged to you,
nor does the maiden destined to die a cruel death move you:
pierce me, and kill me first with the fated blade;
or do you, great Father of the gods, have mercy, and with your
shaft thrust this hated head down beneath Tartarus,
since otherwise I cannot break off this cruel life:
while I hold you, daughter, my only and late-come delight, in my
embrace, lest a graver message should wound my
ears; these were the words the mother poured out at the
last parting: a handmaid carried her, fallen in a faint, indoors.
At this weeping their hearts were shaken, and mournful through them all
a groan arises; Jephthah pities [her], wronged by her lot.
Pondering much, he divides his mind now here, now there
Alas, what is he to do? With what address dare he now approach
his frenzied wife? And with what words should he begin?
On that side love throws him into turmoil, and he fixes his gaze upon the maiden,
On the other side his pledged word presses him, and the vow that must be consecrated
with a maiden's blood; it occurs to him that, once she is slain,
no hope whatever of offspring would remain, for his ancestral
house, and so great an estate, his daughter alone kept safe.
Struck dumb and bewildered by the shifting appearance of events,
and stood gazing silently, suppressing his cares within his troubled
heart; at last, through a mistaken dread of his vow,
he put off his human mind and his fatherly countenance;
you would have said he was reared at brute teats and on the milk of wild beasts.
Sorrowful before the altars, with hands bound behind her back, stands
the maiden, comely with dark-blue fillets and with jewels,
and with the tunic that her mother had spun with soft gold,
running across the fine webs with the shrill comb
now, [as] long ago; but not for these uses was that gift sought;
and round about her, her companions, their hair loosed after the custom,
scatter crimson flowers, and in their frenzy raise the wail.
She herself, unmoving, kept her eyes fixed on the ground.
But while [he] veils his daughter's face with a mantle,
the cruel father, and with trembling right hand
takes up the dreadful axe; the whole house echoes with groaning.
Twice he had tried to hew the girl down with the blade,
twice his fatherly hands fell; but when, on the third attempt,
(shall I speak it or be silent?) the right hand was raised, the girl
her companions lay hold of, fallen in a heap, and the ground with gore
foaming, and the altars sprinkled; a cry rises to the lofty
halls, and rumour runs riot through the shaken city
with lamentations; and with groaning and womanly wailing
the houses roar, and the sky resounds with loud lamentation:
But the band of Dryads, her equals in age, filled the highest
mountains with their cries; beneath the chill caves the
Nymphs wept for Iphis; “Iphis” the riverbanks echoed back.
But God rejects these altars, reddened by human slaughter,
and turns away and flees; he does not drink a maiden’s
blood or devour limbs streaming with putrid gore;
but Pluto, who hates our whole race,
delights in human gore and in bloody feasts.
But God himself learns to grow gentle at the woes of men;
and therefore he sent his dear Son down from heaven,
who, to sprinkle his Father's flames with his own blood,
set himself in the way of death, with none compelling him, and his own
head he offered up; and he expiated all our sin
by his own death, and made the king of black Avernus tremble.
This is the only victim pleasing to the Thunderer most high;
this blood is poured out upon our altars; this is the blood
which we Christians pour as a libation from golden bowls,
wherever the Sun rolls round the measureless year.
Then Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon ruled in peace
the sons of Abraham, until the Ruler of shining Olympus,
provoked to anger, gave them over to a cruel enemy.
But when the people groaned aloud, and sought the Lord
humbly with prayers, he came to the aid of his wretched friends,
and he sends Samson to set his fellows free by arms.

div.p: When the young Samson was going to seek a wife, he killed a lion on the way and, as he returned, found a beehive in its carcass. After being made judge, he burned the Philistines' grain; at Pluto's prompting they conspired against him and bound him. Breaking his bonds, however, he struck down a thousand enemies with an ass's jawbone and carried off the gates of Gaza. Afterwards, enticed by Delilah's blandishments, he revealed his strength to her and lost his hair; thus he fell into the power of his enemies, who gouged out his eyes and consigned him to the mill. Later, while they were performing Dagon's rites, they ordered Samson to be brought into the temple for their amusement. Bracing himself with all his strength against a column—his strength having now grown again with his hair—he brought down the temple and buried all his enemies and himself beneath its ruins. The festival of Dagon is described. Eli, who succeeded Samson, suddenly expired upon hearing of Israel's defeat and the death of his sons. Samuel followed him and, at the people's request, anointed Saul king. Saul had a son, Jonathan, who was very dear to David and put the Philistines to flight. David, meanwhile, struck down with a small stone Goliath, the Philistines' leader, who had challenged him to single combat, and routed the enemy. Afterwards Saul, fearing that David aspired to the throne, kept him under hostile watch and resolved to kill him, but in vain, for David always escaped unharmed. Meanwhile Saul, anxious about the outcome of the war between himself and the Philistines, consulted a witch. She showed him the apparition of Samuel, from whom he learned that he and his sons would fall in battle; this happened the following day. David then gained sole possession of the kingdom, subdued his enemies on every side, and captured many cities through their surrender. Yet he was troubled by rebellions at home, especially Absalom's, which Joab ended by killing him. At last the king, worn out by old age, designated Solomon as his successor. Solomon built the Temple, whose magnificence is described here, and cultivated peace. All these things correspond to Christ.

lg.l: Here Samson was strong in his vast limbs and bulk;
And while, hastening his journey, he head[s] for Timnah
And seeks to join himself in wedlock to the daughter of a Philistine;
An unfed lion, then by chance roaming past the lofty folds,
tracks a wild she-goat or a stag whose antlers are sprouting,
gnashing his teeth he makes for the young man with bloodied jaws.
But he, undaunted, without spear or sword, the lion
laid low with his right hand and left mangled on the sand.
Afterwards, while he was going back to Timnath for his wife's sake,
lo, he saw a portent sudden and marvellous to tell:
through the dissolved entrails of the lifeless beast, throughout the whole
belly, bees were humming, and boiling forth from the burst ribs,
and being drawn out in vast clouds; soon the waxen realms
Samson invaded, and their nectar-filled cells,
their halls, and the cunning-wrought roofs of their combs he plundered,
and with ravening hunger champs the purest honey.
But they, with thick humming and with flashing wings,
swarm about the plunderer, and provoke a fight
with bites and with beaks, and leave their unseen barbs
fixed fast in his veins, and lay down their lives in the wound.
After this he slew thirty men with his right hand,
of the men of Ashkelon, and, proud with the spoils, went exulting,
and the same man yoked foxes together, and to their twisted tails
binds charred brands, and through the tall standing crops
sends them among the Philistines; and suddenly a single
bristling battle line of fire spreads across the broad fields.
A storm raises to heaven a cloud of black murk,
the storm does, and the wind, carrying the blaze, rolls [it] into a mass.
He, seated as victor, looks down upon the exulting flames.
But the army of Hell, harried by shifting cares, and in no way
King Pluto, fearing that Samson might tear down the ramparts of Dis,
and might attempt to raise the structures of Jerusalem’s walls,
ordained by fate; from the Stygian waters he sent forth
the plague of Envy, armed with black serpents.
At once the grim goddess rises from there on dusky wings,
and revisits the lands and cities of Palestine,
carried down on the headlong South wind, and the foul poison
she drives into their bones, and has slipped deep into their inward parts.
Therefore from the several districts of Palestine, all
came together under arms; the king, raging in unspeakable frenzy,
they demand for punishment, with Mars present.
The descendants of Abraham seized him and held him fast with hands and chains,
and hand him over to the Philistines; they from every side around
stream together, and vie with each other in mocking the captive;
and all around him roared with a mighty shout,
at which the crags ring back, and the woods, and great Olympus.
Samson could not endure this; but, bursting his bonds of tow,
he came more fiercely to battle, and anger rouses his strength;
then shame and conscious valour kindle his strength,
and blazing he drives the enemy headlong over the whole plain,
now redoubling his blows with the right hand, now with the left;
and all who massed around him, at close quarters on this side and on that,
driving them off with the jawbone of an ass, he gives over to death the treacherous
bodies of a thousand men: he rages, harsh and relentless in wrath:
monstrous, like a tiger among helpless cattle:
Soon, streaming with sweat, he sought in the burning heat
to quench his thirst from a leaping stream of sweet water;
behold, the white recesses sweat with glassy moisture
[the hollow] of the deadly jawbone; a spring from the hard bone suddenly
flows forth, with which Samson refreshes his parched limbs.
Then, roused with mighty force, he carries off the gates of Gaza:
and he tore away the huge bar and the doorposts from the hinge,
straining with his broad shoulders; for to put to death
the citizens had conspired to kill Manoah’s son; but he himself,
soon, when first repose, midway through the now-spent night’s
course, had driven sleep away, he rose, and, of the city
bursting through the thresholds, the gates together with their high posts
he carried off, and at a run made for the heights of a lofty mountain.
And now, turning over guile and dread wickedness in her breast,
Delilah speaks thus, and in the high chamber of her husband
begins these words, and with her speech inspires a deceitful love.
Do you cherish me, husband, or take pity on me who love [you]?
Why then are you unwilling to entrust your secret thoughts to me?
Ah! why do you keep deceiving me, so often already deceived?
Now at last tell me wherein your vigorous strength
lies, [and] what manacles or chains will hold you?
I am your wife; it is right for me to try your heart by entreaty.
If I had the power that once was mine, and that it was fitting should be mine,
power over your love, for you would not deny me this;
by yourself, by the parents who begot you such as you are,
consent now at last, and let yourself be bent by our prayers;
This last thing I beg, wretched as I am: grant this gift to a lover.
She had spoken, and coaxingly, with snowy arms on this side and on that,
she caresses him as he hesitates in a soft embrace; he at once
received the accustomed flame, and into his marrow the familiar
warmth entered and coursed through his weakened bones:
the wife, glad and conscious of her beauty, perceived [the working of] her wiles.
Then the father, bound fast by unutterable love, confesses
(unaware that Delilah had spoken deceitfully),
that his unconquered strength lay hidden in his fated hair,
and that, while it was unharmed, he could not be bound; having spoken these words
he gave the embraces she wished for, and sought calm
sleep through his limbs, sunk in his wife's lap.
Meanwhile the peerless wife, while Samson was enjoying his rest at night,
summons a servant; he, as Samson lies there,
approaches him and cuts his hair with his right hand; she at once
calls the Philistines inside the house, and throws the doorway open;
hoping, of course, that this would be a great service to her friends,
and that the cause of their old troubles could thus be extinguished.
Why do I linger? They burst in, and from the chamber they seize him and drag him,
and they gouge out the wretched man's eyes, and hold him fast in chains.
But as soon as his hair grew, his strength returned to its former
[state], thus renewed, soon to be [a ruin] to himself and to all
a destruction to his enemies—even though the shrines of Dagon
roared with rejoicing, and the streets with games and with applause;
O human mind, ignorant of fate and of the lot to come,
and of how to keep within bounds when exalted by prosperity!
For on that day, by ancient custom, that solemn [feast]
the joyful Philistine nation was celebrating in honor of Triton.
Here is that monstrous Triton, whose sea-blue conch
terrifies the seas; as he swims, his shaggy front down to his flanks
shows a man; his belly ends in a sea-monster.
First they approach the shrines, then the beasts hallowed with the vine
they slaughter for the flame, and the entrails from [the victims] still living
they tear out, and heap the altars with loaded platters:
The altars grow warm with incense and breathe with fresh garlands.
Then chosen young men, and the priest in clean vesture,
carry the roasted flesh of bulls, and load the baskets
with platters and with cakes, and pour out flowing wine.
Then the Salii, for the singing, around the kindled altars
are present, their brows bound with poplar boughs:
here a chorus of young men, there one of old men, who in song
extol the praises and deeds of Neptune: how first the snorting
horse the earth poured forth, struck by the great trident;
and how to him the rule of the sea, and of the sea's brood,
was given by lot; how he pastures the ugly seals beneath the flood;
and how he yokes the wild beasts to his chariot, and the father adds
the foaming bits, and with his hands lets out all the reins,
when lightly he flies over the surface of the waters in his blue-green car,
with the choir of Nereids attending; and how the monstrous whales

div.note: Dagon, from the word Dag, which means a fish: the same as Triton, or Neptune.

The poplar the poets dedicated to Hercules, because it was well suited to the shields of old. I assign it to Neptune, because it delights in watery places, and the trembling of its leaves represents the trembling of the sea.

lg.l: Nisaea, and Spio, and Thalia, and Cymodoce,
and other figures among his retinue carry out his commands.
How he calms the waves, when he makes the sea-plains ring with his conch:
You are the father of a hundred sons, and you they call the parent
of the winds: your sea-blue consort bore you
all the rivers that glide beneath the great earth.
You raised the faithful Dolphin to the stars, by whose
agency Amphitrite was joined to you in the bond of wedlock.
By your hands were built the perjured walls of Troy;
you care for the sailors who plough the vast level of the sea.
Bring us into the harbors we long for; may we be permitted, safely across the waves, to entrust
our sails to you; give the reins to your favoring chariot.
Hail, great brother of Jove, offspring of Saturn,
and come favourably to us and to your rites with auspicious foot.
Such things they celebrate in their songs; above all they add the dread
brigand, both the cause and the head of the evils,
of such great evils for their homeland, now utterly brought beneath the yoke.
The temple rings, and the echo of their voices strikes and rebounds.
At last, when the sacred rites have been completed, into the temple
they lead Manoah's son, so that, bereft of sight, he may perform for their amusement.
But he was moving toward the temple with his vast bulk.
A lopped pine guides his hand and steadies his steps.
The mighty hero, unable to bear his dishonouring wound;
nor has he strength to endure the mockeries of that savage nation:
fires blazed up in his heart, anger comes upon him to avenge his falling
country, and to exact the punishment due for the crime.
Looking up to heaven, at last he prays aloud thus:
Highest of gods, be present and come to the aid of our toil;
and let me now avenge, by the death they have deserved, the blood
of my gouged-out eye; to blot out the guilty nation
with one and the same blow — let that be granted; it is resolved, whatever of bitterness there is,
to suffer it in death, nor shall Judaea see me dishonoured.
He spoke and called upon God’s help in prayers that were not vain;
for the Almighty Father added courage and strength to him as he prayed
and drove sharp goads within his breast.
Bearing down with great force on the twin pillars at their base,
Torn loose, he freed them from their foundations; then suddenly
he thrust them; at this the roof of the shaken temple, down upon his foes,
suddenly collapsed, and all heaven thunders with the crash,
following the half-dead men to the ground with its monstrous mass.
All die alike—the people and their elders,
mothers and men, boys and unwedded girls
Among the lifeless enemies lies buried the mighty
son of Manoah, and there at last he rests in peaceful death:
So Christ, coming to visit his beloved bride,
slew the Stygian lion by his mighty power.
From it, as from the bees’ dwelling and the latticework of their combs,
he drew forth the heavenly gifts of airy honey.
He subdued every scourge and broke every bond,
and at last, dying, took the life away from the savage foe.
After Samson, Eli assumes authority over the people as their leader;
unhappy both in the wickedness of his sons and in their bloody death.
For as soon as the messenger had filled the father's ears,
[the news came] that both had been slain in the fighting, and that the ark of Jehovah
was lost, and that the whole battle-lines of Jacob had fallen;
He drops down lifeless, and breathes out his life into the air.
Samuel follows him, at whose prayers heaven, set trembling,
crashed out, and fires flashed from the clouds;
there burst down too a black storm-cloud mingled with hail,
which utterly terrified the packed battle-lines of the Philistines, and
forced them, with all their columns, to turn and give their backs in flight.
King Agag, trembling, to the very altars Samuel
drags along, then rises high to strike with uplifted sword,
and with the steel cleaves his forehead down the middle between the two temples,
and his beardless cheeks with a monstrous wound.
A crash goes up, the earth is shaken by the huge weight.
His collapsed limbs, and his armour bloodied with brains,
he lays upon the ground as he dies; and for him, in equal halves,
the head hung down this way and that from either shoulder;
then he flung aside the mangled limbs and the wrenched-off parts.
But now the people refuse to obey the Judges
any longer; they demand a king; the Father of high heaven
gives assent, and to Saul, to take in hand the realms of Judaea,
granted the right; his hair, with the oil running down, Samuel
anoints, and spreads abroad a flowing fragrance of ambrosia;
he gives the sceptre and the robe of state, and the other insignia of kingship;
he lightly kissed the King, and they hail him King

div.note: In the text of the first book of Samuel, chapter 15, he is said to have been slain "before the Lord," that is, before the altar, which was a sign of God's presence.

lg.l: with a shout from those standing by; amid the ranks, King Saul
wheels about bearing arms, and stands taller by a whole head:
like the Ganges, rising high when all seven [streams] are stilled,
the Ganges [flows] through the silence, or the Nile with its rich flood
when it ebbs back from the fields and has now settled into its channel.
He had a son, Jonathan, a most valiant warrior;
who laid low the ranks of the Philistines with sudden terror;
dear to David above all others, and him
he was accustomed to make him his companion in affairs of the highest importance.
They were one in love and rushed side by side into battle;
Jonathan had hung a well-fitting bow upon his [David's] shoulders:
he gives him his own tunic, and fits a sword to his side.
nay, he even sets a golden, studded belt about his shoulders,
and discloses to David all his father's secrets.
And when David was fleeing the King's wrath, his friend's
he clasped his friend's right hand and addressed him with tender affection;
he clung, weeping insatiably, and planted kisses on him:
But when he had heard that one so mighty had been overcome by a grievous wound
in battle; with his garment rent he mourns his comrade
lifeless, and weeping he sang a piteous song.
But Christ far surpassed Jonathan in love;
for he fitted upon us the cloak of his merits, and the sword
of the divine word he girded about our side, and
He lays open all the secrets of the heavenly Father.
Nor did David weep so much for the fate of his comrade,
as Christ Jesus pities the fortunes of men.
Nor was David willing to sink beneath the fates; but rather
Christ, however, was slain for us by an undeserved death;
he alone, pitying the unspeakable disasters of Adam,
he alone was willing to submit to the enemy's hand.
There stood a pointed crag, with rocks cut sheer on every side,
a cave rising on the ridge, most lofty to look upon,
a dwelling well suited to the nests of dreadful birds;
This crag Jonathan mastered by climbing, and the foe
he views more closely — who now on the mountain's summit
settle, where [there is] level ground, and safe retreats,
whether you wish to meet the fight on the right hand or the left,
or to press on from the ridges and roll down great stones.
Hither the young man makes his way along a familiar route,
and with his hands grips the mountain's heights, and the enemy
he attacks, his armour-bearer beside him; and he butchers the first of them
as they lay sunk in sleep; then throughout the camp a panic-stricken uproar
he rouses, and sends flight among them, and sudden fear;
They deal wounds among themselves with great violence,
while they supposed themselves caught in an ambush, and that the whole
battle-line of Abraham's sons had burst in upon them: in the silent night,
while they flee, many tumble from the high crags
headlong; many are trampled under the hooves of horses.

div.note: See Josephus, Antiquities, book 6, chapter 7.

lg.l: Amid blind panic, a breeze brought to the son of Abraham
a mingled clamour; and his attentive ears were struck by
the sound of the enemy in confusion and its joyless murmur.
But after they perceive that the enemy have fled, from their hiding-places
they leap out, press them with weapons, and pursue at a run
the stragglers; a great rush of young men [is made] to the very
bodies, and the half-dead men, and to the place fresh with warm
slaughter, and to the channels full of foaming blood.
But the infernal King [gathered] the citizens scattered on every side
of his beloved Babylon, and mustered them again to arms,
and the scattered captains and the abandoned companies
he urges on with varied words, and begins thus:
O Philistines! what cowardice so great has come upon your spirits?
What fear is this, O you who will never feel pain, O ever-sluggish men?
Does Jonathan drive you in disarray and rout these ranks?
To what end the sword, and why do you carry these useless weapons in your right hands?
But you are not slow for love and the battles of the night,
or when the curved pipe has proclaimed the dances of Bacchus;
to await feasts and the full cups of the table—
this is your love, this your zeal; until the favouring diviner
announces the rites, but a fat sacrificial victim summons you into the lofty groves.
Fired by such words, they take courage and, in close formation,
gathered from every side, they come together.
No less, from the kingdom's various regions, there arrive
the sons of Abraham; and now each armed legion drew out
