its own cohorts, and the battle column stood in the open field;
The battle-lines are drawn up, and far and wide the whole
the earth ripples with gleaming bronze: nor do they yet join grim
battles, but Mars wanders in the midst of wavering arms.
Behold, a Philistine was advancing with his vast bulk,
Goliath by name; and with great strength the giant lifts up
his face, and raises himself amid the great murmur of the men;
his head is covered with bronze; clad in a corselet, with brazen
scales he bristled, and had encased his calves in bronze:
The crest blazes on his head, and from its top a grim flame
pours forth, and his huge shield flashes with vast fires.
He, carrying down an aged mountain-ash from the highest hills,
or a lofty oak, or a cone-bearing cypress,
he advances raging across the field, and in his left hand a shield
he has raised, blazing, and relentless he shakes a spear in his right;
and he displays his broad shoulders, and alternately throws out
his arms, stretching them forth, and lashes the air with blows.
So the Giant lifts his high head into the opening battle.
Another is sought to match him, and no one out of the host of Judah
dares to approach the man, and to provoke a fight with his hands,
but rather with the javelin, and with the arrow that deceives from afar,
than to close hand to hand, and to clash with drawn steel.
But just as that [boar], driven from the high mountains by the hounds’ bites,
a boar driven on, whom pine-bearing Vesulus for many years
protected, and the Laurentian marsh for many [years]; in the woodland
he fed among the reeds; after they had come within the nets,
he halted, and growled fiercely, and bristled along his shoulders:
nor has any man the courage to rage at him or to come nearer;
but they press upon him with javelins and with shouts from a safe distance.
But not with unseeing eyes upon these things, the begetter of men and of gods,
watching, sits on high upon the summit of Olympus;
the Father rouses David, Jesse’s son, for savage battles,
and with no gentle goads incites his wrath.
Him Jesse begot; Jesse was fathered by Obed,
whom fair Ruth, having conceived him by Boaz, brought forth.
This David, distinguished by his beauty and youthful vigor,
keeper of the wool-bearing sheep: who from the lion's mouth
snatched away a sheep and struck down a monstrous she-bear,
in his fury, and laid her dying on the tawny sand;
whose three brothers, from their earliest years, had been sent hither
to arms by their poor father; returning from the sheepfolds, he
approaches them in his eagerness to see them, and gladly greets them.
Behold, once again with a mighty shout he was advancing
in the midst of the field—the Cyclops—and brandishes a weapon,
huge, like a tree, and thus speaks from his savage breast:
Is there none of you who dares to trust himself to the fight,
you cowardly sons of Abraham? What madness has driven you
to wage, time and again, a grievous war against the race of gods
and to wage [war] with unconquered men? Or have you not, routed as you are,
seen deaths enough thus far? See how many cities we have stripped of their citizens,
and how often with the sword we have stripped the fields of their farmers!
If [that] you, deserving [it], have paid penalties enough for [your] crimes
you believe, and if you take care that arms not clash with arms;
and if you, Judaea, dread some unspeakable disaster,
if mothers, and wretched young wives, and the dear hearts
of grieving sisters, and boys bereft of their parents,
curse this dreadful war and the ruin of their country;
then leave it to me, and put away your fears: I will make the treaty
firm with my own hand; mine alone is the right to fight it out. But who
among you dares to meet me alone with the sword,
you sons of Abraham, and to decide it hand to hand with cruel arms,
[to settle] who shall rule over whom? If my enemy strips me [of my arms],
let him have the palm, let him take for himself the first honours of the kingdom;
nay more, my fathers and my peoples and my conquered household gods
shall obey you as their masters, and shall carry out your commands:
But if I am the victor, obey me willingly,
yield your own claim to us, and the royal sceptre;
sue for peace, and hold out your right hands unarmed.
But you worthless souls, you spiritless hearts, why should I press
any further? Is there no one in this whole host, no one
who has any true martial spirit? In whom is courage alive?
Who would now dare to grapple hand to hand? You all
fail; your strength lies broken and numb for battle.
Behold, I now curse you and your God as well. Go,
you to whom sloth is dear, give yourselves to dances,
you half-men; leave arms to men, and yield to the sword.
Him, hurling such words and uttering dreadful threats,
the son of Isaac did not endure; he begs to be admitted to the king;
Making humble obeisance, with downcast eyes, he speaks:
Greatest King, let not this be judged by our years,
what we now bring you; for, bravest one, I do not believe
that you will deign to endure another's commands and such masters;
either to attempt battle, or something great, this long while
my mind urges me, nor is it content with calm repose;
for today, as victor, those bloody spoils of the giant
and his shaggy head I shall bring back, and of our grief
I shall be the avenger, or I have resolved to succumb to certain death.
When he had heard this, the King replied thus with calm countenance:
O youth of outstanding spirit, the more you yourself
surpass others in fierce courage, the more urgently I must
take counsel and, in my fear, weigh every possible outcome.
You are an unshorn boy, far unequal to him in strength;
your downy cheeks, and the fair bloom on your youthful body,
show that under no commander have you endured
soldiering and the heavy work of Mars; nay, you are of small body
You have strength neither in limb nor in bulk; but that Goliath,
bearing his arms, stands a shoulder taller than all his fellows,
neither easy for anyone to look upon nor approachable in conversation.
He is outstanding in war besides; now see how mightily
he rears up behind his shield, with what whirl he hurls his spear.
Will you, a boy, dare to close with such a monster?
David answered: while, as it chanced, my father's flocks
I was pasturing on the lonely mountains, and beneath a lofty crag
I was easing my long labours with lyre and with song;
fierce, with savage glare, a lion — a fleeing beast of the flock in his teeth —
drags it off, gaping enormously, his mane raised, and remains
sprawling over its entrails; I, ablaze with anger,
snatched up weapons in my hand, and the trembling lamb from his claws
I tore away, and laid the lion low in a fight of my own.
Likewise my right hand killed a she-bear; shall I then fear
a half-human Cyclops, spewing out so many empty reproaches?
Either with this right hand I shall send that unspeakable head down to Tartarus,
a monster dreadful and huge: let the Philistines sit and look on,
and alone with the sword I shall refute the charge against us all:
or let him hold us vanquished, and let Judah's royal house yield to him.
Having thus spoken he flung his own cloak down from his shoulders,
and Saul's helmet, and the shield's comely device
He is clothed in it; and fits the gilded sword to his side:
Then, joyful, [he takes] the golden belt with embossed studs,
he receives, and vainly fits [it] to his strong shoulders;
for, slowed by the vast weight of the armour, once more
he strips it off, and lifts smooth stones from the river,
and snatches up his whirring sling for the hard contest,
and a shepherd's oak staff tipped with a spear-point.
Saul answered him briefly: “Now undertake to vanquish the proud man,
and may the Lord attend your mighty undertaking;
you will receive worthy rewards; I shall aid you with lands and wealth,
and besides, you shall have my daughter as your wife.”
When he had said this, David, the bravest of heroes,
stood before God as a suppliant, praying with vows:
O Father almighty, give assent to [my] bold undertakings,
and grant that this disgrace be wiped out by my arms.
Be you now my leader in the fight, do you duly bring near
[your] help, and stand by us, I pray, with favouring step.
you who long since guided my weapons and my hands
against the shaggy she-bear, and the monstrous body of the lion:
grant [me] to lay low with a stone the body of the half-beast Cyclops,
and with a strong hand to tear apart the corselet wrenched from him;
let him see me stripping the bloody arms from him as he lies half-dead,
and let the dying eyes of the monster look upon [me] the victor.
I myself will bring solemn gifts to your temple for you,
and will set before the altars a bullock with gilded brow
A gleaming white [bullock], one that carries its head level with its mother's,
one that now butts with the horn, and scatters the sand with its hooves.
With these words, eager, he runs down from the height of the citadel,
and exults in spirit, already defeating the enemy in his hopes:
just as when, its tethers snapped, [a horse] flees the stalls,
the horse free at last, and master of the open plain:
either he makes off to the pastures and the herds of mares,
or, used to bathing in the water of the familiar river,
he darts forth, and with neck upreared neighs loudly,
exulting, and his mane plays over neck and shoulders.
Then David bids [them] all withdraw utterly from the valley —
the crowd that had poured in — and bids the fields lie open.
All those in between withdrew and gave him room,
and they cut short all delay; David makes ready to go on foot
to close quarters: and as a lion, when from a high lookout he has seen
a bull standing far off on the plains, brooding on battle,
flies at him — no other is the look of the young man as he comes on.
The Cyclops makes ready to go against him, and his quivering spear
he brandishes, exulting, and thunders dreadfully with his weapons:

div.note: That is, from the summit of the hill. Both armies were on hills, with a valley lying between the two. Joseph. Antiq. lib. 6. cap. 10. Hills and mountains were called arces (citadels) from arcere, to keep off — or from the Arcadians, because under Evander they held the best-fortified hills.

lg.l: As huge as Athos or Eryx, or as Father Apenninus himself when, with tossing
holm oaks, he roars, rejoicing in his snowy
summit as he lifts himself toward the sky.
But as soon as he caught sight, closer at hand, of the unarmed youth,
striking in appearance and handsome in body, inwardly
indignant, he rails at the boy, and threatens the boy:
"Where are you rushing, doomed one, daring things greater than your strength?
Your piety deceives you, unwary as you are; is it with fire-hardened oak
that you attack me? Or do you, a boy unequal in strength, dare a man
to provoke? Wild in mind, you drink in an empty hope,
unhappy one, nor do you see that the winds carry off your joys.
Or is your business with dogs, such as you might beat with a cudgel?
May my gods and goddesses destroy you, faithless one; assuredly
I will see to it that hereafter you challenge no one with your voice.
I will make sure you do not suppose your business is with the Solymi and the youth of Canaan —
those whom Joshua subdued in a long war:
I will bury this spear deep in your breast from the front with all my
strength; and your limbs, streaming with black gore,
I will soon give to dogs to be mangled; no loving mother
will bury your mangled limbs and severed members in the ground:
you will be left to wild birds, or, sunk in the depths,
the wave will bear you away, and hungry fish will lick your wounds.”
By such furies he is driven; fire flashes from his fierce eyes.
Just as when a bull, at the first onset of battle, raises
terrifying bellows and tries to gather rage into his horns,
braced against a tree trunk, and challenges the winds
with blows, and with the sand scattered he plays a prelude to the fight.
But David, at the monstrous face and the haughty words,
marvels and stands amazed at the monster, and over the huge body
rolls his eyes, and takes in everything from afar with grim gaze.
And with such words he goes to meet the tyrant's words.
Bitter enemy, why do you taunt me and threaten death?
There is no wickedness in the killing, nor did I come to battle on such terms:
Nor do your heated words frighten me, fierce man, although
you are armed with a shield and girded with a trusty sword;
brandishing a monstrous weapon in your hand you advance onto the level ground,
But I, trusting in the divine aid of God mighty in arms—
the God whom you assail with your words—have come to battle;
I do not fear your hateful face, nor your monstrous limbs;
but my right hand shall thrust your soul down to the underworld,
and I shall scatter your bones mingled with your bloody brains;
and with your own sword I shall tear your head from your neck,
and leave your limbs to wild birds to feast upon,
and scatter the Philistines among the dogs.
Then indeed the Cyclops’s anguish had blazed up with fury and black
gall; he gnashes his teeth and draws near the boy;
but David at a swift run came to meet him.
On this side the battle-lines of the Philistines look on, on that the columns of Judah;
what the outcome of the fight may be, or to whom victory may fall,
all await intently: and throbbing dread drains their exultant
hearts, and the upraised longing for glory;
And just as on vast Syla, or on the height of Taburnus,
when two bulls, facing one another for hostile combat,
charge brow to brow, the frightened herdsmen have given way,
all the herd stands dumb with fear, and the heifers murmur
[asking] who is to rule the flock, whom all the cattle are to follow.
At once David snatches up the little stone from beneath his garment,
and swung the sling around his head by its smooth thong,
rising higher; then the hero, gathering momentum from his run,
hurls it from afar; stones launched from a siege engine never
roar so, nor do such mighty crashes burst from a thunderbolt;
like a dark whirlwind flies
the fatal stone, splitting his forehead between the two temples
and pours out the shattered brain upon his armour.
He himself, heavy, and heavily to the ground with his vast weight,
falls, as sometimes a hollow [pine] falls, either on Erymanthus
or on great Ida, a pine torn up by the roots;
the earth groans, and he, huge, comes thundering down upon his shield:
just as once on the Euboean shore of Baiae
a pier of stone falls, which, [built] beforehand of great blocks,
they cast the built mass into the sea: so it [draws] its ruin
and lies deep beneath the waters, dashed against the bottom;
the seas are churned together, and the black sands are heaved up.
Then lofty Prochyta trembles at the din, and [so does] that hard couch,
Inarime, laid by Jove's commands upon Typhoeus.
The Philistines rise up with a groan, and the whole
mountain round about bellows back, and the deep woods return the cry far and wide.
The son of Jesse rushes up and comes upon him fallen; and the sword
he snatches from his thigh, and hot with fury presses hard on the dying man:
then, standing over him, with his left foot he pressed down the neck,
and between the helmet's lower rim and the upper edges of the breastplate
he took off the head with the sword, and left the trunk on the sand.
At once the ranks are thrown into confusion, and the Philistines, routed,
turn their backs in dusty, panic-stricken flight across the fields:
the sons of Abraham pursue them at a run and with their weapons;
black gore is poured out everywhere, and they lay low the fleeing
bodies of men in great numbers, and the air whistles with spear-shafts.
Half-dead horses roll on the ground, a shout strikes the sky,
[the shout] of young men straggling in flight, and of men falling beneath harsh Mars.
Thus at last the victory passed to the unarmed boy.
Just so, the Ruler of Avernus terrified the human race
He kept terrifying the human race, threatening everyone with death and arms:
But Christ, the great Father’s most justly cherished care,
keeper of a lovely flock, himself lovelier still,
had been sent by Jove to visit his beloved brothers;
no delay: he came down and bent his steps toward the camp;
but not armed with a shield, nor with resounding bronze:
a helmet terrible with its crests and belching flames
he did not want it, or to carry a double axe chased with silver;
Bearing the cross’s stout timber, bristling with knots and rough bark,
and then the sling of the heavenly word, and five deep
wounds in place of five hard pebbles,
he came down, with God leading, between the flame and the foes;
he makes for the Cyclops, on the Cyclops alone he lingers;
him he strikes, and, brought down at close quarters by a single blow,
he tramples him, and lays him out stretched at length in the black cave.
And he tore the head from the shoulders, and shakes the ranks of Dis;
and put them all to flight and filled them with black terror:
And just as when the blast of Edonian Boreas over the deep
Aegean roars, and the wave follows on toward the shores
where the winds have borne down, the clouds give way in flight from the sky:
so, wherever Christ cuts his way, the ranks give ground,
and the battle-lines of foul-smelling Avernus turn and run.
But David, who had deserved well of the proud King,
is driven by the goads of envy and by bitter hatreds.
For the hostile King watches David, and against him
Threatening death, he aggravates the accusation through terror,
namely [the charge] of having aimed at the kingdom; in Saul violence
swells, and it drove the guiltless man over lands and waves.
And when the tyrant was carried along with maddened mind,
at the young man, with all his strength, a whistling spear
he hurls; the other, swift, the blow coming from overhead
foresaw, and, slipping aside with nimble body, gave way:
Into the wind Saul poured out his strength and rage.
So once, harried by the furies of his crimes, that same
companion of the Muses he summons — ( to whom songs always
and the lyre were dear, and setting measures to the strings:
always he sang of horses, and the arms of men, and of Jehovah )
so that, soothing him with the lyre, he may drive away the grim sickness.
But with his song he soothes the burning rage
of the king, and charms his mind with the clear-toned plectrum.
But after, girt with her scourge, the guilty man once more
Tisiphone lashes, exulting over [him], and, brandishing in her left hand grim
brandishing snakes; she summons the savage ranks of her sisters.
since he cannot bend the powers above, to stir up Acheron
he begins, and, impious, girds himself for the magic arts,
and he rouses the nocturnal Shades, and a soul from the tomb—
Samuel's—he summons it from the depths, so that by a sure omen
it may explain the coming war and make its outcomes favorable.
For the witch, out of hollow cloud, a thin shade without strength
into the likeness of the prophet (a portent wondrous to see)
She clothed [it] in the covering of a robe; then set on white
hair with a fillet; a beard combed down over the breast
of the divine head she counterfeits; she gives empty words,
gives sound without mind, and moulds the gait of one walking.
He sees many phantoms flitting in wondrous ways,
while a light phantom rises from hiding places in the earth,
which delivers these grim words to trembling Saul:
Why do you trouble me, at rest now in peaceful death?
And from the place of the shades, of sleep, and of drowsy night
why do you call [me] back? Is it that, unrolling the secrets of the fates,
I should set forth grim disasters and the wars to come?
Then, grinding his teeth fiercely, he thus opened his lips to disclose the fates:
See, the terrible wrath of the divine power harries you;
You will atone for grave crimes committed; therefore, wicked man, you are paying the penalty.
You lift your spirit to heaven, much beguiled by empty hope,
and promise yourself grey hairs, and a kingdom, and years:
but long since God has set himself against you, and your enemy
he has become, and has ordered to succeed to your kingdom
David, because you have scorned the commands of Jehovah,
and were unwilling to cut off Amalek, that wicked nation.
Nay more, the sisters are gathering up your last threads;
tomorrow, unburied, the Stygian waters and the stern river
of the Eumenides you shall look upon with me, and the deep shades below;
And you will sail with [your] offspring in the rust-dark keel."
He spoke; and suddenly from sight, like smoke—
mingling into the thin air—he fled off in another direction; and the other,
while he vainly grasped at the shadows and wished to say many things,
to say, gave way under grief; the warmth left his bones.
But truly the unhappy outcome afterwards taught him
that ashes are not to be disturbed, nor the buried spirits [of the dead],
nor the divine power of starry Olympus to be despised.
For a huge slaughter arose, and the whole
battle-line of the fleeing sons of Abraham was wiped out; there fell in bloody
battle three sons of the King: the King himself, by an arrow
—a deadly one—is wounded and flees; but, slowed by the wound,
he rages, and with the shaft snapped struggles to wrench the weapon
out; but unable to bear so great an agony,
Mad at so great a disgrace, he impales himself on the sword-point
and drives the cruel sword through his ribs.
Him, breathing his last and groaning his final moans, his comrades,
forgetting him, leave him in the obscure dust of the fields.
The Philistines run up, and strip the limbs while they are still warm;
And while they, across the fields, were stripping bare the bodies that lay strewn by the sword,
Saul too, cut off by death,
they find; they strip [him] of his arms, and the crests reddening
with blood they seize; the head torn away from the neck
they fix on a spear-point, following on with much shouting.
Nay, they even fasten the huge, nameless torso
to the walls; so now they have possession of the body and the arms.
But the men of Jabesh, gathered together by night, snatched the corpse
away, and build pyres, and the bodies of Saul
and of his sons as well they burn with fires set beneath,
and buried the men's gathered bones in the ground, beneath a tall
tree, in mourning, and uttered wailings from their mouths.
This [was] the end of Saul's destiny, this the death that carried him off
and Jonathan and his brothers—bravest hearts, but brave in vain—
which so often subdued, with Mars favouring them,
faithless foes, a race intractable in war.
Alas, when Jehovah is unwilling, no man may trust in anything!
After Saul, David takes up the sceptre of Judaea.
He took the earthly Jerusalem by great force, and the Ark
he brought in with great pomp; for he himself went before,
striking a golden lyre, and dances with his feet
beating out, he made Jehovah's praises ring in song.
Countless cities he destroyed in war, and enemies
on every side he utterly subdued with his right hand and victorious arms.
No fearsome form terrified him—not even Goliath himself,
towering, holding his weapons; nor [did they find] him wanting in resource —
as the Philistines, the Jebusites, and the citizens of Damascus discovered;
and the thousand whom, victorious, he sent down to Tartarus in a single day.
He wished to found for Jehovah a temple of solid marble,
but the oracles of the prophet Nathan forbid it.
For [for one] who has come away from so great a war, and from fresh slaughter,
to build temples for the supreme Thunderer is sacrilege;
that this would be Solomon's work Nathan foretold with his voice.
But with shifting cares and a thousand toils him
the Stygian king kept harrying, while turbulent Abner
Mighty in faction, [he] called Ishbosheth to the sceptre.
And while Joab buried his sword up to the hilt in the side
of Abner, after the king had bound him to himself by a covenant.
While Pluto [counsels] the King to break into Bathsheba's marriage-bed,
and urges [him] to send innocent Uriah down to death;
and while Amnon violates a sister's rightful claims of chastity;
whom his brother, more monstrous in crime than all others,
Absalom overpowered with the sword at table, unarmed.
Ahithophel, regarded as no ineffectual adviser
in counsel, advises the young man to thrust his father from the throne,
and, a monstrous wickedness, to defile his stepmother's bed;
and he, upon whom so dread a lust for ruling had come,
then conspires unto his father's destruction with unspeakable
counsel; to what do you not drive the hearts of mortals,
you accursed hunger for a kingdom? But the eternal power of God,
tearing all asunder, and giving [his] counsels, made void, to the clouds,
counsels to the clouds, calms these winds and the swelling seas with a nod;
and granted the King to overcome every peril.
For with the noose of a hideous death both voice and life
Ahithophel himself snatched from himself; soon Absalom himself,
for his monstrous crime against his father, for such daring deeds,

div.note: A change of number.

lg.l: and pays with warm blood the penalty he deserved.
A youth outstanding in beauty, and in gleaming arms,
Absalom, the annals report; nowhere on the whole body
which in whiteness matched the snows, was a wrinkle found.
A boy, marking his unshorn cheeks with earliest youth,
he let his gleaming hair pour down over his white neck.
But his spirit had been bold and capable of enduring danger.
He, after he saw his comrades withdrawing from the fight,
the victorious enemies dealing out slaughter indiscriminately,
and so many leaders casting away their lives to the winds;
no delay: wheeling his reins, in flight he is borne away.
And while he wearies his steed with iron-shod heel
through the woods, bristling far and wide with thickets and dark
holm oak, he had let his hair stream loose to the winds.
(for, dripping with sweat, he had flung away the empty helmet)
Ah, unhappy boy! the boughs of an aged oak
entangled his locks, curled with a hot iron and dripping with myrrh;
from a leafy branch he hung,
wretched between earth and heaven; then Joab
buried three weapons in the breast of the youth facing him.
His blood and life depart by one and the same path;
thus by this killing peace was given back both to the fatherland and to the father.
Not otherwise our Lord, than whom no other more beautiful
there was on earth, hangs aloft in the air
among thieves, as lilies among thorns,
Like white privet-blossoms beside dark bilberries;
through whose breast the mighty iron weapon passes,
bursting the breathing-passages of the soul with a deadly wound;
hence a foaming river of blood glides down to the ground;
with this sacred spring he was washing wretched mortals,
and by this death he led the human race back from death.
So the slaying of Christ was the inviolable pledge
of peace, and of an eternal covenant with us; therefore,
living by his death, I am saved by another's wound.
And now Sheba the leader rouses citizens rebellious against the King in a new
uprising; him, with avenging sword, Joab
pursues, a great phalanx of young men attending him.
He lays Amasa low, off his guard, with a cruel wound,
while he holds him in an embrace and plants kisses on his friend;
for suddenly he drives the strong sword through his ribs.
He falls, spewing streams of blood, and bites the bloodied
ground, and dying he writhes upon his own wound.
Now he has shut himself within the walls and gates of Abel,
Sheba fearing to trust himself to the open field; at once the Jews
press on, and with spirits striving alike, all of them
form a wedge, and are carried against the walls in a great mass;
they demand Sheba for punishment, with the battle upon them.
Unless they give [him] up, they threaten the city with destruction and flames;
all press forward alike, the tortoise driven up,
and they make ready to fill the ditches and to tear away the wall;
Some seek an entry, and [seek] to climb the walls with ladders
some hem in the city's walls with a palisade and encircle them with a siege-mound.
discord arises among the alarmed citizens,
some bid [them] unbar the city and throw the gates open
to the Jews; others press on to defend the walls.
As when a shepherd, [finding] them shut in a hollow rock,
has tracked down the bees, and filled it with bitter smoke:
they within, alarmed for their state, through the waxen camp
run this way and that, and whet their rage with loud buzzing;
a black reek rolls through the dwellings, then with blind murmuring
the rocks resound within: the smoke goes up to the empty air.
Here a heroic woman, heavy with years and ripe in judgement,
soothes their hearts with words, and tempers the rage
of the leader; Sheba's head, cut away from the neck,
she throws down from the walls; so she frees the city from war.
And now the Philistines were preparing to make war again:
from every side they came together; they themselves again into the contest
advance, and send their lives into open perils.
Among these, four from the mighty stock of giants,
young men matching their native firs and mountains,
trusting in their arms, they challenge the enemy with shouts of their own accord;
armed with steel, their high heads flashing with crests,
just as, towering around flowing rivers,
Whether on the banks of the Dee, or beside the pleasant Thames,
four oaks rise up, and unshorn to the sky
lift their heads, and sway with lofty crown.
These battle-lines, and these young men, with victorious arms
David scattered; and the neighbouring nations on every side
he forced, once they were conquered, to accept the bridle and obey.
David bore many perils to his life; Christ
also suffered worse, and God brought these too to an end.
For he tamed the Stygian fury; realms impassable to the living
he beheld; darkness, sleep, and slumberous night
and Chaos, and the waters of Phlegethon he subdued by his power.
But David's eyes were growing dim, and his brow
was rough with wrinkles; snow, spread over his shoulders, covered them,
and the once-ruddy colour left his face.
And because now sicknesses come on, and grim old age
weakens the strength of his mind and alters its vigour:
Solomon is anointed as king, whom the royal mule
carried into the walls of Jerusalem in glorious triumph.
The streets roared with rejoicing, with games, and with applause.
Meanwhile the black house of the deep pit is shut,
and Pluto is bound with a hundred brazen chains,
lest by war he break Jerusalem's peace or her covenants,
while Solomon rears golden roofs for the Thunderer.
And while he enjoyed this pleasant light, the dread
gates of war were shut with tight fastenings:

div.note: A most delightful river in Scotland, famous for its salmon fishery; it flows past Aberdeen.

lg.l: And this state of Jerusalem was a shadow and image of the future
Jerusalem under Christ, which is now called the Church,
in which perfect rest and eternal peace shall flourish.
While Solomon was ruling the peoples in tranquil peace,
an immense, vast temple, lofty with columns of many kinds,
he built, rich in offerings and in the divine presence of Jehovah.
To onlookers it resembled a snowy mountain; and, as
a bright cloud gleams with reflected sunlight, so
the marble gleamed, and the roof-tops blazed with gilded panels.
But with what majesty did the house within shine forth?
Why should I recall the many talents of silver and of bronze?
Or why should I tell the weights of gold, wrought and unwrought?
Great mixing-bowls, tables, and dishes, and crowns,
and embroidered robes, stiff too with purple,
palms, and cedar-wood, and cauldrons of bronze of every sort,
and cups fashioned of silver and embossed with figures;

div.note: A crater is a kind of vessel larger than a cup, used only at libations and more solemn feasts; it is also a vessel in which food is cooked or which is set upon the table: "the mixing-bowl was of red earthenware, the cups of beechwood." Ovid, Fasti 5.

There is no doubt that very many gifts were presented to Solomon, among which it is likely that there were golden crowns; for it was customary to offer costly crowns to kings, as Pliny attests concerning Claudius, book 33, chapter 3. The front of the Temple was adorned with golden crowns, 1 Maccabees 4:57—or with crowns carved upon the stones and covered with sheets of gold.

He abounded not only in tapestries but also in garments woven of many-colored threads and variegated, and adorned with various representations of flowers and animals, such as the palm-patterned robe and the military cloak among the Romans.

lg.l: doorposts proud with barbaric gold and with bronze;
and gilded beams, gems, and embroidered hangings.
Besides, there stood two great Altars, of which
this one was overlaid with gold, that one with flashing bronze.
Furthermore, a bronze basin, resting upon twice six oxen,
spreads out branches and gilded arms.
A lamp scatters flashes of flame throughout the Temple;
Forms of winged youths cling to the shining
walls, their wings give light, and they glitter with brightness.
Everything blazes with gold, flowers are chased in gold,
the tongs are gilded, the incense-boxes gilded,
the golden inner shrine gleams with woven gifts.
Besides, he built structures splendid with royal luxury,
with wide porticoes, chambers, and stately doors,
with gilded beams, and above with panelled ceilings of gold,
adjoining the Temple, and built [them] of Parian marble.
From here to receive the sceptre and to raise the first rods of office
was an omen for kings; this temple was their council-house;

div.note: Here I put Parian marble for the finest of all; so too "Lycian arrows": for I take the species for the genus.

That the King's house was joined to the Temple is inferred from verse 9 of 1 Kings 7, where it extends as far as the greater, or outer, court of the Temple. The King's house, the house of the forest of Lebanon, and the Queen's house, however, were not three buildings, but one building divided into three parts, as Pineda proves in De rebus Salom., book 5, chapter 5. Here places were appointed for administering justice, holding banquets, and storing arms. The basilica was large and beautiful, etc.; he founded it for conducting legal proceedings and deciding disputes, etc. In its midst was a square hall, etc., and in that hall a magnificent tribunal where the King administered justice. Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 2.

lg.l: It was also customary, once the fathers had been summoned, to give laws to the people;
this was the seat for sacred feasts; here, when a ram had been slain,
the fathers were accustomed to sit together at long tables;
here light shields, here gleaming darts hang,
and bronze-plated targes glitter, and curved axes,
swords, and spears, helmets, and plumed crests,
and shields, and wooden shafts, and quivers and Lycian arrows,
he fastened all these arms upon the sacred doorposts.
So Christ, after the conflict had ended and he had brought the nations
to peace, built a temple of living marble.
Here, as in a laver, he washes us clean in clear waters;
here flashes the tawny gold of a blameless life.
Solomon's riches are not lacking, nor the Temple's opulence:
nor the lamp that lights the whole Temple with its brightness,
nor the golden throng of the winged host, nor its arms:
nor the cakes, and dishes, and cups of the full table;
nor feasts spread before the eyes in royal luxury:
Here too, with holy meal and a full incense-casket, we do reverence;
yearly vows also, and solemn processions in due order,
we carry these out, and heap the altars with their proper gifts.
Here is hoary Faith, here a council-house governed by just laws;
laws and magistrates flourish, and a holy senate.
If I were to recount Solomon's riches, and the many talents
of silver and of gold, and the metals of electrum and of bronze,
and the menservants and maidservants who, ranged in a long line, were charged
whose charge it is to arrange the provisions, and to honor the household gods with flames;
and to load the tables with viands, and to pour out the wine.
Sooner will evening lay the day to rest with Olympus shut,
What shall I say of wives, of bridal chambers, and of marriage beds,
of countless cities, of houses raised level with the clouds,
and of varied gardens breathing with saffron flowers,
and of the nations which he then held under his great dominion?
What shall I say of embroidered robes, what of coverings
of gold? Then saffron cloaks and rustling folds
of fine linen, and wools burning with Tyrian purple,
and tunics which Memphis had spun with soft gold.
Then robes of state glittering with sundry gems and with purple,
which a throng of wives, not unskilled in Minerva's works,
had figured with the needle, and had picked out the webs with fine gold.
Add to these so many splendid citadels and the toil of building them;
so many towns piled up by hand upon sheer rocks.

div.note: For greater magnificence, it is probable that Solomon possessed every kind of garment that Egyptian resources, whether fine linen or silk, could supply, or that Tyre, Sidon, the Seres, and other foreign lands could furnish.

The laena is a kind of garment that the Flamens customarily wore while sacrificing. Cicero, On Famous Orators. The chlamys, by contrast, is a military garment shorter than the pallium: "Pallas himself, in the midst of the column, conspicuous in his chlamys and decorated armor." Virgil, Aeneid 8.
For painted and variegated garments Babylon and Egypt were once famous. "Here the land of Memphis gives these gifts; Babylon's needle has now been beaten by the Nile's comb." Martial.
Since he had so many wives and concubines — Egyptian, Tyrian, Sidonian — intent upon luxury and upon the making of costly clothes, they doubtless supplied him with the most exquisite garments.

lg.l: Then the glades, and the living lakes, and cool Tempe,
and the fish-filled pools, and the springs, and the echoing groves.
Besides, he traversed the sea with various fleets;
and he himself prescribed the number and the measure of the ships.
There is a secluded place in Egypt, enclosed on every side by dense
trees and bristling shadows;
Not far from here there is a city on the Red Sea shore, called
Berenice; its walls foam with the salt spray;
a harbour unstirred by the winds' approach, and a berth well suited
for vessels, and for dockyards too; for all the timber
lies by the shore; hither, for Solomon,
Hiram sends craftsmen who knew how to fashion oars
and to fit beams out of the woods, and to frame ships.
The eager Tyrians press on, overturning the deep lairs of wild beasts,
the ancient homes of birds, roots and all,
and groves that have stood idle for many years.
The pines fall, the holm-oak rings, struck by axes,
and beams of ash: with wedges too the cleavable oak
is split: these have laid down curving keels for the vessels,
those renew the thwarts, these with cut oak the ribs
weave together, while others fit the oars and the ropes.
So, once all the keels had reached the open sea,
a wind rising astern follows them as they go.
They wear out nights and days alike with rowing:
and they negotiate various bends and leave behind various
cities and harbours, and skim along diverse shores,

div.note: Ezion-geber was called Berenice in the time of Josephus (Antiquities, book 8, chapter 2); Ortelius likewise calls it Berenice on his map of the Red Sea.

lg.l: and bays, and traverse waters thickly studded with islands.
There lies beneath another sun a land most rich,
which indeed streams of silver and ores of copper
displays in her veins, and has flowed most abundantly with gold,
Here the Sun divides the globe midway between light and shadow;
and here he makes the hours of day and of sleep equal:
and when the rising Sun has first breathed upon us with panting steeds,
there ruddy evening kindles his late lamps.
Here [is] unceasing spring, and summer in months not her own;
twice the flocks are big with young, twice the tree is fruitful.
Here they inhabit great cities, most prosperous realms,
Solomon urged [them] to try these far-off lands.
At length, after various toils of land and sea,
The fleet glides up to the shores of gold-bearing Sumatra.
They turn their prows to the sea, then with gripping fluke
the anchor made the ships fast, and the curved
sterns fringe the shores; an eager band of young men darts out
onto the longed-for beach: some search the sands for gold,
and other metals hidden in veins within the earth:
some — ivory, and black ebony, and glittering gems —
load aboard the ships, together with a vast quantity of gold and elephant bone cut into plates,

div.note: Some maintain that this is the Taprobane of the ancients; others prefer the island of Leilan; some locate Ophir in the Golden Chersonese, and I would prefer it here rather than in Peru.

By "ivory" I understand elephants' tusks; by "cut elephant," elephant bone cut into plates: see Plin. lib. 8. cap. 3. There is also fossil ivory, Plin. lib. 36. cap. 18.; and the teeth of the hippopotamus are equal to ivory, indeed better, Scalig. exercit. 187. 1.

lg.l: An untold weight of silver, and green birds
which utter hoarse, mindless sounds and empty words,
give out; and those animals that mirror men in their faces.
Meanwhile, as the third summer comes round, the fleet
laden with these wares it returns, and has put in at harbour;
and the glad sailors have set garlands on the sterns.
So King Solomon had been the richest of all men,
rich in horses, rich in embroidered raiment and in gold,
he had chariots beyond number, and chosen team-horses
of heavenly stock, breathing fire from their nostrils,
such as would surpass the snows in whiteness and the winds in speed.
Why should I recount the charioteers, and those who in the high stalls
tend the swift four-footed beasts, and with their hands rouse
their breasts, patting them with hollowed palms, and comb the maned necks
the wing-footed steeds, covered with purple and embroidered rugs.
O fortunate king, to whom, from the east,
the farthest region of the world has sent its riches; for whom the Seres
comb fleeces from leaves; whom Tarshish and Ophir serve;
India sends ivory, the soft Sabaeans their frankincense;
the Arabs give gems, Egypt fine linen, Judah

div.note: Most render the word Thukum as peacocks; others as a certain kind of ape; others interpret it as the parrot; Josephus, as Ethiopian slaves.

Tharshish and Ophir are different regions, the one in Africa, the other in India: from the former parrots, apes, elephants' tusks and silver were brought to Solomon; from the latter gold, precious woods and gems. On Tharshish and its riches see 1. Reg. 10. 22. & 2. Paralip. 9. 21.; on Ophir, 1. Reg. 10. 11. 2. Chron. 9. 10.
There were various Sabaeans among Africans, Ethiopians, Indians, Arabs, and Persians.
Diodorus writes, lib. 2. 12., that stones of various kinds, in colour as in brilliance, are produced in Arabia by the working and the power of the Sun.

lg.l: Judah gives balsams oozing from fragrant wood.
An ivory throne shone, borne up on six steps,
enclosed by armrests, and gold encircled the whole throne;
Then on the steps twelve lions' muzzles bristled.
From there, as custom was, the King gave judgements to the peoples summoned [before him].
Great was the glory of King Solomon, great
[his] treasures, but far greater his wisdom in affairs.
Hence he is celebrated with illustrious fame in many lands;
This fame, flitting far and wide, reaches the ears
[of] the queen of the Ethiopians, Candace, whose [kingdom extended]
far and wide to the Indians and the eastern Arabs;
and she held the incense-burning Sabaeans under her sway.
She, longing to look upon Solomon's state and his face,
to address the man and utter learned words;
presses on to Jerusalem with a great throng crowding round her,
bearing gifts: cassia, gems, and talents of gold.

div.note: That this was the common name of the queens in the island of Meroe, Pliny asserts, lib. 6. cap. 29. It is probable that the queens of the Ethiopians were called by this name: Strabo lib. 17. relates the war of Petronius with Candace, the one-eyed queen of the Ethiopians; of another Candace we read in the Acts of the Apostles, cap. 8. "The Ethiopians call every mother of the king Candace," as the Greek scholia have it. By Ethiopia here I understand the Arabian Ethiopia, which is also called the region of Sabaea, and India: for all who dwell on this side of the river Indus are called Indians by Curtius, lib. 9.
So great was the abundance of frankincense and spices here that, in place of brushwood and other fuel, they use cinnamon, cassia, and the like. Strabo, book 16.

div.p: The Queen of Sheba, having entered Judaea, sends envoys with gifts to Solomon at Jerusalem. Learning from them the cause of the Queen's coming — namely, that she might hear his wisdom and see the magnificence of his court — he goes out to meet her with great pomp, receives her kindly as his guest, and shows her the splendour of his court and the various monuments of the city; and she, marvelling at such wisdom and glory, returns home. Solomon's kingdom is compared with the kingdom of Christ, and Christians are spurred on to peace among themselves and to war against the Turk. Solomon being dead, his kingdom is divided under his son Rehoboam, and the king of Egypt storms Jerusalem. Abijah, Rehoboam's son, defeated Jeroboam in war; and Abijah's son Asa overcame the Ethiopians. Jehoshaphat, together with Ahab, is defeated by the Syrians, and the fleet he was about to send to India was sunk; by his prayers he overcame the enemy. Jehoram the idolater kills his brothers; Jehu makes away with Ahaziah; Athaliah seizes the kingdom. The lives of Ahaziah, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah, Joash, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah are briefly set out. Judith beheads Holofernes, overwhelmed by sleep while yet alive, and delivers her besieged country. The Chaldaeans storm Jerusalem and overthrow it utterly along with the Temple; the Jews are led captive to Babylon, where they remained seventy years, during which time God sent to them the Prophets, who prophesy of Christ the deliverer.

lg.l: After the Sabaeans had reached the fields of Judaea,
the queen at once, having chosen from every rank
a hundred envoys to the king’s august walls,
[She] bids them all go, veiled with the boughs of Pallas;
and to carry gifts to the man, and to set out the reasons of their journey.
No delay; those bidden make haste, and are borne on with swift
steps; the queen herself follows at a slackened pace;
And now they were climbing the hill, whose great bulk
looms over the city; from above they gaze at the citadels opposite.
Then they see walls, and towers far off, and the lofty temples
of Zion, which the power of Judaea at that time
raised to heaven's height.
Before the city, boys and young men in the first flower of youth
exercise with horses and master chariots amid the dust,
or draw powerful bows, or with their arms
hurl pliant javelins, and challenge one another in racing and boxing.
When, riding forward on horseback, to the ears of King Solomon
a messenger brings back word that huge [men] in unknown dress
have arrived; he orders that the men be summoned within the house,
and sat at the center upon an ivory throne.
And as they entered, he was first to address them in a calm voice:
Tell me now, Arabs—for we know both the cities
and the race of the Ethiopians—what cause, or what need,
has brought [you] to the lands of Judah and to our thresholds,
so far from your homeland? what fortune wearies you,
or whither do you hold your course? do you bring peace hither, or arms?
He had spoken, and the Ethiopians thus answer his words aloud:
"King, noble stock of David, to build a temple
to whom the almighty Father granted, and to curb proud
nations with justice: not to carry off plunder here
have we come, nor do we approach your shores by chance,
nor has star or shore led us astray in the course of our way;
by set purpose and with willing hearts we are all borne
to this city; your fame, proclaimed throughout the lands, compelled us
through crags and cliffs to seek out your country.
The queen of the Ethiopians, a people mighty in lands and in arms,
ruler of the Arabs, has sent us to your threshold.
She now waits within your borders; her
the breeze of your fame, spread abroad throughout the whole world,
has carried from her ancestral seat all the way to this threshold:
she earnestly desires to see you, and what she has heard with her ears
she now longs to see with her own eyes; may she be granted sight of
your face, O King, and then to hear and offer learned words in reply.
She gives you besides a hundred and twice ten talents
of tawny gold, along with gems and the spices of our land;
gifts small indeed, but they bear witness to a great love."
Then the King answered the envoys with friendly words:
"Does the queen of the Arabs, then, a woman renowned above all,
deign to visit our lands?
And for our sake to give herself to so great a toil,
across so many stretches of land, so many inhospitable rocks,
under a burning sun, and under the star of raging Cancer?
I for my part, young men, do not judge myself worthy of such honour;
but if [there is] so great a longing to come to know our lands,
and the gifts of the mind, if the desire for us is so great;
if she hastens to be joined in guest-friendship and to see an ally,
let her come, and let her not shudder at friendly faces,
For me, touching the Sibyl’s right hand will be a pledge of peace.
Nor do I scorn the gifts; nor let it irk you to have been the first to vie
in service; we acknowledge the queen of the South,
and gladly receive her, and invite her as an ally into our realms,
if only she is willing to settle with me on equal terms in these realms.
We Hebrews do not bear hearts so dull,
nor does the Sun, so utterly turned away from Jerusalem, yoke his horses,
that we should forget to render worthy thanks
for so great a service, or to offer a worthy recompense.
Having spoken thus, the father picks out horses from the whole number,
a thousand swift ones, and such as have been taught to wheel their proud paces
and to prance upon the ground with their hooves under arms.
With these, as soon as tomorrow's light gives itself back to these lands,
he resolves to go out to meet the queen with great pomp.
He therefore orders that a thousand horsemen who will attend him under arms
be assembled; he binds their white necks with gold,
and, as he girds them with breastplates bristling with gold and pale orichalc,
he hangs ivory-hilted swords from their shoulders.
Meanwhile the rising dawn left the Ocean behind.

div.note: The Queen of Sheba is believed to have been one of the Sibyls because of her extraordinary wisdom and expertise in affairs. Cedrenus, in his historical compendium; Pausanias, book 10.

lg.l: As Solomon lingers in his chamber, at the threshold the foremost
of the Saracens await him, in their robes and distinguished armor,
gleaming; quivering crests blaze from their heads.
there stand [horses], in embroidered trappings and spread with purple,
brazen-hoofed, and they roll gathered fire from their nostrils;
golden collars hang let down over their breasts;
covered with gold, they champ tawny gold beneath their teeth.
At last he himself comes forth, fairest of kings,
all ablaze with gems and with refined gold.
His son follows him, another great hope of Judah,
his cloak embroidered with the needle, and bright with Iberian dark-purple.
He calls for the horses, and rejoices to watch them snorting before his face.
Squadrons of young men go before, and all of them in long array
shine on their bridled horses; and after them Roboam
follows next; his flowing locks hang about his milk-white neck,
and a circlet binds them beneath with pliant gold.
A youth of outstanding beauty, whom an Egyptian horse, two-coloured
with white spots, carries; the pasterns of its forefeet
are white, and, standing tall, it displays a white forehead.
The king himself, last, surrounded by the weapons of the swift horsemen,

div.note: By "Iberian ferrugo" I understand purple of the most excellent dusky hue.
Rehoboam, born of his mother Naamah at the beginning of Solomon's reign, being by then a youth of seventeen or eighteen years, or thereabouts.

lg.l: He is borne in a four-horse chariot; on the high towers stand
matrons and men, and they have ringed the walls about in a circle.
Some pour themselves out through the gates, and follow with their eyes
the cloud of dust, and the companies blossoming with bronze.
They, through the thickets, where the nearest turning of the roads lies,
press on; the mountains resound with the blare of trumpets;
and with four-footed drumming the hoof shakes the crumbling plain.
But from another quarter, attended by Sabaean chiefs,
the queen is borne along amid a great throng of matrons,
in a soft-cushioned carriage, encircled with glowing gems,
and wholly agleam with gold; from her head her tresses
breathed fragrance; twisted gold gleams about her neck:
on her head she wears a double crown of pearls and gold.
And as soon as she catches sight of the king approaching, from the golden
chariot she leapt down and, with her lovely features downcast,
she went forward on foot; and her whole company, copying her, with their horses left behind
streamed down to the ground, and followed their mistress.
So the queen walks through the midst of the companies:
even as on the banks of Eurotas, or along the ridges of Cynthus,
Diana leads her dances; a thousand Oreads follow her,
clustering on either side; her quiver

div.note: By Diana leading the dances on the ridges of Cynthus I understand the Moon wandering among the lesser stars. Mount Cynthus was of such height that to those living in the valleys below, the Sun and Moon seemed to touch its summit and to move upon it; whence arose the fable of Latona's childbearing. For this reason I call the stars Oreads, because to those gazing up from the deep valleys they seem to dwell upon the mountains. The queen, then, was among her attendants as the Moon among the lesser stars.

lg.l: She bears [it] on her shoulder, and as she walks she towers above all the goddesses.
The Hebrew companions too, and the young Rehoboam,
come to meet [them]; he himself, fairest before all the rest.
Solomon presents himself as a companion and joins the ranks:
just as when wintry Lycia, and the streams of Xanthus,
Apollo leaves behind, and visits his mother's Delos,
and renews the dances, and about the altars, mingled together,
Cretans and Dryopes roar aloud, and the painted Agathyrsi:
he himself paces the ridges of Cynthus, and with soft
foliage binds his streaming hair, dressing it, and entwines it with gold,
his shafts rattle on his shoulders; no less briskly than he did,
King Solomon went—such splendour shines from his noble face.
After they had come together, and leave to speak face to face was given,
the queen, most beautiful [of women], the reasons for her coming
recounts, and at the same time inquires into nature’s secrets.
She, the powers of herbs and the practice of healing,
longs to know; then how, driven together through the great void,

div.note: I compare Solomon to the rising Sun. Lycia and the Xanthus lie eastward with respect to the island of Delos; he visits Delos when it is hidden in darkness and makes it manifest by his own light—from δῆλος, "manifest." The poets attribute arrows to him and to the Moon because of their rays; to the Sun they attribute the laurel because of the heat innate in this tree, and gold because of the Sun's golden colour at its rising. The Cretans, the Dryopes, the Agathyrsi, and other nations worshipped the rising Sun and consecrated festivals and dances to him.

lg.l: the seeds of earth, and of air, and of sea had been [drawn together],
and of liquid fire together; how, from these first origins,
all things and the tender globe of the world itself grew solid;
then how the ground [began] to harden, and to shut Nereus off within the deep,
and little by little to take on the forms of things.
whence the earth's trembling comes, and by what force the deep seas swell
when their barriers are burst, and again sink back upon themselves;
whence the race of men and of beasts, whence rain and fire,
why the suns hasten so to dip themselves in Ocean
in winter, or what delay stands in the way of the lingering nights;
All this Solomon, tracing it back from its origin, sets forth.
For in his wisdom he came to know the causes of things, and all
things that exist, that had existed, and that are soon to be brought to pass.
But first he resolved to lead the queen to the city.
At last they advance in a mighty procession toward Zion's
walls; he escorts the queen, as his companion, to the royal
palace, and at the same time he decrees honors for Jehovah's temples.
Before the altars, slaughtered bullocks strewed the ground.
Joyful, in the midst of the hall, he arranges the banquets
with kingly splendour: they recline on outspread purple
beneath gilded panelled ceilings; then through the city's
crossroads, he leads the queen, taking her with him through the city,
and displays his vast wealth, and the temple made ready,
and the forum, harbours, towers, forts, and the massive battlements
of the walls, and the rooftops made level with the sky.
The streets roared with rejoicing, with games, and with applause.
The Ethiopians marvel at the massive pile, once mere huts,
they marvel at the gates, the din, and the paved streets;
Candace marvels and readily turns her eyes on everything around;
she is captivated by the places and, delighted, each thing in turn
the monuments of the men of old, one by one.
Then Solomon, the prince, founder of the citadel of Judaea, [says]:
These places Melchizedek once held under his sway;
then the Jebusites, a people hard and rough in their manner of life.
Here father Abraham would have slain his son at the altars,
had not God himself given a sign in the open sky,
that he did not wish his altars to be defiled with human gore;
nor the father to stain his hands with the blood of his son.
Here an angel was flying between earth and heaven,
blazing with a blood-red sword and heavenly arms;
while the expanse of heaven was tainted, there arose a lamentable
storm and a dreadful plague. This ancient city, Salem by name,
and the part of Mount Moriah with its sacred summit,
fell to Benjamin; but Judah holds Mount Zion
holds by lot, and that part of Moriah which slopes toward the south.
These two towns which you see with their lofty walls,
golden now, once rough with woodland thickets,
when a voice from heaven struck terror into trembling Abraham,
commanding him to slaughter his consecrated son for the flames.
Father David founded this city; King Salus founded it
once the enemy had been driven out. Here are those spoils of Goliath,
and the severed head, which the father, dripping with blood,
brought in here, and set up trophies snatched from the enemy.
Then the father, borne in splendid triumph within Jerusalem’s walls,
consecrated to Jehovah an undying votive offering.
When he had said this, turning toward the rising sun,
he points out the cloud-wrapped summits of the Mount of Olives,
where Christ had been raised into the heavenly air
and, departing from the earth, left behind his sacred footprints.
Here too, while the saints were celebrating the annual sacred rites,
Belief in the event is ancient indeed, but its fame everlasting:
quivering flames shone upon the crowns of their heads.
Then the valley with a winding course—they called it Gehenna,
the sons of Abraham — here had been a grove most rich in shade,
far and wide hallowed by solemn religious awe; on every side hills
hollow hills enclosed it; in its midst there blooms a most verdant
plain, and it drinks clear waters from the springs.
Here once a bronze statue of Saturn, with wondrous honour,
was worshipped; in his glowing arms he clasped boys
in a wretched embrace and put them to a cruel death.

div.note: See Baronius under the year of Christ 34.

Molech, or Melech, signifies King. Now Saturn was a king; and from the kind of sacrifices too it is gathered that Saturn was the same as Molech, for boys were sacrificed and drums beaten in the rites of Saturn — a custom which lasted down to the proconsulship of Tiberius. See Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 9.

lg.l: The worshippers, trusting in their piety, through the midst of the fire
advance, and plant their footsteps on many a live coal;
and young men set upon the pyres before their parents' faces
raise dreadful groans to the stars of heaven.
But lest by chance this joyless moaning strike the
mothers' ears, they beat the Corybantian drums.
Then, turning his eyes toward the sinking sun,
he points out the hill whose name is now Calvary,
because the whole hill is white with the bones of the dead.
This hill, renowned by report, is celebrated in many lands,
ever since it was bedewed with the heavenly blood of Christ.
It is believed that here the ashes and bones of the father himself,
the first [of men], were laid to rest; nay, that he himself [came] again to the
ethereal, and to have come beneath the upper airs of heaven;
called back by no herbs, but by the love of the Master,
who wished here to discharge with his blood the ancestral penalty,
and in pity to lift his fallen friend up out of the pit.
So at last they wander everywhere over the whole region
on the plains, and survey the cities and the ramparts.
They see the remains and the monuments of the men of old,
and survey the new citadels which Solomon founded,

div.note: Ahaz, 2 Reg. 16. 8., and Manasseh, 2. Reg. 21. 6., made their sons pass through the fire; others thrust boys into the arms of a red-hot idol to be burned.

lg.l: And when he had led the queen of the Arabs through every particular,
teaching her much, and had cheered her spirits with varied conversation,
he escorts her with great honour to the borders of her homeland.
But she, saddened by the final parting, briefly
halted, and spoke to the king with lowered voice.
I do indeed believe—and my belief is not groundless—O best king of kings,
that the report of your excellences is true after all.
Many things indeed in my own country we heard of your court;
and much about your ability and wealth, but I could not believe it;
but scarcely half of your merits
did I chance to hear; with these eyes we have drunk in far more; therefore
though your fame shines out through the whole world,
yet the fame is far dimmer than the deserts. O King,
All honor to your virtue! O thrice and four times blessed are those
to whom it is granted to stand before the face of so great a King,
and from your discourse to learn true excellence.
He who rules with everlasting sway both gods and men
has willed you to govern [a land] pregnant with empire and seething with war,
Judaea, and to bring her under the laws of peace;
and to curb an untamed people with the strong bridle
of justice: behold with how great a love he has loved Judah!
When she had uttered these words, she journeyed back to her native city.
But if so great was the glory of Solomon, so great
Peace and justice, and prudence in affairs; O Christ,
O glory of the human race, golden light of the world,
defence of the wretched; hope and comfort to us:
In you how great was the majesty, and how great the countenance's
glory of [your] divine countenance, which had revealed the world with light,
and had driven the dank shadow from our sky!
He indeed shone with jewels and in pure gold:
but you shine with divine virtues; for him there was
a royal throne resplendent with gleaming ivory;
but yours is a starry throne, from which, high aloft, you behold all
lands, peoples, and the liquid plains.
Solomon dwelt in marble halls, but you
hold [your seat] in the temple of heaven, fitted with blazing stars.
Him a throng of captains ringed about with gleaming arms,
but you the ethereal forms, without [bodily] image, surround,
standing, matched in number, and singing of the King.
Lavish with wealth and more accomplished in speech, and regarded as no worthless adviser
in counsel was Solomon; but your, O Christ,
opulence surpasses the treasures of the Persians, and the waters
of Hermus, which rolls along sands yellow with gold.
You with the thunder of your speech shake the high summits of the earth,
and your wisdom flashes like lightning through the whole world.
His fame sped forth, spread abroad throughout the regions of the world;
but you, great in fame and greater still in merit, fly throughout all
lands, known from here even to the stars.
To him, an excellent son-in-law, a daughter with worthy wedding-rites
the king of Egypt gave; but the fairest offspring of heaven,
Christ, mighty in his ancestral lineage, marriage with an angelic nature
beauty refused, and hastened on with a wondrous love
to join our nature to himself in wedlock.
Solomon's fame [drew] the queen of the Ethiopians to Zion,
out of her native kingdom, through so many perils:
but your star [took] three kings from quiver-bearing Persia
and led them through to Bethlehem; and in the manger you, the supreme
they recognize as king and as the child of all-spreading heaven,
they heap you with great gifts and worship your divinity.
While you flee your homeland, and the cruel hatred of the tyrant,
the fortunate people of Canopus receive [you] as their guest,
which dwells beside the Nile that forms pools when its waters overflow,
and is carried around its own fields in painted skiffs.
What region on earth, what people so barbarous, to whose
ears the breath of your name has not yet come?
You are known to the Nomads and to the ungirt Africans,
and to the Leleges, and the Carians, and the arrow-bearing Geloni.
Amid the Hyperborean ice-fields, and the snowy Tanais,
and the plains never widowed of Riphaean frosts,
your bright fame thrives; Jesus is venerated by
the Morini, the furthest of mankind, and the two-horned Rhine:
and the untamed Dacians, and the Araxes that resents the sea,
Ismarus, and Rhodope stretched out beneath the mid pole,
the Neptunian land of the Brutus-born. Where …idus, the fields
Amid fields rich in men the Thames flows with a gentle current.
But, not content with these narrow bounds, over all the world's
places far and wide the name of Jesus flies,
where this pole of the world [stands] ever high aloft, and that other one
where Night and the deep shades behold it beneath their feet.
From the sun's rising, where first it scatters the shadows,
right to the bounds of Ocean and the setting sun.
Nor indeed did Alcides traverse so much of the earth,
though he pierced the bronze-footed hind, or of Erymanthus
quieted the woodlands, and made Lerna tremble with his bow.
Nor he who in triumph turns his team with vine-leaf reins,
Liber, driving his tigers down from Nysa's lofty summit;
And do we still hesitate to extend our valor through deeds,
or does fear forbid us to take our stand on Scythian soil?
Wretched Christians, what fortune, rousing you from your peace,
persuades you to provoke so many wars against friends?
You wage a ruinous war, citizens against citizens, and
with indomitable strength—you whom no
battles weary, nor, even when defeated, can you desist from the sword.
Christ had forbidden citizens to clash together in war:
what strife is this against the ban? what fear has urged either these,
or those, to pursue arms and challenge steel?
Does it then not shame you to clash among yourselves with matched
weapons, O you who will never grieve? do you not see
both sides slaughtered in each other’s blood,
razed towns lie everywhere, and Germany again grows warm with our
blood even now, and the vast plains whiten with bones,
Yes, and a time will come when in those borderlands
the farmer, working the soil with his curved plough,
will find javelins eaten away with rough rust:
or with heavy mattocks will strike on empty helmets.
and will marvel at the huge bones in the graves he has dug open.
O you who have scattered abroad the fires of so great a war,
On account of whose ill-omened rule and crooked ways,
so many lights among the leaders have fallen; and we see many
cities sunk down in mourning: now at last give over,
whoever you are — see, I come as a suppliant — and pity your own people,
lay aside your pride and depart defeated; routed, we have seen enough deaths
have we seen, and we have laid waste great cities.
O Germans, the ruin by which [your towns] now lie shattered
is before your eyes, and the towns themselves are in your hands.
O at last, I pray, take pity on your own race,
nor turn your strong might against your country's vitals:
And you—be first to show mercy, you who trace your lineage from the South:
cast the weapons from your hand, [you] blood of the gods.
But if so great an ardour for war possesses your minds and hearts,
and it pleases you to indulge in this mad endeavour,
you may discover what vigorous valour can accomplish.
Enemies, to be sure, need not be sought by us far off:
the Turk stands round the walls of the Christians on every side.
Be bold, and confidently set your breast against the foe.
Break with your hand the spear of the Scythian robber, and him
lay face-down on the ground, and stretch him out beneath the high gates.
We have resources too, and our young warriors are still unscathed;
and various cities and peoples remain to aid us.
Therefore give over joining battle with friends,
and turn your headlong fury against the enemies of Christ.
They believe that, if they drive you from your homeland, nothing will prevent them
from bringing all Europe utterly beneath their own yoke.
But if old age, slow with chill and worn out by the years,
denies you this command, and your strength comes too late for brave deeds,
urge on your son, and those whom blood unimpaired by age
sustains, and whose powers stand in their own unbroken strength.
After king Solomon left mankind and the light behind him:
the barriers of the pit being burst and the chains broken,
borne on a black horse King Pluto flies through all
the gatherings of the sons of Abraham, scattering the fires of hatred.
To him the dead of night had added Tartarean Megaera
as a companion, and gave her wind-swift wings.
She entwined her hair with black serpents, scattering them
among the people; with envy and anger she spurred on
[the man] powerful with twice five tribes from Abraham's race
against the offspring of Judah and king Rehoboam.
On account of whose ill-omened rule and crooked ways,
Solomon's kingdom was divided: for there remained
with the Benjamites only the stock of Judah.
For Jeroboam held the rest under his sway.
With Jerusalem set at naught, they make for the realms of Babylon.

div.note: μεγαίρειν signifies to envy.

lg.l: And they despise God, and worship the godhead of calves:
forgetful of him who, when their fathers had been cast upon the shore of the Red Sea,
received them and so often brought them back from death,
and at last settled them safe on Jerusalem's mount.
Nay more, by the war and the arms of a bold people is harried
Rehoboam himself, because he spurned the commands of the Thunderer.
For the king of Egypt captures Jerusalem and, seizing the gold by force,
plunders the temple and opens up the ancient
treasures, the wealth of Solomon, and carries them off with him;
So God chastises the unjust rule of kings.
The son Abijah succeeded to his father's kingdom.
He, the sluggish peoples of Judah and the hosts unused to war,
suddenly calls to arms, and takes up the sword again,
and overcame Jeroboam, with the battle going his way.
Asa comes after his father, once the kindly light had withdrawn;
he was outstanding in piety, and a leader renowned in arms:
he destroyed the Ethiopians’ vast armies and founded
splendid cities; he shattered the images of the gods;
and protected the people under the ancient religion.
Jehoshaphat follows, outstanding in piety and in arms.
Him the neighbouring nations bind to themselves by treaty,
bringing gifts—talents of silver and gold,
wool-bearing flocks and he-goats. But Ahab persuaded him
that, setting out with him to the wars against the Syrians,
he should prepare to join forces and enter into a firm alliance:
He assented, and both kings were rushing into war.
But the Syrians think no man worth laying low in death
among Abraham’s descendants; in the thick gloom, Ahab alone
they track down; the king alone they summon into combat.
But he, the marks of a king laid aside, changes his arms
and his clothing, covered over with a common cloak,
so that no one might touch him or be able to recognize him.
But while the Syrians shout through their disordered ranks,
and track the man down: then by chance a winged arrow
someone drew out from his quiver, and bent the horn of the bow,
and drew it far back until the bent tips came together
one against the other, and with hands now level he touched
the iron point with his left hand, and his breast with his right hand and the string.
At once the shriek of the shaft, and the air sounding [with it],
trembling Ahab saw, and the point sticks fast in his body,
none knowing by what hand it was sped, by what whirl driven home:
[nor] who had brought the Syrians so great a glory without slaughter
of their own; the signal renown of the deed was left unspoken.
The king speaks to his driver, who guides the chariot and the reins:
Turn the horses about, he says, and have the chariot carried back
swiftly out of the field, for now a bitter wound
is consuming me, and everything around grows black with darkness.
He spoke, and little by little loosed himself from his body,
and with welling blood poured out his life over his armour.
Jehoshaphat returned, meaning to send a fleet to the Indies.
But of a sudden there rose a squall shrieking out of the North,
which falls upon the sea, and lifts the waves to the stars;
And the shallows leap up, and are churned by the swell with sand.
At once the ships, their beaks plunged under, [seek] the sea's
make for the lowest depths; with the joinings of their sides sprung, all
take in the hostile flood, and gape open at the seams.
And while Moab threatens the King with ruin and death,
he importunes God with vows and prayers, asking him to overwhelm
the enemies; and taught the people to praise Jehovah.
Relying on these weapons he drove back, with memorable slaughter,
the enemies, gleaming in arms and swollen with empty pride.
After him his son Jehoram assumed the rule of Judaea.
He stained his house with his brothers’ blood:
He scorns God, while the images of the dead
he worships with gifts and vows; the whole male line
fell, save for the younger son, heir of his father's
rule, and no less heir to the vices of his forefathers,
Ahaziah by name, whom Jehu put to death.
Hereupon his mother Athaliah rages, and butchers the whole
stock of David, and lays hold of the reins of the kingdom.
One of Ahaziah's sons had escaped; him
Jehoiada proclaims king by the herald's voice.
They greet the boy with applause, and rejoice as they gaze on him,
the sons of Abraham, and recognize in his face the features of his royal father;
and the queen soon paid with her blood the penalty of her crimes.

div.note: That is, of forefathers, as often in Virgil.

lg.l: Joash orders all the monuments of Jove to be destroyed,
and he tore down the altars of the Sun, and all the images:
and worshipped Jehovah with pure devotion.
But after faithful Achates yielded to fate,
he plunges headlong into every crime and scorns the Thunderer,
and put the high priest’s son to a cruel death.
forgetful both of his own honour and of his faithful father;
who [had gained] for him this realm, such as it is, who the sceptre and God
had won for him; the queen, her heart swollen by the kingdom she had seized,
he slew, and brought Joash himself back from death.
How little gratitude many people retain for a former service!
but soon he paid the penalty with his sacrilegious blood;
for the army of the Syrians invaded Judah, [and] the fields
it laid waste far and wide, and widowed the cities of their citizens.
And while the king himself, weighed down by disease, lay upon his couch,
his servants burst into the chamber and butcher their lord
Amaziah succeeds him, who [was] the greatest avenger of his father's
murder, and destroyed the mighty battle-lines of Edom.
Of these he hurls down headlong from a high crag
ten thousand, and as many he sent down to the shades by the sword.
But Joash threw him into confusion with a sudden disaster,
the king in Samaria, who forced the enemy ranks to bare their backs in flight

div.note: In 2 Chronicles 24 he is called Baal; this was the god of the Phoenicians, whom they call Beelsamen, that is, lord of heaven; the Greeks, however, call him Jove. Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 1.7. Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17, bears witness that all the gods are traced back to the Sun.
Samaria takes its name from Simron, or Mount Sameron, which Shemer sold to the Israelites.

lg.l: the enemy battle lines, and carried the king away to the city
untouched by so great a war and resting there unscathed.
He demolished the walls, and a mass of silver and gold
he carried away. The citizens of Zion conspired against the king,
whom, once captured, they struck down with a deadly wound.
His son Uzziah, illustrious in war and in arms,
extended Judah's dominion and rebuilt its walls.
He built up forts, and towers raised to the stars.
And he grafted pear-trees, and set vines in their rows.
His care was to look after the calves and the herds,
and the young of the sheep, and the she-goats that scorch everything bare.
He digs wells and channels streams into the fields,
so that clear springs or grass may not be wanting to the flocks.
He devised engines for the walls; but in his impiety he dares
to offer incense, and to touch holy things with profane hands.
Hence God in anger struck him with leprosy, and
cast him out of the temple and banished him beyond the city's walls.
He breathed out his unhappy life, and all
right to the kingdom passed to his son; he, under favorable
auspices, took up the reins of his father's kingdom,
and Jotham always paid honor to Jehovah.
All his enemies feared him, and year by year
they paid out many talents of gold and of silver.
In the manner of a camp he girds with battlements and rampart
his towns; then he founds various strongholds in the mountains.
And when the king laid his head down in death, he left the sceptre
to Ahaz, who possessed none of his father's virtue,
no true martial mettle, none of his ancestral religion.

div.note: He carried Amaziah off to Jerusalem.

lg.l: The living bodies of his sons — an abomination — by the unspeakable custom
of the Phoenicians he was wont to burn with flames set beneath.
He bars the priests from the house of Solomon,
and fills the city with forbidden altars of the gods.
Enemies on this side and enemies on that, by the offended divine power
sent forth, they lay Judaea waste with conquering arms.
Assyria is implored for help; gifts are sent —
treasures, an untold weight of silver and of gold —
by Ahaz in his trembling; but nothing was achieved by all
the outlay of such great undertakings: neither gifts, nor gold,
nor did great prayers avail; for when the city of Damascus
had been stormed, Assyria ravages rich Judaea:
His son Hezekiah, a man most observant of what is right,
holds the sceptre after him; he unbarred the Temple, and therewith
restored his fathers' worship; solemn vows
he paid to the King of the heaven-dwellers in the house of Solomon.
Then to sacrifice seven bullocks from an untouched herd
he ordained, and as many sheep chosen after the custom.
Seven lambs, seven shaggy-bodied he-goats.
And he tore down the altars, and the empty images of the gods.
He overthrew the groves; beneath the iron two-edged axe rings the tall
ash, and he cuts down the pines grown up to the stars.
He broke the serpent to which
the faithless nation rendered solemn honours; an army with weapons of every kind
