under Sennacherib invaded Judah, and threatens Jerusalem.
But the King, as soon as the plains smoking with dust
he descried far off, and saw the gleaming columns,
and he heard the approach of footsteps and the snorting of horses:
straightway to the Temple and to the high citadels of Solomon
he advances, a great throng of nobles attending him;
and he kindles the altars with vows and makes [them] steam with incense.
And from the high threshold he pours out sorrowful words.
While he implores Jehovah's help against such great hosts,
others dig trenches before the gates, or stones and stakes
they bring them up; the walls have been encircled by a motley ring—
matrons and boys: the last struggle calls them all.
But meanwhile the huge army of the Assyrians, in a lofty
camp, takes up position before the city and invests its walls.
Behold, the almighty Father sent down from heaven a servant,
a winged one, who in a single night laid low so many thousands,
and God took away all the enemy's force and all fear.
Hereupon his son Manasseh raises the sceptre and the rods of office,
unlike his father, and a contriver of crimes; this is he
who in his savagery paid worship to the king of hell,
who so often stained Jerusalem with human blood,
and cast his own children onto the pyres, and burned them alive,
and worshipped all the stars in the dark-blue sky:
and he sets the image of the grove in Solomon's temple;
he consults too the lowest shades of Acheron in Avernus.
He observes the cries of birds and the omens of their flight,
and he observes forbidden days, and into the opened
breasts of beasts, gazing eagerly, he consults the still-breathing entrails.
Nor would he have set either number or limit to his vices,
Had the king not been led captive to Babylon and confined
in tight chains, acknowledged his guilt, and of his own accord,
called, suppliant and humble, upon the God of his fathers.
The Almighty, overlooking such great crimes, heard from high
heaven the groans and words of the man who called.
At last he pardoned him, and sent the king back into his own kingdom.
Then the king overthrew the altars of the gods, tore up
the groves, and purifies Solomon's temple and the city.
But savage Amon follows in the footsteps of his wicked fathers
and worships gods bereft of light.
His own servants conspired for his destruction,
and the king received their sword-points in a welter of blood,
and spewed out his wretched soul; then Josiah took up
the sceptre; in piety he was second to none of his fathers.
the images, the altars, and all the monuments of the gods
destroys, and in prayer worships the great godhead of Jehovah;
moreover, as a suppliant he lays an offering upon the altars.
The bones of the priests, dug out from their tombs, he burned.
When he had heard the law, he tore his own garments;
he restores the temple, and joyfully provides the feasts
of the Passover; countless kids and lambs he shares out
among the people, to which he had added three thousand bullocks
the gifts and the gladness of God.
The nobles too, each according to his means, gladly
bring gifts, and load the altars, and slaughter bullocks;
The Levites lay the sacred offerings upon the flame.
Duly the priests, sprinkling the doorposts with blood,
while others set the bronze cauldrons in order and tend the flames.
Afterwards, when he had attacked the king of Egypt on an ill-judged
plan, [and was] fighting in the midst of thousands — alas,
a dreadful thing — an arrow, gliding in and whirring on its wings,
runs him through, and lays the king low with a deadly wound.
O you destined to return to Zion as its grief and great glory!
This first day gave you to war, this same day takes you away,
though even so you leave behind huge heaps of Egyptians.
And now flying Rumour, the herald of so great a grief,
shook Jerusalem, and set the city ablaze with wailing;
the houses roar, and the sky resounds with loud lamentation:
no otherwise than if, with the enemy let in, all
Jerusalem were falling, or ancient Hebron, and raging flames
were rolling over the rooftops of men and over Jehovah’s temple.
Alas for that piety, alas for that ancient faith, and that right hand
unconquered in war! No one could have confronted him with impunity,
when he was armed, whether he went on foot against the foe,
or dug his spurs into the flanks of his foaming horse.
His son Joasus succeeded to his father's kingdom;
whom the king of Egypt carried off captive, entrusting the reins

div.note: In the rites of Osiris, Egypt is called Chemia, as though Chamia, from Ham. * The Pharians are so called from Pharos, an island of Egypt.

lg.l: entrusting the [charge] of affairs to his brother; this is that Jehoiakim
against whom the Chaldaean king directed harsh force and chains,
and left the ancestral kingdom to his son Jehoiachin.
Him too the tyrant, from his father's sceptre and his throne,
drove out, and called Jehoiachin's brother Zedekiah to the throne.
And about this time the neighbouring peoples on every side
Holofernes terrifies with arms, and in his pride compels [them]
to accept the bridle of Babylonian rule; but through cunning
[she] overcame Holofernes, sunk deep in sleep and wine,
great-hearted Judith, and beheaded him with a sharp blade.
For with a strong hand, in a long siege, he was pressing hard
Bethulia, [that] Assyrian commander, and a great fear

div.note: This Jehoiakim surrendered himself to Nebuchadnezzar when besieged, at the end of the third year of his reign or the beginning of the fourth, after hostages had been given—among them Daniel and the three youths—together with part of the Temple vessels. Dan. 1. He was left in his kingdom as a tributary; but after defecting to the king of Egypt, he was captured a second time by the Babylonians and died in the eleventh year of his reign.

This Jehoiachin, or Jechonias, surrendered himself, together with his mother, to the Chaldaeans in the third month of his reign and, being taken to Babylon with his entire family, inaugurated the seventy-year captivity.
Zedekiah was the son of Josiah and the uncle of Jechonias, 2. Reg. cap. 24; but by a Hebrew idiom he is called his brother, 2. Chron. 36. 10.

Here I follow Genebrard, who refers this history to the time of Nebuchadnezzar. In the thirteenth year of his reign he sent Holofernes into Judaea and Samaria; in the nineteenth he removed the remnant of the Jews to Babylon. Earlier too the Jews had been scattered under Sennacherib, and it is of that dispersion that Achior speaks in cap. 5 of the book of Judith, and perhaps Isaiah in cap. 1. Others refer this history to the times of Cambyses or Ahasuerus; but the kings of the Persians were never called Nebuchadnezzar. Genebr. Chron. lib. 2.

lg.l: he let loose upon the citizens, who dare neither trust themselves to the open field
nor close hand to hand, but [choose] the broad walls
to defend them with a rampart and interpose walls against death.
Equipped with wiles and conscious of her beauty, this maiden
plans to capture the commander by guile and envelop him in flame,
and turns such arts over in her heart;
first she washes herself in running water, then,
with her bared limbs drenched in oil, she glistens.
Then, as customary, she curls her hair with a hot iron.
She braids her hair with gold; over the top of her breast runs
a pliant circlet of twisted gold about her neck;
a golden brooch clasps up her purple robe.
Judith thus, gleaming with gold and comely in purple,
at last goes forth, a serving-girl attending her;
and she cuts short all delay; as these two go, the whole
company of the chief men at the gates, of young and of old,
escorts them with prayers; on the wall and on the high towers
stand the frightened mothers, and follow them with their eyes as they go
toward the foremost ranks and the squadrons bright with bronze.
When the sentries of the camp see these women drawing near
they run to meet them and ask the reason for the journey and her name;
and they pick a hundred young men out of the whole column
to bring Merari['s daughter] unharmed to the commander's tent,
but he, alarmed by the sudden sight, asks them both

div.note: A woman is called "virgo" even after she has been joined to a husband: as "Ah, unhappy maiden, what madness has seized you?" &c., Eclogue 8, of Pasiphaë.
Judith, the daughter of Merari.

lg.l: He asks of what race she is, from what home, what cause compelled her
to venture upon difficult paths through weapons and enemies.
The warrior-woman, answering him with her heart composed,
with her gaze lowered to the ground, speaks thus:
"All things indeed, my captain, whatever I shall confess to you, will be
true,” she says, “nor shall I deny that I am one of Abraham’s descendants;
nor will you find me false or deceitful. This, first of all, I
foretell you, and, repeating it, I will warn you again and again:
that these towns cannot be razed by Assyrian weapons,
if Abraham's sons keep the precepts of the holy prophets,
if they remain pure in the religion of their fathers.
But if our own band shall violate the holy things of Jehovah
and the Jewish people prove contemptuous of God,
then a great destruction is to come upon us and upon our children —
this we know, and that those fates await our descendants.
See, now Abraham's sons have profaned the temples of Jehovah,
they have seized the ritual fare, and with bloodstained hands
have dared to lay hold of the firstfruits and the consecrated beasts.
For dreadful hunger, together with the wrong done to the heaven they have scorned,
drives these men to devour the consecrated tables with their jaws;
the wicked have spurned the laws and the commands of the Thunderer;
therefore the Lord has abandoned Jerusalem and the Temple
as plunder for its enemies, and threatens that he will overthrow its highest towers
that he will overthrow the cities of Judah and consign them to destruction.
But you, for the rest, lay aside all anxiety;
Prepare yourselves in spirit for battle, and anticipate the war with hope.
I shall hand over to you the towns of the Jews, captured by force.
Either I shall now win praise for rich spoils seized,
or for a glorious death; now lead the young men out of the camp,
Cross this ridge, and I will bring you there by a safe path.
Judith had said this; the commander had long been scanning the speaker’s face and eyes
and her whole body with his gaze,
staring in astonishment at how regal finery
clothed her smooth shoulders in purple, how her milk-white neck
gleamed with gold, and how her hair was bound with gold;
but above all the grace of her beauty moves him, and her youth,
as do her cheeks, aflame with a blush, and her feigned words.
And while he hangs on her with his eyes, and fixes his gaze upon the maiden,
the wretched man burns, and frenzy has coursed through his bones.
And now one day and then another had passed, and they
They discussed many things among themselves in varied speech,
But more and more the wound of love grows raw;
he burns, helpless in mind, and is eaten away by a hidden fire.
So when he felt himself held fast by such a plague,
the commander Holofernes prepared a banquet in the midst of the camp
and, beside himself, inflamed his unspeakable passion.
He invites Judith, and receives her in a golden chamber;
and the commander himself and all the young men roar with joy.
Sated with the feast, he pours out the Lenaean offering.
And he drains gilded bowls of foaming Iacchus.
After he had passed this last night amid false rejoicings,
heavy with sleep and dripping with wine,
the ill-starred bedchamber held him, and as he lay there weighed upon him
sweet and deep repose, most like to peaceful death.
Then the watchmen settled themselves in the chambers; silence falls
in the night, and sleep enfolds their weary limbs.
Meanwhile the heroic woman, still awake, came upon Holofernes,
draws [it] from beside his head, and tears the sword from its sheath;
and she twisted his hair in her left hand, and with her right the flashing [blade]
she raised, and cleaves the neck through with a double stroke.
Then she herself carries off the wretch's head, and left the trunk
as the blood spurted; warmed by dark gore,
the ground and the couch are soaked; then the head, to be carried away, to her maidservant
she handed over; she withdraws from the camp and makes for safety.
So she returned victorious, and by this death subdued the godless.
So the Stygian king held the human race under a vast siege,
until Christ came down from heaven,
and by his own power, not by craft, or guile, or arms,
conquered the world and cut down the King of hell:
then he returned, flying on high, and triumphing over the enemy
he left us peace and liberty.
After this, from the vents of cruel Dis burst forth
so many forms of wickedness, so many dreadful monsters, as had never before
had never before come beneath the starry vault of heaven.
For the almighty Father, deeply stirred, and kindled with
terrible wrath, because the faithless race of Jacob
had so often scorned the law and the answers of the prophets,
and so often worshipped the images of the gods — prone to every
sin, and always to deadly crimes:
forsook the offspring of Judah, and left Jerusalem
as prey to her enemies; to Satan was granted the power
to plunder the city and to despoil the proud temple,
and [that] the treacherous race should pay for its sins with deserved punishments.
Without delay the Stygian King, founder of the city of Babylon,
rouses the Chaldeans against Jerusalem, and they in a dense column
fall upon it, and assault the high city with siege-works.
Now the trumpet, far off, with its ringing bronze, a terrible sound
blared out; a shout follows, and the sky bellows back,
the enemy press on all together, their tortoise formed,
and they make ready to fill the trenches and to tear away the palisade.
Some seek an entry, and [seek] to climb the walls with ladders
where the battle line is thin and daylight shows through the ring,
not so densely packed with men; the citizens pour every kind of missile against them,

div.note: The city was taken three times, in the reigns of Joachin, Jechoniah and Zedekiah, and the people three times carried off to Babylon by the Chaldaeans, whose empire lasted only seventy-eight years. There were but three kings, namely Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, and Belshazzar.

lg.l: every kind [of missile], the citizens, and to drive them back with stout pikes—
trained by long warfare to defend their walls.
They also rolled down rocks with deadly force, in hopes that somehow
one might break through the shielded formation, though they all
are content to endure whatever comes beneath the close-packed tortoise.
The enemy hurl every kind of missile and raging flames against them,
and repeatedly batter the walls with a ram.
Within, the wrath of God raged with unseen shafts,
while plague, while ill-counselling hunger carry off so many thousands.
The citizens do not escape death, but on the very threshold,
within their native walls, and among the safe places of their homes,
pierced through, they breathe out their lives — a pitiable sight!
God has withdrawn, leaving these shrines and altars behind,
he by whom alone this dominion had stood; the citizens tried to bring help
in vain, and some rushed into the midst of the fighting.
The one deliverance for the conquered is to hope for no deliverance.
Some stand within, to right and left, before the towers,
armed with steel, their high heads flashing with crests;
These throw open the gate and invite the enemy to the walls;
those dare to close hand to hand and to charge out from the walls.
But others—so great is the confusion—try to close the gates,
and dare neither open a way for their own, nor within the walls
receive them as they beg; and a most wretched slaughter arises
as some defend the entrances with weapons and others rush upon those weapons.
Shut out before the eyes and the faces of their weeping parents,
a part, with the crush pressing on, into the sheer trenches
is rolled headlong; a part, blind and driven on with reins let loose,
batters against the gates and the doorposts stiff with their bar.
The mothers themselves, from the walls, in the utmost struggle
(love of their fatherland, falling in this pitiable disaster, shows [them the way])
in their alarm hurl weapons by hand, and with hard oak
poles and fire-hardened stakes, imitate iron;
headlong, and they are the first to dare to die in defense of the walls:
Alas, every effort is in vain, and vain the weapons
wherever they hurl them, for Sion's last night has come:
The enemy throw down the walls and lay the ramparts open
with great force; no longer do the closed walls shelter the citizens;
nay more, within the gates, and on the very
embankments of the walls, they join battle, and flood the trenches with blood,
a way is made by force; they burst the entrances and slaughter the foremost,
the enemy pour in and fill the place far and wide with soldiers.
They plunder the houses, they hurl flames to the rooftops.
The ancient city falls, that held sway through many years,
and everywhere along the streets very many lifeless
bodies are strewn, and through the houses and the hallowed
thresholds of the Thunderer; grim slaughter is done with no distinction.
Untamed Mars rages; in the midst of the thousands blazes
pale Tisiphone; Vulcan, with the reins let loose,
rages wildly and sends a black cloud bursting up to the sky.
smoking with a pitch-black whirlwind and glowing ash,
and he heaves up balls of flame and licks the stars.
The sons of Abraham, meanwhile, tear down towers and the roofs of houses,
and their gables; with these, when they see that the end has come,
they make ready to defend themselves with weapons, now in death's extremity.
When the King sees the fall of the captured city, from the palace
he withdrew by night, attended by a few friends.
Then he hastened his flight in the woods and trusted to the night.
And when he seemed to have escaped disaster and completed the whole
journey, not far from Jericho a shout reaches his ears;
he hears horses, he hears the din and the signals of pursuers;
and an enemy band, amid the confusion of a sudden uproar,
through the treachery of the terrain, in the dim shadow of night,
carries off the overpowered king as he attempts many things in vain, and
led him to the king of Babylon; the latter, before the father’s very
eyes, put all his sons to death,
and seized the father himself, as he wept and lamented bitterly,
in close-fitting manacles, and deprived him of his sight.
And now Nabuzaradan, a savage commander flashing in arms,
marches up against the city of Jerusalem with many thousands,
to demolish the temple and every building from the rooftop down.
Conspicuous on his horse amid the ranks and elated by success in
battle, he charges forward.
Before the very entrance, on the temple’s outer threshold,
he exults in his weapons, gleaming with the light of bronze:

div.note: He succeeded Holofernes in this position.

lg.l: Like a snake when, fed on noxious grasses, it comes forth into the light,
which, swollen, cold winter kept covered beneath the earth,
now, his slough laid aside, made new and glossy with youth,
he coils his slippery back, his breast reared up,
towering toward the sun, and darts his three-forked tongue from his mouth.
He himself, among the foremost, seizing a two-edged axe, breaks through the hard
thresholds and wrenches the doorposts from their hinges,
bronze-clad; the door totters under the ram's repeated blows; at last
the house comes into view within, and the long halls lie open.
And now the priests, in vain around the altars,
rushing headlong like doves in a black storm,
packed close together; but no sacred fillet shields them,
through the sanctity of the place; but without any distinction he
slays, and has defiled the temple with human blood,
and plundered all the treasure and the ancient sacred monuments,
and set fire to the temple, and to the temple's inner sanctuary.
At once the devouring fire, driven by the wind, up to the topmost gables
rolls on; the flames tower upward, and the blaze rages to the sky.
After Jerusalem was seen collapsing into the flames,
the leader returned bearing the spoil, the greatest treasure
snatched from the burning inner shrines: Jehovah's tables,
and mixing-bowls of solid gold, and captured vestments.
So the city, once proud with so many peoples and dwellings,
queen of Asia, the golden house of Jehovah, in war
renowned, has collapsed, and been laid low from her high summit.
So Babylon, the head of a Stygian empire, at last
overthrew Jerusalem, and tore her up entirely from her deepest
foundations, and kept the citizens oppressed beneath its mighty rule.
For seventy years, as the months rolled on, he jeered at them
with unremitting arrogance, while forcing the unarmed—
unknown, broken by war, and driven back by fate—
to endure another's commands, and to obey proud masters:
So the king of hell holds sway over the whole world.
But the almighty Father, not forgetful of the promise long ago
repeatedly made to Abraham, nor of the covenant struck
with Judah, sent prophets who sang of things to come
concerning Christ, who, the flower of the men of old and the valor of heroes,
will destroy the empire of Satan, and will found heavenly
walls, and will call [them] Christians after his own name,
Christians, masters of the world and a toga-clad nation,
so it is decreed; an age will come, as the lustres glide away:
when the house of Abraham [shall press] Rome and proud Babylon
into servitude, and will rule over conquered Hell.
For God will transfer Babylon’s kingdom to the Persians, and from there
will transfer it to the Greeks, and from them at last to Rome.
Christ and his companions will bear many hardships, long
exiles, and disasters, and in the end every form of death
under the Hectorean race, for three hundred years, to be exact:
Then Christ will, from its deepest foundations, Satan’s kingdom
uproot, and with mighty power fortify the holy city.
Then too it will be a joy to raise up the fated masses of the walls,
and to carry the stones of Judaea up on their shoulders.
Thus at last the king—Christ—will conquer black Avernus
and with his voice will bridle the tyrant of hell.

div.note: Down to the times of Constantine the Great.

div.p: After the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity had elapsed and the Jews had been granted permission to return to their homeland, the Temple was rebuilt together with the city, while Satan tried in vain to cause delays. And although the Jews, both during the captivity and after their return home, were often brought into extreme peril, partly by domestic dissensions and partly by external enemies, God nevertheless, mindful of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church, raised up various defenders and champions of his people: namely Esther, Alexander the Macedonian, Ptolemy Philadelphus, Mattathias with his sons Judas, Jonathan, and Simon Hyrcanus, who were types of Christ, the champion of the heavenly Jerusalem. But when God had been provoked by the crimes of King Aristobulus and his successors, he permitted Judaea to fall under Roman power; for the empire of Babylon had by then been transferred to Rome, where Pluto is accorded various honours and his kingdom is spread far and wide. With Jerusalem reduced to servitude, the family of the Maccabees extinguished, and the line of David removed, Judaea was subjected to Idumaean kings. Meanwhile Christ, so long awaited and so often promised, was conceived by the Holy Spirit at the angel's annunciation and, after various portents had preceded his birth, was born of the Virgin Mary. A digression is made in praise of Christ, and he is shown to be the sole God of the Jews and the Gentiles. The vanity of the Greeks in multiplying gods is condemned; the Jews are admonished and exhorted to acknowledge Christ as their Leader and Shepherd.

lg.l: After it seemed good to Jehovah to overthrow Jerusalem’s state and Solomon’s kingdom—
though it deserved destruction—and the proud Temple fell,
The Temple and Zion’s entire royal palace, collapsed to the ground, are smoking;
then, weeping, the remnant of Abraham’s descendants leave the fields of their homeland
and wander through unfamiliar cities;
until at last, when the unhappy years were spent
of exile, the Persians suddenly laid aside their fierce
hearts, by God’s will; above all, the king himself
assumes a peaceful disposition and a kindly mind toward the wretched;
to whom he grants the freedom to build temples for the Thunderer;
and to build Jerusalem’s strongholds and renew its houses;
and to return to their longed-for homeland; but against them
the Stygian King sets himself and contrives reasons
for delay; but he who wields the reins of the world
scattered Satan's attempts into the fleeting winds,
tearing them all apart and consigning his futile
plans to the clouds; for the lofty homeland of Zion saw them return,
and they build for the Lord a temple of marble,
but unequal to the first; and the law and the commandments rehearses
Ezra; Nehemiah chastises with bitter words
the ungrateful people, which, restored to its fathers' shores,
disregarded God’s benefactions and, of the evils of old
forgetful, was rushing headlong into the sins of the fathers.
Fierce Haman resolved to destroy in a single massacre all who were of Judah’s blood,

div.note: Cyrus permitted the Temple to be built; Cambyses obstructed it, and Darius furthered it. Artaxerxes (concerning whom, see Daniel, chapters 9 and 14; Ezra, chapters 4, 5, and 6; and Nehemiah, chapter 2) sent Ezra to Jerusalem.

lg.l: to destroy [them] in a single slaughter, did not a loving care resist,
the care of the King of the heaven-dwellers, who the affairs of men and of gods
governs with eternal sway, and terrifies with the thunderbolt.
For the maiden Esther, of surpassing beauty, the tyrant
softens, and her own people from the abominable treachery
sets free, guiltless as they are; and the [death] which he was levelling at the Hebrew,
that death Haman himself, the contriver of the crimes, undergoes.
The leader Zerubbabel, a scion of David’s noble blood,
from whose ancient stock Christ descends,
brought back from Babylon, bound fast in long servitude,
his companions into their ancestral kingdom, and rebuilt the Temple.
Moreover, foremost amid such labours, he
urges on his wavering companions and girds himself with like arms:
Thus, after a long exile, from the shores of Babylon
Jesus led us into our homeland, the heavenly Jerusalem.
While Alexander the Great thunders in savage arms
against the Tyrians, after subduing the Persians, and threatens to cast down the greatest
cities of Judah he will cast down and give over to destruction,
all ablaze in vestment and insignia, to meet him
comes Jaddua, at that time high priest by lot,
When the King saw him, he worshipped him with lowered face.
For the one seen by him in his sleep, in that very dress,
is the Almighty Father, who [foretold] that the King, with fortune favouring him in war,

div.note: This king of the Persians was Artaxerxes Longimanus, the son of Xerxes and grandson of Darius Hystaspis. See Joseph. Ant. l. 11. c. 6.
Zorobabel had two sons, Rhesa and Abiud: from Rhesa came Mary, from Abiud Joseph; Luke follows the former genealogy, Matthew the latter.

lg.l: He had foretold that he would subdue [his] enemies, and would be great.
Thus the city escaped, untouched by war and resting unharmed,
but it found Egypt’s tyrant to be no such man—
for he, after entering the city by guile,
carries off abundant booty and deprives of their cultivators
the neighbouring fields; but Philadelphus sent those men back to the longed-for altars
of their longed-for homeland, safe and rejoicing.
Then [he gave] a table of solid gold and mixing-bowls to the friendly
he gave to the High Priest; he in turn gave gifts to the King,
and the Law, which the King had long desired to see
translated into Greek; but the ruler of hell
afterward shook the city with dissensions and surrendered it as spoil to its enemy,
Antiochus, who immediately disfigured everything
with slaughter and with flames, profanes the holy things,
strips the Temple bare, defiles the altars with slaughtered
swine, and orders the ancient monuments to be destroyed.
Mattathias, his mind maddened, could not bear this sight,
(who had a mighty lineage from a hundred forefathers, and illustrious was his father's
reputation for valour, while he himself was most fierce in arms)
but he armed the young men, and broke down the accursed altars.
There gather those whom either cruel hatred of the tyrant,
or keen fear drives; but the harshness of death
suddenly carried him off; Judas took up the war,
his son; he, with success ever favourable, the hostile [ranks]

div.note: Ptolemy the son of Lagus, that is.
Concerning the high-priesthood, that is. See Josephus.
For he was of the tribe of Levi, and the son of John, who was the son of Simeon, begotten of Asamonaeus, who gave his name to the whole family of the Maccabees.

lg.l: He scattered the enemy ranks; no vast army
of Antiochus the Great terrified him; nor the arms and threats
of Antiochus's son; but with Simon, through the enemy
drawn up against him, he charges; his headlong momentum bears him onward,
and the breeze tosses his streaming crest as his chariot charges head-on,
and both dye their flashing swords with the blood
of the enemy, and turn whole columns to trembling flight.
And just as fires let loose from different quarters
in a parched wood, and thickets crackling with laurel,
or when in swift descent from the high mountains
the foaming rivers give out their roar, and run down into the sea,
each having laid waste its own path; with no less speed do both,
Judas and Simon rush through the fighting; now, now
rage seethes within; their hearts, which know no defeat, are bursting;
now with all their strength they press on to inflict wounds.
He restores ancestral worship and revisits the temple,
now left desolate, and Judas purifies the altars,
and orders solemn processions to be led to the temple.
Many a victim falls in sacrifice to God before the altars at Judas’s hand;
Moreover, in ancestral song he proclaimed the honors God deserved.
Antiochus, beaten, to enter into a treaty with Judas
is compelled; but after the treaty had been struck, and all
the terms settled, the treacherous man violated them;
and he tore down both the walls and the bulwarks of the temple;
and shook the whole city with great lamentations.
Those who were now hoping for rest from war and safety for their fortunes
again demand arms and complain of the king
as faithless, and they pity Jerusalem’s unjust fate.
After this Demetrius, but not unpunished, challenges
[challenges] Judas to battle, who scorns Bacchides’ army,
and who destroyed Nicanor's squadrons, and him
with a lightning shaft sent down to the gloomy waters.
Now the martial hero was leading a thousand men,
when a fresh army, gleaming in arms, invades
Judaea, and over the plains a savage dread more and more
grows; [he sees] a cloud billowing up in black dust,
and darkness rising across the whole sky.
Yet confidence did not fail bold Judas,
although many had deserted him out of terror.
But he girds himself, and at the same time equips his comrades with arms.
They were few in number, but their courage was vigorous in war;
when he saw them massed together and daring to enter battle,
he began as follows: “Young men, ever most valiant at heart,
you see now what fortune attends our cause;
let us die for our country, and rush into the midst of the fighting.
Though we have not as many lives and hands [as they],
yet let us not be disgraced by base fear, nor
lose heart,” he says, “now, after so many valiant deeds,
and wars won, and such great dangers endured:
for God will come to the aid of us and our people,
whose aid we have so often proved in times of need."

div.note: This was the son of Seleucus, who seized the kingdom of Syria after King Antiochus and Lysias had been killed.
Bacchides, governor of Mesopotamia, a friend of Antiochus Epiphanes.
Nicanor, Demetrius's most trusted friend, who accompanied Demetrius in his flight from Rome.

lg.l: Is it not better to pour out life with much blood,
than, with arms laid down, to obey proud masters?
Or you, O comrades, you who have followed me and my arms —
shall I bare my back in flight and leave [you] to unspeakable death?
Shall I turn my back, and shall this land see Judas in flight?
Is death so very wretched? I am resolved to endure whatever bitterness there is
in death rather than drag out a shameful life;
never shall I return inglorious to my native city.
He spoke, and hurled his spear against the enemy facing him,
as he charges: the whistling cornel shaft sounds and through the air
cuts true; at that very instant a tremendous shout rises,
they clash together with a horrifying roar; with the blare of trumpets
terrible, the mountains resound; blood on every side in streams
is poured out, the earth groaned, and is covered with the bodies
of the falling warriors; the sky is shrouded in a darkness of missiles.
But in the midst of the slaughter Judas exults,
engaging one after another at close quarters; this man from afar, that man from afar
he lays low with deadly javelins, and brandishes his sword,
a lightning blade, foaming with much blood, until at last
he scattered the central ranks in shameful panic.
As soon as the enemy saw this — those who keep the left [wing] in check —

div.note: The left wing.

lg.l: the columns, and soon they swept their whole battle-line against Judas,
assailing him from behind; all their strength closes upon one man.
Overwhelmed by their vast number and engaged in an unequal
fight, Judas has strength neither to withstand so great [an onslaught] with his shield,
nor with his right hand: so, with weapons hurled in from every side,
he is overwhelmed: about his hollow temples the helmet clatters with unceasing
ringing, and under the javelins the solid bronze gives way,
and the plumes are struck from his head; nor does the shield-boss hold out
against the blows; they redouble their spear-strokes, and wear down his back,
those enemy squadrons; then over his whole body the sweat
streams down and pours a pitch-black—nor can he breathe—
stream; labored gasping shakes his weary limbs.
At last he succumbed, overcome by superior force and a wound.
And he laid down his head, taken by death, leaving his arms behind.
Our Judas restored the heavenly Jerusalem —
Christ — and the spoils, as a trophy, from the slain and routed [foes]
he wrested from the enemies by dying; glory came
at the cost of much blood; thus he did not allow his wounds to go unavenged,
but through wounds he sought a glorious death;
by this he subdued the king of hell and the Stygian battalions,
with these arms alone he even strikes terror into hell;
with these, exulting, he breaks through the sanctuaries of dread Dis,
and with these, as victor, he returns thence to his Father's abode,
thence to come back again, blazing in the clouds; at their
horrifying flash the columns of Dis will tremble.
And when they see Christ and his gleaming arms, through the air
the enemies, thunderstruck, will flee with howling uproar.
They will long to be hidden in the mountains and in dark retreats;
These are Christ's returns and the long-awaited triumphs.
Jonathan succeeded Judas and, with success in battle,
scattered two thousand men, and who drove out all
the enemies from Judaea, and made a treaty with Bacchides.
His friendship Demetrius courts, and that same friendship
Alexander courts it with gifts; the leader Jonathan preferred him to Demetrius,
the leader Jonathan; but after Demetrius withdrew to the shades,
Jonathan bound to himself by a firm treaty
his son Demetrius; victory always went to him;
until, captured through Tryphon's treachery and cunning,
he met his death. Simon took his place, who ringed the walls
of Jerusalem with siege-mounds; then he tore out from its lowest foundations
the citadel standing on the sheer height, and reared up to the stars
from the topmost hills; from there the Greeks used to hurl
every kind of missile against the temple and the roofs of Zion.
He besieged Tryphon and destroyed many towns that he had captured
by force, and he frees his homeland from every tribute.
Always with the success he wished for he fought against the enemy.
But at last by the treachery of his son-in-law, amid the cups, by the sword
he fell; his son Hyrcanus succeeded him; he

div.note: This Alexander was the son of Antiochus Epiphanes; coming into Syria, he seized Ptolemais and defeated Demetrius.
This Demetrius, the son of Demetrius, with the help of his father-in-law Ptolemy Philometor, overcame Alexander and recovered his father's kingdom.
Tryphon was one of Alexander's generals; when Demetrius had been captured by the Parthians, he treacherously seized Jonathan. * Namely, Ptolemy's [son-in-law].
John, the son of Simon, called Hyrcanus from a certain Hyrcanus whom he had defeated.

lg.l: Antiochus, who was then keeping the city under siege,
he won over with gifts and sought peace.
And since he no longer placed his hope in his own arms,
the affairs of Italy and the triumphs of the Romans
having been heard, he renews the treaty that the fathers once struck
with the people descended from Aeneas; he captured many towns
and overthrew their power, and laid low from her height the lofty
Sebaste; at last, his enemies utterly beaten, among the shades
he lies dead; after him comes, bearing the emblems of kingship,
his son Aristobulus, defiled by his mother's abominable death
and no less defiled by the blood of his brother Antigonus.
who met a wretched death, vomiting gore from his mouth.
His brother Alexander took up the kingdom, and he,
his own brother slain, bloodies himself with much slaughter
of the citizens; but at last they, exhausted, confront him as he rages abominably,
and stand round him in arms; he, relentless in his wrath,
rages against innocent and guilty alike with haughty
command; and when he attacked Ptolemy under unfavourable
fates, he lost the battle and was forced into a shameful flight,

div.note: This was the man surnamed Pius, who granted the Jews a seven-day truce for the Feast of Tabernacles; he also sent bulls with gilded horns, and cups of gold and silver filled with spices.
Samaria was named Sebaste by Herod in honour of Augustus.
Aristobulus was the first to set the diadem upon his own head, 481 years after the return from Babylon; he killed his mother by starvation, etc.
Ptolemy Lathyrus, who, driven out of his kingdom by his mother Cleopatra, held Cyprus.

lg.l: he was forced to turn his back in flight and leave his comrades as prey
for the enemy, and to be punished with a wretched death; to tell it
I shudder [to relate] — how, to be feasted upon, he ordered set on the fathers' tables
the bodies of their sons: Ptolemy ordered it, and none avenged it.
At last, seized by a wasting sickness, down to the realm of death
he sent his unhappy soul, leaving his kingdom
to his wife: from her the sceptre and the strongholds are wrested by her son
Aristobulus by name; the elder [brother] content with the office
of high priest: but discord fell upon the brothers
by the counsel of Antipater, on whom Caesar many honours
bestowed. Aristobulus, twice an exile, his kingdoms having been taken away,
at last, after enduring various reversals and wars to the end,
drains cups drugged with Lethean poisons.
Neither your piety, Hyrcanus, nor your priestly fillet shielded you,
whom the tyrant cut down under a false [charge of] treason,
although the worn-out strength in his body was already growing cold.
Earlier his nephew had mutilated the wretched man about the temples by tearing off
his ears — Antigonus did it — and then drove him from his native shores.
Nor does Antigonus rejoice for long; his uncle’s fate too
awaits him, and soon he occupied the selfsame ground.
Scipio cuts down Alexander, and the Triumvir his brother
Antigonus; when the axe struck his neck, in him

div.note: When Alexander died, his wife Alexandra succeeded to the kingdom. * Hyrcanus. † See Josephus, Antiquities, book 14, chapter 15. ‡ Herod the Great. * Antony.

lg.l: The kingdom of Jerusalem and the renowned house of Judah have been overthrown.
For the King made away with his wife Mariamne, and
Thus Judah’s line was extinguished; and at last
Caesar transferred Judaea’s sceptre to an Idumaean tyrant.
And now, a foreigner having gained possession of Jerusalem and the sceptre,
and the memorials of the Kings done away with, and the senate [as well],
the Stygian King, hoping that Zion had utterly perished,
exults; the seat of his empire, to the city of Babylon —
which enclosed seven citadels together for herself within a single wall—
he had transferred it; three hundred shrines for him throughout the city,
all very great, glow with incense; fires keep watch upon the altars,
the everlasting sentinels of the gods, and with the blood of beasts
the ground [was] rich, and the thresholds breathed with varied garlands.
In every temple, a chorus of matrons; in every temple, altars:
Before the altars, slaughtered bullocks strewed the ground.
They worshipped countless gods, and Erebus, and Chaos,
and threefold Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana:
the Dirae, the mother of the Eumenides, and the great sister
(she who is called the mother of the gods, whose delight is Dindymus
and tower-crowned cities, and lions paired at the reins.)

div.note: These were the children of Alexander, whom Scipio killed.
By the mother of the Eumenides the poets understand Night; by the great sister, Earth.

lg.l: and Latona's twofold offspring, and two-faced Janus,
and the sacred springs and rivers, and whatever of the high aether
worship [there is], and the deities that are in the azure sea;
These Pluto taught the ancient Latins to worship as
divine powers, and [taught them] this rite of sacrifice: that duly consecrated
beasts they should slaughter in the flame, and from the living [victims] the entrails
they should tear out, and heap the altars with loaded platters.
These taught their own sons; from them thereafter mighty
Rome received [them], and preserved the ancestral honour;
and no nation celebrated the honours of Satan so fully.
But the due time came when Christ Jesus,
King of Jerusalem, held the temples and the lofty Capitol.
The sacred images of the gods and the Phrygian household gods,
which from Troy, and from the midst of the city's fires, with him
Aeneas carried forth, Christ cast out of the temples; and the dominion
of Hell he utterly overthrew, and the rites of their worship
he changed; with his voice he drove Satan down to Tartarus.
He commanded the proud Italians to obey the followers of Christ.
And when Stygian power had been broken and Fortune withdrew,
many followed the Christians and their victorious arms.
And when proud Babylon had at last been led in triumph,
Jerusalem shone, adorned with well-earned trophies.
The Greek-born had filled the world with altars of the gods,
If I wished to run through every one of their names,

div.note: Sometimes they worshipped the Moon by herself, sometimes together with the Sun: hence a little earlier I made mention of Diana alone, but now of her joined with the Sun.

lg.l: Sooner will evening lay the day to rest with Olympus shut,
Alas, the ignorant minds of the seers, and the empty powers
which, at Christ's coming, fled in fear down among the shades.
For Christ is that God of gods—and Jupiter himself,
who shakes earth's heights with his thunderbolt, sending flames
forth from the clouds and mingling dreadful rumblings:
He is Aeolus, king of tempests and of the raging East Wind,
driving dread-sounding waves up to the stars.
He is Neptune, tamer of the sea; cleaving a path through deep
waters, he reins in the monsters beneath the flood
and the chafing wave, its roarings laid aside.
He is that Atlas—you who bear upon your shoulder the spheres
of heaven, who by his nod turns the stars of the universe.
He is that Pallas, the wisdom of the great Father,
whom God poured forth, conceived within his eternal head.
He is Mars mighty in arms, [who] musters the ranks for battle,
and drives them on; the same one ends war by an offered treaty.
He is Vulcan, master of fire; for fiery is
his strength; he will come down again from high heaven,
giving horrifying flashes, and noise, and terror;
he will seize the whole world with crackling flames.
He is Phoebus, [who] scatters the pale shadows from the sky:

div.note: "Having beheld the preaching of the truth, they fled like deserting soldiers and left their ambushes bare," &c. See Theodoret, ad Graec. in fidel. Serm. 10. de oraculis.

lg.l: And we know him as the discoverer of medicine; he
taught mortals to soothe their hardships with song.
And as victor he laid the serpent low with a deadly wound.
He is the true Mercury, whom a radiant maiden,
brought forth in childbirth as a heavenly child beneath the light-filled skies,
a woman filled with God; sent down from bright Olympus
this messenger bears commands through the swift air.
Then he takes his rod; with this he calls forth from Orcus the souls
that are pale, and sends others down beneath gloomy Tartarus.
This is that conquering Alcides, the renowned offspring of Jove,
tamer of monsters and subduer of wild beasts,
and laying low the ranks of Tartarus with his mighty club:
He crushed under his heels the head of the ancient serpent,
and Cacus, belching out empty fires in the darkness,
he seizes him and locks him in a knot, embracing and clinging fast as he throttles him,
until his eyes are forced from their sockets and his throat is drained dry of blood.
What region on earth is not full of his labour?
Christ, first descending from ethereal Olympus,
is himself that Saturn who ruled in tranquil peace
an unteachable people, scattered abroad over the high mountains,
once believed to be Pan, the god of the fields and of the flock,
religious awe of whom terrified the fearful country folk.
But Christ is that Pan, the God whom we ourselves have seen
reddened by bloody rods, by thorns, and by nails,
whom wool-bearing sheep attend, and shaggy she-goats.

div.note: By the Rod I understand the divine word, which to some is the odour of life, to others of death.

lg.l: When joyful summer has come at the call of the Zephyrs,
he sends both flocks out into the glades and into the pastures.
Then, when the fourth hour of heaven has gathered thirst,
and the plaintive cicadas rend the thickets with their song;
he leads the flocks back to the wells or to the deep pools,
and in the midday heat he shelters [them] with the shade of the branches.
Then once more he gives them a little water and lush pastures
toward the sun's setting, when the cool evening
tempers, and the dewy Moon now revives the glades;
With him as guardian you will not fear the fierce Molossian hounds,
or the night thief at the folds, and the onslaughts of wolves.
Of his own accord he gave his life for the fat lambs,
for the flock of bleating sheep he bore hard labours.
Why should I recount the other deceits and the sweet thefts
of the Greeks? The light [they drew] from our annals
they wrapped in the shadows of errors and in black clouds.
O you who care both for the sheep and for the keepers of sheep,
and who with your crook draw back the tender lambs from the folds
that stray, and gladly carry them on your shoulder back to the pastures;
behold, I, keeping up my bleating now on the high mountains,
now in the dense wood and among the silent thickets, wander.
Therefore search deep with your eyes, seek out the sheep
that strays through the frozen fields with no keeper.
where so many beasts perish from the cold: no
grass appears on the plain, nor leaves upon the tree.
Always winter, always the north-west winds blowing cold.

div.note: Of those sheep the wolf carries off none, the thief steals none, the robber kills none, &c. August. in Johan. tract. 45.

lg.l: Then the Sun never scatters the pallid shadows;
nor when, borne along by his horses, he makes for the high heaven,
[nor when] he bathes his plunging chariot in Ocean's ruddy water,
Therefore take me into the fold, out of the wild glades of this
deceitful world, filled on every side with so many briars;
where [there are] so many bristling thickets, and the deep lairs of wild beasts.
Then to lay healing hands upon the wounds
let it not irk [you]; curb faults with a word, before
the dread contagion creeps through the unwary crowd.
Do not disdain to immerse this soul in the healing river
of blood, and to free me from every stain.
And I beg you: take up stones in your hand, take up clubs, shepherd:
and, as it rises menacingly and swells its hissing neck,
strike down the plague-bearing serpent; defend the sheep;
lest an unfed lion, raging through the crowded sheepfolds,
when maddened hunger drives him on, should chew or drag
the soft flock, dumb with fear; and roar with bloodied mouth.
O race of Abraham's sons, renowned house of great Judah,
for a thousand six hundred years now you have been turning the wheel
around every shore of the earth, around all the seas,
wandering as exiles, like sheep without a master.
Now at last recognize the voice of your shepherd,
while he calls you into the fold: do you then spurn the God who calls,
you unbridled race? What madness has seized you?
Jesus is scorned by you, nor do you ask who he may be,
how rich he is in snow-white sheep, how abounding in milk.
Ah, unhappy Judah, who now wander in the mountains,
if you have any care for your shepherd, return.
Here are cool springs, here soft meadows; through the grass
clear streams glide down in winding turns.
See, fair Jesus feeds sheep upon the grass.
beside a stream of water, and beneath the canopy of a spreading beech
he rehearses a woodland song on a slender reed-pipe.
And as he sings, the echoing valleys carry his song up to the stars:
and with his song he draws stiff ash-trees down from the mountains.
O offspring of Judah! you care nothing for the songs of Christ,
songs which can draw the moon down from the sky,
halt the water in the rivers, and turn the stars backward?
With these songs he summons the shades of night; you will see the earth bellow
beneath your feet, and cities tremble upon lofty mountains.
Thracian Orpheus would not have outdone him in songs,
he who soothed tigers and drove the oaks along with his song.
By songs Circe transformed the companions of Ulysses,
from human form into the faces and backs of beasts:

div.note: By the Moon I understand the Roman empire; by the stars, the lesser kingdoms subject to Rome; by the ewe-lamb, the multitude of the peoples; by the shades, the dark and barbarous nations, now converted to Christ by the preaching of the Gospel as if by an incantation. But the Jews are still deaf asps, harder than the stones with which they stoned Saint Stephen, their own charmer, and they did not hear the voice of the one charming. Augustine on Psalm 57. The Moon was drawn down from heaven at the time when Rome was thrown down from the highest degree of honour and dominion, on account of her slaughters and her cruelty against the Christians. Cicero uses this expression in the 6th Philippic: you have dragged your colleague down from heaven.

lg.l: But Christ, by his singing, wolves and tawny lions,
and bristled boars, and bears in their stalls,
stripping them of their four-footed shape — wondrous to tell! —
changed [them] into the faces and features and limbs of men;
therefore come to our sheepfolds and pens;
range over our mountains and through the deep valleys;
Here unfamiliar fodder does not put the heavy offspring to the test;
nor is there cold ice here, nor snow-bearing winds;
nor are burrs or caltrops at hand, nor do diseases
seize their bodies; no flocks die in the grass,
or give up their sweet lives at the full mangers.
But while the shepherd sings to the breezes beneath the high rock,
see, in troops they wander through the winding valleys,
cropping the grass far and wide, snow-white in their brightness.
Come to our wells and meadows; for both [flocks]
let there be one fold, and let there be one shepherd for both;
thus at last, O sons of Abraham: [the land] which [first bore] you from the stock of your fathers,
the land [which] first bore [you], that same [land] with joyful bosom
shall receive you on your return; seek out Christ as your leader.
The awaited day had arrived, and in the clear light
Phaethon's horses were already bringing on the auspicious Dawn;
a kindly day, which with new light had uncovered the world
and the mind's darkness, and had dispelled the laws, those shadows.
For there were no fires of the stars, nor was the pole bright in the ether

div.note: The condition of the Jewish Church was by now utterly corrupt, and the whole world lay in darkness. By the Stars I understand the Doctors; by Heaven, the Synagogue; by the Clouds, the Ceremonies; by the Moon, the World.

lg.l: the pole [bright] with starry radiance, but clouds [hung] in a darkened sky,
and the dead of night kept the Moon shut in a raincloud:
until, with the gateway of starry heaven burst open,
a star, seen by none, runs down along its swift track:
which first illumined the untouched womb of the Virgin:
then, shining upon Jerusalem, destined for everlasting peace,
it burned up the Mars-born walls of mournful Rome.
The realms of Babylon are thrown into turmoil with a great uproar;
the Tartarean abodes and the lofty gates of Dis tremble
as God draws near, and the whole sky bellows back with thunder.
Grim fires out of the clouds strike terror into their minds:
the immovable rock of the Capitol was struck by lightning;
and the ivory weeps mournfully in the temples, and the bronzes [sweat];
Romulus and the native gods of the fatherland, and mother Vesta,
scarcely [keep guard over] the Tuscan Tiber and the Roman Palatine;
for suddenly the images of the gods fell down in terror;
and the she-wolf with the twin boys, her neck bent back,
licking them each in turn, and shaping their bodies with her tongue:
the bronze columns burned, together with the tablets of the laws.
But while the golden Sun was traversing the middle of his circuit,
dewy Iris ringed him about with her saffron wings.
Nay more, oil was seen to flow from deep wells,
and three suns to blaze in the middle of the sky.
resembling a crown of thorns (wondrous to tell!),

div.note: Christ the morning star.

On these and other prodigies, Dio writes in books 37, 41, and 47; Suetonius, in his Augustus, chapters 94 and 95; Orosius, History 6.18; Eusebius, in his Chronicle; and Suidas, under the entry "Augustus."

lg.l: A fiery ring encircled the orb of Phoebus,
portents of the God to come, and of the king to be,
under whose happy auspices renowned Judah
will make her rule equal to the earth, her spirit to Olympus.
Yet through varied trials—alas—and frequent deaths,
the harshest realms of Satan remain to be vanquished;
and through fire, and weapons, and thorns dripping with blood
lies our road into heaven; thus is the way to the stars.
O you whom the great ruler of those above, sent down
sent down, willed to endure such great toils,
O Christ, God—a greater order of things is arising for me,
a greater work I set in motion — I pray, breathe favour on me as I sing,
open Helicon to me now, and set the songs in motion,
and unfold with me the vast reaches of my subject,
while we encompass your deeds in Maro's verses.
There was an ancient city, settlers of Zebulun held it,
Nazareth, built upon the leafy summit of a hill;
A maiden distinguished in beauty and bodily form dwelt there,
whose name was Mary; already of marriageable years,
already ripe for a husband; to be joined in the bond of wedlock
to Joseph: descended from David, he alone was the most righteous man
who lived on earth, and the most devoted to justice.
But Mary — if we give any credit to what is reported — Anna
bore; the priest Mattha, with Maria as the mother,
begot this Anna; her mother’s nobility gave her a proud lineage,
was bestowed by her maternal nobility, for she was born of the illustrious stock
of David, of which line Judah was the founder.
Thus the lineage of both branches off from a single bloodline.
But lo, Gabriel the messenger, sent by Jove himself,
sails on; he, swimming through the winds and the stormy clouds
on golden wings, he sees the summit and the steep flanks
of Galilee’s lofty mountain; amid black clouds, its
airy head is beaten by both wind and rain.
Here first, poised on balanced wings, the Angel of Jove
halted; from here, headlong with his whole body, toward the city
he flung himself, like the bird that around the shores, around
the fish-teeming rocks flies low beside the waters;
no otherwise between earth and heaven was flying
the winged messenger, and cut through clouds and winds.
As soon as he had entered through the little doors of the gracious
Virgin, at last [he] spoke thus with a human voice:
O happy one, alone above all others, most holy Virgin,
to whom a new offspring is sent down from high heaven;
from you shall be born Christ, of heavenly origin,
dear offspring of gods, great increase of Jove,
he shall mount the ancestral throne of his father David,

div.note: Christ the offspring of gods, that is, of Kings, who are called gods.

Christ is called the increase of the Father not actively but passively: the Father did not grow by the addition of the Son, but the Son grew, as man, in wisdom, grace, stature, virtues, and glory. God, best and greatest, is truly Jupiter, because truly a helping Father. "Zeus, Olympian father of all things" — Sophocles. So too Sallust. Du Bartas calls the true God Neptune: qui vray Neptune, &c.

lg.l: and he shall rule a world made peaceful by his father's excellence.
For him God will set no bounds of dominion nor spans of time,
he has granted him dominion without end.
The Spirit nourishes you inwardly by sacred power; and the Mind, infused through the limbs,
animates the tender fetus and mingles itself with the little body;
Do not doubt, for what you hear is true.
When he had spoken these words, lifted into the air on his wings
he passes on high into heaven; but the Virgin, in terror,
stood dumbstruck, her hair stood on end, and her voice caught in her throat
turning many things over in her mind, she worships the divine power of Olympus.
Going from there, she makes her way to her kinswoman's threshold
across rocks and crags and through sunken valleys;
for the whole region is bristling with woodland thickets.
It swells with airy mountains, and with lofty crags threatens
toward heaven; yet the Virgin, through the mountain's steep
wastes, hastening along the ridge, comes to the town,
and enters the house of her kinswoman Elysa.
And when she had gone in, and leave was given to speak face to face,
she, herself heavy with child, greets the pregnant woman with a joyful cry;
but as soon as Mary's voice struck the mother's ears
of her kinswoman, behold, the eager infant gave a leap in the womb;
who, though shut in by darkness and a blind prison,
yet felt beforehand the dawn risen for mortals,
and the Sun breaking out from amid the thick clouds.
Not yet had he drunk in the sweet light of heaven and its airs,
And yet he saw God in clear light:
his ears had not yet opened, yet a voice is carried to his ears.
How varied are the wonders that shine forth in this boy—
he exults in bondage, and is free in the midst of his prison,
without an ear he heard, without light he saw the light.
Then the mother thus began to speak: O you, blessed alone
among beautiful maidens, and blessed [is] the child
whom you carry in your womb; is it me, then, that at last
the gracious mother of the Lord will deign to visit? Behold, all at once,
as soon as your voice reached my ears,
the child, leaping with joy, beats with its foot within the womb.
O happy [woman], whose trust never gave way! for
the almighty Father will keep his promises and his word.
Then the virgin, her face lowered, briefly speaks:
See, new joys now thrill through my silent breast,
behold, my spirit is kindled with love of praising Jehovah.
O may the last portion of my life endure so long,
and may I have breath enough to tell of your deeds,
you who deign to honor your lowly handmaid so highly;
not unacquainted with suffering, you rejoice to come to the aid of the wretched.
Therefore, as long as heaven sustains its varied stars,
always shall your honour and your name and your praises endure.
All peoples—those whom the remotest land, with the encircling
Ocean, keeps apart, or those whom the zone stretched out among
the other four—the zone of the merciless sun—separates;
All these women will call me three and four times blessed.
You, Father, take pity on us lowly ones from heaven on high;
You have strength of spirit, you have such great power, for us
to spare the conquered and subdue the proud;
to cast pitiless tyrants down from their high seat,
to lift from the ground the poor whom shameful want presses hard.
You call back their strength with food, those whose mouths are always
pale with hunger; and the man rich in gifts and in the bounty of the gods
you strip bare, [while] the servant you will help with aid and with means,
This you have promised, and no change of purpose will turn you.
But when by no doubtful signs he began to perceive —
Joseph, that Mary was with child — the marriage agreed upon
he fears to carry through, and grieves to make public the shame
of the Virgin: so in his mind he wavers now this way, now that.
But while his mind is led into every anxiety,
and black night, borne aloft on her two-horse car, held the sky;
the form of a winged minister was seen descending from heaven
and suddenly pouring forth these words:
You who draw your line from the high blood of David,
Joseph, do not scorn to join this girl Mary
to yourself in lasting wedlock, and to claim her as your own
now, for she is pregnant by wind and by the breath of the Deity.
She will bring forth an offspring on whom you will lay the name Jesus,
since he is indeed the highest salvation of his own people.
He had spoken, and fled like smoke into the thin air.
Joseph did exactly as he was bidden, and all
his life he passed with the Virgin without intercourse.
Meanwhile the Sun rolls round the great year,
And icy winter roughens the waves with the north winds;
indeed Night, borne onward by the hours, was approaching the midpoint of her circuit;
and indeed ten months had brought the mother prolonged discomfort,
when the pregnant Virgin gave birth to a little boy
in a stable, since they are barred from entering the shelter
of an inn—so great is the poverty of the newborn child,
who nevertheless had been the richest in all the world;
He now bounds his dominion by the Ocean and his fame by the stars:
Thus at last was born the undoubted Son of God,
whom the Greeks call Christ, while by the name Jesus
the sons of Abraham call him; his mother is a Virgin—wonderful to tell!
whom no love, no wedding-rites ever swayed,
but, remaining unwed and cherishing a love of virginity,
undefiled, she gave birth to her offspring while still intact;
beautiful, she reclines on the ground, while her beautiful newborn at her breasts
begins, with a smile, to recognize his untouched mother.
Behold the world swaying beneath its arching mass,
and the lands and the reaches of the sea, and the deep sky,
behold how all things rejoice at the age to come.
For this boy is that one so often promised to the world,
who will rule the peoples in peace, and the proud nations
will curb with justice, and will hold far and wide under his sway.
He will bring the world under [his] laws; then first the iron [race]
shall cease, and a golden race shall rise up in all the world.
He will give laws: with iron and close-fitted fastenings the dread
gates of war shall be shut, and impious rage within
Sitting upon savage weapons, and bound with a hundred brazen
knots behind his back, will roar, dreadful, with bloody mouth.
Not furnished with steel, not resplendent with gold and purple,
nor exulting in a weapon, nor flashing with brazen light;
but mighty in piety, beyond both the Garamantes and the Indians
he shall extend his dominion: a land lies beyond the stars,
beyond the paths of the year and of the sun, where heaven-bearing Atlas
turns on his shoulder the axis [of heaven], studded with blazing stars.
At his coming even now both the Caspian realms
shudder at the divine oracles, and the Maeotic land,
and the trembling mouths of the sevenfold Nile are in turmoil.
Sons of Abraham, hard men from the hard stock of your fathers,
receive this in a few words and pay attention; I shall instruct you.
This is that dove let down from a mother's womb,
which holds out in its beak a branch of peace-bearing olive.
This is the Sun of righteousness, who lights up with his lamp the minds
of men, and dispels the dense shadows and the darkness.
This is the true dawn, which had brought to wretched mortals the kindly
light, lighting up their works and their toils.
This Morning Star has raised his holy face from the heavenly height,
whom God loves above the other fires of the stars.
This is the Manna, surpassing swans in snowy whiteness,
which the golden urn of the ever-Virgin enclosed.
This is the flame that, doing no harm, licks with soft touch
the Virgin's bush: he is the stone torn away from the mountain,
But without a mortal hand, or hard toil.
Why should I unfold to you the foretellings of the prophets of old?
All the seers sang that he would be great;
and indeed this glory of the age, [he] who shall found the ages
golden, for whom all the earth shall bear all things, and for whom
the field shall little by little turn golden with the soft ear of corn,
and the reddening grape shall hang upon untended briars,
and hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey.
Under his guidance, if any traces of our guilt remain,
they shall be effaced and free the earth from perpetual dread.
No wolf [shall plot] ambush against the flock, nor any nets
devise a trap for the deer; the vineyard [shall feel] no pruning-hook,
nor shall the soil endure rakes; but then the sturdy ploughman shall loose
the yokes from the bulls; every grove shall grow green,
[and] timid does shall come to the drinking-places along with dogs.
The mountains themselves, in gladness, their voices to the stars
shall fling: the very crags shall echo back the songs.
Therefore, Judaea, acknowledge this mighty Lord:
prevail with unceasing vows, bring as a suppliant gifts
undefiled, to God. God—oh, he is God, you profane men!
And he shall always be God to me; his altar
I shall ever tend, and kindle with the flame of burning love;
though no lamb from my sheepfolds shall wet it [with blood].
For piety, and ancient faith, and a kindly heart —
these are no less dear to you, O Christ, best of boys,
than if many a victim went out from my pens.

div.p: This book contains prophecies concerning Christ's nativity, life, miracles, death, resurrection, ascension, and so forth, and concerning the greatness, power, and splendour of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, of the Church and kingdom of Christ. Here, occasion being taken, a digression is made in praise of Kings James and Charles, the nursing fathers of the Church. Here too Virgil inveighs against the sacrilegious plunderers of Jerusalem, who in this rapacious age, driven by an impious frenzy, have torn away the Church's goods with grasping hands.

lg.l: Him the chaste Sibylline prophetesses sang of long ago.
And of these she who was most learned in speech, the daughter of Glaucus,
Deiphobe, the prophetess of Phoebus (for whom, when she raves, the Delian
is wont to shake the reins and ply the goads beneath her breast),
foretold that Christ was to be begotten of a pure Virgin,
and willingly loosed her voice and lips.
But the maiden did not write these prophecies upon leaves,
lest, thrown into confusion, they fly as the sport of the rushing winds.
Him too Balaam sang of, the aged soothsayer,
to whom the entrails of beasts, to whom the stars of heaven give heed,
and the tongues of birds, and the fires of the foretelling thunderbolt:
It shall raise its holy face, he says, from the stock of Jacob—
a Star; and from the seed of Judah there shall burst forth a rod
of gold, which shall strike down the proud kingdoms of the world.
And so the star of the Prince of Jacob's line came forth,
A star at which the princes of heaven will rejoice, and which
will lead, from the sunlit borders of the Persians,
kings all the way to Bethlehem, to the cradle of our Lord.
When the evil serpent in the glades of Paradise poisoned
the primeval father, Jehovah himself proclaims
that Christ will come, sprung from a woman's seed,
who will crush with his heel the head of the monstrous dragon;
but the gore will hurt Christ, and the venom of the hard
tooth, and the scar marked on the bitten heel.
This is he, Shiloh, whom Jacob with trembling voice
foretold would come, when, pale with the death then at hand,
he lay down upon his bed and spoke his last words.
This is he, Jesus, the Interpreter between men and Jehovah,
a prophetic seer, whom Moses the lawgiver once
foretold would be like himself and would be great.
This is he, the son of King David; this is he
who will found the temple; whose dominion will remain
without end, as Nathan the prophet openly declared.
This King will curb the nations with justice; this is that
Son — this day the Father begot him — and on Zion's
lofty summit set him, and called him King;
to whom he gave the bounds of Ocean and the nations to rule.
He will exult in triumph, and will rest in this hope,
that the Father will not leave this soul in Stygian Orcus.

div.note: Genesis 3, verse 15.
Shiloh shall come.
I will raise up a prophet like you.
2 Samuel 7, verse 1; 1 Chronicles 17.
Isaiah 32, verse 1.
Psalm 2, verses 6, 7, 8.
Psalm 16, verses 9, 10.

lg.l: Nor will he suffer the holy flesh to rot in the ground.
Not a man but a worm, whom on every side fat bulls
surround, and butt with the horn, and provoke the fight;
a throng of savage lions gnash their teeth,
and roar, and the barking of hounds rages into the air;
the warder of Tartarus, whose neck bristles with snakes,
pursues him relentlessly and harasses him with
dreadful barking, and, hot in pursuit, presses his foot close upon the trembling man's:
just as when [a hound] has come upon, penned in by a river,
a stag, or one hedged about by the terror of the crimson feather,
the hunting dog presses hard with the chase and with baying.
But he, terrified by the snares and by the high bank,
flees and doubles back along a thousand paths, and the keen Umbrian hound
clings open-mouthed; now, now he has him, and as though holding him
he has snapped his jaws, and is baffled with an empty bite.
Tormentors of every kind mock him; some with a twisted lash
assail the wretched man; some tear his garment, and among
themselves divide it by drawing lots.
Some taint his food with gall; others mingle vinegar into
cups of wine, together with harmful words;
But others, his hands and his feet being pierced through, lay open
the hidden recesses of his breast, where [my soul] may rest in the night
on the last [night], after my soul has done with its perils;
Behold, the moles, blind of eye, have dug their chambers.
This is he, that mighty Prince of surpassing bodily form,

div.note: Psalm 22, verses 6, 12, 13, and 16.
Psalm 22, verse 18.
Psalm 69, verse 21.
Psalm 22, verse 16.

lg.l: Christ, powerful through grandsires and great-grandsires, and noble in arms;
and who stands above all mortals, fairest of all,
grace is poured out upon [his] lips, glowing with purple.
He will fit the gleaming sword to his thigh, to wear it,
and, bravest of heroes, will drive his foaming horse,
distinguished by the trappings of justice; whom a hide
linked with bronze scales into feather-work shall not cover, nor gold;
but ancient faithfulness, and mercy, far better than tawny
gold, and than arms, and than embroidered coverlets.
Borne thus on a caparisoned horse, he will rush over the whole plain,
trampling upon his terrified enemies; and no small glory will follow,
when, under the happy auspices of the city of Jerusalem,
he shall extend his dominion; wondrous throughout the whole world,
his right hand shall make high heaps of slaughter of the rebels.
He, holding a bow in his hand, and swift arrows,
will hurl piercing darts with his strong right hand,
against the King’s hostile enemies, lodging them in their breasts,
until all fall prostrate, and a beseeching right hand
they stretch out in lowliness, and worship the King's divine power.
The throne of his rule stands fixed for ever, on into the ages;
and the sceptre flashes with justice, not with comely bronze,
not with gold that a craftsman's skilful hand has fashioned;
with justice he has bridled the peoples, and he hates the wicked.
Joys thrill through [his] mind, because the ruler of Olympus

div.note: Psalm 45, from verse 2 to verse 10.

lg.l: Him he has anointed with oil above his companions of equal age;
fragrant with aloe and cassia, and dripping with myrrh,
the ivory palace shall send forth purple garments;
and coaxing joys shall soothe the mind held in suspense.
Nymphs sprung from royal blood shall stand by,
among the honoured handmaids, to carry out commands;
All [are] in gold, all girt in embroidered garments.
But close at his right side stands the royal consort,
wrapped in a purple cloak with an embroidered border;
her tunic is of gold, her hair is knotted up in gold;
a golden band gleamed with sky-blue gems.
Indeed, the king’s daughter is altogether most beautiful in form.
Her eyes flash with light, glory shines from her excellent face,
but more pleasing is the virtue that proceeds from her beautiful body.
She shines in Phrygian robes, which earlier the girl
had made, and had picked out the webs with fine gold.
with a chorus of maidens attending her and the favorable applause
being redoubled by that chorus, the royal palace shall resound when
the King receives her, glad, in his ample porticoes.
He shall restore the shattered walls of Judah,
and shall found the city of Jerusalem, and shall set the dwellings
of Abraham’s descendants, and shall give a name to the nation and hang up his arms.
In our mountains, under that King, there shall flourish
peace and justice, and the people shall revere him,

div.note: Psalm 45, verses 13, 14, and 15.
Psalm 69, verse 35.
Psalm 51, verse 18.
Psalm 72, from verse 3 to 18.

lg.l: While the moon gathers her returning fires month by month,
and while the Sun brings back the day and puts it away once it has returned.
As the rain falls, poured out from the clouds of summer,
onto the mown grass, so shall Christ come down from heaven;
whose dominion is stretched out over the whole world,
where the dark-blue wave resounds afar over the ebbing sea,
and the proud kingdoms of the Ethiopians and the Arabians shall worship him.
The Sabaeans, bringing gifts of gold and of frankincense,
[their] kings, shall come in supplication; and, grovelling at [his] knees,
the enemy shall worship [him]; and, calling upon [him as] lord in their prayers,
the nations, submissive, shall offer kisses to the ground.
He shall ransom the wretched at a price, and defend the needy.
[A harvest] which shall answer the prayers of the grasping farmer,
on the mountains and the crags the harvest of grain shall bristle.
And as the cedar of Lebanon rises through the clear air toward the sky,
just so shall the stalk lift itself with its countless ears.
All nations shall make solemn vows to him each year,
in supplication; and he too shall bind them by vows.
And while heaven’s life-sustaining light traverses the world,
always his honour, always his name shall be celebrated,
and in him the nations, and the peoples, shall be made blessed,
all those whom Nereus encircles with his back-flowing waves.
And devotion and ancient faith are joined together in him;
and the Virgin returns, and the reign of Saturn returns.

div.note: Psalm 85, verse 10.

lg.l: Indeed kindly Faith shall lift her head up from the earth, under that
king, and the Virgin shall come down from the highest heaven.
He who had once been the keeper of the fold among the mountains,
the son of Jesse, leaving the tender lambs with their mothers,
succeeds to the throne, and takes up the kingdom of Judaea;
The Almighty anointed his temples with fragrant nard
and gave him the sceptre and the kingdom’s crown:
so Christ, once the keeper of the flock, [holds] all things;
The Father comes to his aid and protects him with his right hand,
lest the forms of wickedness and violent hearts harm him.
He will crush his enemies and force them to turn their steps
back, and will dye his sword-point in enemy blood.
Neither devotion nor ancient faith will ever desert him.
He will bring the conquered nations from both shores
completely beneath his own yoke, under his Father’s auspices;
lightly he flies over the surface of the waters in a dark-blue chariot,
and the raging waves with their mighty roar
he will curb with everlasting rule; and will hold in chains
all the rivers gliding through the great lands.
Euphrates, gilded with twin horns upon his bull-like face,
will serve him; and the Nile, with its black sand,
making green Egypt fruitful; and Rhine and Tagus,
Eridanus, king of rivers, and the streams of Xanthus.
Him too the swift Oaxes of Crete shall acknowledge,
and the fair Ganges, and Hermus turbid with gold.

div.note: Psalm 78, verses 70, 71.
Psalm 89, from verse 20 to verse 31.

lg.l: And Jordan too, with the rustic glory upon his head,
bearing blossoming fennel-stalks and tall lilies,
shall acknowledge Christ, and shall pay the honour due,
so too dark Galaesus, watering the yellowing tilled fields,
and the Don, where it rolls among pearl-bearing sands;
and swift Rhone, veiled in grey-green reed,
and turbid Ister, whirling along his yellow sands.
Father Tiber himself, and the streams of Anio themselves,
and Hypanis sounding over his rocks, and snowy Tanais,
these rivers, struck with wonder, shall lower their waves
before Christ's authority, whose commands they shall obey.
Among these, Thames, the river most pleasing to heaven,
his locks adorned with flowers and bitter parsley,
shall acknowledge Christ, and shall worship [him] with his glassy waters;
and on the neighboring bank they shall worship him; for whom lilies in full
baskets—see—the Nymphs shall bring; for whom, fair Naiad,
plucking pale violets and the topmost poppies,
and shall join the narcissus with the flower of sweet-smelling dill,
then, interweaving [them] with cassia and other sweet herbs,
[and] shall paint the soft hyacinths with yellow marigold.
To him too the sturdy farmers shall carry gifts,
and on the green bank they shall set temples of marble
beside the waters, where once from the grassy turf

div.note: The Don, the other river of Aberdeen, famous for its pearl-fishery.

lg.l: Altars were smoking with the blood of men and of beasts.
A hundred and twice ten shrines throughout the august city
they will found for Christ, fashioned of ancient stone,
relics of the faith and memorials of the fathers of old.
which piety will set up, as long as they fear the sacred rites and God,
the Christians, or as long as [religion] terrifies the fearful country folk;
but the accursed hunger for possessions will follow,
together with contempt for God; piety will be forced to seek deserted lands.
Then it will be lawful to plunder property
and to contend in hatred and lay waste ancestral homes,
to plunder temples, and to overthrow consecrated altars
will be lawful, and to tear the hallowed gold from the temples.
The Caledonians will lay the temples that neighbour the sky
level with the ground, and lofty citadels too, once their defenders have fallen,
