while the untamed and base rabble rages to arms.
Alas, the madness of war and the dreadful lust for possession,
and superstition—the cause of such great evils!
But my mind shudders to recount it and recoils in grief.
Holy Father, lay these low by your power, and let them fall
headlong like a wheel, and like an axle whirled on in its course,
those who dare with rapacious hands to violate consecrated shrines;
make them cast from their hooked talons
the houses they seized and the loot they denied taking,
and turn away such a plague from our lands.
And as a storm whirls the light stalk and flying stubble,
the storm hurls them, and as fire, amid crackling flames, having escaped into the lofty
foliage, rolls its blaze through the whole forest
and veils vast Olympus with smoke;
just so, pour out the flames of your wrath, and with your
whirlwind tear these men up from their deepest roots.
Yet at last you will console this grief of ours;
for one day time will bring us, in answer to our longing,
help and the coming of God, who will lift the tottering temples
up from the ground, and will renew the ancient honour of Jerusalem,
while the black dogs bark around in vain.
He himself, seated upon the snow-white threshold of gleaming St Paul’s,
let him wear branches of laurel on his brow, and be golden:
for, relying on this man's piety, he lifts his head the higher,
St Paul’s, soon to be seen in splendid attire.
Charles, long since the royal court of heaven
begrudges you to us, and complains that you care for the triumphs of men;
for you have deserved to be raised by fame above the upper air,
see, for you the altars of the Muses smoke with holy incense,
and they build temples, and adorn [them] with fresh garlands,
the Castalian maidens, and they carry your sacred name to the stars.
And my Calliope sings of you on a rustic reed
among the Pierian leaves, and the throng of her sisters,
while she sits by the sacred spring: but (if life remains)
she will set up a temple, and ordain honour for the temple,
where the spring waters the ridges of Parnassus with glassy waves.
At its center you shall be a god to me and occupy the temple.
I myself, my head adorned with the leaves of the clipped olive,
shall bring gifts of incense, conspicuous in Tyrian purple.
On the doors I shall fashion, in gold and solid ivory,
your mighty deeds, great King, and benefactions so great
toward Jerusalem, and the work of piety by which the ancient temples,
built by pious hands, but now, whether by war or by [fire],
torn down, you restore, and enlarge with fresh gifts.
I shall also add columns rising in naval bronze,
and Neptune's realms made subject to your keels;
and the holy plunder snatched from the robbers' gullet,
whom wicked gluttony drives to devour our tables—
never sated with sacred blood.
Fed on the entrails of the wretched and on so much blood,
they sprawl over bones half-gnawed by their bloody jaws.
If you drive these monsters, great King, out of your coasts,
you will be fortunate, and a second Charles after him,
who restored the Latin state and recovered the fasces,
and brought peace back to Jerusalem and restored its majesty.
Then I shall add Parian marbles, statues that breathe.
Nay more, the likenesses of the old forefathers, rank on rank,
[carved] from ancient cedar: Brutus, Fergus, and
Bruce mighty in arms; and the other kings from the line's beginning,
who suffered the wounds of war fighting for their country,
shall stand in the entrance-hall; there shall stand the image of the father,
in gold—the man who established these golden ages for us,
and shut the gates of war with close-drawn fastenings,
the strife among neighbouring peoples having been laid aside.
Sicilian Muses, offer lilies by the handful;
let me scatter purple flowers, and the soul of James
at least heap with these gifts, and discharge a fruitless duty—
by [his] gift; for he has made this peace for our country and for us.
Great father of Jerusalem, you who guard the holy palaces,
be gracious, and (I pray) ward off the enemy's fury,
and keep the King safe for us and for our fatherland.
Do not forbid this young man, at least, to come to the aid of the ruined sacred institutions;
we have paid enough for the sins of our fathers,
enough punishment has been endured; have mercy on Zion
now at last, have mercy, good shepherd, on your own fold;
for the tender lambs, by their bleating, rouse the wolves
who devise snares for the flock; in gore the whole
sheepfold swims, and warm limbs quiver beneath their teeth.
Alas! the high house of Zion has been made a cave of wild beasts,
ghastly with the gore of Christ's people and with bloody feasts.
Hunt down these wolves, kindly Father, with fierce Molossian hounds,
and with your shafts lay the savage lions low:
snatch back the half-eaten prey; lest with the slaughter of your own
the soil of Jerusalem grow fat any further, we beg you.
But now let me return to Christ and the oracles of the prophets.
The Almighty will honor this one above all kings.
All the loving Father's care rests upon this son;
whose love no day, no force shall turn aside,
however things shall fall out; nor will he break peace or covenant,
whose offspring, [sprung] from a great stock, shall abide,
and [his] throne [shall abide], so long as the sky shall feed the stars in its vault;
While the Father upholds the heavenly spheres with his nod,
offspring shall fail him, and [his] royal seat,
[only] when Phaethon's horses shall cease to breathe fire from their nostrils
and to open the kindly day to mortals,
and the Moon [shall cease] to be borne among the stars in her four-horse chariot.
Here is that eternal Priest of gods and of men,
Melchizedek, just as the ruler of Olympus has sworn;
who, set fast at his Father's right side, shall put Avernus
beneath his feet, and shall crush all his enemies under his heels;
he shall receive the sceptre, and on Mount Zion the rods of office
shall raise them, and from there shall rule over all lands;
him all the nations, rejoicing in a full throng,
shall welcome as victor with applause; then in comely robe
the whole world shall serve him of its own accord.
As the dew, most welcome to the flock, upon the tender grass
comes down from on high in a hidden and wondrous way,
so we believe that Christ, gliding down from heaven's citadel,
traveled hidden paths through the Virgin's womb.
He, wreaking his wrath, with deadly wound shall lay kings
low, and shall cause great battles and carnage.
He shall fill the steep trenches with abundant blood.
And he shall be the judge, and shall learn the lives and the crimes
of the nations, and with unconquered blade shall cut down tyrants.
And while he pursues the fleeing enemy, and from his body the sweat
streams down, and laboured panting shakes his weary limbs:
at once he shall drink clear water from the stream,

div.note: The whole of Psalm 110.

lg.l: And he will quench his thirst and raise his head high toward the stars.
This is he whose love is sweeter to me than wine,
for whom the sweet breeze of his fragrant name blows,
and for that reason the Nymphs are set aflame with love of him,
and the Naiads zealously search out his tracks.
My soul burned for the beautiful shepherd Jesus,
the delight of men, and had nothing to hope for,
not knowing where he, reclining in a green cave,
might be pasturing the sheep as they sought shade and coolness
in the midst of the heat; until, over the glad pastures,
the shepherd led my wandering soul to well-fed flocks and sheepfolds
[my soul] as it strayed, and made it rest in the cool shade.
As the apple tree is a glory to the trees, as [the grapes are] to the vines,
and as the roses to the fields, as the white lilies to the valleys:
so Christ is every glory to his own, beneath whose covering,
reclining, I gather apples white with tender down.
This is that stag, leaping upon the high mountains,
with branching antlers, and feeding among the lilies.
Whose head is wet at night, and his hair with dew.
Who surpasses the snows in whiteness, and purple in redness,
golden is his brow; from his crown there quivers dark
hair, blacker than the dusky wings of ravens,
like a gem that gleams, dividing the tawny gold,
or such as the eyes of a dove white with milk
beside the watering streams in the chill valleys:

div.note: Song of Songs 1, verses 2, 3, 7, 8.
Song of Songs 2, verses 3, 9, 16.
Song of Songs 5, verse 2.
Song of Songs 5, from verse 9 to the end of the chapter.

lg.l: Such are the eyes of Christ, comely and without blemish.
Behold, his cheeks are always fragrant with perfumes; behold,
the white lilies of his lips drip with myrrh;
and his fingers, heavy with gems, glitter with gold as well.
So his belly gleams with gems and shining ivory,
and his gilded legs call to mind columns of marble.
He walks forth as great as Lebanon, or such as upon the high
mountains the cedar lifts its crown toward the sky.
Therefore no one surpasses Christ in beauty;
none dearer to our languishing spirit; he
breathes forth sweet fragrances from his divine throat.
Sweet is moisture to the sown fields, the arbutus to weaned kids:
the pliant willow to the breeding flock, to me Jesus alone.
The wolf is harmful to the folds, rain to ripened crops:
winds to the trees; so is his anger to us.
Come then, Christ, God, my light, my sole delight:
lo, the golden Sun has driven routed winter down beneath the earth;
and now every field, now every tree, is giving birth,
now the woods are in leaf, now the year is at its loveliest.
Let us make for the fragrant gardens, the vineyards, and the fields:
and let us sit among the hazels on the soft grass.
The ground pours forth flowers, now the white poplar over the cave
overhangs [the cave], and the pliant vines weave shady bowers.
Now the varied concert of birds is heard in the fields,
and the glad flocks, and the thrushes exulting in their throats;

div.note: Song of Songs 2, verses 11, 12, 13; and Song of Songs 7, verses 11, 12; and Song of Songs 6, verse 11.

lg.l: And the shores resound with the halcyon, and the thickets with the goldfinch,
and now the chaste turtle-dove moans from the airy elm.
Now the fig-tree pushes its tender green figs out of the bark,
which burst their thin skins; now it breathes out fragrance —
the vine-leaf, and the buds swell on the joyful vine-branch:
And now for you the whole sea lies levelled and silent, and all —
look—all the murmuring breezes have died away.
The garden, then, breathing with crimson flowers,
let us enter together, and let us pluck mellow fruits,
lilies, soft chestnuts, and waxy plums.
Cups foaming with new milk, dewy honey;
Lenaean liquors, and let us prepare sweet perfumes:
nor let the tears of myrrh be wanting, nor pomegranates.
But while the snub-nosed she-goats crop the shoots;
while beneath the dark holm-oak the flock chews the pale grasses,
and the copses ring with hoarse cicadas;
let us taste kisses; with me you will give yourself to love,
you will give the embraces I long for, and hold me with your right hand;
take me into your bosom; you can rest with me through the night
upon green foliage; let us sing of love,
and on a slender reed let us practise the rustic Muse.
For love wastes me away; what limit can there be to love?
Nor is cruel Love sated with tears, nor the grasses with streams,

div.note: Song of Songs 5, verse 1. Song of Songs 4, verse 16. Song of Songs 6, verses 2 and 11. Song of Songs 2, verse 5.
Song of Songs 1, verses 1, 13, 16. Song of Songs 2, verses 5, 6, 14.

lg.l: Nor are the bees sated with clover, nor the she-goats with leaves.
[It] is fiercer than the grave and mightier than death itself,
Who will be able to quench with springs so great a fire,
as it rolls an untamable flame and such vast conflagrations?
Neither the strength of heroes nor rivers poured upon it can do so.
Love conquers all things, and let us too yield to love.
He will set a mountain upon the mountains, and the high halls of Zion,
to which in dense column nations and peoples will fly,
rejoicing to settle bristling wars by a treaty.
And he will restore the honour of the ploughshare and the curved pruning-hook.
Out of their fathers' swords they will make plough-beams, and spears
they will turn into sickles; a golden race will rise up for the world.
This shoot of Jesse, which comes forth from the lowest roots,
will shelter Jerusalem with the vast shade of its branches;
nor will the wolf plot ambush against the flock, under that
King, nor will the viper spatter its venom upon children;
for indeed he will take the evil venom away from the black serpents;
The cold snake will do no harm, although it lurks hidden in the grass;
undaunted, children will play above the asp's den,
and monstrous wild beasts will live among the defenceless flocks
harmlessly; and after the manner of an ox the lion shall chew straw.
This is that true Immanuel, whom the radiant Virgin,
the daughter of Jesse, will bring forth, conceived by the Holy Spirit.
This is he, so great a son begotten by such great parents,

div.note: Song of Songs 8, verses 6, 7.
Isaiah 2, verses 2, 4.
Isaiah 11, verses 6, 7, 8.
Isaiah 7, verses 14, 15.

lg.l: one who would eat curdled milk, who would eat clinging honey.
That Boy is born who the proud emblem of kingship
bears on his shoulders, and as he walks towers over all the gods.
The Spirit anoints him with flowing oil, that ailing
hearts he might soothe with his words, and to the righteous tidings
of joy might bring back, and might restore liberty
to the captives, and might relieve those bound by fear and by fetters.
And that the dark house may be laid open, its doors wrenched away,
the house of hell; he will come, and will lead the nations out of prison.
To the nations he has been given as a kindly light, and [as] the glory of Judah.
He holds the key of David, with which the thresholds of the king
of hell he alone unbars, he who again those same [doors]
shuts fast. To what man has such great power been granted?
This is he whom, as he comes from Bozrah, a purple robe with drops
of blood stained covers; he who with the blood
of the enemy dyed his bare legs, his buskins torn off.
He alone, exulting, has trodden upon the necks of his enemies.
See, the vintage of blood foams in the brimming vats.
He will not quench the smoking flax, nor by the wind's blast
will he break the battered reeds: with shouting his anger
the gentle one will not sharpen, nor will he provoke anyone with his voice:
but those shut up in darkness and bound in a dark prison
he will lead out, and will show the blind the way to the stars.

div.note: Isaiah 9, verse 6.
Isaiah 61, verse 1.
Isaiah 9, verse 2; Isaiah 49, verse 6; Luke 2:32.
Isaiah 22, verse 22; Revelation 3, verse 7.
Isaiah 63, verses 1, 2, 3.
Isaiah 42, verses 2, 3, 7.

lg.l: No outstanding beauty of form, no strength [was] in him,
but sick with heavy cares and a thousand griefs;
and bearing those many wounds which he received for his beloved
Jerusalem: despised, lowly, destitute,
stricken, dragging out his life in darkness and mourning,
slain for us by many blows and by death;
and [he] who healed our wounds with [his own] wounds.
Like a plant he will rise from dry ground into the air,
whose life will flourish with everlasting foliage.
This is the shepherd David, of whom, unsealing his lips in prophecy,
the son of Buzi sang long ago—he whom the royal
herds obey, and to whom the keeping of the field far and wide is entrusted.
That good keeper seeks the lost sheep through desert trackless places,
and has taken it up on his shoulders; and the lambs he has found
he himself cherishes in his bosom and carries to well-filled mangers.
With him as keeper we shall not fear to stray through the fields,
the deserted wastes of Libya, [nor] the thief and the onset of wolves,
nor then shall we shudder at misshapen she-bears at our back.
Gentler in the open fields, the lioness forgetful of her cubs
will roam, dealing no havoc and no deaths,
and snow-white bullocks will crop the thickets in safety.
Then one may take gentle sleep beneath the open sky,
or may choose to lie unharmed upon a woodland ridge amid the grass,
unharmed, while the vast shade of the branches shelters [us]
from the sun's blaze, and while the whispering swarm coaxes
sleep to steal in, or the whistle of the approaching South Wind does.

div.note: Isaiah 53, vers. 2, 3, 4, 5.

lg.l: Then God will come down from heaven in abundant rain,
at whose coming the fields and every grove will grow green.
[The prophet] wrote that under Christ there would be golden ages:
the lame man will leap, and the deaf will hear, and
the blind will see, and the mute will break silence.
Nay more, the land left desert by thirst will flower like white
lilies; horned streams will course through the grass.
Crags and stones will be turned into a rich plain
that pastures snow-white swans on its grassy stream.
And where once the lairs of dragons and the deep dens of lions
men used to shun, where the deadliest tigress and boars
and ill-omened dogs and baleful birds
roamed; now herds of cattle and bullocks that have served well
are pastured there, and flocks of sheep, and the shaggy she-goats
and here the fat cows let down their milky udders.
Every field brings forth, every grove grows heavy with its yield,
and the untended woodland haunts redden with blood-red berries;
and the sacred violet-beds drink from watering springs.
As Lebanon, pouring out cedars and cypresses for houses,
so the wastelands will grow green with lofty trees.
This is that shepherd of the flocks, whose care [for them] is greatest;
he supplies the flocks with grass and with fresh-running streams,
and with abundant straw and bundles of fern he strews the hard ground beneath,

div.note: Isaiah 35, vers. 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 9, and Jeremiah 35, vers. 12, and Ezekiel 34, the whole chapter.
Jeremiah 23, vers. 3, 4.

lg.l: he strews the hard ground beneath them, lest the cold ice harm
the tender flock, and bring on scab and foul foot-rot.
But in the midday heats to seek out a shady [place] in the valley
he does not shrink, if perchance an oak of ancient timber
stretches out its huge branches, or wherever a dark
grove of thick holm-oaks lies low in sacred shade.
Nay more, all the plagues and diseases of the flocks the master
keeps in check, and with healing hand takes the infections away.
Or he plunges the whole flock in fresh streams, or the fever
he wards off by opening a vein that spurts blood.
With this shepherd slain, there spies around the sheepfolds
the wolf, a menace to the stalls; the herds and flocks flee
across rocks and crags and through sunken valleys;
This is he whom Daniel, turning many things over through the night,
saw borne up to the clouds of the ethereal heaven,
whom all the heaven-dwellers lead, in their midst, to the stars;
and here, on a flaming seat, the aged Thunderer
he saw; delicate linen clothed him in a snow-white garment,
and purest wool covered his hair;
round whom a rushing river runs with scorching flames,
and fiery wheels; his fiery face pours forth burning heat.
Around him countless children of starry heaven
chant holy songs, and lead Christ to his Father's threshold:

div.note: Zechariah 13, v. 7. Matthew 26. 31.

lg.l: Whom the Father willed to rule the peoples and rebellious nations with eternal authority;
whom the vast world
acknowledges as Lord, powerful far and wide.
After six hundred years have passed, an age
will come when, as they turn their fleeing backs in fear,
Christ will call the sons of Abraham back to Jerusalem, and all
guilt he will curb, and will expiate sins by [his] death.
Eternal justice will plant its footprints upon the earth;
with [his] blood he will confirm the predictions of the pious prophets.
The interpreter of the gods will cease to recount portents;
understanding will forsake the prophets’ ignorant minds:
Then with the flowing juice of ambrosia the most holy hero
will be anointed, as he enters the sanctuaries of highest heaven:
But after the Prince has undeservedly succumbed to the cruel shades,
the Roman will raze to their deepest foundations
Jerusalem’s earthly walls; inside, the triumphant enemy will rule
and will overturn the whole city from its seat;
and the citadels will fall headlong in the enemy's fires:
As a torrent in swift course down from the high mountains
rushes down with a dreadful roar, sweeping along with it whatever it meets,
rolling [all in its path] along with it, lays waste the fields; it will bring ruin
to the trees and devastation to the crops; thus, far and wide, the hostile storm
will lay everything low—towers and men,
the temple raised to heaven’s height, and the sacred inner shrines.
Then Christ will bind the nations to himself in a peaceful covenant,

div.note: Daniel 9:24–27.

lg.l: which neither force nor length of days will have power to abolish.
Him too Zechariah, foreknowing the age to come,
foretells, and calls him a Branch; but that Branch is golden,
of its own accord, with no human compelling it, from a field
that is barren, lifting [its] head as high as the stars of heaven.
A bud is thrust forth from the bark of the untouched mother [tree],
a most beautiful root is thrust forth from the dry wood,
a golden-haired offspring sprouts from the consecrated tree,
the gleam of this gold shone far and wide across the lands:
just as in the woods, in the cold of midwinter, the mistletoe is wont
to grow green with new leaf — a thing its own tree does not sow —
and to wreathe the smooth trunks with saffron growth:
such was the look of the gold putting out leaves on the shadowy
tree; so the [gold] foil rustled in the gentle wind
throughout all the lands that Phoebus sprinkles with his light.
The Virgin's kindly field knows no seed of generation,
and yet, behold, it swells; for with hidden showers he himself,
descending into the bosom of his consort, the ruler of Olympus,
the Great One, mingled in body, nourishes the great offspring,
and the heavenly Zephyr loosens her folds, and huge
the tree has risen up to heaven with its fruitful boughs,
which supplies foliage for the flock and shade for the shepherd.
Nor indeed can all lands bear all things;
willows by rivers and alders in thick marshes

div.note: Zechariah 3, verse 8, and chapter 6, verse 12; Isaiah 4, verse 2; Jeremiah 23, verse 5, and chapter 33, verse 15.

lg.l: grow; barren mountain-ashes [rise] on rocky mountains.
the shores are most joyful with myrtle-groves; lastly, the open
hills Bacchus loves, and yews the north wind and cold,
But Christ chose lowly Bethlehem; in that [town]
this Shoot willed to be born, not in lofty cities.
To the trees their homelands are allotted apart: India alone, black
ebony bears; the frankincense-bough belongs to the Sabaeans alone,
but Judaea, a very rich land, bore Christ:
His [is] this tree, rising from no seed,
and stretching its boughs and arms far across the world.
That [tree] no winters, no blasts, no rains
uproot; it stands unmoved, and through all the years,
rolling on through many generations of men, by enduring it prevails.
The ash is fairest in the woods, the pine in gardens,
the poplar by rivers, the fir on high mountains:
but if, beautiful Christ, you visit my soul again,
the ash in the woods will yield to you, [and] the pine in the gardens:
Joshua bears a double crown of gold and silver,
he builds the temple, and has taken his seat on a high throne.
Behold, Judah, your King comes, most gentle, but not
borne on a foaming horse does he come, one that in its racing the winds
might challenge, or, winding the alternating coils of its legs,
and, compressing the gathered fire, might roll it beneath its nostrils

div.note: Zechariah 6, vers. 11, 12, 13.
Zechariah 9, vers. 9, 10.

lg.l: But with no din of arms, nor blare of trumpets,
he enters Jerusalem, borne along on a slow she-ass.
Him all the peoples shall see returning in a cloud,
these too, who [dared] to defile with iron the sacred recesses
of his breast, and dared to bore through his hands and his feet,
shall mourn, and shall lift a mighty groan to the stars,
with breasts beaten, and with a savage howling uproar:
such bellowings as when, wounded, he flees the altar —
a bull, and has shaken the ill-aimed axe from his neck;
or such tears as a most sorrowing mother pours out
who has lost her firstborn son to a cruel death.
He shall climb the heights of the Mount of Olives, his foes
cut down, and shall lay open the bowels of the split mountain mass;
the ground shall burst apart, then the foundations shall gape open
of the thunderstruck mountain; one part of it shall slope toward sunrise,
another shall slope toward its setting; but a third toward the heights
the Rhipaean heights and Scythia, while a fourth shall recede toward the South.
He himself, on high, blazing in a triumphal rainbow,
shall review all the crimes of the peoples, and he himself,
a just King, shall visit punishments upon his enemies,
and shall render to Jerusalem's people the rewards of the palm they have merited.
Then rivers shall glide beneath the walls of Jerusalem
into the sea that lies above Judah and that washes it below;
thus shall Jesus hold sea and land alike under his sway.

div.note: Zechariah 12, verse 10.
Zechariah 14, verses 1, 4, 5, 8, and 9.

lg.l: This is that stone cut out of the crag, which one day
will shatter the enormous image; this image, on a slumberous night,
was seen to stand before the eyes of the King as he lay,
terrible to look on in his sleep, and flashing all over.
whose face was gold, its breast silver, its belly
bronze, but its legs stood stiff with gleaming iron:
This stone into an immense mass and, moreover, into a lofty mountain
grew, and vast it stretches out over the whole world.
A dominion has been raised up, to abide through all ages,
by the Almighty — a dominion which shall destroy all the kingdoms of the earth,
and which the long lapse of ages cannot change.
This is he whom Micah sang of with inspired lips,
the Prince of Bethlehem, who one day in power was to prove
outstanding, who by his might should take possession of the whole world.
He too, the fallen roof-tops of David's cottage,
shall raise up, and Jerusalem's downfall and her sorrowful ruins
shall set to rights, and rear her towers to heaven as of old.
Then the reaper, like the stooping ploughman, will keep the same
seasons; for at the same time the ploughman will entrust seed to the furrows,
while at that same time the reapers will harvest the wheat crop and hardy spelt;
with Saturn’s sickle, and they will overload the groaning wagons.
But while he cleaves the earth with the curved plough,
then on the sunny hills the grape will take on its colour,
and every vineyard will grow fat with abundant yield;

div.note: Daniel 2, vers. 31, 32, 33, 34.
Micah 5, vers. 1.
Amos 9, vers. 11, 13, 14.

lg.l: And then the vine-dresser will stain his legs with ripe grapes;
and the mountains will run with the sweetness of milk and new wine.
The captives, brought back to their homeland, to plant vines
will begin, and to soften wild fruits by cultivation,
and everywhere they will gather the fruits, each beneath his own tree,
and they will lie beneath the spreading fig tree and beneath the pliant vine.
From the bowls Arvisian wines will pour, a new nectar.
They will not fear the clash of arms, nor the wrath and threats
of the foe, nor the number of captains, nor the sound of trumpets,
but they will pass a peaceful life through untroubled ease,
these in a green field, those among the shady woods;
others beside the waters, where, wandering in slow windings,
the Jordan fringes its banks with tender reed.
Here beneath a high crag the pruner will sing to the breezes,
there, among his sheep, the shepherd will rest in the shade,
playing what he would, carefree, on his rustic reed.
As fire pants forth from the hot furnaces,
such shall be the coming of the Lord, and all the profane
will burn like stubble as well: like the lamp of Phoebus
the Sun of righteousness will shine, flashing with healing wings;
with those saving [wings] he will heal his sick servants.
The righteous will go forth rejoicing in a full throng,
as fat calves leap in lush pasture;

div.note: Micah 4, vers. 4.
Micah 4, vers. 3. Isaiah 2, vers. 4, and Isaiah chap. 11, and Isaiah 32, vers. 17, 18, and Isaiah 35, v. 10, and Isaiah 49, vers. 10, etc.
Malachi 4. verses 1, 2, 3.

lg.l: And they will trample the enemies underfoot like dust.
That day will tear up the enemy from his deepest roots,
and will strip the growing [plant] of its fruit, and scorch it as it bears.
Who has strength to bear the blaze of him who comes from on high,
the great winged one, who ratifies the covenant with blood?
That fire, refining the ores of silver and of gold,
and while the silver runs in streams; and the golden mass
of the Levitical stock melts in the vast furnace.
He himself, seated, skims the dross from the molten silver and gold;
then the Priest will duly sacrifice the beasts to Jehovah.
So all the Prophets sang with one voice
that Christ would be High Priest, King, and Prophet,
and would be begotten of the Virgin’s blood and of pure aether.

div.note: Malachi 3. 1, 2, 3, 4.

Lucretius, Virgil and other poets call the supreme God "aether"; and him whom Plato named Θεός from running, Aristotle named αἰθήρ from everlasting running — not from burning, as Cicero did. Here, therefore, I do not attribute to Christ an ethereal body, as the Marcionites do, but an ethereal Father, as the Church does.

div.p: The angels announce Christ's birth to the shepherds, who, as commanded, hasten to Bethlehem to the child; on the eighth day Christ is circumcised. Meanwhile a new star leads the Magi from Persia to Jerusalem. Herod, however, disturbed by the report that a new king has been born, kills the children of Bethlehem through his henchmen. Joseph and the Magi, meanwhile, warned in a dream by an angel, fled: the former with the child and his mother into Egypt, the latter by another road to their homeland. After the Magi had worshipped Christ, Simeon embraced him in his arms when he was presented to the priest. In his twelfth year he was found by his parents among the teachers in the temple, and with his parents he lived a private life until, upon completing the thirtieth year of his life, he was baptized by John in the Jordan. John's solitary and frugal manner of life is commended. Pluto assails the fasting Christ with various temptations; after Pluto has been defeated and driven away, the angels offer their service to the Lord. Christ chooses twelve companions of modest means; the character of Christ's kingdom is described; the poet condemns war among Christians and interweaves various divine and pious meditations.

lg.l: It was night, and throughout all lands the weary creatures,
the race of winged things and of flocks, deep sleep held fast.
Certain shepherds — their tender lambs upon the mountains
while, wakeful, they guard [them] — behold, suddenly poured all about them
a new light flashed out; just as when a dark-blue cloud
kindles with the sun's rays and gleams back far and wide:
at once the angelic squadrons, rejoicing, in their ranked array
They soothed the upper air with song, and flew through heaven,
and with lofty praise they extolled the Heaven-dweller and King.
They were stunned in their hearts, and a chill tremor ran through their inmost
bones: a sudden voice was heard from heaven on high:
Shepherds, call back your spirits, and your sorrowful fear
put away, for God has sent us from bright Olympus,
he himself bidding [us] bear these tidings: pass them on through the swift breezes:
Behold, today, brought forth by birth into the light of day,
is Christ at Bethlehem; he will rule the conquered world,
and will press kings and rebellious nations into servitude.
Nay more, he will bring even the shades below completely under his yoke,
and with his right hand will thrust the King of Hell down to Tartarus.
Go now, and make your way from here to Bethlehem's threshold,
and look upon the Child lying in the deep manger.
Saying this, Gabriel then flies through the vast air
on the oarage of his wings, with a whole throng accompanying him
of winged youths, who gleam with bright light
and in their assembly ringed the sky about, and gave forth songs:
as snowy swans sometimes amid the clear clouds,
when they bring themselves back from feeding, and through their long
necks give out tuneful measures; the river resounds, and far off the Asian
marsh, struck [by their call].
Meanwhile they seized upon the road where the footpath points [the way],
the shepherds; they climbed up to the town and were approaching the dwellings.
They marvel at the words of the winged one; they marvel at Jesus:
and at the radiant countenance of God and the Virgin's face—
they cannot satisfy their minds, and they burn as they gaze,
And they are moved alike by the face of the Child and of the Mother.
Holy Child, are you that God whom the palace of heaven
does not hold, and yet you lie back in a little manger?
Beneath the gables of my narrow breast’s dwelling
enter, and come into our home, my guest,
Here, Child, is your stall, here is your cradle: sleep.
And now the eighth Dawn a kindly day for wretched mortals
had brought forth, and with her rays had unveiled the world.
He sets about to cut away with the blade the tip of the foreskin
of the infant Christ — the Priest, after the custom of the nation.
Attendants of various sorts stand round about, on right and left,
they make ready warm water, and the tepid blood
they catch in a bowl; even then the name Jesus
they lay upon him, and they wash the infant's wound and anoint it.
Christ Child, even now you are the begetter of men and of gods:
therefore even now grow accustomed to be called upon with prayers.
You had scarcely entered upon this pleasant light of life,
when from your tender body you pour out drops of holy
blood, and, torn by the hard point, you weep.
It is I who earned this wound; mine is the guilt to be expiated,
for the guilt is wholly mine; my parents begot me such as I am.
But your mother was holy, an untouched maiden;
and your soul is holy, knowing no guilt of any kind.
You, by a word, to cut away for me the primal stain
are able, Christ; if you wish to prevent the contagion of sin
from harming me and to ward off such a plague.
I shall not be unmindful, nor shall the thanks for so great a deed
slip from my breast, so long as breath rules these limbs.
Straightway the report travels through Judah’s great cities:
that at Bethlehem [there is] a Boy sprung from royal blood.
who will hold both sea and lands beneath his universal sway,
as so many holy oracles of the prophets have foretold.
Moreover Magi, who held the Persian realms,
while they watch the stars gliding in the silent sky,
behold, they saw a new Star with abundant light,
blazing, and gliding from the summit of highest heaven,
and marking out the road which leads into the city of Jerusalem.
But indeed the kings, weighed down by a wavering dread,
resolve, through the realms of the Arabs, through inhospitable rocks,
to make for Judaea, and to venture upon lands set far away.
So they carry through the journey begun, and draw near to Jerusalem,
and keep pace with the Star as it advances with steps that do not falter.
They had not yet entered the city when the Star turned aside and passed
from their sight, like smoke into thin air:
Then briefly the kings pour out these words from their lips:
Great sons of Isaac, stock of Abraham mighty in arms,
tell us, since we have come into your lands:
what region holds Christ, what place [holds him]? For his [sake]
we have come, and have crossed the dry fields of the Arabs.
Us hither a glittering star — yet not without the divine will —
has led us from the East, from its peoples and the Red Sea shore;
this Boy, a King ruling far and wide and mighty in word,
we declare him; he alone shall have dominion over all coasts;
For that reason we bring him solemn gifts.
After this report had been spread abroad through the city of Jerusalem,
discord arises among the alarmed citizens,
which with a sudden commotion shook the city to its foundations.
The King, troubled by this commotion and by the words of the Magi—
what King they say is born, what gifts they have prepared—
ponders much, and [turns] his mind now this way, now di[vides it that way],
and pulls it in different directions, turning it over from every angle.
As when the trembling light of water in bronze basins,
flung back by the sun, or by the image of the radiant moon,
flits far and wide over every place, and now up into the air
is lifted, and strikes the panelled ceiling of the roof above;
To him, wavering between alternatives, this plan seemed preferable:
the chief priests, and the scribes, [to be] summoned within his halls
he orders, and took his seat in the midst upon a high throne;
he asks many things concerning Christ, and seeks out the land
of the Lord's birth; to him inquiring with heart now calmed
they answer him, “At Bethlehem,” just as the foreknowing oracles
of the holy prophets had often warned, knowing beforehand what was to come.
Herod called the Kings to himself, into his halls,
secretly asking when the fiery star, as it rose, had lifted
its sacred face to highest heaven and dispelled the darkness.
Go, he says, illustrious Kings, whom the star has driven
to attempt unknown roads; search out Christ,
I will follow you, and let us render him the honours he has earned.
After setting out, they see that beneath a clear sky
all is calm; once more, with abundant light, there sped
the blazing star, until at last it stood still above the dwelling
of the Virgin, and lit up the roof far and wide with its lamp.
Then the Kings, glad beyond their wont with sweet delight,
burst through the inner thresholds of the house, and the kindly
Child they behold, whom his divine mother, in her arms,
as he smiles, cherishes in a soft embrace; and he in turn
gives his mother embraces, and plants sweet kisses [on her].
When the Virgin caught sight of the three monarchs coming
she was struck dumb at the first sight: then, with fire,
a deep blush rose beneath, and ran across her heated face:
just as if with blood-red purple one had stained Indian
ivory, or where many lilies blush mingled with
the rose, white [as they are]: such were the hues the Virgin's face gave forth.
They marvel at the Child, and fix their gaze upon the Virgin,
the Kings do so humbly, and worship the holy Godhead.
In the Child they mark the signs of divine beauty,
and note his burning eyes, what spirit is his,
what a countenance, and what a sound of voice; it delights [them] to gaze without end
at the maiden's face, how she shines forth with rosy neck,
and how her gleaming hair flows down over her milk-white neck.
Then gifts of gold, with myrrh and Sabaean frankincense,
they give to the Child, a memorial and pledge of true love.
And these are the beginnings and, sacred from the race of Japheth,
the firstfruits, which the tents of Shem shall soon receive.
For this is the nation which, by Christ's own blood,
shall bear his name to the stars, and from whose stock descendants
shall see all things beneath [their] feet, where the Sun, returning in his course,
beholds [either] Ocean, [this nation] shall see turned and ruled.
Little Child, yet vast in fame, vaster in deeds.
Though you are the greatest ruler of the gods, and the world
you govern with everlasting sway, and terrify with the thunderbolt,
Yet you do not shrink from the lap of your needy mother.
Nor do you flee her embraces; but you lay kisses on your mother,
while with tender lips you drain her white breasts.
You leave your Father’s kingdom and the blessed abodes,
that you may snatch men from death, and break their chains:
What thanks, what thanks shall I render you for such a gift?
I can repay neither worthy thanks nor the gifts that are due;
but I set before you small gifts with no adornment:
the frankincense of prayers, the myrrh of tears, and the gold of the heart.
Meanwhile the heaven wheels round, and night rushes up from Ocean,
wrapping in its great shadow both the earth and the sky,
and the wiles of the sons of Romulus, and the wicked arts of Herod,
who ponders various outcomes in his heart
while sleep held the rest of living things throughout the earth.
It was the hour at which the first rest for weary mortals
begins and, the gods’ most welcome gift, steals over them.
while the kings were relaxing their limbs in tranquil repose:
In their dreams, behold, before their eyes a winged messenger from Olympus
stood by, and seemed with his voice to warn them thus:
You who mark, gliding through the silent sky,
the stars, and who watch the settings and risings of the constellations.
Wake at once and take flight; return to your kingdom,
to your homeland, by another route;
He spoke; then the youth hid himself high in heaven,
making for the stars; black night and sleep left the Magi.
They rise, obey the counsel, and carry out what they were commanded;
and they hasten headlong in flight, and traverse woods and glades,
lest by chance Herod should pursue them at a run.
For, raging in his mind, deceived by the trickery of the Magi,
who meant to return to their own country without consulting him;
to destroy the boys of Bethlehem by a pitiable death
he resolved, and to mar the fathers’ faces with the death of innocent
infants, and to fill every house with mourning;
Alas, can anyone be guilty of so great a crime?
Then the mother went to Solomon’s temple and, carrying the blessed
child in her own bosom, fell prostrate at the altar;
and to the priest the devout Virgin, twin doves
offered as the redemption-price for her son, according to ancient custom.
Here, weighed down with years and ripe in mind, Jesus
Simeon received into his lap, and thereupon speaks thus:
In your peace let your servant depart, just as
you promised, since the begetter of gods and of men
I have drunk in with these eyes; this light you have prepared before the face
of all, that the longed-for lamp might light up the nations
and that it might be the sole glory of his own sons of Sarah.
And many things besides he sang from his inspired mouth,
the long-lived prophet: with his eyes and with his whole heart
he clings to the infant, and cherishes him in his lap, planting kisses.
Anna too was there, heavy with age, most holy,
foreknowing what was to come; she, suppliant and lowly, was accustomed to call
upon God with her voice in the Temple, by nights and by days,
and she was filled with a more immediate power of God, when
she prophesied much concerning Christ, and the Thunderer’s warnings
She set them forth in words and foretold the deeds that were to come:
to whom belongs surpassing glory, and whose temples twin flames
pour forth in gladness, and his Father's star is disclosed upon his head.
Be present, holy Child—may it be granted me to put my arms around your neck
and to cherish you, Christ, in my lap:
may you breathe a hidden fire into me, so that I may receive you with all my heart;
and I embrace you as Lord through every adversity.
O Child, how I revere you! for the face you bear is not
mortal, nor does your voice sound like a boy’s: you are God himself.
Never indeed would I be torn away from your sweet embrace,
Christ, but would spend my whole lifetime with you.
Meanwhile, while the king tosses in a surge of wrath,
there came to Joseph in his sleep the likeness of Gabriel,
in all things like the heaven-dweller, both in voice and in colour
and in golden hair, and limbs graceful with youth.
Then he addresses him thus, and there is a smile in his voice as he gives this warning:
Holy old man, can you sleep on amid such a crisis,
and not see the dangers that from now on surround you?
King Herod rages, driven on by monstrous anger,
He broods in his heart over a thousand stratagems and a dreadful crime.
Do you not flee headlong from here, while there is power to hasten away?
Come now, break off delay: the Child, together with his Virgin mother,
take these as companions of [your] destiny, make for the realms of Pharaoh:
There is a place which the sons of Abraham call by the name Misraim,
an ancient land, mighty in arms and in the richness of its soil;
Ethiopian men once dwelt there; now the report is that later generations
called the nation Egypt after their leader's name;
here you may lie hidden, until by a safe path I set you
back home to your own land; now in the silent shadows of night
take up your journey, and tear sweet sleep from your eyes;
lest the Dawn overtake you lingering in these lands.
The angel, having spoken thus, mingled himself with the black night.
But aged Joseph, terrified by the sudden shades,
springs up from his bed and urgently rouses Mary:
Shake off sleep at once, Virgin, and the tender boy
take with you as a companion in exile; God, from heaven on high,
has sent a wing-bearing servant of surpassing form,
who urges [us] to hasten our flight and to depart from our homeland;
See, he urges us on again; we follow you, gracious winged one,
whoever you are; we gladly obey your command.
O be near, graciously help us, and guide our steps;
He spoke, and amid such words the mother [took] the infant
took [him] up as companion of her exile, whom in the shade of night
she herself, carrying [him] before her at her breast, sought the long ridges
of lonely woodlands, her husband the Carpenter going with her.
Thus the two advanced together through the dark stretches of the roads,
shielded by the darkness and by the gift of friendly night,
cover the space between, and draw near to the land
of Egypt, which the river makes fruitful with black silt,
and, rushing apart, runs out into seven mouths —
the Nile, flowing down all the way from the dark-hued Indians.
But the cruel king roars, bristling, with bloodied mouth,
and holds immediate death over the defenceless boys;
But my mind shudders to remember, and shrinks back in grief from
the unspeakable slaughter and the savage deeds of the tyrant,
yet I will set them out in these few words, and unfold the matter in order.
After he had conceived fury and savage anguish in his heart,
Herod himself works out within himself the time and manner,
and lets loose every rein of his anger.
He drives the men to arms and spurs them all on with these words:
O brave young men, word has come to our ears
that at Bethlehem a Boy is born of the blood of kings;
whose descent they reckon up from the ancient stock
of David—he who will establish the cities of Judah by laws;
but it is to drive you from your realms that this heir is sought,
and to stir up quiet citizens into war.
Upon this King the rebel sons of Abraham will turn their eyes
and their faces, and, with the peace defiled, will raise up tumults.
Now, O chosen band, cut out with the sword the root
of this dissension, and the King, the head and the cause of our evils,
take away, lest the citizens, restored in arms and in spirit,
turn their steel against me and against their masters, the Romans.
Each of you, kill two boys as soon as possible;
let none of you take pity on the new-born King;
take javelins in hand, and gird the sword to your side;
now lift up your spirits, and turn glad minds [to my words]:
no one out of this company shall go from me ungifted;
Thus fury was added to the young men’s hearts; from there [they went],
plunderers in a black mist, whom the belly's relentless
rage has driven out blind, and the cubs left behind
wait with parched throats. After cruelly entering the city,
they break through the entrances and butcher every
(O the crime!) infant, and fill the places far and wide with death.
But the trembling mothers pressed their children to their breasts,
and raise huge groans, and in wretched uproar
were throwing all into confusion; the cry strikes the golden stars:
now they disfigure their breasts with fists, now their faces with nails;
and cradle their boys in their arms and comfort them, pressing kisses upon them.
Who could unfold so great a disaster, who could tell of such deaths,
or could match such sorrows with tears?
O young men savage in war, and O bloodstained King!
Do you not shudder, with the blood of children, to defile your foul
hands? Cruel father! Or did any
of the Myrmidons, or of the Dolopes, or soldier of the harsh [Ulysses],
ever rage against his own offspring? What barbarian ever
spattered his household with so great a slaughter of boys?
What so great [wrong] could this holy Child commit against you,
what could the boys do? — on whom the soldier so many cruel
wounds inflicted, burying the steel in the tender lung.
Blessed are the boys who suffered so many wounds for Christ’s sake;
you, having no share in sweet life, and snatched from the breast —
a black day carried [you] off, and sank [you] in untimely death.
But now, borne aloft across the clear upper air,
among the dwellers in heaven, you all hold the heights above.
Illustrious souls, if my songs have any power,
no day shall ever take you from the memory of time.
So long as the house of Abraham the lofty heights of Zion
shall dwell beside, and the heavenly Father shall hold dominion.
But as soon as the cruel King's life, [passing] through the air,
went down sorrowing to the shades, and left the body behind:
and as soon as the infant, with the first soles of his feet, his steps
had planted:
behold, again in sleep, with the same face as when he came before,
the winged one's form soon presented itself to the Carpenter, bidding him
return to his homeland: the holy commands he takes up,
Joseph does, who had great hope of seeing again the realms
of his fathers; he sets out: in [his father's] right hand little Jesus
entwined himself, and follows his father with steps not equal to his.
Behind comes the Virgin, turning over the whole tangled journey [in her mind],
and at last the threshold of their native dwelling was reached.
But when the report flies that through the cities of Judah there reigns
cruel Archelaus, and, fearing to settle in his native land,
Joseph chose to settle in the realms of Antipas
Herod; unnoticed in the town of Nazareth
that boy lay hidden who draws his lineage from Olympus.
Little boy, whose fame is greater than your years,
though unknown you lay hidden in a secret dwelling;
you are small, yet you are also the great King of great Olympus;
you are poor, yet rich in gifts; the Son, and at the same time
the almighty Father; a servant, yet the world's greatest Creator
You are the Author and the Lord, whom farthest Thule shall serve.
Though such is [your] ethereal vigour and heavenly origin,
yet you do not shrink from taking on a mortal face,
and from dwelling in earthly limbs and dying members.
But, Christ, with what praises shall I exalt you to heaven?
[You] who from the height of heaven descended to the lowest shades,
so that you might be able to lift from us Satan's manacles and his tight
bonds; a thousand hard labours for our sake
under an unjust nation, by the deeds of wicked Herod,
you had endured; all enemies, and the hostile camps,
the pale shades of Erebus, and the deep night,
you hold down by your rule, and curb with chains and prison.
The Stygian lakes trembled before you; you throw open the realms
of pallor; you are the Lord of all things; you are the greatest.
You alone who by dying restore our fortune.
Hail, true offspring of Jove, glory added to the gods,
and come favourably, with auspicious step, to us and to my undertakings.
When Christ’s first year after his eleventh had begun,
he went up to Jerusalem, and bent his step toward the walls.
There stood in the city a vast temple of solid marble,
whose bronze thresholds rose upon steps, and whose beams were joined
with bronze; the hinge creaked on brazen doors.
The walls are covered with gold, gold gleams from the doorposts,
the coffered ceilings of the sacred building shine with gold;
and the Temple’s inner sanctuary blazes with magnificent hangings.
Here Christ, turning over the records of the men of old
bearing a spirit and a manly concern beyond his years,
sat down in their midst; then with calm speech the teachers
he addresses them, and delights to listen and to reply.
All fell silent and fixed their attentive gaze
marvelling at Christ, because he has by God's gift
such a mind, and an understanding of things greater than his years.
They discussed many things among themselves in varied speech,
who was this new guest that had taken his seat in the sacred building,
both bringing teachings and ready to answer.
Indeed, the boy's excellence recurs to their minds, and so too does the abundant
dignity of his countenance; his features remain fixed in their hearts,
and his words; nor can their hearts be satisfied with gazing,
and they believed — and the belief was not empty — that he was of the race of the gods.
But for the lost boy his parents, weary and grieving,
search three days, calling him again and again.
This way and that they turn their eyes, and range over the whole
of Jerusalem with their gaze; beneath the central vault of the Temple,
raised high upon a seat and teaching the law,
they find him at last; but they stood amazed and silent,
and turning their eyes upon each other they held their faces still;
with joy and fear, eager to touch Christ,
they burned; but the matter, being unknown, troubles their minds.
As soon as the most holy Virgin could speak,
she addressed her son and poured forth these words from her lips:
"Dear boy, where has your care for us gone?
Whom are you fleeing, or who keeps you from our embraces?
Alas, son, you do not know what great sorrows by your departure,
you have brought upon us; as for my restorative sleep, anxiety
has broken off; my brow was far from glad, and my mind was troubled,
nor were my cheeks free of tears; while I search through all
Jerusalem for you, and stray from the familiar quarter of the streets,
in case you had by chance gone astray; at last it is granted [me] to look upon
your face, my son, and to hear and return familiar words.
So spoke Mary; but to Mary her son began thus in reply:
What does it profit, O mother, to give way to so great a toil
that you should track me down in tears? I could not believe
that by my departure I brought you grief as great as this.
The care you bear for me—this, best of mothers, I beg you for my sake
to lay aside, and to let your son endure toil for his Father,
gracious mother—for it is right for me to undertake my Father's commands.
I have made ready to obey the command of the great Father,
May this please us; this is my only delight
and my solace in trouble; nor will that toil weigh me down.
When he had spoken these words: the Virgin and her elder husband
then make their way back home and ponder the boy's
words within their minds, and kept the care pressed down beneath their hearts.
But he, planting his steps with cares to match,
follows after, and carries out the commands of his father and mother;
and he lived out his years with his Father, without glory,
in obscurity, until ripened age had made him a man.
After Christ had completed thirty years, their months having run their course,
he soon makes his way to the winding waters
of rushing Jordan, which with brimming flood was grazing
its green banks, and cutting through the rich tilled fields
Sky-blue Jordan, the river most pleasing to heaven.
Here a vast throng, streaming out to the banks, came rushing:
mothers and men, boys and unwedded girls
As many as the leaves that in the woods at winter's first chill
drift down and fall; or, toward land from the deep sea,
as many birds flock together, when the cold
[season] drives [them] across the sea, and sends [them] to sunny lands,
They stood praying to be bathed in the sacred river.
Here in the woods, among the wild beasts' desolate
lairs and dens, John drags out his life, the King of Olympus’
herald: barren parents begot this prophet.
Bristling in coarse hair, and covered with a camel's hide,
He foretells many things and proclaims the grim wrath to come.
The ground pours forth easy nourishment; woodland honey
the branches give, and plants feed [him] with roots torn up.
His cups are clear springs, and streams swift in their
course: not Ceres, nor the Massic gifts of Bacchus,
does he crave, nor has he loaded his tables with rich feasts:
yet in spirit he matched the wealth of kings — O best of prophets,
happy in your lot, you who have come to know the country life,
and Pan, and old Silvanus, and the sister Nymphs.
Royal feasts set before you have done you no harm,
but [you are] content with leafage and the food of simple plants;
you spurn the luxury which the age of iron has brought forth.
No golden bedposts gleam for you on festal couches.
But amid dense beeches, their crowns thick with shade,
beside a running stream of water you lie down on the green grass:
or you sit beneath a high rock, or at ease in a cave
you sleep, and no care breaks off your wholesome slumbers.
This life the men of old once practised, before
both the frenzy of war and the lust for possession followed.
Golden Adam led this life upon the earth,
and golden, as men relate, under that King were
the ages: so did he rule the peoples in tranquil peace.
when the impious race had not yet feasted upon bullocks,
The fruits that the branches and the willing fields themselves
bore of their own accord, he plucked; then the fields were
subject neither to men's mattocks nor to any tending
then no husbandmen broke up the rich fields;
nor indeed to mark out, or to divide the field by a boundary,
was lawful; they sought [their gain] for the common store, and the earth herself
yielded everything more freely, with no one asking.
O fortunate beyond measure, if only they had known their blessings,
those earliest fathers, nurslings of the all-parent earth:
who amid cool springs and sounding groves,
and the couches of the riverbanks, and meadows freshened by streams,
far from the din, and far from discordant arms,
lived out their lives amid the deepest silence.
Until little by little a worse and tarnished age
came on, leaving behind the foul traces of deceit.
whereby [it bade men] essay Thetis [the sea] with ships, whereby to gird with walls
the towns, whereby it bade [them] cleave furrows in the earth.
Then for the first time the rivers felt hollowed alder boats.
Then the sailor made numbers and names for the stars,
the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the bright Bear of Lycaon.
Then how to catch wild beasts with snares and to trick [birds] with lime
was discovered, and how to ring great woodland glades with hounds;
and now one man lashes the broad river with his casting-net;
seeking the deep pools, while another hauls his dripping nets through the sea;
and unrelenting toil, conquering all things, hammers out various arts,
as does want, pressing hard amid adversity.
Then some delight too much in the breezes of popular favor,
and another delights to ravage neighboring homes with the sword.
Another seeks wealth, and drives his way into the bowels of the earth,
blind with a mad love of silver and of gold.
Neither the shade of tall groves, nor soft meadows
could stir their hearts; nor the stream which, rolled over rocks,
clearer than amber, makes for the open plain:
But this prophetic seer, to whom no acres of inherited
land belonged, no weights of gold wrought
or unwrought, content with the shady covert of the groves,
lived out his life, and feeds himself on unbought fare.
He did not grieve in pity for the poor man, nor envy the man who has;
nor does he stand thunderstruck at the rostra, nor does applause, as he gapes,
through the theatre’s tiers—for it is doubled—from commons and senators alike,
seize him; but the son, content with his native air,
does not seek a homeland lying beneath another sun.
Christ, coming up to him, addresses him with friendly words:
Offspring of Zechariah, into whom a great mind and spirit
the almighty Father breathes, and opens up what is to come,
To you I flee for refuge, and as a suppliant now in living water
I beg to be dipped; sprinkle my body with the river's water.
John replied: “Yours, O great King, is the task of deciding what you desire;
for me it is right to carry out commands.”
But it is I whom you should instead immerse in the healing river;
indeed, I do not deem myself worthy of the honour
of pouring abundant water upon shoulders so sacred.
But if the longing in your mind is so great, if so great the desire
to sprinkle your body with water, and to enter the rushing river,
I will obey; follow me, and I will lead you there by a safe path.
When he had spoken these words, Jordan, in his pleasant stream —
now aged (but a god’s old age is vigorous and green),
eagerly raising himself up among the poplar leaves
was seen; fine linen veiled him in a blue-green mantle,
and a shadowy reed covered his hair;
And when he saw Christ coming toward him across the grass,
he lowered the horns upon his bull-like brow,
humbly venerating him, he invited him to his glassy hall:
Then at last Christ cast himself headlong, with his whole body,
into the river; Jordan, with his pure flood,
received him as he came, and bore him up in gentle arms.
But behold — a sudden portent, and marvellous to tell:
for Christ sees the mid-heaven tear itself apart,
and a new light run across the vast sky,
moreover he beholds a dove on high in a cloud,
which gives a mighty clapping with its wings, and gliding down from heaven
flies down, and stood above [his] head; and then the lofty
[the lofty] heavens thundered, and a voice was uttered and borne to [their] ears:
Behold my strength, my great power—he alone;
behold—the beloved Son of the Most High Father. Listen to him,
O nations, all [of you], carry out [his] commands:
These things done, he seeks the deserted caves of wild beasts:
Here among vast crags and bristling wild haunts
for forty full days a long fast
he endured, and as many nights without any food.
Here at the foot of the crag, wearied, Jesus
sat down, awaiting the enemy from the Stygian abodes.
This is the Stygian King, once of the highest race
of the heaven-dwellers, whom, while he was claiming divine honours,
the Almighty drove headlong with a monstrous whirlwind
together with his companions, who now are rolled in the lowest depth.
They, chafing, with a great roaring, around the barriers of Dis
rage; in heaven’s citadel sits Jehovah,
holding the sceptre, and he softens their spirits and tempers their rage.
Were he not to do so, the seas and lands and the deep heaven
they would surely sweep away with them in their rush, and whirl them through the air.
But the Almighty Father hid [them] in black caverns,
fearing this, and [set] a mass and lofty mountains on top [of them],
placed [upon them], and appointed a king who, under a fixed compact,
would know, when bidden, both how to tighten and how to give slack reins.
This is Pluto, the Prince of darkness and of shadowy night,
Lord of the Tartarean abode, of stagnant Avernus
the dweller, who the lowest shades and the silent souls
holds down with dreadful rule; to whom grim wars,
and wrath and ambushes and guilty crimes are dear at heart.
He is wont to arm brothers of one mind for battle against each other,
and to throw households into turmoil through hatred; a thousand names are his,
a thousand arts of harming; and now he was ascending, and lo,
the cavern roared horribly; the earth, gaping open by force,
unbars the abodes below and throws open the realms
pale [realms], hated by the gods, and above, the monstrous abyss
is seen; meanwhile he transforms himself into the features
of an old man in dreadful squalor, on whose chin abundant
unkempt white hair lies; his eyes stand fixed in flame;
a filthy cloak hangs knotted from his shoulder,
and he ploughs his foul brow with wrinkles, rolling his fiery
eyes, then making his way across the grass with trembling step
he opens his pestilent jaws, and with haughty voice
addresses the King of heaven and, agitated, begins thus:
"Son of the highest Father, who by [your] power turn the heaven,
make these harsh rocks into grain snatched by the waves,
Christ replies to him: men cannot sustain their life
with the gifts of cultivated grain, but with the words from the mouth
which the almighty Father pours forth; by these they can live;
these provide sweet nourishment to mortals.
Then the fierce enemy, with a loud screech through the air,
lifts Christ aloft; he flies through the vast expanse of air
And at last, light [of wing], he alighted upon the Temple's height.
With these words he approaches Christ, and asks such things as these:
Son of the highest Father, cast yourself headlong, with your whole body,
send yourself down to the ground; God from the high heaven
will send winged sentinels, who in a close-packed throng
will guard you; you will not harm your body with any wound.
To this Christ replies: “In vain do you try to deceive the King of high heaven
to beguile with such snares. As he was speaking such words
[Satan] snatches him up, not timidly, and lifts him high into the clouds:
just as when either a hare, or a swan of gleaming white body,
Jove's winged [bird] has carried off, making for the heights, in its hooked claws.
or [when] a lamb, sought by its mother with much bleating,
the wolf of Mars snatched from the stalls: just so did Satan seize him,
who is the Father of humankind and of gods, the eternal Power,
and lifts him toward the high clouds.
Christ is borne aloft in the clear air;
then, set down far off upon the lofty summit of a mountain,
he halted; from there, the sail-winged sea, and the lands lying [below],
and the shores, and while he looks down upon the peoples of the world far and wide,
the King of murky night addresses Christ once more:
These things indeed are mine; if you will worship me with vows,
we shall grant you these kingdoms; accept them, and give laws
to the peoples, and establish customs and walls for men.
At these words Christ, deeply stirred, [orders him] to depart
he commands, and followed him as he fled with such a voice as this:
Hasten your flight, and go beneath gloomy Tartarus,
instigator of crimes; worship with prayer the Divinity of heaven;
Sing your vows to God alone, and the mighty Lord
win over with suppliant gifts. But grim Avernus'
King goes off in confusion, flees at once swifter than the East Wind
and makes for hell; fear gave wings to his feet:
And just as that one, before the enemy's weapons give chase,
straightway, off the track, hid himself in the high mountains —
the wolf, when the shepherd or a great bullock has been slain,
knowing his own bold deed: and, drooping his tail,
tucked it quivering beneath his belly, and made for the woods:
just so Satan, distraught, withdraws from sight,
and, content with flight, mingled himself in the midst of the shadows.
But Christ the victor remains undaunted, the enemy
huge [enemy] to flight by his might, and stands firm in his own bulk:
Then the princes of heaven came flying from the sky
on swift-borne wings; in the upper air they soothed [him] with song,
and to God the victor they serve wine and bread.
After this Christ, making his way to the nearest shore,
calls Andrew and Peter, while they are handling their nets;
they obey the call, and follow Christ.
Then with his voice he calls John and his brother James,
swiftly they leave their father, worn out with age,
and do not refuse to obey the Lord's commands.
Besides these, Thomas, Matthew, [and] the eldest son
of Alphaeus, and Simon, Thaddaeus, and Philip,
Bartholomew, and Judas himself, the contriver of the treachery:
all these, their homes and their goods left behind, to Christ
join themselves to him as companions, having pursued no lesser aims.
All these had one love, and one and the same toil for all,
namely, to bring the nations utterly beneath their own yoke;
and to hold sea and lands under total sway:
He sends these twelve ambassadors out into the world,
equipped with no art, [girded] with no shining arms;
girded; they carry no javelins, no [darts] gleaming with iron;
they do not fit blood-dripping crests to their helmets.
They hollow out no helmets and bend no willow wickerwork
for shields; none of them fashions bronze breastplates
or fashion smooth greaves from pliant silver.
[Christ has] no need of barbaric wealth, nor of many-coloured arms;
does Christ have need; he will not stir up battle lines and slaughter.
He brings with him neither violence nor the forces of the East and remotest Bactra;
and, with his triumph won, he was going with his mother.
But lowly and suppliant he comes, without any forces at all,
lacking city, home, and food, and in want of everything
he learns what poverty is and how to endure hard labors,
and all the threats of sea, of land, and of Styx.
O you sprung from the race of the gods, the throngs [of birds] flying through the empty air
of birds have set their sweet nests in the grass:
and the foxes too have dug their lairs beneath the earth;
but you, who have no hearth, no household gods,
nor the roof of a poor hut heaped up with turf,
do not know where you will be able to rest the whole night through,
do not know where you might lay your bowed neck.
Other commanders choose men to follow them into war,
they choose men outstanding in valour and stout of heart,
and such as are strong in arms and in wealth; but Christ [chose] unarmed men
who had neither breeding nor refinement, but whose livelihood,
about the gliding rivers of fish-teeming Judaea,
was their craft, and their house was poor; nor were the mighty men's
gifts known to them; mighty Jesus chose such a retinue,
these he willed to join as partners in the highest affairs.
The kings of the earth, stiff with figured work and with gold,
take their seats on ancestral thrones, the people thronging round;
golden sceptres they bear in hand, and about the neck they wear
golden collars; then double crowns of gems and gold
they set upon their heads; and in a row the likenesses of their ancient forefathers,
[fashioned] of ancient cedar, or of gold, or of flashing bronze,
stand in the forecourt; and embossed in gold
[are] the brave deeds of the fathers; but Christ, the greatest King of the world,
who now restrains the sea and the land and the heaven with fear;
No gilded robe gleams, nor is his milk-white neck
entwined with gold; never did Jesus wear
garments wrought with art and with proud purple,
nor a veil bordered about with saffron acanthus,
nor did he bear fasces or sceptres; no palace of his shines
with luxury; nor do arms hang upon sacred doorposts:
no captured chariots, and no curved axes.
Nor helmet-crests, nor the huge bars of gates,
and spears and shields, and beaks wrenched from ships' hulls.
Far other was his temper, and different the
condition of Christ's kingdom; never [did] so dread a craving
Yours, O Christ, was [the desire] to rule the heavenly kingdoms,
[was your] desire, and you subdue the peoples with heavenly arms;
and you scorn to trouble yourself with the mad triumphs of men;
seeing that here right and wrong are turned about, so many wars across the world,
so many faces of crime, no honour worthy
of the plough; the fields lie squalid, their farmers carried off,
and curved sickles are melted down into the rigid sword.
How many strong nations come together for grim battles?
Discord arose among the kings in a mighty upheaval;
Germany grows fat with its own blood: the Belgians
are still sharpening their darts, and urging one another to arms;
not yet sated with the blood of so many young men, they go on
still to clash with one another with matched weapons;
the cities of Italy, the compacts between them broken,
take up arms; unholy Mars rages over the whole world:
as when the four-horse teams have poured themselves out of the starting-gates,
they fling themselves along the course; and, hauling on the reins in vain,
the charioteer is carried away by his horses, and the car does not heed the reins.
What frenzy, O citizens, what madness of war so great?
what mad Discord, with her mantle rent,
goad you, and Bellona, raging with her cruel scourge?
Do you forever forge your fathers’ swords in the furnaces?
and does it please you to carry the standards, and to hear the blare of trumpets?
O best Leader of the Christians, while you are safe I shall never
admit that our fortunes or our kingdoms are conquered:
what grief so great, I ask, rouses untamed wrath
among the wretched sons of Christ rushing into wars?
These were not the promises you had given your servants as you departed,
but an everlasting peace, made fast by a sure covenant,
you had promised; what purpose, then, has changed your mind?
Surely there was no deceit in you, whose faithfulness in deeds
and words is supreme; but the accursed love of gain,
and pride along with it, and our deadly crimes,
have sunk us in these evils; these drive us into battle.
Sons of Christ, do not school your hearts to such wars,
nor turn your strong might against your country's vitals:
but let the harsh ages grow gentle at last, with wars laid aside;
now, in gladness, settle a peaceful covenant.
And you, great Father, have mercy on your own holy ones:
glide down from heaven, Christ, and visit the Latin borders,
where a grim battle is joined under an ill-starred omen.
Make them unite in friendship and conclude treaties;
grant everlasting peace, let the reign of Saturn return,
only look upon us, and set an end to [our] toil;
command that hereafter no war-trumpets be blown, nor that
swords laid upon hard anvils ring out,
that hereafter the fields grow fat no more with our blood:
For throughout the world we have suffered enough unspeakable punishments
and have paid every penalty for our crimes.
But where have sweet love of country and longing for peace
carried me in my weariness? Now the time demands that we turn back
and return, Muse, to the point from which we digressed.

div.p: Having summoned the twelve ministers together, Christ instructs them with various teachings and precepts and emboldens them against the malice of their enemies. The power of the Divine Word in the mouths of the Apostles is described, through which Pluto's kingdom collapses. At the wedding in Cana of Galilee, Christ turns water into wine; afterward he drives the merchants from the Temple with a whip; he preaches the Gospel and cures every kind of disease. He has a divine conversation with the Samaritan woman at the well; but when crowds converging from every direction pressed upon him, he boarded Peter's little boat and taught the people from it, confirming his teaching by a wondrous catch of fish. He raises a widow's only son from the dead. While he was sleeping in the boat, however, with a storm stirred up, Pluto tried to drown him together with his companions; but Christ, awakened from sleep, rebuked the winds and calmed the tempest. He cast demons out of two young Gadarenes; the demons plunged a herd of swine into the waters. Through contact with his garment he heals the woman with an issue of blood. He restores Jairus's dead daughter to life. He frees the weeping Magdalene from demons. From a distance he heals the ruler's son. While teaching in his own country, he is placed in mortal danger; the Baptist is imprisoned and beheaded. Herod's banquet is described, and the deeds of Herod the Great are celebrated in passing.

lg.l: After Christ had gathered his companions on the shore,
first of all he gives the charge that from their ancestral threshold
they should not depart, but should range over the whole region of Judaea,
proclaiming the laws of peace and bearing joyful
tidings of salvation, wonders, and spectacles of events,
and teaching that the heavenly kingdom was drawing near,
he bids them drive every disease out of the body.
The brothers begotten of Night, and the grim monsters of the Pit,
let them cast out with a word; and bodies bereft of life
let them call back to the light, and greet each one by name.
But he forbids them to carry two tunics, or a shepherd's staff
to take; likewise to carry about heaps of gold, of silver,
or of bronze, and he forbids binding their feet with the buskin.
And when they have entered the threshold of a house, let them
offer peace; and if anyone scorns it, [let them attest] that man's house
by tossing a little dust, to be unworthy of the olive
of Pallas unworthy, or of the laws of peace.
But at the same time he shows through how many hazards of fortune
they must make their way, and how often they will be compelled to expose their heads to danger,
how often hostile enemies will demand punishment in blood;
but let them protect themselves like a snake
hiding itself among brambles and in winding coverts;
and if perhaps, caught on the way on the dry shore,
a bronze-shod wheel has run across it sidelong, or with a heavy blow
a traveller with a stone has left it half-dead and mangled:
still, as it flees, it gives long writhings with its body,
fierce in its uninjured part, its eyes blazing, and lifting its hissing neck
high, although its wounded part holds it back
as it knots its coils and folds itself upon its own limbs;
Thus he bids his companions to be so prudent when savage dangers press:
to hold their course through the midst of their enemies
and to hasten their flight, when they threaten slaughter and war;
Just as a dove, suddenly startled from her cave,
whose home and sweet nestlings are in the honeycombed rock,
is borne flying out over the fields, and in her terror makes
a great clapping of wings within the covert, then, gliding on the still air,
skims her clear path and never stirs her swift wings.
As a wolf plots ambush against the flock, so the enemy
will ply a thousand wiles against them, and harry [them] with unjust hatreds.
Or as a wolf lying in wait beside a full sheepfold,
when he growls at the pens, having borne winds and rains.
Past midnight, while the lambs, safe beneath their mothers,
keep up their bleating, he, fierce and relentless in his rage,
rages at those beyond his reach; a ravenous hunger, pent up
for a long time, torments him, and his jaws are dry of blood:
just so will they summon the guiltless companions to dreadful
punishments — tyrants, hostile and cruel of mind:
Then he heartens his frightened companions with kindly words,
teaching that there is need of such courage, and of a steadfast heart:
that they must not waver, nor let trembling seize their limbs before the trumpet,
nor yield to evils, but go against them the more boldly;
for God himself (he says) will supply courage and favouring strength,
and will give them fitting words to utter;
without whom not even birds glide down from the sky on their wings.
Nor shall a hair fall from your head; nay more,
a sure glory awaits you, and he shall have his reward
who holds out cups of cold water to one who thirsts;
The reward for so small a deed cannot grow old.
You too — great rewards await you in our realms,
here is your dwelling-place, that is the sure rest from your labours:
therefore call back your courage, and gloomy fear
put away; fear betrays ignoble spirits. He—
He, I say, is the only one you must fear — the reins
of heaven he guides, and to him the shades and the silent souls
and Chaos and Phlegethon, places silent far and wide in the night,
are obedient — his is the rule over souls and over the body; therefore
endure, and keep yourselves for better times.
Furnished with such counsels, yet destitute of all
human aid, or of arms to defend them,
he sends them out from a poor land into a great dominion.
Namely, that they may subject Judaea first, then foreign kingdoms,
to Christ, but without force, without the slaughter of men.
The ambassadors of kings, with a great throng attending,
advance, all wreathed in Pallas’s olive branches,
bearing gifts and talents of ivory and of gold:
but these men carry neither branches of peace nor gifts,
but the almighty word, the inviolable sceptre of the Kingdom,
which no human force nor the wicked power of Dis
withstood; but a way was forced through weapons and fires,
