with every barrier burst and the chains broken
with which Satan held the human race for so many ages.
Not so, when its banks are burst, does a foaming river
burst forth and overcome with its flood the barriers set against it,
sweep raging over the fields in a swelling mass, and through all the plains
drag the herds along with their stalls. Fallen are the proud
temples of the gods, the oracles of trembling Phoebus have fallen silent,
and every interpreter of the gods, who perceives false divine powers—
nay, the tripods and the Clarian laurels—he who reads the stars,
and the tongues of birds, and the omens of the auspicious wing.
When the dread trumpet of the word, from afar, with tuneful mouth
rang out with its blast, on a sudden all things seemed to tremble —
both the lights and the laurel of God — and the whole
mountain round about to be shaken, and the cauldron to bellow as the shrines were flung open:
Then all the plagues of Erebus fled, leaving
the earth behind; and they are hidden once more in familiar Orcus.
First Grief departs, with downcast eye, with loosened
hair, and breast bruised by hard fists.
Next follows Fear with ears pricked up, out of his senses
fearing all that is safe, whom every breeze, every sound startles.
After these, pale Diseases and gloomy Old Age
have fled; the avenging Cares have left their couches.
Then Dread, and ill-counselling Hunger, and shameful Want,
shapes terrible to behold, and Death and Toil;
Then Sleep, the kinsman of Death, and the mind's evil
Joys, and Mars mighty in war, his spear-point flung away.
The Eumenides, armed with black serpents, make for Orcus
with horrid shrieking, and go back to their chambers
[made] of iron; and Discord follows with mighty stride,
[with her] viperous hair resting upon bloody fillets.
And many monstrous shapes of varied beasts besides.
Centaurs return to the stall, and the two-shaped Scyllas,
and hundred-armed Briareus, and the beast of Lerna,
hissing horribly, and the Chimaera armed with flames,
Gorgons, and Harpies, and the form of the three-bodied shade

div.note: By the Centaurs, half men and half horses, I understand men given over to brutish pleasures, slaughter, plunder, and drunkenness. By the two-formed Scyllas—of whom one was the daughter of Nisus, betrayer of her country and her father, and the other the daughter of Phorcys, caught in adultery with Neptune—I understand parricides, traitors, and adulterers. Briareus, who attempted to drive Jupiter from heaven, signifies seditious men, who resist the gods above, who resist the higher powers. The Hydra, the beast of Lerna, signifies an untamable and rebellious multitude. The Chimaera signifies heathen idolatry and the worship of demons, which had three parts: first, the flame-spewing lion's head, signifying the terrors inflicted upon an untaught people and the cruel sacrifices of beasts and human beings; second, the goat's belly, marking promiscuous and unspeakable lusts; third, the serpent's tail, indicating their poisoned doctrine concerning God and their crafty statecraft. Bellerophon—that is, Christ, the missile-bearer—slew this monster with the Pegasus of the Gospel (for the Gospel is an ever-flowing spring and swifter than any Pegasus). The Gorgons, whose hair was once beautiful but later serpentine, and whose appearance was grim, denote the allurements of pleasures, which at first sight appear beautiful but soon torture men as though they had been poisoned and turn them into stones. These were overcome not by Persius—that is, Perseus—son of Jupiter, but by Christ, the son of Jehovah; not with Minerva's shield and Mercury's sword, but through his own wisdom and eloquence in the preaching of the Gospel. The Harpies signify the greedy rich, who are always squalid, famished, and rapacious. Their faces are pale because they are tormented by unremitting cares. They are winged and swift to seize, and have hooked hands to hold fast; beneath a maiden's face—that is, under an appearance of honesty—they conceal sordid avarice. The preaching of the Gospel and the working of miracles drove these men away, just as Calais and Lethes—that is, Zetes—the winged sons of the North Wind drove away the Harpies. Three-headed Geryon, moreover, signifies Satan's threefold power over men's souls, bodies, and fortunes: Christ, the true Hercules, destroyed him and by his own power placed all the aforesaid plagues beneath his feet.

lg.l: This pestilential throng, from the very jaws of Orcus,
the Stygian king Satan sent forth into the upper air,
after [she] had plucked the fatal fruit from the tree,
Eve our first mother; but Christ, taking pity on Adam,
sent these furies back again to the waters of Acheron.
So then, after the horns had blared with the hoarse note
of the terrifying word, the nations laid aside their fierce
hearts, God so willing, and they carry out Christ's commands.
Then the Father, ruler of highest Olympus, by no means willed
that these should stray too freely through the airs above:
but because of the sins we have committed they often burst through
the black vents of Dis, and are carried up to the vaults above,
God permitting it; but when again he gives the command, they all
more swiftly raise their wings, which hiss with serpents,
and make for the seat of Cocytus, and leave the heights above.
Be my God, then, O Christ, and best King of Kings,
you who by your voice can bend the powers above and stir
Acheron as well: bend me by your breath, I pray,
and now govern my mind with your words, and soothe my heart.
Others will fashion breathing bronzes more delicately,
I do indeed believe it: they will draw living faces from marble;
others will plead cases and trace the courses of the sky
with the rod, and shall tell of the rising stars:
do you meanwhile remember, King Christ, to rule the world,
not by sword or sceptre, but by the word and the Holy Spirit.
These shall be your arts, and to lay down a settled order for peace,
to spare the conquered and subdue the proud;
After Christ fell silent and, having ended here, rested,
then he swiftly carried out his Father's commands,
showing by various signs that he was Jehovah’s offspring.
There is a city the Hebrews call Cana by name;
here there was a wedding; Christ and his companions, invited,
are present, recline at the feast, and set their cares aside.
After hunger was banished and the desire of eating checked,
the wine was drained; Christ orders all the cups that had been cleared away
orders all the cups [to be set back], and sweet water from the springs
to be poured into six jars; soon the water began to redden,
and the water becomes draughts of foaming wine:
they marvel at him as he pours out the flowing wine,
and fills the bowls with pure wine; the unaware crowd is astonished,
and once more [he] poured on the table an offering of the liquid.
An uproar arises in the halls, and they send their voices rolling through the spacious
halls; lamps hang down from the high panelled ceilings.
The young men redouble their applause, and the maidens follow suit;
Going from here, he made for Jerusalem, and visited the Temple again.
Here, where they ought to have laid the offering upon the altars,
they traded their wares; where [the people had once been accustomed] duly to stretch upturned
their upturned hands to heaven along with their voice,
while selling cattle, they made the Temple profane.
Yet not with impunity; nor did Jesus tolerate such things
He makes ready twisted lashes, and scourges young and old alike,
now redoubling his blows with the right hand, now with the left;
no pause, no rest: as thick as when with heavy hail the storm-clouds
clatter upon the rooftops, so with close-packed blows the Hero,
again and again, he strikes with both hands and drives the profaners about:
and put them all to flight, and thunders from his mouth:
"This is a place for prayers, and not a robbers' den."
Then Christ ranges far and wide through the whole region,
teaching many things, and pitying in his heart the unjust lot
of the helpless populace; various works and miracles
he performs, and brought aid to suffering mortals,
while he delights to lay healing hands upon their wounds.
All those whose bodies languished with grim disease,
and those who bear foul scab and shameful gout,
and those whose limbs a parching fever eats away,
leaving their sweet lives behind, or dragging along their ailing
bodies; moreover, the deaf, the mute, and those with wasting limbs.
And the blind, or those whom stupor renders helpless—
from this side and that, all mingled together, gather into one throng,
seeking Christ's help with a great outcry.
But he comforts his wretched friends with words,
and for them all, with a word, he checked every disease.
not [even] if I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths
and a voice of iron, [could I] encompass all the cruel plagues,
or run through all the names of the diseases
which the Lord relieved by his own power, not by [any] art.
Now the swift Dog-star, scorching the thirsty Indians,
was blazing in the sky, and the fiery Sun had consumed half the circuit of heaven;
the grasses were parched, and the hollow rivers, with dried-up throats,
warmed by the rays in their [dry] channels, were baked down to the mud;
when Christ, worn out by the long journey, sat down
at Jacob’s well, so that he might enjoy the cool shade.
Within [were] sweet waters, and seats of living rock.
By chance there was a woman nearby who was seeking from the spring
cups of sweet water; then, distressed by the fierce heat
and blazing with thirst, he asks for fresh water.
“Woman, let me quench my thirst from the bubbling spring,”
says Christ, "and we shall give you [drink] from an unfailing spring,
whoever shall taste cups of its sacred water,
fiery thirst driven through his inmost veins shall not oppress him."
To him then the woman, entreating, used these words:
"Whoever you are — not, I think, hateful to heaven — you draw
the breath of life, you who have come to our city;
why, then, do you address me unbidden,
when you are sprung from the illustrious blood of Judah?
For Samaria, rich in resources and most fierce in the pursuits of war,
called Sebaste, brought me forth into the light.
Are you then greater than father Jacob, than whom no other
was more righteous in devotion or richer in flocks?
All the flocks of bleating sheep and every herd
to drink the running water from holm-oak troughs
Here he gave the order; and father Jacob himself was wont
with his servants and sons to draw water from the spring.
But if you are a prophet, foreknowing what is to come (and indeed
you are not ignorant of prophets nor unaware of the age to come,
for you know all the secrets of my deeds),
or if you are the Christ, [hold out] cups of this holy water,
hold them out, that I may not thirst again, or be forced to come back
to the well with parched throat. Jesus answered:
I am he whom you hear promised so often,
Christ the light of the world, the glory of the Jewish nation.
Seek me, and you will receive waters flowing without end.
During this exchange of words, Phoebus dips his rosy horses in the flood
dips them and brings back night as the day declines;
His companions draw near; the woman hurried to the town,
and told what Christ had said, and laid the matter out in order.
At once the report is spread abroad through the shaken city;
all the citizens pour out through the two-leaved gates,
and, mingled together, they ringed Christ round in a thick circle.
All fell silent and fixed their attentive gaze
while he taught, and unrolling the secrets of the fates disclosed them;
then towards nightfall they make for their dwellings and refresh their bodies.
And now one day and another day went by, and thereafter,
departing, he came again to the regions of Galilee.
There is a sea which washes the walls of the city of Tiberias
with its waves; into this the roaring Jordan, with its lovely stream,
with swift eddies, and yellow with much sand,
flows in; to these shores Christ directs his steps,
and alone, by himself, he paces upon the dry sand.
And the fame and the name of renowned Jesus [had roused] the neighbouring peoples;
had gone out [among them]; they had filled the shores with a joyful gathering,
[come] to see Christ, and all of them ready to hear him.
Around him countless nations and peoples made a din;
And just as in the meadows, when in calm summer bees
settle on flowers of many kinds and pour around the white
lilies; the whole field hums with their murmuring:
Just so the children of Abraham, and the Roman youth as well,
gathered from every side, come together, and were pressing upon Christ.
Now by chance two boats were standing on the shore,
one was Peter’s; Christ boarded it and sat down on the high
thwarts, and from the boat he taught the people;
Then, after Christ had made an end of speaking,
he commands Peter to set a course under sail and leave the harbour,
and to lower the nets into the deep sea.
Peter answered him: Although the night has witnessed our labours
(but in vain), yet since your heart’s desire so inclines,
I shall obey, and once again give myself over to hard toil.
When Peter had spoken these words, he quickly orders all the
masts to be raised and the yardarms spread with sails;
all together they trimmed the sheet and unfurled the left-hand
and then the right-hand folds; together they swing the lofty
yardarms around and back; their own breezes carry the ship onward.
But lo, of a sudden the watery race of the vast Deep
were all swimming up together and cleaving the waves.
And from afar they recognise the King, and circle [him] in dances.
The Nymphs hasten to meet him, and all from their glassy seats
(Without delay) they leapt forth from their own seats and fly across the waves
more swiftly than a javelin, and than an arrow that matches the winds,
and all hasten on their courses here: Cymodocia,
and Thetis, and Melite, and Doto the Nereid too,
and Galatea cleave the foaming deep with [their] breast.
The companions marvel as they watch in the flood the fish
sweeping the waters with their tails, and cutting through the surge.
And now the whole throng, streaming out, was rushing to the ships —
the offspring of the boundless sea — and it fills the nets.
Soon Peter and his companions haul in the dripping nets,
and both boats are filled; every kind of swimming thing,
bearing down on the sterns, with monstrous weight the boats
was engulfing in water, and to sink [them] in the vast sea
it begins; but Peter's limbs go slack with chill,
he groans, and stretching out both palms in dread
he utters such words: You whose divine power they adore —
the throngs of the Nereids and of Phorcus, and the maiden Panopea,
and the aged company of Glaucus, and Palaemon son of Ino,
and the swift Tritons: depart from this guilty ship;
leave the polluted lodging and the minister of crimes,
grant help, O Christ, and come to the aid of our toil,

div.note: By these terms I understand not fictitious sea-goddesses but fish. Cymodocia takes her name from the waves; Melite from a honeyed flavor; and Galatea from a milky color. Thetis is called by Homer Νηρηῒς Ωκεάνης, "a daughter of the sea," because fish are born in the sea (Hymn to Apollo). Doto is numbered among the kinds of fish by Hyginus in his book of Fables.

lg.l: Rescue us in our misery from death, and forgive every sin.
To whom Christ [said]: take heart, Peter, and [let] all fear
[be gone]. You used to catch the watery race with a snare;
soon you will learn to catch men, and to beguile them with the word;
follow me, and embrace me as Lord in every circumstance,
no glory will be sought for your deeds apart from Me.
When these words [were spoken], they make for harbour, and the favouring
west winds stretch the sails; the ship is carried swiftly through the flood,
the anchor is cast from the prow, the sterns stand on the shore.
Christ goes forward, a throng of companions pressing about him.
With a healing hand he cured all failing limbs,
and brought present help both to masters and to servants,
and heals children and breathless old men alike.
And now he was drawing near to the walls and gates of Nain;
a mourning widow coming on with a great press of people
he catches sight of, marvelling at their number, both matrons and men.
This wretched mother had but one son, one male child,
only one, and he was snatched away in the first dawn of youth;
the body of this man, cold and bereft of life,
they carry out from the house, and lead the sad funeral train.
the unhappy mother is led along, worn out with grief,
now disfiguring her breast with her fists, now her face with her nails:
and, out of her senses, uttering much in her mournful frenzy,
she wept over the pitiable body of her dead son.
But Christ, shaken by the mother's bitter misfortune,
He groans and bade her lay aside her sorrowful cares.
Then he touched the bier, and that the pitiable body be lifted
he commands; and the lifeless youth, laid back upon the bier,
he addresses, and bade him rise to the threshold of life.
The lifeless youth heard, and suddenly came back to life from death,
reverencing Christ as a suppliant, with eye cast down.
Here the people, terrified at the sight, stood fixed a little while,
wavering between hope and fear, whether to believe he lives,
or, deceived by a false appearance, that he was suffering his final agony;
At last they recognize their companion called back from death,
and that they were not deluded by an empty hope; straightway all
in gladness fling their voices to the stars of heaven,
and praise the great and memorable name of Christ.
These things at last performed, presently from the walls the hero,
almighty Christ, with many attending him, bears himself away,
making for the familiar shores; then a ship that chanced to lie ready
he seized, and bids his companions take their seats on the thwarts;
swiftly they unfurl the sails; lands and cities fall away;
the companions strike the sea in rivalry, and churn up its waters.
Meanwhile in the stern, and beneath the cold vault of heaven,
while Christ, troubled in his heart by many cares,
lay down, and gave his limbs late rest;
and while they too lower their eyes in sweet sleep,
Beneath their oars the sailors sprawled along the hard benches,
when at once Satan, who for so many years against one race has been
waging war—whose mind, not yet sated with hatred, finds no rest,
so that he may sink Christ in the sea;
into the homeland of the storm-clouds, places teeming with raging south winds,
he comes to Ocean’s regions; from there, rains and raging winds
he stirs up, and sends black fumes bursting forth to the upper air;
and these, beaten back by the cold of the clouds, with a vast
roar he brings down upon the lands and the deep sea.
Thereupon at once the rushing winds, as though in ordered column,
rush out through the gateway granted them and blast the lands with a whirlwind.
They have swooped upon the sea, and the whole of it from its lowest depths
the East wind and the South together heave up, and, thick with squalls,
the African wind, and they roll huge billows to the shores;
there follows the shouting of men and the shrieking of the ropes;
in a moment the clouds snatch away both sky and daylight
from the sailors' eyes; black night broods upon the deep;
the heavens thundered, and the upper air flashes with fire upon fire,
and everything threatens the men with death at hand.
But the sailor’s blood, cold with sudden fear,
froze; their spirits sank, and trembling grips their limbs.
Peter himself quakes with fear, while on the arching swell
he is lifted to the sky and looks upon the dew-dripping stars,
and, the wave drawn away beneath him, sinks down to the lowest shades.
He tore sleep from Christ and importunes him with his voice:
Son of God, can you sleep in a crisis like this?
Alas, see with what great perils of the sea we are tossed:
how huge a sheer mountain of water comes on in a heaped mass?
See how you hang upon the wave, and how the gaping wave
lays the ground bare amid the billows; the surge rages with sand.
We, your wretched companions, borne through such great dangers,
implore you: keep the maddened waves away from the ships.
Look upon us kindly, if you are moved by any prayers;
give your help, Christ, and snatch us from death.
Christ replied: Take heart again, and cease showing through your pleas
that you doubt my power. Where has your trust
in me gone, Peter? For I can do all things; the Father did not
set me over land and sea to no purpose;
for he granted [me] to soothe the waves and to raise them with the wind,
by everlasting command — the Father of gods and King of men;
and he makes [me] master of the storm-clouds and the tempests.
When with these words he had soothed Peter’s glad heart,
he calls Eurus and Zephyrus to him, then speaks thus:
Has so great a confidence in your own race taken hold of you?
Now, winds, heaven and earth, without my sanction,
do you dare to confound, and to raise up such great masses?
You—! But it is better to settle the waves once roused;
later you will pay me for your offenses with a punishment unlike this one;
Hasten your flight, and say this to the Stygian King:
The dominion of the sea and the savage trident were not given to him,
but by right to me. He holds the monstrous rocks
and the infernal dwellings; in that hall let
Lucifer vaunt himself and reign in the dark prison of the Furies.
When he had spoken these words, the lofty house of those above falls silent,
and the earth is shaken to its foundations; lofty heaven is still,
then the west winds subsided; the sea holds its waters calm;
and he puts to flight the gathered clouds, and brings back the sun,
ruddy, and, more swiftly than a word can be spoken, calms the swollen seas:
gentle, so that after the manner of a pool and a still marsh
he might smooth the watery surface, so that the oar need not struggle:
And just as, often, when among a great people there has arisen
a riot, and the base crowd rages in its passions;
and now firebrands and stones fly, fury supplies the weapons:
but if by chance a man weighty in piety and in services rendered
they have caught sight of, they fall silent: and stand with ears pricked up.
He rules their spirits with his words and soothes their breasts.
So all the sea’s roar died away after he looked upon the waters
and stilled the murmuring of the rushing wind.
The crowds marvel who he is to whom such power
and dominion over the sea have been given, and who with his voice restrains
the struggling winds; and the roaring storms.
O you who govern the blasts of the winds, at whose
command the waves obey and carry out your orders:
stretch out your right hand to one perishing in the midst of the waves,
whom Pluto drives onto the Syrtes — a pitiable sight —
and dashes him against the shoals and hems him in with a bank of sand;
let the waves subside and the storm clouds flee across the vast sky,
so that I, worn out by cares and burdened by illnesses,
may at last be received by you in a safe harbor, most gentle one.
After all the fury had died away, and the raging wave grown still,
soon, under full sail, he approaches the landing-place of the Gadarenes.
Here two young men run to meet him, raving in mind;
Their fierce hearts swell with madness; the unclean spirit shakes them inwardly,
turning goads beneath their breasts.
Neither their countenance nor their color remained the same; continually it torments
the raving mouth, subduing their fierce hearts, and shapes it by pressure.
Here they dwell among the tombs and foul corpses,
and set up dreadful groans; fire flashes from their fierce
eyes; they break the iron and the chains they drag.
Nay, they themselves, while the spirit rages within, their own
— may the gods grant better to the godly, and that madness to enemies —
limbs, torn asunder, they were mangling with the hard rocks.
So both are borne headlong to Christ along the winding
shores; then they broke out with such words from their breast:
"Son of the most high Father, who turns the stars of the world,
why do you press us with cruel punishments before the day?
Not yet has the last day, nor the inescapable time,
come, when, shut up in darkness and in a lightless prison,
you will torment us with punishments through all the ages.
But if you bid us go from here, if you wish to drive [us] from our
lodging, because the desire in your heart so inclines you,
we obey: but let [us] be allowed to enter the swine
which we see poised far away on the high cliff.
To this the son of Mary assented; then more swiftly all
The brothers of Tartarus enter the swine in a full column,
and headlong they rush from the mountain's highest peak
into the neighbouring sea, and beneath mid-water they sink
the bristly swine, and fill the cities with fears.
And now a sudden report flies through the Gadarene towns,
that Christ had scattered them into the waves, and in the vast flood
had drowned the swine; through the opened gates rushes out the whole
throng of old and young, with prayers and upturned hands,
was begging the Lord to depart from the Gadarene land.
Meanwhile, a woman wasted by extreme emaciation,
the poor creature, whose blood had been flowing from all over her body
for twelve years, seized her opportunity and followed Christ,
sick as she was; amid the thousands surrounding him
on every side—for the crowds had enclosed him in a dense ring—
she sought him out and longed to touch with her hands the hem
of the garment that covered the Lord with a light wrapping.
Wherever, then, Christ made his way through the middle of the crowd,
there the woman comes up behind, and silently traces his steps.
For a healer's hand, and the potent herbs of Phoebus,
she had often employed them in vain; all her expenditure had accomplished nothing
over all those years; neither skill nor Apollo, its inventor,
came to her aid, nor herbs sought out over all the mountains.
But as soon as, trembling, she touched the sacred garments,
at once the whole fury of the disease gave way, and the sick woman
felt the help: and suddenly from her body there fled
all the pain, to be sure; the blood stood still, all of it, deep in her belly.
But he, perceiving that power had gone out from [his] body,
cast his gaze this way and that, and speaks thus:
"Someone defiles me with an unclean touch, and the same one
dares to touch with her hand the hem of my garment,
for I feel that power has flowed out from my body."
The woman, marvelling at Christ's venerable divine power,
and, humble and suppliant, extends her gaze and her pleading right hand;
Christ, after no long delay, gives his right hand
to the wretched woman and strengthens her spirit with this immediate pledge.
But behold, a messenger is brought to Christ, filling
the place with mournful outcry, and reporting Jairus' daughter
reporting that Jairus’ daughter was dead; Christ bade them hope for deliverance
and take greater confidence amid adversity.
Then he touched the dead girl's right hand, and called [her] with coaxing
words; she lifts her heavy eyes and, in the high
heaven, sought the light and rejoices upon finding it.
Then the anxious mind of the dead girl's father is in turn
pervaded by soothing joys; glad with the sweetness,
the crowds marvel and exalt Christ to the stars.
After this, while Jesus was restoring his strength with food,
Magdalene came, tainted with the poisons of the Furies,
and, clasping Christ's knees and grovelling at his knees,
she clung, her shining eyes suffused with tears;
she pressed kisses on his feet, and drenched them with weeping;
and her golden hair, poured down over her white neck,
she caught up, and dries his feet, sighs, and anoints [them].
Christ, who hast ever pitied the heavy toils of men,
to these tears thou grantest life, and pitiest one who loves:
See, I groan, and drench my face with a broad flood [of tears];
grant pardon to a wretched man, and look more closely on our case:
to Thee I flee for refuge, and as a suppliant I entreat thy divine power;
gracious one, I pray, have mercy, for thou canst do all things; so shalt Thou
ever be honoured with my worship, ever be celebrated with gifts.
From there Christ departs, and revisits Cana.
Here a nobleman of illustrious blood met him,
sighing, and drawing his voice from the depth of his breast,
and thus he briefly speaks: Snatch my son now from death,
Christ, I pray — whose body languishes with a grim disease.
Alas, shall he fall before his day? If any care for a wretched parent
can touch thee, take pity on the son, and on the father.
Christ replies: Take heart again, for he breathes the air
of heaven, and does not yet lie among the cruel shades.
At these words his cares were removed, and, driven out for a while
from his sad heart, the grief departs; straightway to him
a messenger comes up, who brings back sure and joyful news:
that his son enjoys the longed-for light and has been recalled from death.
Departing from there, Christ returned to his native city,
and when he had entered the synagogue and was teaching many things,
but the fierce race of the Pharisees heaves with a tide
of wrath, and the base crowd rages in its passions.
Gathered from every side, young men and old alike, [they assail] Christ
They rush upon [him]; madness drives the blinded citizens:
no otherwise than if, with a great roaring, a flame
a brushwood flame is fed against the sides of a seething bronze cauldron,
and the waters leap up with the heat; within rages the force of the water,
smoking, and the stream brims over high with foam;
and now the flood cannot hold itself in, the black steam flies up to the air.
Then they drive Christ to the heights of the summit,
to hurl him headlong from the summit of the cliff; but
a cloud wrapped about with thick shadows hides him,
dulling mortal sight, and, damp, all around him
growing dark; but indeed a thicker darkness on their
minds lies heavy; they are darkened by the murky shadows
of errors — how great the storm-clouds that have girdled their hearts?
since they cannot see Christ, who for wretched mortals the world
unveils with light, and puts the night to flight.
So he tore himself away, and fled from the hostile
towns, and withdraws himself from the shores of his ungrateful country.
Meanwhile Herod wrongfully put to death
John, while the king indulges an unspeakable love
for an incestuous wife, and violates the holy laws of chastity;
for he seized his brother's marriage-bed and a forbidden wedlock.
John therefore blazed out into righteous anger,
saying it was unlawful to defile Philip's marriage-bed:
but the king, rolling waves of wrath beneath his breast,
the guiltless prophet, in chains and a lightless prison,
orders him shut up, because he forbade the unchaste bonds.
And when the birthday came, by ancient custom
He makes his yearly vows and duly performs the solemn processions,
and heaps the altars with his gifts.
Then the inner house, splendid with royal luxury,
is furnished; and in the midst of the halls he prepares a banquet.
coverings wrought with art, and with proud purple;
a great mass of silver on the tables; on the high festal
couches, golden supports gleam, and splendid tables shine
with the dishes set upon gold; the drinking-cups flash,
and the bowls, wrought of silver and rough with figures.
The nobles and captains assemble with great pomp;
the King was receiving them in his spacious colonnades.
And at last the Tetrarch settled himself amid proud hangings
upon a golden couch and took the central place.
Now the nobles of the kingdom, and the Roman youth as well,
recline at the royal table upon outspread purple.
The servants pour water for [their] hands and [set out] bread in baskets;
serve out [bread], and bring towels with close-shorn nap.
Inside are fifty maidservants, whose charge it is to set out
the provisions in a long array and honor the household gods with flames;
a hundred others, and as many attendants matched in age,
to load the tables with the feast and to set out the cups.
Herod feasts, and the nobles and the joyful youth;
they fill themselves with old wine and with rich game:
They set out great mixing bowls and fill them to the brim with wine.
An uproar arises in the halls, and they send their voices rolling through the spacious
courts; lamps hang down from the golden panelled ceilings,
lit; and the torches overcome the night with their flames.
Here the King himself called for [a bowl] heavy with gems and with gold,
and filled the bowl with unmixed wine, and straightway eagerly drained it
foaming, and gladly drenched himself from the brimming gold.
after the King, the nobles [drank]; the praises and deeds of his father
of Herod the Great, a servant who made them ring out on a golden lyre
stood by, [singing] how the wars had been fought in their proper order.
how he was pressing the city of Solyma with a mighty siege,
and the citizens rushed to arms for liberty:
he marches to war; the same man had shattered famous cities;
and how, after triumphing over Zion, to the lofty Capitol
with Caesar as his companion and the whole cohort in attendance,
the lofty Capitol of the sons of Romulus, resplendent with gems and gold.
How a Temple lofty, immense, of polished marble
he built; and columns rising in gleaming bronze,
the city Sebaste, and the Antonia tower, and the temple
called Caesarean, which the King named after the Roman Caesar,
and the city Caesarea, glad in so great a name,
and he sings of countless citadels gleaming with marble.
And he adds many temples built of ancient stone,
renewed by Herod's hand; then the paved ways,
the gates, and the bridges, and the bulwarks for war,
the immense menace of the walls, and a gleaming eagle,
golden, on the lofty summit of the shrine, spreading its wings
and threatening new wars with its hooked talons.
Then harbours dug out by skill, and for theatres the deep
foundations laid he sings of, and huge columns
hewn from the cliffs—lofty adornments for future stages.
He adds the cities of Asia subdued, and the brigands driven out,
and the Parthian trusting in flight and in his arrows turned back,
and so many trophies seized by hand from different enemies,
and the nations triumphed over from the neighbouring shore.
Then he sings of the bronze-beaked fleets, and the wars of Actium,
and how Augustus Caesar, leading the Italians into battle
with the Senate and people, the household gods and the great gods,
had stood upon the stern, with flickering flames from the crown of his head
terrible; and how grim Antony, with motley arms,
victor from the peoples of the Dawn and from the Red Sea's shore,
Egypt, and the Eastern battle-lines, and the arms of Memnon
had brought with him; and how there followed — abomination! — his Egyptian consort
in gilded ships; and how the vast sea foamed,
torn up by the oars and by the shrieking beaks:
and how at that sudden terror all Egypt, and the Indians,
every Arab, all the Sabaeans, were turning their backs;
then he sang of the Nile, his mighty body in mourning,
opening the folds of his robe and beckoning with all his raiment
the vanquished into his blue lap and his sheltering streams.
He sings in measures the seven distinctions of notes,
and plays those same notes, now with his fingers, now with the ivory plectrum.
Here meanwhile Paris, with his half-man retinue,
his chin and perfumed hair supported by a Maeonian turban,
enjoys his stolen prize and gives himself up to dancing,
whose garment is dyed with saffron and gleams with purple,
to whom lyres are dear, together with the pipe that gives its twofold song.
Never by trumpet, horn, or drums of war
to rouse men with bronze and kindle battle with song
had he dared; but he was bold in love and in the battles of the night.
Moreover, the king's adulterous consort danced in time,
beating out the dances with her feet and singing songs.
Impious Herod prolonged that night with revelry, song, and wine,
and he drank deep of forbidden love.
The wretch burns; an unlawful flame devours his marrow,
and an unspeakable wound lives beneath his breast;
doomed to ruin, and caught by shameful desire,
he swore that he would give whatever she should ask.
But since the causes of her wrath, and her bitter resentments,
had not yet fallen from her mind: there remains, stored deep in her heart,
the prophet's verdict, and the insult to her scorned marriage.
Without delay she demanded the head, torn from the neck, of the prophet
John; so her wicked mother had commanded.
Cruel love, to what do you not drive mortal hearts?
For neither his own piety [saved] the prophet, nor a life untainted by crime,
nor his virtue shielded him from the tyrant's sword,
but he tore the head from the shoulders, and left the trunk
sobbing out its blood: and, streaming with black gore,
the man's face, in a dish full of foaming blood,
he handed—ah!—to the wretched lover the promised gift.
She—horrible to tell—more monstrous in crime than all other women,
gloats over the head and mocks it with bitter words.
Then, lifting up to her mother the face, pale in ghastly fashion,

div.p: When Christ had heard of John's murder, he withdrew from Galilee into the wilderness, where he miraculously fed a vast crowd of people. He walks upon the sea and rescues Peter as he was all but sunk. He teaches and heals the people; moved by the prayers and the faith of the Canaanite woman, he restores her daughter to health. He brought back to health a man at Bethesda who had laboured under his disease for thirty-eight years, and he cures a man with dropsy. The Pharisees, stirred by envy, sent certain officers to seize Christ; but they, themselves taken captive by Christ's words, returned with nothing done. Afterwards he is assailed with stones by a raging populace. On Mount Tabor he is transfigured; coming down from the mountain, he frees a boy from a demon and rebukes the Apostles. Having entered Capernaum, he pays the tribute with the money found in a fish's mouth. While he teaches in the Temple he is stoned again, but withdrew himself and came to Bethany, where he raises Lazarus, already dead—

lg.l: she brought it; they cannot sate their hearts by gazing.
But his companions the huge trunk, and the body without a name
— a sad service — take up, and lay away in a tomb;
afterwards the Christians, far and wide throughout the cities,
driven by heavenly portents, paid due rites to his bones;
Thereupon—if it is worthy of belief—in a temple of solid marble
they appoint chosen days named after the prophet;
and they raise a tomb and render solemn rites at the tomb,
and the Baptist's name flourishes for ever through the ages.
But indignant within himself at the death of his innocent friend
Christ, rolling beneath his breast great surges
of cares, when the image of dear John rose before him,
breathing out his life in a cruel death; sorrowing,
he burns to be gone in flight, and to leave the land of Galilee.
In silence he makes the boat ready, and gathers his companions to the shore.
Then, when the sea is first to be trusted, and the winds
grant calm seas, and the softly rustling South Wind calls them out to the deep,
his companions board the boats and leave the shores behind;
straining [at the oars] they churn the foam and sweep the blue water.
Then he makes for empty places, set apart in a vast retreat;
and here [he sees] that a huge throng of people had streamed together,
and wondering at their number he finds them, mothers and men alike.
From every side they had gathered, ready to pay attention
while he teaches his companions and rehearses the precepts of the men of old.
With attentive ears they hang upon the speaker’s lips;
nor is it enough to have heard it once, and it delights [them] to linger on;
But now rosy Phoebus, with his weary horses in the Iberian flood,
dips them and brings back night as the day declines;
He grieves, pitying the destitute; then with his voice the Master
calls Peter and his companions to him; then he speaks thus:
"Since evening draws nearer as the sky slopes downward,
and the people have not regained their strength with food, I think it wrong
to send the unfed crowd away into the towns:
Come then, O companions, bring out the bread, and [all] the people
all of them, now duly seat them on a seat of grass.
They do just as commanded and have seated the people
upon the green foliage: Christ shares out among them all
the gifts of toil-won bread, and serves out the fishes.
Christ too eats, and with him the youth of Judaea:
So on five loaves and two fishes all of them,
sated, return home by night and put their cares aside.
After hunger was taken away, behold, twelve baskets
they load with the remnants of Ceres [the bread], and serve out the fishes:
Then Christ was bidding his companions give their sails to the winds.
But he himself, through the friendly silences of the still moon,
alone on foot seeks the steeps of an airy mountain.
That night he passes sleepless; nay, from the bottom of his breast
poured out prayers and invoked the Father in supplication.
As soon as he had spoken, he fell silent with closed lips;
he makes for the familiar shores, daring to trust himself to the waves
by a path unfamiliar to mortals; swiftly the mighty
sea settles down, nor does the broken wave murmur back.
While Christ goes on foot through the vast pools of Nereus,
cleaving [his] way, he rises above the whole wave,
which on its glassy back bears up the tamer of the world,
who with his countenance checks the fury of sky and sea,
Meanwhile Peter was cleaving the waters in the middle of the night,
He himself sits there, holding the tiller and tending the sails.
(such shapes as rumour says flit about once death is met)
he thinks he has seen, and he watches the step of the one walking,
how through the midst of the sea, poised upon the swelling wave,
made his way and did not wet his swift soles in the sea.
But while, not knowing what was happening and not knowing his master,
he stood thunderstruck and amazed, presently a cold shudder
shakes his limbs, and his blood congeals chill with dread.
And for his companions too, when they saw the Lord through the
dim shade (such as one who, at the beginning of the month,
either sees, or thinks he has seen, the moon rising through the clouds —
their chill blood stiffened with sudden dread.
Then Christ, unbidden, chides his trembling companions,
lifting their spirits with these words: let all fear be gone,
why have your hearts failed? It is I, not a ghost; therefore
endure, and keep yourselves for better times.
These things Christ [said]; and when that voice came to Peter's ears
he flung himself headlong into the sea from the high stern,
and with light feet glides across the surface of the waves,
But while he treads the high waves, and walks across the sea,
already a savage dread has hemmed Peter round in mid-passage.
For suddenly the winds roll up the sea, and great waters rise —
soon Simon, flung out into the midst of the billows,
cries aloud: have mercy, I beg, come to the help of your servant,
O Christ, tamer of the sea and of the roaring storms.
Without delay he gives his right hand to the trembling man, and lifts him from the waves.
Then the winds fell, and all at once there sank
every blast, and the oars labour in the sluggish marble [of the water].
Christ makes haste to turn the prow toward land;
soon he makes his way, straight along the shore, to the harbour of Gennesaret.
From every side, eager to see him, the Judaean youth
pours round him in a throng, and the shores are filled with crowds:
nor can they be torn away from Christ, until the dewy night
turns about the sky, studded with gleaming stars.
Here the deaf, the dumb, and those whom an unholy frenzy within
convulses — these he relieved with healing hand, or with his garment.
After this, a Canaanite woman follows the departing Master
for a long way, weeping, and, as a suppliant, begs him
that he would be willing at once to help her wretched daughter,
who, driven mad by frenzies, raves wildly through the city.
But he gave no answer at all to her as she begged.
She presses on, weeping, and again and again entreats him;
he says nothing in reply; all the more she wears down
as he hesitates; at last his companions urge him to look upon the afflicted woman,
but he, unmoved, heeds nothing:
And just as, when an aged oak with its strong timber,
the Alpine north winds, now with blasts from this side, now from that,
strive with one another to uproot it; a creaking resounds, and thickly
the leaves strew the ground as the trunk is shaken,
[yet] the tree itself holds fast to the rocks, and as far as with its crown it reaches to the airs
of heaven, so far with its root does it stretch down toward Tartarus;
not otherwise, with unceasing voices from this side and that, the hero
is battered, and still will not hear her as she calls.
But she, seeing that her tears were rolling down in vain,
raging after the manner of a rushing flood, or of a black whirlwind,
toward Christ—for the whole crowd of men, packed close, concealed him—
she hastens at a run, breaking through the midst of the ranks,
and clings, having embraced his feet, and again she pleads,
crying aloud, and with deep groaning she filled all heaven.
Then Christ briefly rebukes [her] with bitter words:
The sumptuous dishes and cups from the full table
of the children—is it right to offer them to unclean dogs?
To him the woman: I confess it is true, and I do not gainsay your words;
But let the dogs consume, with their hard jaws,
the leavings of the bread, if any fall from the high
tables, while their masters feast on rich fare.
O woman! great is your faith, cries Jesus;
be of steadfast heart; what you ask shall be given, Canaanite woman.
See, the unholy fury out of the failing body of [your] daughter
has gone out; you will find the girl saved from the affliction.
Thence he presses on the journey granted [him], and revisits Jerusalem,
here a pool is enclosed by five proud porticoes,
to which come together all who are sick in body,
on this side and on that, grim diseases have laid their couches;
and the sick wait, until the winged Spirit, gliding down from high
heaven, has stirred the healing waters;
and whoever was able to swim into the hallowed pool first,
for him, quicker than it can be said, every disease flees from his body.
There was one man, seized in his body by a grim disease
for thirty-eight years, and he lay on his back.
Stretching out his hands with a cry, he prays to Christ
that he would pity a helpless man, and raise him with his right hand,
for there is no one, he says, to lift me from the ground,
and set me down in the midst of the muddy pool's waters.
At once Christ soothes the grieving breast,
and bade him lay aside the sad cares from his mind.
“Rise,” he says, “and sling your familiar bed over your shoulders.”
But he rose without delay and took upon his neck
the raised bed; filled with great delight,
he goes on, and with his praises exalts the Lord even to heaven.
After Christ’s departure thence, wasted by extreme emaciation,
the strange figure of an unknown man, pitiable in appearance,
He comes to meet [him]; dreadful [his] filth and [his] untrimmed beard;
fluid discharge streamed profusely from his body and drew into itself all
his bones, broken down bit by bit by disease.
When Christ caught sight of him, without long delay
he gives [his] right hand, and with a word drives the disease from his body.
But the report of Christ seizes the ears of the Pharisees,
and spreads so many deeds far and wide upon the lips of men.
Indignant, they roar with loud murmuring around the Temple’s
barriers, and with various rumors they whet their anger
and scorn all Christ’s miracles.
Stirred by envy, they join bitter hatred to their words:
nay more, they urge young men tried in war to arms,
and kindle their anger and fill them with boldness.
Such commands they then give: either kill Christ with the sword
or take him captive in chains and bring him straight to us.
They fly off at once; frenzy and anger hurl their minds
headlong: one snatches a helmet from the house;
another carries flashing javelins and puts on a shield and, triple-woven with gold,
a breastplate, and girds himself with his trusty sword.
So all of them, swift against Christ, are borne on in full
column, nor are they far apart from one another by many paces.
But as soon as they saw the Lord teaching the crowds
they all fell silent, and stand by with ears pricked up:
They turn many things over in mind; then their hearts, swollen with anger, subside;
and they stood fixed with astonished minds, while he soothed with words the hard hearts of the cohorts; and no longer now in arms
do they trust, but with vows and prayers to sue for peace
they are compelled; and they worship Christ and exalt him to the heavens.
But among the leading citizens discord arises;
some accuse Christ, others praise the miracles;
meanwhile the crowd is split into opposing parties.
At last, when the people, overcome by grief, had conceived a frenzy,
it rages, bereft of reason, and, inflamed throughout the whole city,
runs riot; they press Christ hard with huge stones.
In fear his companions make again for scattered shelters across the fields:
And just as, when storm-clouds with a burst of hail
come rushing down, every ploughman scatters from the fields,
and every farmer too, and the traveller lies hid in a safe stronghold,
or on a river's banks, or under the vault of a high rock,
while the rain falls upon the land, so that, when the sun is brought back, they may be able
to ply the day's work: so Christ, overwhelmed on every side
endures the whole cloud of stones without a wound.
But after he secretly turns away unharmed and removes himself
from their sight, he heals a blind man with mud, and thence
having gone off, he straightway unstopped the ears of a deaf man.
From here he makes for the cloudy summits of airy Tabor.
Him, through crags and rough rocks, there follow
only three companions: God delights in an odd number.
After they had come into the high mountains and the trackless coverts,
behold, suddenly a new light shines out, and Christ's
countenance flashes and casts blazing light beneath the clouds.
In face and shoulders he is like gold; nay, his very comely
hair shines like the lamp of Phoebus,
and his milk-white robe surpassed the whiteness of snow.
Whiter than swans, more beautiful than white ivy
was his body; it had breathed glad beauty upon his eyes:
such grace as hands add to ivory, or as when with tawny
gold, silver or Parian marble is encircled.
But the companions strain toward Christ, while their eyes see Moses
and Elijah, clothed in white garments.
They discussed many things among themselves in varied speech,
then Peter broke forth with such words from his breast:
Here let us set up three tents with snow-white canvas;
on these mountains may we be allowed to settle together with you;
here indeed I would spend my whole life long with you;
Scarcely had Peter spoken these words, when a shining cloud,
poured around them and glittering, clothes the whole region in
purple light; and such a voice is uttered and borne to their ears:
This is my Son, my great and only delight:
therefore let his words sink down into your hard ears.
But a fierce dread stood all about the trembling companions;
they sink down in the midst of the vision, the warmth left their bones;
but Christ raises the wretched men themselves up from the ground,
and lifts their spirits with words, and soothes their hearts.
These things done, at last they arrive from the mountain heights,
Christ with his companions; he finds that a vast number of new followers
have gathered—mothers as well as men.
among whom, drawing groans from the depth of his breast,
and clasping the pitiable body of his own son,
a sorrowing father stands; and then speaks thus to Christ:
Behold my son, whom a wicked spirit within [vexes],
and ravages his limbs with a grievous disease;
and it casts him into water and into fire; then the terrified child
writhes and vomits from his mouth blood mixed with foam;
at the same time he lifts horrifying cries to the stars.
I kept urging [your] companions to bring aid to my wretched son,
but in vain, for they have no such power; wherefore
with suppliant prayers I beg: have pity on sufferings
so great, have pity on a soul bearing what it does not deserve.
Then with weighty words Jesus rebukes his companions,
calling the father and the son to himself, and at once he upbraids
the hellish monster itself, and forces it to depart from the boy.
But the spirit quakes with sudden dread, and thereupon,
departing thence and gliding down into Tartarus in swift flight,
it returns to the pallid shades and the deep night.
And now once more he presses on toward the city of Capernaum;
Here Christ had no chased silver at all.
Then he addresses Peter thus, and lays on him these commands:
Go now, Peter; quickly make for the shore at a run,
seek the deep waters, and cast your dripping lines into the sea;
Open the throat of the fish that you catch first;
you will find silver; pay it for Me and yourself.
He had spoken; the other made ready to obey the great God's
command, and goes willingly to the shores he knows.
He puts out from the harbour, lets down his nets into the waters;
Then the sea-born race of Nereus, through his vast waters,
cleave the foaming billows and play through the waves;
like the many thousands of birds that hide themselves in the woods,
when evening, or a wintry rainstorm, drives [them] down from the mountains.
And while the gleaming dolphins cut the swell in a ring,
one of them raised its gleaming head from the midst of the water,
rolling its scaly back with breast reared high,
and turning its burning eyes with a blue-grey glare
upon Peter, it opens its jaws laden with silver.
Peter snatches the proffered treasure from the fish's throat,
Peter, and with this price he redeemed Christ and himself:
You to whom Neptune sends treasures from his glassy hall,
and [whom] the scaly race enriches with hidden wealth;
I ask no gold or silver, nor of a fertile field the
yield, by which I might ransom myself from the prison of death;
let another lay up riches and brood over his wearied gold,
let others churn unknown seas with oars, and rush
into armed combat, and penetrate the courts and thresholds of kings;
let one seek to destroy cities and their wretched homes,
that he may drink from a jewelled cup and sleep on Tyrian purple:
But I, for whom there is no lofty house with proud doors
spewing back from its halls at dawn a wave of morning callers,
and garments inwrought with gold, and Ephyrean bronzes,
nor is white wool stained with Assyrian dye,
nor is the use of clear olive oil spoiled with cassia,
You I seek, Christ, solace of every care and mischance;
and you I follow; now there is no delay — wherever you lead, I am here.
If I may have you, Christ, if you do not refuse to go as my companion,
while I live and carry on my life through every hardship;
if, when the harsh cruelty of death snatches me away,
you receive me and show me the paths of heaven and the stars;
then not, gaping at doorposts varied with lovely tortoiseshell,
shall I canvass for the people's fasces; and kingdoms doomed to perish,
but I shall scorn both the world's threats and haughty arrogance,
and all fears, and inexorable fate
I shall place beneath my feet, together with the roar of greedy Acheron.
You are untroubled rest, you the life that knows not how to deceive,
You too are rich in resources of every kind; and a single drop of your blood
drop avails more than the Mede's most wealthy land,
and fair Ganges, and Hermus turbid with gold,
and all Panchaia, rich with its incense-bearing sands.
After this, with his companions, he presses on to the city of Jerusalem,
and while he teaches the peoples beneath the high vault of the Temple
and says that he is greater than Abraham, at once with rage
the people rages beside itself, and the Pharisaic throng
seethes, and fierce resentment burns in its inmost bones.
A storm-cloud of stones follows; fury supplies the weapons,
The shaken city roars, and a shifting tremor ran across
the troubled faces of the scribes; as rocks hold back
the swift rivers, a murmur rises from the pent-up flood,
and the neighbouring banks roar with the crashing waves.
But God then fenced Christ about in darkened air,
and poured around [him] a thick mantle of mist;
so that no one may see or touch him.
He withdraws, enclosed in mist—wondrous to tell—
through their midst, and mingles with the men, and is seen by none.
The Jews, out of their senses, run through the paved streets,
casting their gaze this way and that around every house,
and they track the man in vain, covered as he is by darkness:
as when a black swallow, through the great mansion of a wealthy master,
flits and on her wings ranges through the lofty halls,
gathering tiny morsels, food for her chattering nestlings,
and now in the empty colonnades, now about the damp
pools she chirps; like her, the maddened crowd through the midst of the city
roars and, flying, ranges everywhere at a rapid pace.
O blind sons of Abraham! what madness has seized you?
Where are you rushing, wretches? what frenzy unsettles your mind?
Is it you who assail with stones him who watches your stony hearts
from the hollow cloud with a groan, shrouded in mist?
Do you hope to pour out his life with your own right hands —
to whom alone belongs power over death and life?
Shall he, immortal, meet death by a mortal hand,
he who fills heaven and earth with his very own divine power?
He walks upon the ground, and hides his head among the clouds.
Has so great a confidence in your own race taken hold of you?
Alas, how dreams mock the sleeping senses!
This is to drive a skiff with oars against the river's current,
which the foaming channel sweeps headlong down the descending stream,
Every attempt is fruitless, and to no purpose your
stones fly; you beat the empty air with your blows:
And just as in sleep, when at night a languid rest has weighed
the eyes down, in vain to stretch out our eager course
we seem to wish, and in the midst of the effort, faint,
we sink down: the tongue has no strength, nor for the body do the familiar
powers suffice, and neither voice nor words follow;
So it is with you: by whatever means you try
to crush Jesus and slow the peaceful course of his kingdom,
God himself denies [you] success; but the hour draws near [which]
he will not fear, although he will perish by a death he has not deserved.
After this Christ bends his steps toward the walls of Bethany,
and at him all the young men, streaming out from houses and fields,
and the throng of mothers marvel, and gaze after him as he goes.
And while [He] pressed on, hastening His journey, Martha, most sorrowful,
groaning much and wetting her face with a copious flood,
runs to meet [Him], and pours out from her breast such laments:
Christ, God, I believe that He sent You down from heaven —
the King of heaven, who governs heaven and earth by His divine power—
so that, pitying the human race in its neediness,
You might help it with counsel and with aid; he would not be without the light [of day],
my brother, if he had felt Your divine power present.
Now he lies lifeless, and rests in peaceful death;
this is now the fourth day since his pale limbs
we buried in the earth and enclosed in his ancestral tomb.
Now I know that through prayer You can move the Father;
Put it to the test: whatever You ask, He will give You for the asking.
In such words she was praying, and such tears, most wretched,
Martha sheds; but Christ consoles her with kindly words,
answering her thus, briefly:
Why are you so troubled, and, sick with enormous cares,
why do you pour out tears? Easy is the descent to Avernus,
night and day the door of dark Dis stands open;
but to retrace one’s steps and escape to the upper air,
this is the task, this the toil; yet, best of women, I will make
[your] brother rise from the infernal regions to the light of life,
he who believes that I have drawn my descent from bright heaven,
and [that I am] the offspring of the great Father, who the stars of the world
rules with eternal dominion — although the kindly light has withdrawn
from his eyes, and though an iron sleep weighs hard upon him,
Yet his eyes shall not be closed in everlasting night,
but he shall live, and shall draw out his life through all the ages.
When he had uttered these words, he went with many thousands
to the tomb, in their midst, a great throng attending him.
Here, seeing that Mary had wept, and the grieving crowd,
Christ lifted his burning eyes to heaven,
giving a mighty groan, and with tears welling up he speaks thus:
Holy Father, never does your care for us depart from you;
therefore I pay you worthy thanks, because you hear [me]
when I call upon you aloud and, as a suppliant, implore your divine majesty;
now, Father, do not withdraw your help from us; in doubtful
straits be at hand: give your assent to [these] bold undertakings.
So he speaks, weeping, and the body of his lifeless friend
he calls forth from the tomb: the body — wondrous to tell —
as soon as Christ's voice reached the ears of Lazarus,
comes out, leaving the cave, and once more into his marrow
warmth entered and coursed through his weakened bones:
not otherwise than when at times, burst open by flashing thunder,
a fiery crack, glittering, runs with its light through the storm-clouds.
Christ himself orders the man's manacles and his tight
bonds to be lifted off: he greets Lazarus, called back from death,
Then indeed through the trembling breasts of all a new
dread steals in, when they saw Lazarus moving
stretching out his hands and invoking Christ in his prayers.
Straightway the report travels through Judah’s great cities:
Rumour, an evil than which no other is swifter,
thrives on movement, and gathers strength as it goes.
Small at first through fear, soon it lifts itself into the air,
and he walks upon the earth and hides his head among the clouds.
The ruler of Orcus, from the seat of the dread sisters,
sent her forth, swift of foot and nimble of wing:
a monster dread and huge, who has, as many as are the feathers on her body,
so many watchful eyes beneath, wondrous to tell.
She has as many tongues and just as many sounding mouths, and pricks up as many ears.
By night it flies in mid-heaven: and over the earth through the darkness
shrieking, nor does it close its eyes in sweet sleep.
By day it sits as a watchman, either on the ridge of a high roof,
or on lofty towers, and terrifies great cities;
as tenacious of what is false and perverse as she is a herald of truth.
She then kept filling the peoples with talk of every kind,
rejoicing, and sang alike what had been done and what had not:
that this Christ had come, sprung from royal blood,
who would hold the lands of Judah under his whole dominion,
who gives laws to the people, and makes his way toward heaven
while he teaches the idle crowd; what is more, credulous hearts
he beguiles with false shows, and turns over in his breast new
designs, so that he may overthrow the nation of Jacob.
The foul goddess spreads these things everywhere upon the lips of men.
Straightway she turns her course toward the wicked Scribes:
and she inflames their spirits with her words and heaps up their anger.
And now the chief priests and the whole council
were holding council on the highest affairs of the Kingdom.
Then Caiaphas sat down in their midst upon his ancestral throne,
whose temples the priestly headband bound about with its sacred fillet;
and shaking his head, he poured out these words from his breast,
Since the pitiable crowd follows this Christ,
and to roam too freely up through the airs of heaven
if we allow [him]; then upon us, and upon our descendants one day,
the Roman stock will let loose great destruction:
we shall be compelled, our homeland abandoned, to obey proud masters—
we who now sit settled at our ease in our fields:
Take counsel for the common good, and come to the help of our weary fortunes
There is no safety in war; we all ask you for peace.
Shall a godless soldier hold these fields so well tilled?
a barbarian these cities? See to what point discord has led
the wretched citizens! Alas, what great madness it is to support Christ
to aid with heart and wealth, while we are set at nought?
Take these words of mine to heart, then, and fix them firmly there:
To the matter at hand—for I speak to the point—we have, for war, brave
hearts and courage, and young men tested in action;
From among them, having chosen by lot a picked band of men, secretly
let us send them, so that Christ, off his guard and fearing nothing of the sort,
they may secretly overpower him with the sword, or, with his hands bound fast by a rope,
Let them bring on punishment; but he pays [it] not without blood;
One life shall be given for many.
With such words Caiaphas pleaded, and all the Jews roared
with varying assent, as when the first gusts,
caught in the woods, roar, and roll blind
mutterings, betraying to sailors the winds to come.
When he had spoken thus, then straightway from his golden throne
he rises, whom the sons of Sarah escort in their midst to the threshold.
But because the last day and the inescapable hour
of Christ had not yet arrived, the Jews make many vain attempts
against the Lord, assailing him with guile and force
from every side and hurling futile abuse,
so that the savage nation may leave nothing untried, all to no purpose:
And just as one who assails a lofty city with siege-works,
or encamps under arms around mountain fortresses,
now these approaches, now those, and ranges with skill over
the whole ground, and presses on unavailing with assault after assault:
just so the sons of Abraham attacked, now by force, now by fraud,
the Lord, to no avail; he remains undaunted,
and stands firm like an unmoved rock of the sea;
as a rock of the sea, when a great crash comes on,
which, with many waves baying about it, holds itself
fast by its own mass: in vain the crags and the foaming
rocks roar around, and the seaweed, dashed against its flank, is flung back:
So Christ bore the threats of the people and of the fathers,
weak, beyond the strength and lot of created
nature, if courage and favoring strength were not
supplied to the Son by the Father, King of high heaven.
But when he declares himself one of our race or blood,
we all recognise in Christ the defects of [his] nature —
defects without defect, fault without fault.
Hence desiring and fearing, grieving and rejoicing, he confesses
that he is flesh of our flesh and bone of our bones:
hence he sits at the well, and sweet waters from the springs
he awaits with dry throat — he himself the everlasting spring.
And he who promises the believer waters flowing from his belly,
and pure rivers of everlasting water.
Thus among deserted crags, to set his teeth
upon scant bread the lack of food compelled him.
Yet he — men and cattle and the throngs of flying things,
and the monsters the sea bears beneath its marble surface,
the herds of Neptune, and the ugly seals beneath the flood;
and those that inhabit the clear lakes far and wide and the rugged
countryside—these living creatures he feeds with rich fare.
He loads the tables with feasts, and fills the cups,
and gladdens our banquets with abundant wine —
he who by his nod [upholds] heaven and earth, and the flowing plains,
and the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars—
He bears [it]; yet, worn out, he often sank down to rest.
He who with his countenance clears the sky and the storms,
often groaned in grief, and, sick with mighty cares,
often wet his bosom and his face with bitter tears.
He who so many times made all Olympus tremble at his nod
himself trembled with fear, veiled in our likeness.
O You, who have often grieved with our grief,
whose cheeks were wet with tears, who from the bottom of [your] breast
have often uttered mighty groans for us:
now unseal the springs of my eyes, and with bitter
mourning shake my heart; let pain burn in my inmost bones,
let sad rivers burst out from the fountains of tears;
that I may weep for Thee night and day, and that thy wounds with water
I may wash, and embracing Thee cherish Thee at my breast; for
alas, I was the cause of thy death; my guilt, of sufferings
such great sufferings, [guilt] which so great a flood of blood
poured forth, [my guilt] which has undone me, wretched as I am, and Thee, alas!
If I did not weep for Thee, I should be harder even than stones,
rougher than butcher's-broom, cheaper than seaweed cast ashore,
for Christ slain by a cruel death the Temple's
veil bewailed; the golden Sun wept, looking out
from mid orb, and borne along through the open sky
he shudders, and thunderstruck gives rein to his plunging team.
Then he veiled his golden-haired head with a black mantle,
bringing night and storm, and the upper air bristled with darkness.
Yet the audacious people did not lose confidence,
nor is it struck dumb with amazement, nor to Christ, bearing what he did not deserve,
does it grant reprieve, nor does anyone pity the guiltless Jesus;
though the sun withheld its gaze, and turning away shrank back from
those foul offices, and hid itself in blind shadows,
and the impious ages feared everlasting night.
Should I not weep for you?—you whom [the crags, shaken] from so many deepest roots,
wept, and the earth herself,
while, shaken from her foundations, she opened the gaping tombs,
and the stones of proud Judaea themselves wept.
Nay more, the shades howled from the lowest seats of hell,
and the thin ghosts and the phantoms of those bereft of light.
Christ, that even the furies of the abyss groaned at your
death, Ausonians and Greeks alike declare.
But whither have we turned aside in our weeping? the wandering of love
has led [us] off the path; no wonder — [our] eyes with weeping
grow dim, and through tears everything round about darkens.
But now it is time to turn the steaming necks of the horses
and to retrace our step.
Go on, then, to recount the annals of Christ's labours,
Calliope, and to bind our calves with the buskin.
After it had conceived a frenzy, overcome by grief —
(will you believe it?) the offspring of Judah, whom the glory of Christ,
with sidelong envy and with bitter goads, kept driving on —
Christ silently resolved to leave the accursed land
and abandon Judah's polluted dwelling.
There is a region left desolate by drought, withdrawn in a far recess;
On either side vast crags and varied cliffs loom threateningly
toward the sky, and monstrous wild haunts bristle.
Not far from here is a town called by the name of Ephraim,
up to which Christ went, and his companions follow.
Here lay hidden he from whom nothing lay hidden; not the inmost
realms of Dis, nor Neptune's monsters in their secret lairs.
Whatever Ocean embraces in his vast belly,
and whatever lies covered in the blind bosom of the earth,
all this lies open to his eyes; nay, the hall of the breast
and the house of the heart within, and its dark chambers, lie open.
Turn yourself into every shape, and gather up whatever
power you possess, whether in courage or craft: choose to pursue
the lofty stars on wings, and to conceal yourself enclosed in the hollow earth,
yet you will not escape Christ's all-seeing eyes;
from whom nothing is hidden, for he alone knows all things —
what is, what has been, and what is soon to come.
He alone knows the wandering Moon and the Sun's eclipses:
whence comes the race of men and of beasts, whence rain and fires,
[he knows] Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears,
why the suns hasten so to dip themselves in Ocean
in winter, or what delay stands in the way of the lingering nights;
whence the earth's trembling comes, and by what force the deep seas swell
the barriers burst, and again they settle back into themselves.
But I, who only in the pursuits of ignoble leisure
flourish, and long to give myself up to unremitting toil,
namely that I might come to know the causes of things;
and not wholly unversed have I tried human arts;
for, so that I may not be able to draw near to nature's realms,
behold, the cold blood about my heart stands in the way,
and earthly limbs and mortal members dull [my mind],
and the mind's keen sight grows dim; nay more, there stands in the way
for all men, this brief and irrecoverable span of life.
Therefore let it be granted me, with you, most beloved Christ,
to live, and to shun the frenzied tumults of men.
You pass a life untouched by the marriage-chamber, without blame;
you inhabit woods and terrifying caves among the crags,
setting aside the halls of kings and the proud gates
of cities, where an unending love of getting drives the citizens on.
O if only I might be allowed, with you, to inhabit the humble countryside
and lowly cottages and the haunts of wild beasts.
Not the thresholds of kings, nor Roman palaces to heaven
made equal, nor towers gleaming with Parian marble,
shall I so much as seek after. The strongholds the rich man has founded
let him himself inhabit; for us let the woods please above all things.
Only be with me; without you, cool Tempe,
caves, living lakes, or rivers are of no avail;
or the lowing of cattle and soft sleep beneath a tree.
It is resolved: in the woods, among the dens of wild beasts,
to choose rather to endure with you, and, inglorious, all my years
to spend them, and to endure the harsh labours of the countryside;
rather than without you to receive the sceptre, or to raise the torches.
For neither the people's fasces nor the purple of kings
swayed you, when, by unanimous assent, the people wished to entrust you with
the reins of government; you fled and, in the high
mountains—even there—chose rather to spend your years.
In them discord never troubles faithless citizens;
no wars rage, nor do you behold iron laws,
nor do you behold a mad forum, or the people's record-offices.
Yet you do not wear away untroubled leisure in the thick groves
like a wild beast, although amid the beasts’ wildernesses
you inhabit their haunts; you do not compose a woodland song on a slender reed,
stretched out in a green cave,
and reclining amid the grass beneath the canopy of a spreading beech.
Mossy springs, and grass softer than sleep,
and the green arbutus that shelters us with its thin shade,
do not thrill you through with an empty sweetness, nor make you glad;
but amid such things you kept tossing various cares in your sorrowing
breast; you press the deep grief down in your heart.
Nay more, an uncivilized people and settlers scattered through the countryside
you set in order, teach laws, and expound the Father’s precepts;
and you also roam throughout the whole region,
secretly healing mortals as you go along.
But it is not with Paeonian herbs or any
medicated produce that you call mortals back from the grip of wasting death;
Our masters knew the arts that had been sought out—
Chiron, son of Philyra, and Melampus, son of Amythaon.
But no one has been able to drive diseases from a languishing body
by touch or word except you; for indeed
You are our Physician; you alone are the cure for madness.
After this, reclining at the feast in Simon's house
with Lazarus, he sees the people approaching in a great throng
so that they might see Lazarus recalled from death;
Souls crowd around, in throngs to right and left,
but Mary shed abroad the flowing fragrance of ambrosia,
with which she anointed Christ's sacred brow; but from his
carefully arranged hair a sweet fragrance breathed forth.
And his ambrosial feet, wet with the dew poured over them,
breathed fragrance forth; Judas, shaken with bitter anger,
seethes, and rebukes Mary with bitter words.
But Christ, although he tries to soften Judas's fury
with words, and to bend his savage mind —
one whom neither length of days nor any devotion softens,
nor is he pliable enough to hear any words of Christ;
he, turned away, kept his savage eyes [averted] all the same,
nor is his expression moved any more by the speech begun
than if hard flint, or a Morpesian crag, were standing there;
but his mind is agitated, and made wild by the monstrous things it has undertaken.
At last, rolling his bloodshot eyes in a savage glare,
he tore himself away and made for the lofty
halls of the Priests, and openly accuses Christ,
whom the traitor of his own accord promises to catch by a plot;
and while Judas turns over in his breast new devices, new
designs, [to see] whether he can deceive his guiltless friend,
borne on an Ass the hero seeks the City again, in no way daunted,
whom his anxious companions accompany with matching steps.
But as soon as [he] looks up at the rooftops of the lofty city,
Christ, and gazes down from above on the citadels facing him,
he gives a mighty groan, and thus speaks as the tears well up:
O [city] too fortunate, if you will come to know your own blessings,
Jerusalem! you who cruelly butcher all
the messengers whom we send to you—with the sword, alas!
Why do you refuse to let my words sink into your hard ears?
Where are you rushing? or who keeps you from our embrace?
For your sake I shed tears; for your sake too
I chose to endure so many misfortunes, to undergo so many hardships;
yet you, most wicked one, threaten me with death, although
I taught you as the day came on, taught you as it departed.
Alas, Solyma, Solyma! what madness has seized you?
Will neither our love move you, nor my words move you?
Have you no pity for me? Do you finally force me to die?
See — since you are moved neither by our prayers nor by our tears,
the final day presses on, and the inescapable time
when this immense and enormous temple, from its lofty summit,
will crash down, and the enemy will lord it in the conquered city.
Apart from shattered masses, and stones wrenched from
stones, you will see nothing else, together with smoke mingled with dust;
the Roman — the walls, and the whole city from its foundations —
will tear down; alas, what carnage, how many deaths everywhere!
the dying bodies of many thousands of men, and moreover
I see the Jordan foaming with red blood,
and far and wide the plains white with the bones of the Jews;
because your mind is never content with quiet peace.
Such laments he poured forth from his breast.
Christ, with tears and with prayers I seek your peace,
grant [it], Father, and bind this peace in an everlasting covenant.
See that no day violates this peace or breaks the covenant,
however events may fall; and may no force turn You, resolved as You are,
aside—not even if it should pour the earth into the sea,
mingling it with a deluge, or dissolve heaven into Tartarus;
I shall not shudder at the empty din of wars, nor at enemies,
though all things threaten present death,
but untroubled I shall live my life amid open perils.
And now, having completed his journey, Christ was drawing near
to Zion’s lofty towers and roofs and approaching the wall;
when suddenly crowds, with palm branches cut on every side,
runs to meet him and raises its cries to the stars.
They strew the streets with their garments and, bearing palms,
advance; all around them boys and unmarried girls
sing holy songs; and with the roar of men and the zeal of those cheering
the whole grove will ring out; vast halls roll the cry around,
and the hills, struck by the shouting, echo it back.
Then mothers, pouring out in their eagerness, and the unarmed common folk,
and feeble old men thronged the towers and rooftops;
others stand at the lofty gates.
Soon the Pharisees’ anguish had flared with fury, from black
gall; and they gnash their teeth in savage wrath.
But Christ, going up into the Temple, and having made a whip,
drove out those exchanging wares and, furthermore, rebukes them.
And while he is pressed by hunger he caught sight, in a rich field,
of a fig-tree spreading its boughs and its aged arms,
but no fruits were hanging on the whole tree;
because the eastern Atlantides [the Pleiades] are not yet hidden away.
