Therefore he curses it with bitter words,
and forbade that hereafter it should grow green with new leaf:
nor thrust forth buds, nor unfold any blossoms.
At this word the tree withered from its lowest roots,
the leaves slip and fall, and the life-giving moisture fails.
Neither the light rains nor the force of the scorching sun,
fiercer still, nor the piercing cold of Boreas, sears it
to such a degree as does the speech from your divine mouth,
O Christ, God, whom alone the vast world acknowledges
as author of the harvests and as master of the seasons.
Ah me, what a field the heart is — how it bristles with thorns!
No fruitful tree in its fresh bloom clothes itself with
fruit; or, if Autumn provides any ripe fruit,
they all deteriorate, forgetful of their former flavor.

div.note: Autumn had not yet come—the season when the Vergiliae, which stand in Taurus and are also called the Pleiades, set cosmically according to Virgil and rise acronychally according to Ovid.

lg.l: In the furrows to which we have often entrusted the barley of the Word,
unhappy darnel and barren oats hold sway.
In place of the soft violet, in place of the purple narcissus,
the thistle rises up, and the thorn-bush with sharp prickles.
I am like a tree in the woods cut away from its stock,
bereft of its mother, stripped by the iron of its foliage and its bark;
never putting forth shoots of light leafage, nor any shade.
O you who teach mortals to turn the earth with iron,
when acorns and arbute-berries fail the sacred
woods withhold; now to the furrows of [my] heart the seeds
that are owed do you commit, and from the deepest roots
tear out the darnel; and may the Holy Spirit, with warming breezes,
now cherish the whole field of my breast;
moreover, may he descend abundantly in a glad shower;
so shall I be fruitful, so a tree serviceable for its fruits.
But the tribe of the Pharisees burns implacable,
rolling beneath its breast a vast mass of wrath:
as when the wave begins to whiten at the first wind,
little by little the sea heaves itself up, and higher its waves
it rears, then from its lowest depth surges up to the sky;
a thousand plots they turn over within themselves with kindled heart,
[to see] whether they can make away with Christ by any death whatsoever.
And now he is said, as a suppliant with upturned hands, to have prayed to the Father
that he deem his Son worthy of deserved honour;
and he was pondering many hard things in his sorrowing heart;
had the Father himself not given a sign from the open sky:
For suddenly a lightning bolt, hurled from the upper air,
came with a crash, and of a sudden all things seemed to be falling in ruin;
they look up; again and yet again the huge thunder-crash rolls out.
But while the almighty Father, shining from heaven on high,
thundered, and a cloud ablaze with rays of light and with gold
he himself, shaking it with his hand, displayed out of the upper air,
behold, from the midst of the cloud an answering voice is borne to their ears:
I have always held you in honour, and so shall I always hold you.
The others were stunned in their hearts, but the greatest hero
recognized the thunder and the promises of his great Father;
then he speaks: that crash thunders for your sake.
If you ask what event the portents bring — the world's
turbulent Prince is cast out; I am summoned to heaven.
And now the day was at hand on which the Jewish people used
to sprinkle the doorposts with the blood of a slaughtered lamb;
Neither customary feasts nor these great solemn rites
did vain superstition, ignorant of the true Jehovah,
impose; this nation, preserved from cruel perils,
while the winged Spirit slays the firstborn of Egypt,
makes its yearly vows and was renewing the honours duly owed.
From Bethany Christ sent his companions ahead into the city,
bidding them make a room ready, and a tender lamb from the sheepfolds.
They at once fly off and take up their orders:
first, rich with pine-brands and split oak,
they built a huge fire, while they roast the flesh;
they lay the table, and serve out bread and wine;
they cut the lamb into pieces; Christ and his sorrowing companions
stand round about, and feed on the lamb and on bitter herbs.
After hunger was taken away, and the desire of eating was checked,
Christ lays aside his garment; at the same moment he himself begins
eagerly to pour water over the feet of his companions,
and makes ready to dry them wet as they are; for the best of heroes,
wrapping about his shoulders towels of long nap,
brought the pure stream down in gleaming basins;
and bending down upon his holy knees, with his sleeves drawn back,
his head bared and his eyes cast down, like a suppliant
he himself washes and dries their feet, and rebuts Peter,
who refuses to be washed with water. After he has washed them all,
Christ rises, and draws his tunic over his limbs
and reclined upon the couch, and broke forth with this utterance from his breast:
You have seen me wash [your] feet with water; in turn
do this among yourselves; let the love in you all be the same,
I pray; may harmony secure eternal peace
among you. Learn courage and true toil from me,
for dangers must be faced by you for my sake.
Whatever shall come, every fortune must be overcome by enduring it.
You will leave the borders of your homeland and its fields, compelled
to seek distant places of exile and deserted lands,
uncertain where the fates may carry you, where it may be granted to halt,
through diverse trials, through so many dangers
you press on toward heaven, where the fates will reveal peaceful
abodes; but overcome all your hardships,
and take heart; for this right hand of mine will always
keep you safe and lead you among great rewards;
endure, and keep yourselves for better times.
In me is your hope and your peace, yet hard things you will bear
[You shall have] afflictions in the world; but rejoice, because the round
world, and the head of savage hell, we have stormed.
I hasten to heaven’s dwelling and the lofty house of my Father;
here I will make ready for you both a sure home and seats;
I wish you to dwell together with me in these realms.
If ever toward the Father, with your voice, upturned palms
you stretch out, breaking forth in laments in my name,
He will hear at once and from high heaven will show mercy.
Nor will I leave you stripped bare: there will be sent from Olympus
the Spirit — He, the solace of every care and mischance,
will govern you, and He will console your long labours.
Behold, I am the Way that leads into the heavenly city,
and the life-giving air that you breathe; I am that messenger of
truth, and I fill the mind with truths; assuredly, in me
there is neither wavering care nor uncertain hope of the future;
therefore bend your minds to it, and these my words in your breast
fix fast; obey my counsels willingly.
The world is glad with some empty sweetness or other,
while you are melted in tears, while [your] breasts, wounded with cares,
give out groans; but your mourning will pass over
into applause, and the great river of tears will be dried up.
When a woman has brought forth a male child in her travail,
she exults with gladness, forgetful of all her pains:
so you, after the various labours of land and sea,
once they are endured, sweetness of spirit will soothe you as you rejoice,
and no force of men will have power to snatch it from you.
If the world hates you, it is no wonder: it hates Me first.
Is a servant greater than his master, a house-slave than an envoy?
I am the greater; it is right that you, [my] servants, obey me.
Those [words are mine]: I am the vine planted by the Father, the husbandman,
you [are] the branches; bring forth from the vine-shoot worthy fruit.
In your fruits the Father's glory rises.
But without Me neither does the field flower, nor the tree bear,
nor without Me does the vintage foam in the brimming vats.
That plant is fruitful which, to grow into our bark
has been taught, and the vine thrusts buds out of the rind;
but fallen leaves and pruned shoots are burned.
I do not call you servants but friends, for servants
do not know what purpose stands fixed in their master's mind.
But to you I have laid open all the Father's secrets.
The Stygian King begrudges you the heavenly citadels,
hence he rages, and stirs up the whole world against you.
He rouses wars, and forbids [you] to settle in your native land,
and takes it ill that you seek realms abroad.
You are souls of little worth to the world, an unknown crowd—
what wonder is it if the world, with hatred and ever-unjust accusation,
harries you, if it strives to overthrow your fortunes from their foundations,
if it compounds its crime with death and wounding?
By these I am despised, and none of them asks who I am —
not one of them; yet he longs to devour Me, though innocent, with unspeakable
envy; they have known neither Me nor [my] Father.
See, the Father is spurned when the Father's image is spurned.
But a brow scarcely broad, and eyes in a downcast face,
compel me to bring out in words the grief I had covered over;
Cares press on, and my mind is distraught by death,
what we have always feared must now be gone through;
someone from this company has resolved to hand me over to death,
who along with me breaks with bold jaws the round
of the fated crust; that man strikes me with his heels.
To take this life, and to release me from these cares,
I permit; but a time will come when he will wish he had bought
me unharmed at a great price, and when those crimes and that day
he will hate. Meanwhile, should my body be robbed of light,
I do not fear it; rather, through many wounds I shall seek death.
I have lived, and the course you had given, kindly Father, I have run to the end,
and now my noble shade will pass beneath the earth.
yet nowhere shall I be absent, nor will I abandon you in death,
but when cold death has parted my limbs from my soul,
see, I shall be present in every place; lay down your cares.
Such things he utters aloud; and, sick with overwhelming cares,
he comforts his companions; he presses the grief down deep in his heart.
All were struck dumb; at once pallor seizes their faces.
Mary weeps, a mother terrified in heart by no means without cause,
and stirred by the threats of Abraham's sons and by the savage uproar;
They discussed many things among themselves in varied speech,
[asking] which companion Christ was accusing; then the greatest hero,
rebuking him, holds out to Judas the fated morsel;
he snatches it, opening his wild throat in ravening hunger.
Then Judas’s mind, driven wild by frenzy, lest anything remain unattempted

div.p: Supper ended, Christ withdrew with the Apostles into the garden of Gethsemane, where, as he prayed and sweated blood, an Angel consoles him, and holds out to him a cup filled with deadly wine, which the heavenly Father himself had mixed. The cup, wrought by the Angels, is described in the poetic manner; upon its rim are chased the martyrdoms of Christ, of the Apostles, and of many Christians. Christ's passion in the garden is described, whom Judas, in that same place and attended by a cohort of criminal soldiers, betrayed with a kiss; but at Christ's voice they all fell to the ground; at last

lg.l: or any crime or guile left unattempted,
he goes out, and soon sells his master's life for silver,
And now day had withdrawn from the sky, and kindly Phoebe
was traversing lofty Olympus in her night-roaming chariot,
when Christ serves out Ceres and Bacchus to his companions:
which he shares out among all [as] memorials of his death;
so that they may attest to mankind Christ’s enduring love;
and with varied words he soothes their grieving hearts,
and many things besides, foretold by the prophets of old,
he unfolds from his divine mouth and reveals what is to come,
and kindles their minds with love of the coming Spirit.
Then he recounts to the men all that is afterwards to be done,
and how they are to avoid or endure each hardship.
Meanwhile the Father was mixing a bitter draught,
and prepares to send down from the stars a deadly cup
to [his] Son, that for us he may drink down the wrath [we] deserved.
Within the smoking walls of the storm-clouds' homeland, lofty,
there is a house; within, the flame rages in dreadful furnaces;
and this [flame], as often as it bursts through the tower's dark-blue barriers,
it roars, indignant, through the air with dreadful thunder.
In these furnaces the almighty Father, with his fiery right hand,
forges thunderbolts, of which very many across the whole sky
he hurls down upon the earth; a winged troop of spirits
here was plying, amid the thick clouds, the shafts
of the thunderbolt, and was hastening to shape the pliant mass.
Shaped by these hands, with one part now polished,
there was a thunderbolt, but a part still remained unfinished;
Three rays of twisted rain, three of watery cloud
they had added, three of ruddy fire and three of the winged south wind.
Now terrifying flashes and noise and dread
they were blending into the work, and wrath into the pursuing flames.
Now hither the Lord of Fire came down from high heaven:
“Take everything away,” he says, “and carry off the tasks already begun,
you winged youths, and turn your minds this way;
leave off now, Brontes, and Steropes and naked Pyracmon;
for a bowl must be made for my son; make it wide enough
to hold Lenaean liquor—the bowl that I have duly prepared;
that bowl he will drain for wretched mortals; therefore
cut short delay: now there is need of all your strength,
now of swift hands, now of all your mastering skill;
show how much fires and the bellows' blasts avail, how much
can now be wrought in iron or in molten electrum.

div.note: Although lightning and thunder arise from natural causes, it must nevertheless not be believed that they occur without divine command and the ministry of angels; for the things that fools suppose to happen by chance in this world happen only at God's bidding and carry out his word. Augustine, on Psalm 148.
These names, taken from the nature of the thunderbolt, may be attributed to those angels, because they have been appointed by God to the forging of the thunderbolt.

lg.l: He had spoken; and they, making ready to obey the command,
all bent to it the faster, and the labour alike
having shared out; the bronze flows in streams, and the ore of gold;
while they lift their arms, the air groans with blow upon blow,
and the steel fabric flashes: they dip the hissing
bronze in the trough, and turn the mass with the gripping tongs.
They take in the breaths of the air, and give them back with the bellows.
Thus they fashion a huge bowl, which alone [might hold] the liquor
could hold, of divine wrath, and the deadly wines.
When the work was done the Father himself called for the immense [bowl],
and filled the bowl with unmixed wine; then he chooses one
out of the whole winged company, to whom he gives this charge:
Go now, servant, call the west winds and glide down on your wings,
and the Son, for whom the sisters are gathering the last threads,
address, and carry my words down through the swift breezes.
Let him not shrink from sinking down in cruel death, nor
from draining this drugged wine; for it brings sleep
upon the limbs, but lifts the mind to the stars.
He indeed shall be the first: this [bowl], sprinkled with his own blood,
he shall drain this bowl and drink deeply from the brimming golden vessel;
Afterward the other leaders will be able only to taste it
with the lip alone; but let them not fear to touch it, for
I have rubbed the mixing-bowl with the healing juice of ambrosia.
Whoever shall have sipped this unmixed wine with the tip of his lips,
shall lose his mortal form and trample tyrants beneath his feet
he shall trample in triumph, and shall pass his age among the stars.
He spoke, and everything rang with the mighty applause
of the heaven-dwellers, who sing the deeds and the praises of the Thunderer.
There was once a garden, most luxuriant with varied herbs,
Gethsemane, and nearby, the Kidron, with its rushing waters
running down, stirred a murmur over the smooth stones;
Whenever it, swollen to its banks by rain-bearing south winds,
overflows and blankets everything far and wide with a coating of mud,
it paints the soil with violets and with other green-growing plants.
Thither Christ withdraws, sorrowful now, away from the city,
and his servants, faint [with dread], attend their master's steps.
The first Adam, by going astray, barred heaven in a garden;
the second Adam, by praying, opened heaven again in a garden;
here he groans, and stretching both palms toward the stars,
he utters such words aloud: Most holy Father, I beg you,
rescue me from death, if such is the will you bear in your heart;
nor steep the cup in Lethean dew; away from me
let it pass, or at least mix it with heavenly nectar,
for you can do all things; yet let the purpose stand fixed in [your] mind.
You are the Father; it is right that I obey you. As he prays
in such words, at once there flows on every side in streams
cold sweat, and blood flowed over his whole body;
and stains the earth with gore. Soon, having descended from heaven,
on the oarage of his wings, look, there flies through the great air
an angel, bearing the Father’s fateful gifts to his Son;
to him, with a suppliant expression, he presented an enormous bowl
foaming with wine, and added these words:
Do not flee the cup, though this draught be bitter
and soporific; for the Father himself mixed it
with nectar and drenched it in the liquid fragrance of ambrosia.
Its chief power is to bring upon the limbs the numbness
of death and to take away the feeble senses; but that same draught
soon bears the soul above the stars, and doubles the vigour
of the mind, and one day it will call the body back from the shades.
Be honoured, then, for your valour: this is the way to the stars;
and do not hesitate to summon fierce death to battle,
whom you will overcome as victor, exulting, and the Stygian tyrant with her.
He spoke, and having soothed Christ's heart with his words
he raised himself again into heaven on balanced wings.
But Christ, turning his sorrowful eyes over each detail,
marvels, and turns about between his hands and arms
the death-bringing cup of gold, glittering from afar.
Here winged spirits, versed in the prophets and in the destiny to come,
had fashioned annals of the sufferings to come:
for around the rims of the cup there are chased in gold
the brave deeds of the Christians, and triumphs over death.
Here Jesus recognised himself hanging on the wood,
stretching out a hand and calling aloud upon the Father.
Round about stand grieving mothers, their hair unbound,
they beat their breasts; from their eyes silver
rivers flow; then Mary, pale at the coming death
of her guiltless Son, the winged spirit had chased [there].
He catches sight, not far from here, of a tomb cut out in the rock,
And the mothers bringing the last rites to him after his death.
Then he sees himself descending to the deepest shades of the dead,
and bringing back trophies from Dis and from death,
and soon rising again, and above all the stars of heaven
borne up, and set on high in his Father's seat.
Then he saw Stephen praying amid the stones,
stretching out his hands and holding his eyes up toward the stars.
Stones fly about his ears and his temples; the sky,
torn open overhead in its midst, shows Jesus
standing at the Father’s right hand in clear light.
Here lies James's head, torn away from his neck,
gurgling with blood; here, having descended from high heaven,
an angel leads trembling Peter out of prison;
the gates are flung open, the chains fall away, the guard
stands wretched and thunderstruck; nearby Damascus is engraved,
toward which Paul presses on with hurrying steps; on a white
horse he rides, whose bridle gleams with silver, while Christ's
trembling ministers he pursues with sword and flame.
Him, like one full of wrath and like one threatening,
you would behold; but a cloud hangs over him,
white; then a sudden lightning bolt is hurled from the upper air,
which throws the young man from his horse, and presently took away his sight.
But the same man, beaten with rods for the name of Christ,
stood with Silas, his body stripped bare; close by,
the prison's dark house is carved with its doors thrown open.
For the huge doors of the house opened in the night
of their own accord, while each stretches [his] palms to heaven
and pours out prayers; onto the sword the frantic gaoler
was now about to rush, had not Paul's care held him back.
Amid these scenes one could see the blue seas encircling vast lands
and white waves rising to the stars.
As rain pours down, a black storm from above
is depicted, together with dense clouds encircling the sky.
Here the ship in which Paul had been tossed upon the deep
sea, as the brine now overpowers it, riddled with cracks, breaks apart;
all make haste to turn the prow toward the land,
they bend to the oars and cut the restraining cables with steel.
At last, driven upon the shoals, while it hangs on a treacherous ridge
precariously poised, long held up, it wears out the waves,
it breaks apart and casts the men out from amid the waves:
the prow indeed held to the shoal; but the stern, by the waves,
is shattered; these grasp with their hands the floating thwarts,
many [grasp] the fragments of oars, and on broken planks
leaning, they swam to shore, and now held safe ground.
Some [seemed] to watch for the ebbings of the slackening sea
and seemed to entrust themselves to the shallows with a leap.
Here, rising from the sea, the Cnossian land is chased in relief,
past which Paul sailed, skirting its shores;
you would think the ship was moving forward with sails set evenly.
Facing this, Melete appears amid the waves,
an island rich in resources and most fierce in the pursuits of war,
which Paul and his companions, storm-tossed and destitute upon the shore,
welcomes them and treats them hospitably; the fire flares, and a huge
viper leaps from the logs at Paul, clasping his right hand
gently, and harmless in its soft touch,
it is shaken off, while the whole crowd of bystanders marvels.
And not far from here you would see Rome and the lofty Capitol,
and the flock of the followers of Christ, and Paul paying the last
penalty, and the whole ground dripping with blood,
and the head torn from the shoulders, and the body without a name.
Peter is seen clinging to the wood, face upward,
breathing out his life for the Lord, whom he had denied with his voice.
And his brother Andrew ends his life upon a high beam.
And Philip breathes out his life by the same fate.
They tear the skin from his ribs and expose his entrails,
and at last they sever Bartholomew's neck.
Thomas, run through with barbarian spears, into the fire
directs his steps and plants many footprints on the glowing embers.
Behind Matthew stands a barbarian soldier, driving in
hurling [it], and with the embedded shaft pierces his breast.
While the other James was being overwhelmed by a storm of stones
and was praying on the shore with outstretched hands,
a barbarian coming up, and armed with a scorched brand,
struck him down, and stretched him dying on the tawny sand.
Jude and Simon, on the accursed threshold of the Temple,
lie laid low by the sword; for as they were entering
into the Temple, the images of the gods gave way and fell.
Matthias is battered with stones, and by the sword his head
is struck off, and drops of holy blood trickle down.
Plunged into boiling oil — wondrous to tell —
John came out unharmed, while the people looked on.
Mark is depicted in relief, mangled throughout his body.
Manacles are put upon his hands, and about his neck a rope
[for] bonds; along the ground both his neck and his hair are dragged,
and his holy entrails are hauled over the hard rocks.
You would have seen the briars dripping with streams of blood.
But fierce four-horse teams, pulling in opposite directions, had torn Hippolytus
apart; before the raging lions Ignatius
stood undaunted, but they were gnashing their teeth,
and now, at any moment, seem to be tearing the man's limbs apart.
Not far from here an iron gridiron was forged, white-hot,
Lying upon it over a slow fire, Lawrence
is tormented; close by stood an impious band of young men,
thrusting live coals beneath his side and scorching his flesh.
Why should I recount Luke, Justin, why Cyprian;
Christopher, Vitus, Martin, or why Nicetas;
or why Gregory, Victor, Pantaleon;
and countless others who, for their Master's glory,
sacrificed themselves, and of their own accord gave up their lives for their King?
these the flames consume, those the whirlpool swallows in the sea;
these perish by the sword; those are prey for the lions.
Dread hunger harries others, or squalid destitution.
Others, lifeless, are hung aloft and exposed to the winds;
Others, headlong from the mountain’s lookout onto the rocks far below,
are thrust; the ground grows bloody with their brains,
and, spattered with gore, swims [in it]; do not seek to be told
what they suffered, or what punishment or fortune overwhelmed the men.
Others are battered with stones, and on the spokes of wheels
hang stretched out; they are beaten with rods; before [your] face
of the cauldron you would have seen limbs [flung], and members torn away,
eyes gouged out, and temples ravaged by the tearing away
of the ears, and nostrils cropped with a disfiguring wound;
and entrails burning with pitch, and tongues cut out
from the throat, and inward parts smoking with hot lead.
An iron crop of weapons covers this one; that one wears a crown
of iron glowing white-hot upon his uplifted head,
If time were not fleeing—brief and irrecoverable time—
While, held captive by love, we range over all things,
you would not depart uncelebrated in my songs, Dionysius,
holy one; nor would you, with your offspring and dear wife,
whom the brazen Bull on high tormented with fire.
Sooner will evening lay the day to rest with Olympus shut,
than anyone could run through all the names of the punishments one by one;
But on the other side Constantine stands in gold,
towering, leading his column, whose proud emblem of war
is a golden cross, blazing at the summit of the clear sky;
against Neptune, and Venus, and against Minerva
holding his weapons, and [against] all the gods of Babylon and of Orcus

div.note: Christopher.
Eustace.

lg.l: [his] command; Pluto rages in the midst of the battle.
Before him the enemy turn their backs in trembling dread,
in whole columns; Licinius himself flies off,
no delay — with reins wheeled about he is carried away in flight,
But Christ, seated in a clear quarter of heaven
upon a snow-white cloud, and looking undismayed on the enemy
strewn across the plain, and in their own blood
rolling themselves about, spewing back waves of hot blood —
they who have so often drunk deep of Christ's blood, and so many
thousands of Christians they killed by a cruel death;
whose souls, standing before Christ in white robes,
the Angel had fashioned, adding to their victorious hands
flourishing palms; then he binds their hair with gold.
And also the maidens, slain by a cruel death,
stand by, who beyond their strength and their frail sex,
brave, poured out their virgin blood of their own accord.
But a choir of the winged ones in radiant raiment was singing
of Christ, the overthrower of Pluto's kingdom and city;
and likewise of Christ's people who suffered wounds for Christ;
the slender strings rang beneath the clear-toned plectrum.
Heaven exults, and earth, and sea, and air.
The Cynthian redoubles the applause, and the stars follow after,
the throngs of women exult with verdant palms.
At such things upon the cup, gifts of the Divine Father,
he marvels at, and delights his mind with the picture of these things,
while he carries in his hands the fame and the destinies of his own.
But not for that reason have the divine fires yet laid aside their unconquered
strength; deep beneath his breast there rages
the Father's wrath, and the dread of death, and deep within, the marrow
grief devours, and the affliction goes down through the whole body;
but this grief of the Lord is, for the servant, the medicine of grief
amid delights, and amid sweet fragrances.
O Christ, from your cheeks you water with tears and with blood the flowers
as they grow pale; in pallor you surpass the violets; the hyacinth,
sweetly blushing, did not blush so deeply as the body of Jesus,
now drenched with bloody dew; happy at last [are]
the lilies which bloom, painted with the blood of Christ.
Happy violets, and O happy hyacinths,
steeped both in glassy waters and in red nectar:
O for one to set me in the sacred garden of Gethsemane!
the garden where blood-red buds swell upon the vine-shoot:
for Christ is the vine-shoot; let us be your boughs,
and grant that that warmth of yours open the channels and the hidden
breathing-pores, by which the sap may come into new limbs;
and when the shade runs riot with a luxuriance of foliage,
exert your rule, and check the branches as they stream out;
strip the foliage with the word, not with iron, and shear the boughs;
And you whom gardens, breathing with saffron flowers,
invite, or whom the shade of the branches shields
from the rays of the burning sun, if flowering fields,
and [if] well-watered streams in the valleys please [you]:
While you snatch soft sleep beneath the open sky, or while
you gather flowers, and the strawberries springing up on the ground,
let not his face slip away from your heart —
he who, among soft violets and white lilies,
mingled with roses, cassia, and the blossoms of sweet-smelling dill,
then shut in by marigold and by other fragrant plants,
grows red with bloody sweat; whose breath, drawn from the depths of his breast,
strikes his sides with sobs.
The wild nard does not stir him, mingled though it be with rose-beds
of crimson; nor the soft marjoram, breathing out a sweet fragrance
from its flowers, nor the vine weaving its shady bowers;
Nor is he captivated by the gentle breeze of the murmuring wind.
O You who are the keeper of our poor garden,
who for my sake pour out a bloody dew in the garden:
come now into my garden, now with a rain of blood
bedew the plants that thirst so greatly in the heat.
O that my mind might breathe fragrance with the flowers of the virtues!
O Grace, if only you would strew the soil of my heart with flowering plants,
of Grace, so that this garden, growing wet with the dew of tears,
may pour forth the violets of the virtues, the lilies of the virtues:
so that you may lie at rest among the lovely flowers beside the streams.
It was night, and weary bodies were taking peaceful rest
throughout the lands, and the woods and the wild
seas had grown still, while the stars wheel on in mid course,
when all the countryside is silent, the herds and lovely birds—
both those that inhabit the broad, clear lakes and those that inhabit
lands rough with thickets—settled in sleep beneath the silent night—
were soothing their cares and their hearts, forgetful of their labors.
But now Christ—who turns over in his sorrowful mind
so many cares, whose marrow divine wrath devours—
is not released into sleep, nor does he receive rest in either his eyes or his heart;
does he receive; his groans redouble, and ever there returns
the horror of death, and he tosses on a great tide of griefs.
He who was willing to bear for me so many bitter griefs,
and to leave the borders of his fatherland, and the sweet realms
of the dwellers in heaven, and to suffer death, and the Father's wrath:
He was not lying among the willows beneath the pliant vine
upon green foliage, nor among the familiar streams
and sacred springs was he seeking shady coolness.
No hedge, its willow-blossom grazed by the bees,
was urging [him] with its whisper to enter refreshing sleep;
But cares redouble, which from his eyes and breast night
they snatch away; the deadly shaft clings in his side —
of the wrath of God; his immortal liver was being seared by
a devouring fire; the wound lives on, silent, beneath his breast.
Alas for me! the frenzy of sin blazes, scorching all
his inward parts, nor is any rest given to his fibres; his marrow
a relentless flame sears his marrow; a panting fire rages in his bones.
Oh, may the flame at last breathe forth from the shattered furnaces,
hidden within, which now boils up from the very depths of the heart.
You whose inward parts burned with the Father's flames
for me, O Christ — I pray in tears — blot out the accursed
traces of my sin, and seize me with this flame
with which it seized you, and which clung to your bones eaten away;
Or let a rain of water burst from my eyes; let my streams swell
from clouds torn open; let it grow wet with a fountain of tears —
[this] heart, scorched by sin and black with soot.
But his companions let their limbs relax in peaceful repose;
then, as they lay worn out with cares and weighed down by sleep,
Christ comes upon them, and presses them hard with friendly words:
Up, men, be watchful; now [there is need] of a steadfast breast,
now there is need of courage, for a hostile force draws near;
I see blazing shields and bronze flashing.
Scarcely had he said this when suddenly the repeated sound
of footsteps seemed close to his ears; for dread Judas,
leading armed foot-soldiers and horsemen, draws near.
They all beset the doors with drawn blades.
The horsemen throw themselves in the way at the familiar crossroads,
on this side and on that, and ring every approach with a guard.
See, the blood grows cold and congeals in his companions’ hearts;
But Christ, who now to yield to certain death
willed of his own accord [to submit], himself with himself the time and manner
determines, and did not repel Judas as he approached; but he,
When Judas caught sight of Christ, he stretched out both hands;
(for they had many torches, and the road shines with a long
line of flames, and marks off the fields far and wide)
and Judas holds him in his embrace, and plants kisses upon him.
To him Christ, briefly: do you plant kisses, friend,
and betray me with your own voice? And having spoken no more,
He halted, and with his eyes encompassed the thronging ranks:
Then at last he cries out: “Here I stand before you—the one you seek.”
At this voice they all fell, foot soldiers and horsemen alike,
to the ground; the earth trembled beneath the vast weight,
the men roared aloud, and gave a groan as they fell.
Every horse reared itself up, and with its hooves the air
lashes, and, itself following close upon the unseated rider,
entangles [him], and, its shoulder wrenched out, pitches headlong down upon [him].
Then Christ [said]: If you wish to lead me away into the city,
let these companions of [my] fate go. At once they
rush upon him with a great shout and restrain him with manacles.
But when Peter saw him seized by their hands and bound in harsh chains,
fury and anger drive his mind
headlong; he knows not how to bear so great a grief.
What is he to do? by what force, with what arms should he dare to snatch Christ
away? Or should he, ready to die, into the midst of his enemies
hurl himself? And hasten a noble death through wounds:
He could not bear this sight; he rushes into the midst of the ranks,
as a wild beast which, fenced about by a dense ring of hunters,
rages against the weapons and knowingly hurls itself
to its death; then with a leap it clears the hunting-spears.
Or as a boulder headlong from a mountain's summit
when it falls, torn loose by the wind, whether a turbid rainstorm
has washed [it] loose, or age, creeping on with the years, has worked [it] free,
the ruthless mass is borne headlong down the steep with mighty impetus
and leaps up from the ground, sweeping woods, herds, and men
along with it: through the scattered ranks Peter
charges — just so — ready to die, into the midst of the enemy
he charges: and where he sees the weapons thickest, there he makes his way.
Making for Malchus with drawn sword he looms over him, and
with his left hand seizes the hair of the panicked foe,
and pressing his knee down, straining, pins the man to the ground,
and briskly cuts off the right ear with the unyielding steel.
But Jesus rebukes Peter with weighty words,
and bids him bury the lightning blade in its sheath.
What would you have? What purpose so dreadful, most wretched Peter,
has driven you to gird yourself with these weapons? or where are you rushing? he said.
Not of such help, nor of defenders of that sort,
does the hour have need; presently the ear of Malchus, and his temples, by the steel
mutilated, Christ healed them with a healing hand, not by art.
Not, I say, by human resources, nor with art as guide
are these things done; nor does your own right hand save you, Simon:
One greater—God—is at work, and sends you back to greater tasks.
Meanwhile he is led away, his hands bound behind his back,
to Caiaphas's father-in-law; while the latter presses him with many questions, there stands nearby
a soldier, who struck that noble face with the flat of his hand.
His companions scatter, and are hidden by the shadowy night.
But Peter alone, stricken by the cruel turn of events,
follows at a distance, shedding tears and pitying Jesus.
Yet soon — alas — Peter three times with his own voice denied the Lord
while he stood close by the fire (for it was cold) in the hall;
the Master had foretold from his divine lips that this would be.
From there Christ is led away to the house of Caiaphas.
Here false witnesses bring their charges, and the Priest himself,
aloft on his throne, addresses Jesus with these words:
Whoever you are, now tell me these things truly as I ask,
(for I adjure you by the divine power of great Olympus;)
Are you that Christ, the offspring of Jove almighty?
To him Christ [replied]: I am indeed the undoubted offspring of God,
whom hereafter you shall see on high in an airy seat,
girt about with clouds, and adorned with resplendent light.
At these words, the elders' minds were troubled and their hearts shaken,
and their wrath was roused by no gentle goads.
Soon Caiaphas began to tear the garments from his shoulders,
and to call men to his aid, and to stretch out his palms;
and to load the guiltless Christ with malicious words,
whom he accuses of many things, falsely: then from every side a shout
with dreadful roaring lifts itself, huge, into the air,
just as in a lofty grove, when by chance a flock
of birds has settled, or on the fish-teeming stream of Padusa
the hoarse swans give out their sound through the babbling pools.
There is no need of further witnesses, for outrages such as these.
“For your crime,” Caiaphas cries, “you shall pay the penalty, villain.”
Young men run up, and vie with one another to mock Christ,
this one spits from his mouth, while another thrashes him with blows:
others muffle his face; Jesus stands sorrowful,
with lowered countenance, and has fallen silent, his lips shut close:
they jeer, and about his ears and temples there ranges
the hand, thick and fast; his cheeks crack beneath the hard blow.
Ah me, what he was! how greatly changed from that
Christ who once sprinkled with light the mountain
Tabor, and breathed out fire from his holy nostrils.
O true Light of men! O most faithful Hope of the world!
Who chose to exact punishments so cruel?
Who was allowed such power over you? Why [do I see] your hair with blood
matted with blood? What unworthy cause has marred your serene
has marred [your] features? or why do I behold these wounds?
Or did the almighty Father, ruler of those above, will
that you, sent down from heaven, should bear such great trials?
Is it thus I behold you, O Christ, my only delight
and solace of my sorrow: have pity on your King,
sons of Abraham, if there is any pity [in you]; against me hurl all
your weapons, and break off this wretched life as soon as may be.
What so great [wrong] could my Lord (alas) commit against you?
What could he have done, that he should pay such penalties with his blood?
Me, me — here I am, the one who did it — turn your steel against me,
you Jews; the whole guilt is mine; he neither dared anything
nor could he (this heaven and the stars that know I call to witness):
he only loved too much an unhappy friend.
Therefore Thee, O Christ, O God, now with my whole heart
I receive and embrace as Lord in every circumstance;
No glory shall be sought in my undertakings without you,
whether I make peace or wage war: you shall have my fullest fidelity in deeds
and words; with tears your wounds
I bathe, and with unceasing prayer adore your great divinity.
But Bar-Jonah’s mind, long wounded by care,
feeds the wound in its veins, and is consumed by a hidden fire:
The man’s great courage recurs to his mind, and so too does the great
dignity of his countenance; his features remain fixed in his heart,
and the words; nor does care grant his limbs quiet rest.
Alas, what is he to do? In vain he tosses on a shifting tide,
and conflicting cares call his mind in opposite directions.
In the middle of the courtyard, from pinewood and split holm-oak,
they have built a huge pyre; sorrowful beside the fire stands
Peter, for his blood has congealed with icy chill;
but in his soul a far harsher winter rages; rigid
with ice stands his former faith; frozen solid by white hoarfrost
his mind lies prostrate; his confidence is buried under snowdrifts.
His love lies numb, like water frozen by cold—the love that lately in the garden
blazed like fire shut in raging furnaces.
O Simon! these were not the promises you had given to the Master,
you who kept declaring that you would be faithful even in a cruel death,
and no deserter of Christ so long as life should remain.
When, then, trembling seizes your limbs at a servant-girl’s voice,
why do I see you thus disgraced on the very threshold,
fall away? Look, a maid accuses you; three times aloud you denied
that you had ever known the man, or had been his companion.
This teaches what trust there is in human affairs.
Christ, [my] God, this heart frozen hard with so great a cold
dissolve into tears; let it melt in the furnace of love,
and let these eyes, warmed by Thy rays, that have long been
dry, flow, and let this head scatter bitter dew.
Alas, the pools of my head have turned to solid ice;
a grim winter has curbed with ice the running of the waters;
it lies numb under a mass of snow; the heart, the breast lies numb with cold.
Hard crusts congeal in the stream of tears.
Meanwhile Dawn, borne on her rosy four-horse car,
had already crossed the mid-point of the sky in her heavenly course.
Now the morning song of the birds beneath the roof-top
rouses the farmers; now with hoarse throat the cock
plies his crowing, shaking his wings with loud clangour;
and that clangour lashes Peter too with a mighty stroke,
and rouses his heart, lulled asleep, out of deep slumber.
Oh, if only that same bird, with that same song, would break open
my breast, and this soul lying in an untroubled heart
rouse from sleep, beating with the stroke of its wings.
But as soon as, in terror, he drank in the noise of the wings
of that dread-sounding bird, and its deathly songs, Peter:
at once there came to his mind what had lately been said to him by
Christ: that he would deny the Lord three times with a trembling voice
before the crested bird had crowed twice.
And as soon as he turned his eyes, with their grey-green light,
upon Peter, Christ gives a groan from the depth of his breast,
a mighty one, and filled his bosom with welling tears.
Me also, great God, look upon me with the light of your countenance,
and turn your twin eyes hither; the inmost chambers of my heart
illumine, Christ, with the rays of your eyes,
that I too may be able to wet my face with abundant weeping.
May a spark from your eyes fall upon the dry
kindling of my heart, and may you catch a flame in the tinder;
so that my kindled breast may breathe out the flames of love;
break this soul of mine now with the flashing thunder of your word,
[and] let a fiery cleft run through my clouds with its light.
Scarcely was the following day sprinkling the highest mountains with light,
now risen, when first from the deep flood rise
the horses of the Sun, and breathe out light from their lifted nostrils.
And now the high priest, the eldest in years,
Caiaphas, a great council and the foremost of his own people,
summoned at his command, he gathers within the lofty halls.
They assemble, and recline upon outspread purple cloth.
Some armed men lead Christ out from the prison,
some stand at the open double gates, gleaming in bronze;
others have blocked the narrows of the streets with their weapons;
set against [them]; a line of steel stands with flashing point,
drawn, ready for slaughter, should anyone lay a hand on Jesus.
to seize [him] by force; they threaten instant destruction and death
if anyone should so much as approach Christ, and they terrify [the people],
Then once more the Lord declares from his divine lips
that he is begotten of the King of the heaven-dwellers; the frenzy and anger of the elders
drive their minds headlong; all gnash with their teeth,
and on a false charge they condemned Christ to death.
At once Tisiphone, girded with a scourge, strikes guilty Judas,
leaping upon him and brandishing in her left hand grim
snakes; she summons the savage ranks of her sisters.
Megaera, born of Night, hisses with countless serpents
and made her lashes crack; then the Fury rolls her fiery
eyes, planting smoking brands beneath his breast.
Alecto revealed her grim face and frenzied limbs,
and slipped deep into Judas’s innards.
By these frenzies he is driven, and from all his blazing face
sparks fly forth; fire flashes from his fierce eyes.
Raving, he is driven through the midst of the cities, and the high
temples he seeks, like a hind struck by an arrow,
whom, off her guard, from far off among the Cretan woods has pierced
the shepherd pressing her with darts, and he left the flying iron [in her],
not knowing it; she in flight ranges the woods and the glades
of Dicte; the deadly shaft remains lodged in her side.
Then Judas fills the air with quavering howls,
crying aloud that he himself was the cause, the crime, and the source [of the evils]
the things that had befallen the innocent Lord; because he had sold Him
to [His] enemies, he accuses himself, and suddenly gives back
the silver, and, driven by the furies of his crimes, he went away;
and from a high beam he ties the noose of hideous death.
The wretch's entrails burst: a misshapen corpse
bristles with dreadful squalor: a cloak hangs down,
filthy, from his shoulders; a stupor weighs on his lifeless eyes,
his features are strangely pale; a heavy breath from his dark
body, pouring itself forth, was rising toward the vaults above,
and his life fled, resentful, beneath the shades of Tartarus.
Meanwhile Christ, with the arms of foot-soldiers escorting [Him],
is led to the lofty house of savage Pilate.
The judge urges [Him] to say of what blood He is sprung
or what He brings; let Him tell what confidence a captive has.
He, laying fear aside at last, speaks these words;
Power over Me, Judge, has now been granted you,
but the Almighty Father, Ruler of Olympus on high,
has granted it to you; from what founding ancestor our race
we derive, you do not know; My descent is from Jove most high;
I too have kingdoms, but not earthly ones; nor does
Christ, Himself girt about with arms, any men to arms
rouse, nor drive bronze-clad battle-lines into the fight;
there is no such violence in My heart, nor does one defeated possess such pride;
I do not come with a close-packed band of My followers (believe Me);
[were] My kingdoms many and earthly, or [My] towns many,
Or if [my] mind burned with a youthful love of war,
the peoples long inactive, and my ranks unaccustomed to war
I would call to arms for freedom;
I would urge that war be waged with this dreadful nation,
which conspires to the open destruction of one wretched man;
My servants would snatch me from death, or heaps of the slain
they would strew through the cities and through the fields; but the royal house of heaven
is both the home and the fatherland that I seek. With such words he
declares himself born a King, and [tells] his name and his lineage,
and what he seeks, and what he himself brings; but an enemy of Caesar
the Jews proclaim him to be, and to wield power through sedition;
an overthrower, they say, of the Galilean nation, and [they say] that he himself
flings unwary citizens into open dangers.
At such words of the sons of Abraham, Pilate holds his face fixed
in a stare, and motionless he stays fastened to the ground,
turning his intent eyes about; then he sends Jesus
to King Herod; the cruel King, from his high throne,
asks Christ many things, but to answer the one asking
he would not deign; roused to anger, the King has Jesus clad in white
garments and mocked, and sends him back.
Then the foot-soldiers, dragging Christ along with a great shout,
set him before the doors of the Roman judge; he
leads Jesus down into the midst, into the people's full view,
proclaiming him innocent; in reply all press on with their shouts—
the sons of Abraham, enraged, and [they demand] punishment with blood;
they cry that he is guilty of death, and an enemy of Caesar.
Overcome by their unceasing clamour and compelled by their entreaties,
he hands [him] over to the torturers to be beaten with rods; they
at once fall upon [him], and strip bare his white breast,
and among themselves lift their arms with great force
in rhythm; copious blood flows from his body.
the Hero is pounded unceasingly with blows from this side and that;
he groans, and labouring gasps shake his holy limbs.
Alas! with many a wound they have violated the body of Christ;
many [strokes] they redouble on his hollow side, and from his chest they
make mighty sounds; around his ears and temples darts
a fist striking again and again, while his jaws crack beneath the hard blow.
Nor do they desist until, overcome by the repeated lashing,
he stiffened, and fled the light of day, and the warmth left his bones;
at last, alas, he sinks down, and only after a long while speaks,
and just as, high on the mountains, a huge ash tree,
when hacked by iron, while farmers press on with repeated axe blows,
vying to uproot it: still it threatens to fall,
and, its foliage trembling, it nods with shaken crown,
until, little by little overcome by its wounds, it gives a last
deep groan and, wrenched from the ridge, crashes down in ruin.
Who, O Christ, could recount thy groans, who thy wounds, in words,
or could match such sorrows with tears?
Who with dry eyes the warm stream from his body
could look upon? and the ground foaming with so much blood?
Yet Judea is not moved by this death of the Lord,
nor did she groan at Christ's weeping, nor turn her eyes,
nor did she give her life over to tears, or take pity on the master;
nor does anyone feel such cares deep in the breast.
Sarah was no mother to you, nor Abraham the founder of your line,
faithless one; but the bristling Caucasus begot you from hard crags,
Caucasus, and Hyrcanian tigresses put their udders to you.
O if only my eyes might hold out under weeping as great
as your body, O Christ, streamed with blood:
I would drench [your] sacred wounds with my drops, and [your] limbs
dripping with blood I would wash with a spring of tears.
After the torturers had mangled Christ with scourges all over his body,
they cruelly mutilate him about the face—
his face, both ears, and temples ravaged by thorns;
(for they set upon his head a crown woven of thorns)
and over [him] purple robes, the coverings of kings,
they throw; then Christ sat upon a lofty throne;
a sceptre of reed he bears, the King who rules all things,
our victim is slain before the cruel altars,
whose head they bind about with garlands, and crown with funereal
foliage, and gird his temples with red fillets.
Our King is covered over with a purple cloak;
behold the Prophet who reveals the decrees and the Father’s answers,
whose swan-like breast is soothed with song.
Behold the High Priest, now bearing our sins,
look upon the bloodied tunic of our Joseph,
dyed not with the gore of a kid, but with his own blood;
your brow, Jesus, bristles with a wreath of thorns,
[you who are] more worthy — whom the two-coloured poplar, with its Herculean shade,
should veil, and who should bear the palm, and your hair, dripping
with blood, should press [it] with a wreath of laurel, or of the rich olive,
and should have your temples shaded by the civic oak.
But for this reason (alas) that noble head is torn by thorns,
because my own mind bristles with thorns and with thick briars.
In a thousand ways the barbarous people mock Christ; some
strike his face with their fists; one spits [on him]; and another
beats him with a reed rod, and hails him as King:
Meanwhile the blood flows from his veins in streams on every side.
But the torturers—Christ, dragging his weakened knees,
and tossing [his] head to either side, and [spewing] thick gore
spitting [it] out from his mouth, along with teeth mingled in blood,
led him into the midst of the people's assembly; but they
(O race born of tree-trunks and hard oak)
raise an immense shout, and the banks and the pools
echo all around, and the whole sky thunders with the uproar;
They all goad Pilate on with their zeal and their roaring,
that he should be willing to make away with Christ by death as soon as possible.
He long holds out, like a rock unmoved:
The Jews press him hard in their fury and wear the man down:
Straightway, in defiance of all right, they demand that guiltless Christ be put to death,
against the commands of God, with will perverted, they demand him.
Pilate had a wife, joined to him in enduring wedlock;
to her, behold, in her sleep the most sorrowful likeness of Christ
appeared, lifting up a face pale in strange fashion;
and drawing groans heavily from the depth of its breast,
the apparition itself seemed to pour forth abundant tears.
A matted beard, and hair clotted with blood,
and bearing all those wounds—so many—which from hard rods
he had received; the woman, terrified by the grim sight,
is startled out of sleep; with tears and prayers her husband
she presses, [begging him] to pity the plight of guiltless Jesus.
To him, as soon as he had taken his seat on the golden throne,
a messenger came from his wife, bearing this message:
O judge, and husband dearer to me than the light,
Scarcely had unexpected sleep begun to relax my limbs,
when strange dreams terrify me, held in dread:
for suddenly before my eyes Christ stands, most sorrowful,
his whole body dripping with holy blood;
his features were growing strangely pale at his impending death.
Thunderstruck at this sight, and terrified by great portents,
I filled the place with my cry, and weeping I seemed
to address the man, and to utter sorrowful words:
O almighty Christ! scion sprung from the exalted blood of kings—
Why does black night hover about your head with its gloomy shadow?
Who dared to tear your rosy cheeks, who to disfigure your body with a wound,
or to befoul your hair with blood?
Do you present yourself to me as a true form, a true messenger,
O one born of God? Are you alive? Or, if kindly light has departed,
what has piety, what has ancient faith availed you? did you not
were you not accustomed to surpass men, to surpass even the gods, in piety?
Is this the reward of piety? At last he offers the frantic woman only a few words
in reply and, troubled, parts his lips in halting speech:
I do indeed live, nor do I yet leave men and the light,
but I shall leave them: for us, to whom he has granted heaven’s citadel,
the Almighty Father leads us through slaughter and wounds,
and through fear and cares, and sicknesses, and a thousand toils:
and through the waves, while the sea surges high, and through pathless rocks;
This is our road to Elysium; so one goes to the stars.
It is not crimes and deceit that have dragged Me through these punishments,
but My own virtue, and the holy oracles of the Father.
But as for the hated nation, which, though I deserve no such thing,
wounds Me, and delights to strip this body of the light,
Soon flames will consume it, and the hostile sword will drink it dry.
What penalties shall you pay Me, Judah? How many beneath your waves
shields of men, and helmets, and brave bodies shall you roll,
O horned Jordan, king of the rivers of Abraham's sons?
Alas, how great a slaughter is at hand? How many bitter deaths of your people
bitter deaths of your people will you behold? Rome’s great ruthlessness
will overthrow her power and cast Jerusalem down from her height.
When it had spoken these words, it covered its head with a black mantle,
groaning much, and hid itself in the shadows of night.
So it left me weeping and wanting to say many things,
and the phantom withdrew into thin air,
equal to the light winds and most like winged sleep.
Then a chill sweat ran over my whole body.
I snatch my body up from the bedding, and stretch out upturned
hands to heaven with a cry, and pour out offerings
undefiled upon the hearths; and I burdened the air with vows.
Now [I beseech] you by the sweet light and breezes of heaven,
by our marriage, by the nuptials we began:
if I have deserved anything well of you, or have been anything
of mine [was] sweet, have pity on a soul that bears what it does not deserve,
I beg, and if there is still any room for prayers, put off that purpose;
forbear to defile your hands, now spare the blood
that is guiltless, for this is Christ, than whom no other is more just
nor does any excel him in piety, nor is any greater in word and deeds.
And me, I swear, this man’s phantom—whenever with dewy shadows
night covers the earth, as often as the fiery stars rise,
warns in dreams and, agitated, terrifies me.
When she had spoken these words, the judge fell silent in bewilderment,
and his hair stood on end with horror, and his voice stuck in his throat,
thunderstruck by so great a warning.
Alas, what is he to do? With what address would he now dare approach the raging people?
with what address should he dare to approach them? And what opening words should he begin with?
He indeed had tried to let Christ go,
but in vain; the heavy wrath, and the insatiable heart
of the Jewish people cannot be swayed by any entreaties.
It is not enough that Christ has suffered every punishment,
but they want to rob him of life, and they demand the last drops
of his sacred blood; such blind madness
drives them headlong; with such wrath the wicked one rages against the peoples.
Therefore, when no power is granted to overcome their blind
counsel, and [them] going on at the nod of the impatient people,
he calls for water and asks for towels with clipped pile.
The servants give water for his hands; then he washes off the blood
that is innocent, and swears that he is exposing this man to death
unwillingly; driven, he says, by your shouting
I hand this life over to you; put [him] to death yourselves.
You yourselves will pay these penalties with sacrilegious blood.
O wretched men! For you, Judah, the sacrilege, for you a grim
punishment shall wait, and you will worship God with vows too late;
for my rest has been won, and my entire haven is at hand.
With these words he shut himself within [his] house; and now the cohorts
of the Romans move out in a long column; Christ
comes on behind, bearing on his failing shoulders — alas! —
the beam of his doom, and his garment drenched with gore—
Two thieves go along with him; the rest of the crowd
follows after; mothers, boys, and unwed girls
They raise a womanly outcry to the stars of heaven;
and tears stream down their cheeks—small consolations
for an immense grief, yet not undeserved by Christ.
Yet, chiding them, he addresses these women with friendly words:
Why do such tears roll down in vain, O wretched women?
Pour them out for yourselves and your descendants.
A time will come for you when you will call barren women thrice and four times blessed,
around their breasts you will see no boys
hanging at play and licking the milk-white breasts with necks outstretched;
you will wish the lofty mountains
to plunge headlong upon you, and the sloping hills;
so that, covered by darkness and by the gift of shadowy night,
you may lie hidden in the lap of the earth, safe from the enemy.
When untamed War and the sons of Aeneas rushing upon the houses
you behold, and the Temple besieged beneath an advancing tortoise formation,
and the fall of the captured city, and, wrenched away far and wide,
the thresholds of its houses, with the enemy in the heart of its inner chambers;
what groans, what lamentations and tears there will be?
A time will come when Vulcan, with the reins let loose,
will rage through towers and roofs, while a vortex rolling along the timbers
will billow toward heaven and engulf the temple,
and the whole land of Judaea will sweat with blood.
Do not the barren woods dread the two-edged axe
of the farmer, if the green tree is cut down by the iron?
But sick with cares, and utterly terrified by the sad fate
of her guiltless son, the Virgin Mother weeps, most wretched,
Her burning cheeks bathed [with tears], and beating her breast.
Most holy Virgin, dear to me above all others, [your] son —
do not, I beg, with such great tears, nor with so great an omen
attend him as he goes into the contests of hard death;
for on behalf of wretched me, for me, he was paying the cruel
penalty, and — alas — expiating my faults by his death;
yet with this you will console yourself for your son's undeserved death,
that he falls by the great Father’s right hand; he willed
the innocent one to undergo cruel punishment in place of the guilty;
and by his command he compels [him] to go through the pallid shades,
through places rough with decay and through deep night;
Yet the Father will not leave you, O Christ, without honour
now in a death from without: nor [shall] this death [be] without renown
among the nations, nor will you, unavenged, endure such report.
For whoever has violated your body with a wound
pays for it with a deserved death; nay, in death itself he watches over
you — the almighty Father: for as soon as the third [dawn] in the sky,
borne on crimson wheels, shall glow red,
bursting through Tartarus, he will lead [you] out to the upper air.
But Christ, pressed down by the weight of the fatal wood,
began to give way — a pitiable thing — and for him, trembling, his slow
knees give way, the once rosy colour leaves his face;
he sinks down bloodless, and over the limbs of the dying man a cold
sweat broke out.
The savage companions run to help, and the Lord, as he falls,
they take him up; the crowd compelled a certain man of Cyrene,
Simon, to carry the cross; but the sins of the world,
these, heavier than the wood, you, Christ, bore on your shoulders.
Me too, through flames and a thousand pursuing weapons,
you carry to safety on these shoulders and wrench from the midst of the enemy;
me, worn out by every misfortune, in need of everything,
[he] joins to the throngs of the heaven-dwellers; to pay thanks
that are worthy is not in our power, nor in that of whatever exists anywhere
of the human race, which is scattered over the great world.
While the rivers run down into the seas, while shadows over the mountains
shall range the hollows, while the sky pastures the stars,
always shall your honour and your name and your praises endure.
They had come to the hill which now bears the name Calvary,
in the midst of thousands he stands, sweating with much blood;
as once a consecrated goat, led by the horn to the altar,
whose horns dripped with drops of blood,
sprinkled by the high priest's hand: so Christ Jesus
took his stand before the cross like a goat, or like a lamb,
innocent, like young cattle with neck untouched [by the yoke].
He himself is the altar, and he himself is the victim, and he himself the Priest:
who offered himself in sacrifice to the Father as the honour due.
[He] offered incense, and warm gore smoked at the altars —
which [is] far more excellent than all the blood of cattle,
with whose holy sprinkling the nations now foam.
But after he had lingered a little in tears and in thought:
Shall I speak or keep silent? Jesus, fastened with nails,
clings to the wood, and strains toward heaven his burning
eyes, for the sharp iron has bored through his palms.
That hand, to hurl swift fire from the clouds,
which once was accustomed [to do so], is pierced through with iron; that
foot, transfixed with rigid nails, clings fast to the wood —
the foot that trod the vast waters of deep Nereus.
He who clothes the painted birds, who clothes the lilies:
the lilies with leaves, the birds with all their many-coloured wings,
and who girds kings about with gleaming purple:
he himself, nonetheless, hangs inglorious without any garment,
gashed in brow and temples by bloody thorns.
The people give Christ in his thirst draughts of gall—
he who was wont to quench that people's thirst with a leaping stream
of sweet water flowing from his venerable mouth.
a copious shower of blood is poured down from his veins,
and rushes like a swift river from the mountain tops.
The barriers burst, the deep seas of blood swell high,
and doubtless this expanse of a red sea must be ploughed by us,
if we desire our homeland's shores and quiet harbours
to gain: the oar must be bent in the bloody wave.
Over the purple sea, be my Portunus as I go,

div.p: Christ, fastened to the cross, is raised up between two thieves; the title is written above him. One of the robbers mocks, the other confesses Christ and prays, and to him Paradise is promised. And while Christ prays for his enemies, he catches sight of his mother in heavy grief and commends her to John. The miraculous eclipse of the Sun is described, and the blindness of the Jews; at last the Lord, having suffered pains beyond number and beyond telling, breathed his last: the earth quakes, the rocks are split, the tombs are laid open, and the veil of the Temple — which is here described — was rent apart. The Centurion, moved by these prodigies, acknowledges Christ to be the Son of God; and while the thieves' legs are broken, Christ's side is pierced by a lance, out of which flowed blood and water. Christ's descent to the underworld is described, and his burial; likewise the piety of Joseph, of Nicodemus, and of the Mothers, and the most bitter sorrows of the Virgin Mary. On the third day Christ rose again, the guards struck with terror by the earthquake. The Angels announce the resurrection to the women, and they to the Apostles; Peter and John run to the sepulchre. But the watchmen, corrupted with money, spread the lie that the Disciples had carried off the Lord by theft. The malice of the Jews against Christ is described. Magdalene stands weeping at the sepulchre,

lg.l: that, with You as guide, my mind may take shelter in the deep harbour
of the heavenly fatherland: is there any [land] more welcome to me,
to which I should long all the more to send down this weary soul,
than the land which keeps for me Jesus, [my] leader.
And in the bosom of father Abraham [it] embraces all
the men marked out by piety, lovers of virtue.
BUT to raise up, as soon as may be, the vast mass of the cross
the people set to work, and strive to rear it up to heaven —
this altar, between whose horns God himself poured out
his crimson life and consecrated the offering;
A shout is raised to heaven, and the whole
mountain bellows all around; with quavering howls they fill the sky.
Then the people set above him the charge for his death, to be read
by all the Hebrew peoples, and by Greeks, and by Latins;
This is the King of the Jews, Jesus the Nazarene.
So he who had deserved nothing hangs aloft in the air
between two robbers; one of them, jeering at Jesus,
says, “Now help us—and yourself—
you who save others!” The other rebukes him with words—
the thief who hung from the tree at Christ's right hand:
and he groaned, and gave forth these words from the bottom of his heart:
Both of us are justly paying the penalty for our crimes,
but who will say that this man has paid for a crime, he deserving it,
when not a single trace of crime was ever seen in him?
But he took away the world's ingrained stain, and washed away all
bodily plagues, and all deceits.
Alas, Christ, you have paid too much—alas, too cruel a penalty,
though innocent of such great crimes; why then
do you, the Lord, die for servants, the innocent for the guilty?
Only love for us, and the glory of redeeming the world,
plunged you into these sufferings and into this bitter death.
Then he wept, and as a suppliant pours prayers from his breast:
Let it not irk you to remember me, kindly master of [all] things,
when it shall fall to you to take possession of the throne and sceptre
of the kingdom of heaven’s inhabitants, and to raise your Father’s emblems of authority.
Christ replied to him: with me you shall dwell amid shady groves;
you shall reach the resting places on the banks and meadows freshened by streams,
and shall drink sweet water from the springs,
before night covers the lands with dewy shadows.
And while, mocking Christ as he hangs upon the cross,
his enemies shout things worthy and unworthy of telling;
he utters his final groans, and from the depths of his heart
poured out prayers and invoked the Father in supplication.
Forgive them, Father, for wicked frenzy has robbed them of
their bewildered reason. Having thus spoken, Jesus
cast the burning glances of his eyes over the crowds.
Here Mary, shaken by undeserved grief for her son,
stands weeping, and lamenting much, and beating her breast;
she prays for death; she is weary of looking upon the vault of heaven,
and upon her son’s grievous death and such great sufferings;
for the mother’s blood flows from her son’s wound.
And as the interpreter of these sorrows and one privy to them,
Simeon once foretold: through the mother's heart passes
the spear-point, and driven home it drinks deep the maiden's blood.
When he saw her sick with overwhelming cares,
he shed tears and was moved by sweet love.
“Behold your son, woman”; then, as it happened, John—
he caught sight of John and at once addresses his ardent friend with these words:
“Behold your mother.” Struck to the heart, the bystanders
shed tears—John himself before all the rest;
and the image of filial devotion touched his heart.
Then he began to comfort the destitute woman, and to succour her, [left] alone,
and to honour her as his own mother; so the devoted hero
was unwilling to leave his mourning mother alone,
but, weeping, entrusts her to his kinsman and friend.
Happy in your lot, John, happy in this mother,
and happy the home blessed with such a guest,
namely the mother of God, a virgin most beautiful in form.
But while Pluto stirs up violence against Christ, and with anger
and with missiles rages, his companions give way in dread,
and abandon their leader, so that he may endure the whole storm
of weapons; and Peter deserts him as he lies dying,
for whose sake he had lately drawn his lightning sword.
But he, undaunted, kept stretching out an unarmed right hand
With his head bare, and calling on the Father with a cry,
he alone bears up under the enemy's blows and wounds.
Stretch out over me this conquering right hand, Master,
while the enemy hurl their weapons and drive [me] back from afar;
may this, like a shield and buckler, defend me, me against all
may defend [me against] the weapons of darkness, and the columns of Dis;
for my mind, without thee, to strive against so great a force
has no strength, though doomed to die, nor dares beyond its powers;
Therefore may you interpose yourself before the right hand of Pluto as he rises to strike,
before his sword-point, and hold him at bay,
so shall I, the Lord's servant, come away protected by [thy] right hand.
The Sun, who with his flames surveys all the works of the lands,
this unspeakable deed the Father does not look upon with unmoved eyes;
but he covers his shining head with dusky gloom.
the high heaven is buried away into darkness by the mist;
for heaven grieves to behold the Lord's cruel death,
and is ashamed that mortals have no shame.
The palace of heaven was shaken with immense mourning,
when the Sun failed, sorrowing, in mid Olympus;
and he veils his golden locks with a mantle of darkness.
And while a trembling runs right through the whole bodies
of Phoebus' driven horses, and they breathe no light from their nostrils,
the round world, now robbed of light, mourns:
and the Temple, like a wife bereft of a dear husband,
rends its consecrated vestments with its own hand, doomed to die.
The rocks burst apart; a cold shudder shakes the earth's
shakes the earth’s limbs, and the sea, chilled, stands numb with fear.
From the crags the frightened seals flee into the blue [waters].
At once every field falls silent; the pathless countrysides do not
ring now with the song of birds, nor the sloping hills
with the bleating of flocks, nor the rivers with any lowing.
She herself is stunned, treacherous to man in her winding lairs,
the viper, and the water-snakes, aghast, their scales standing on end.
Everywhere there was grief, on every side fear and on every side weeping.
But hapless Judah, alas, harder than the very rocks,
than the viper's brood, and than the heavily breathing water-snakes
more savage, is moved neither by portents so great nor by tears;
his mind stays unmoved, the tears roll down in vain.
Night so thick, borne aloft by her two-horse team, held the sky,
that while the Sun is wheeling in mid-heaven, through the houses
lamps are lit, and the cities blaze with fires;
The farmer, suddenly marveling amid the blinding gloom
at the sky snatched from his eyes, and night brought back,
when the Sun had not yet dipped his weary horses in the flood:
strikes a spark from the veins of flint out in the fields:
and he caught the fire in leaves, and round about dry
kindling he supplied, and caught the flame in the tinder,
and at Jerusalem they kindle torches, and the proud King himself
burns fragrant cedar above, for the lights of night.
But blacker night, a greater shadow, flies about
the sons of Abraham; their minds wander in blind darkness,
while they do not recognize [him] dying and bearing dire
torments, him, the true begetter of men and gods;
but some mock [him], some urge [him] to come down;
this one divides his garment, presently another holds out vinegar.
Alas for me, who am wrapped in such deep darkness and shadows
beneath a burning sun, and while it wheels in mid-course
dark night holds my mind, nor does my breast flash with love's
fire: now, Christ, light me with your lamp:
dispel my darkness, make the cloud poured round [me] suddenly
split itself apart, and clear away into open sky.
That torches blaze out, and that breasts glow with the flames
that are yours — make mine so, Christ; make [these] lights conquer the night:
Who could look on this death with his eyes, who on these wounds?
Almighty Father, did you hold him worthy of so great a charge,
and did you will that he pay such penalties,
though guiltless? The Father his Son — wondrous to tell —
called to punishment for the sake of our freedom.
Love for the world prevailed, and the boundless
care for our salvation; but alas for wretched me, what earth is now deep enough to gape open
for me, who was the cause of your death, Jesus.
For it is I, Christ, who have stained your name with crime.
I ought to have paid the penalties for my own crimes,
through every kind of death I myself should have paid [them] with my guilty soul:
but I live, and draw my life from your wound.
Did so great a desire to die possess you, Christ,
that you were willing to succumb to a sorrowful death for me?
You [are] the Lord: am I, your servant, saved through these wounds of yours,
living by your death? What worthy thanks could I express,
or what thanks could I adequately render? Never shall I be unmindful
of such great merits, while the golden Sun rules the world;
while Phoebe crosses Olympus in her night-roaming chariot.
Sooner, then, shall nimble stags graze in the upper air,
and the seas shall leave fish exposed upon the shore;
sooner, after the territories of both have been traversed, shall the exiled
Parthian drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris,
than Christ's face shall slip away from our heart.
At last, worn out with cares and with much pain,
he calls aloud upon the Father, and with a deep groan uttered these [words]:
Holy Father, why do you forsake Me as I die? Thereupon
he groaned again, and spoke his last words;
This soul I commend to you, Father of high heaven.
At these words, all things round about grow black with darkness,
pallor takes hold of his face, his limbs are loosened with cold;
and with a groan his life vanishes into the thin air.
A harsh repose settles upon his eyes, and through his fair limbs
the blood runs, and his neck, sinking down, falls back upon his shoulders:
as when a crimson flower, cut down by the plough,
grows faint in dying, or as poppies with weary neck
have let their heads droop when they happen to be weighed down by rain.
This was it, this, Judas: it was at me you aimed with your treachery,
when you, faithless one, willed to betray the just Lord.
See, that cross is made ready for me, these nails, and thorns.
What shall I, forsaken, lament first? Or did you, Master,
scorn as your companion in cruel death a servant
who deserved so many deaths? If only you had called me to the same fate,
the same anguish on the wood, and the same hour, would have carried us both off.
Let the enemy tear me with thorns, let him pierce me with nails,
and hurl the wicked spear into my breast;
I have destroyed you and myself together, and the people of Zion
and the fathers and your city; grant me your wounds, Christ,
grant them: I will dry them with my tears, and will wash your body.
Ah! where now are the fires of your eyes, where the once-gleaming
hair, and the flashing lightnings of your fair countenance?
The eyes are buried in darkness, the face in gloom;
and black night has taken away the rosy color of your face.
Christ, always dearer to me than life itself so long as life remains—
Christ, tried by countless afflictions:
you stretch out your arms and lower your face to receive kisses;
do not refuse to put those arms about our neck.
Give your embraces, Christ, and plant your kisses;
O, if only with the dew of your dripping blood you would wash away all
the stains of [my] soul; if with the living stream
of your tears, O Eternal One, you would dry the wounds—
the wounds which even now hiss in me, fixed fast beneath my breast.
Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one, and hold out heaven to me
stretch it out to me (for you can), and protect your faithful servant;
give your right hand to me in my misery, and take me with you through the stars,
so that at last I may rest in peaceful dwellings in death.
But the sorrowing mothers, their hair loosed according to custom,
raise a mighty groan to the stars, with beaten
breasts; the upper air rings with great wailing.
What feeling was yours now, mother, as you beheld such things?
Or what groans did you utter, when you
beheld the pitiable body of your son, drenched with so much blood,
and [saw] his beautiful limbs defiled with shameful wounds?
Maiden, glory of women, most dear to our heart,
you grieve in your inmost heart; your lovely eyes cast down,
you groan much, and wet your face with a copious flood [of tears],
striking your breast, and filling heaven with your complaints:
Just as the nightingale, mourning beneath a poplar's shade,
laments her lost young, which a hard ploughman,
watching, has dragged unfledged from the nest; but she
weeps through the night, and, sitting on a bough, her pitiful song
renews, and fills the places far and wide with mournful laments.
Just so the Virgin, terrified by her son’s fate,
stands weeping and calls these men cruel by name—
