who, before her very face, the death of her guiltless son
made her behold, and defiled a mother's face with that death.
Here something else, greater and far more to be dreaded, [is set] before the people,
is set before [them], and troubles unsuspecting hearts the more;
For as soon as Christ entered the hidden regions of the earth,
the ground began to bellow beneath [his] feet, and the ridges
of the woods to stir; cities trembled with unwonted shocks;
and the earth was shaken to its foundations, and rocks torn from the crags
come crashing down; the bowels of the quivering earth opened.
You would have seen souls coming forth from the deepest tombs.
Once, too, a voice was heard as silent night fell,
proclaiming that Pan had been cruelly slain;
and as soon as that voice was sent forth through the clear air,
lo, suddenly a dreadful groan strikes the sky; you would think
that the neighbouring fields had rung again with the howling of wolves.
Within, the inner sanctuary of the holy temple lies open to view;
for now the veil is torn apart of its own accord; it
was wrought with art, and interwoven with gold.
Embroidered with the needle, and with threads of many colours, the world
is seen: here air, earth, sea, and fire
are engraved, and clear showers fall from the clouds.
Here forests put forth leaves, animals roam the mountains,
towers rise up, the roof-tops of the farmsteads smoke;
rivers flow down through rocky valleys,
Amid these the image of the swelling sea stretched far and wide,
all golden; but its blue waters foamed with white surf,
and round about, dolphins bright with silver, in a ring,
swept the level waters with their tails and cut through the tide.
Arching above these, the silver orb of heaven
holds the stars, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears,
and it encompasses Orion armed in gold.
Here the golden Sun runs among the twelve constellations,
and his sister wanders through the sky with blunted horns,
five interwoven zones, of which one, with the flashing
sun, is red for ever, and for ever scorched by fire;
around which, outermost, to right and left are drawn
[two zones] congealed with blue ice, and with black rains;
Between these and the middle zone, two were given to suffering mortals
by the Ruler of those above; and a path was cut through both,
along which the slanting order of the signs might wheel.
It was customary for this veil, on festal days,
to be hung up according to custom; now it is torn apart in grief. Troubled by these
portents, a certain Roman (who in former days
was accustomed to lead a hundred young men at a time into battle,
his head gleaming with bronze, and bristling on its crown with crests
blood-red, marked out too by his shield and his flashing sword —
gives warning and declares in a loud voice through the ranks:
I do indeed believe, and the belief is not empty, that he is of the Thunderer's stock,
this man whom you have put to death with torments and a lingering death.
Meanwhile, while the executioner breaks the legs of the robbers,
so as to loose the struggling soul and the bound limbs,
a young Roman, experienced in war and arms,
mounted on a horse, [hurled] with mighty strength a huge spear
hurled into his side and into the innermost recesses of his sacred heart,
and with the spearpoint laid open the hidden seat of life,
driving through the ribs, and bursting the white breast.
Behold, a strange stream flows from the fair body,
of blood and of water; warmed by the plentiful gore
the ground is drenched, and the wound planted beneath the breast hisses.
What do you want, soldier? Why do you defile with a wound a body
already lifeless? It is right to spare one stripped of life.
There can be no contest with the conquered, with those bereft of the air of heaven.
[It befits] Romans, lords of the world, and the toga-wearing race,
to spare the conquered and subdue the proud;
it is not fitting to trample on a wretch, nor on one destroyed by a death
undeserved: this victory has no praise at all.
There was a stag of surpassing beauty, enormous in his antlers,
whom, as he wandered far away, the rabid hounds of dark Avernus
roused; with javelins and pursuit they wear him down—
the hunters. From his curved bow a Roman soldier aimed his arrows
at the body before him; and behold,
through the belly with a whir, and through the flanks, the shaft comes,
Alas, with how many keen-scented hounds does Pluto hunt me!
Each for himself, my enemies draw out their shafts from their quivers,
and against me they bend their bows with all their strength.
Do you not see the flying arrows clinging in my back?
O Christ God, a hurled phalarica comes whirring,
driven like a thunderbolt, which neither three layers of bullhide
nor a dependable breastplate of threefold scale and gold
can withstand; lodged in the throat, it passes deep into
the breast; the cavern of the black wound gives back a wave,
foaming, and the iron grows warm in the pierced lung.
Probe deep into the weapon's hiding-place; the flows of blood
dry up, and wash the wound, then sprinkle on the healing
juices of ambrosia, and the fragrant all-heal
of [your] blood; pour in this oil, good Samaritan,
upon our wounds, pour out these flowing wines.
This is he whose back with the plough
the ploughmen dared to tear open, and to cut long furrows [in it].
He, his buskins torn off, [stained his] legs with new must
he dyed them, and he alone as vine-dresser trod the grapes.
Once a dark rain-cloud stood over the world,
bringing night and storm, and the wave shuddered in the darkness;
the helmsman himself, Christ, now from the high stern
orders the tackle gathered in, climbs the mast, and seeks
a wide lookout far over the sea, catches the air
with his ears, tests the winds, and keeps watch on the stars,
and takes care that the ship should not run in upon dreadful shores,
nor, driven upon the shallows, be broken apart amid the waves.
You whose is the dominion of the sea, whom the ruler of Olympus
makes master of the storm-clouds and of the tempests,
see what mighty storm-clouds have ringed the sky:
shifted [winds] roar across our course, and from the black west
the winds rise up, and the air is packed into cloud;
and we lack the strength to struggle against them or make sufficient headway
while the storm and rainy Orion rage,
and the ships are battered, and the sky is past all handling.
Alas, your ship is now driven by the winds and the waves
onto rocks and crags, and it hangs upon an uneven ridge,
taking in the hostile flood, and gaping open at its seams,
We, Christ's wretched people, carried by winds over every sea,
pray [thee]: settle the stirred-up waves with thy trident.
Let the breezes blow evenly, and let there be an hour for rest.
And thy Ship, driven by so many storms,
for so many days made uncertain by blinding gloom,
wandering on the deep, and as many starless nights,
bring through calm waters into the longed-for harbours,
lest she come under the Sirens' cliffs and the sounding rocks;
nor let her now give way as such waves rise against her.
Drive the vessel thyself with the pole, and tend the sails,
and fill the canvas at last with favouring winds.
Then me, saved out of the waves, to the shores of heaven
direct; grant [me] to enter the quiet harbours of the Fatherland.
See, now the door of the ark stands open; now the steep rock
pours out waters, struck by Moses' willow rod.
Now the Pelican beats its breast with sharp beak,
that it might feed its unfledged young with its own blood.
Behold, the physician opens a vein pulsing with blood,
doing so himself for thee, that he might turn the fever’s heat away from us.
Now our Jonah is plunged beneath the foaming wave,
lest the South Wind hurl the sailors he has swept away against hidden rocks,
and lest a swift whirlpool swallow the ship upon the sea.
While Moses eagerly stretched out both his hands,
behold, the victor lays low in death all the rebels,
and exacts just punishment from the enemy's blood.
Our Adam rests, laid to rest in untroubled peace,
While the soldier drives the cruel spear through his ribs,
while he pierces the rib cage with steel—behold,
there comes forth suddenly from the wondrous wound a maiden,
now ripe for a husband, now marriageable in her full years.
Behold the lamp lifted high upon the lofty tree-trunk
that it may light the world lying in darkness and night.
This is that ladder of Jacob that touches heaven;
upon whose lofty summit Jehovah stands,
and a choir of winged youths glides down from the stars
along it, and again along it, ascends to the stars.
Here a huge altar, beneath the open vault of heaven,
has been raised and stained with a calf’s foaming blood.
Hither souls, like doves in a black storm,
gather, free from care; this altar will protect them all.
The bitter pool of divine wrath grows sweet
by the power of this wood; now Aaron's rod puts out leaves,
though cut in the woods from the base of its trunk,
it lacks its mother tree and has lost its foliage and branches to the blade;
And this tree has raised its head as high among the others
as cypresses are wont [to do] among the pliant wayfaring-trees.
Behold one who had come neither to ravage his country’s homes with the sword
nor to carry captured spoils to the shore,
hangs among robbers; no one more righteous than he
has lived on earth, distinguished in devotion and countenance;
whom the Father of heaven’s host himself now marks with his own honor.
Once among the thickets and among the bristling wild haunts,
driven out by envy from his native land and his father's roof
Ishmael and his mother, ignorant alike of men and of places,
were wandering: in that whole region of paths there was no one
who might teach [them] under what sky, on what shores of the world
they were being tossed; there is no spring to moisten the grass
with its waters, and no rivers rush down from the mountains.
but the grasses thirst, and the lands gape open with the heat.
Then the young man, burning with thirst and terrified by the heat,
fell to the ground beneath the branches of a tall tree.
But the mother stretched out her palms to heaven with a cry,
and poured tears down her cheeks; presently an angel, unasked,
appearing, a clear spring on a sloping track
pointed out, stirring a murmur over the smooth stones.
Thus Adam, driven from Paradise, his ancient homeland,
in the world, as in a wood that bristles with briars,
and with the thick darkness of branches, and with high crags:
wandered as a fate-driven exile for many years,
he could not find the way that leads to the stars;
nor [could he find] clear springs, nor pools green with moss
beneath the burning sun, and beneath the grim star of Cancer,
by which, in his thirst, he might turn so fierce a heat away from himself;
but at last Christ, pitying Adam's fall,
shows an unfailing well flowing from the rock;
This holy fountain a soldier dares to unclose,
from which flowed our only salvation as we lay dying;
who, as soon as he struck holy Christ with the wicked spear-point
He drove [the spear] into [his] side; lo, the waters, as if in a formed column,
where an opening is given, rush forth, and cleanse the world with their flood.
Christ, [our] God, that holy fluid flowing from [your] breast,
more radiant than gems, purer than any amber —
let it now with glassy springs soften the parched fields
of the heart, and water us in the midst of the burning heat, I pray;
let this moisture not forsake the barren sand of the mind.
let not the thistle bristle with thorns in our fields,
nor burdocks and caltrops amid the flourishing tilled fields;
let no mildew harm the stalks, nor any rough thicket,
while the grain swells milky in the green stalk.
After the Shunammite woman's child had breathed out his life,
at once the warmth left the wretched mother's bones;
the shuttles were struck from her hands, and the wool-work unwound;
the unhappy woman rushes out, and with a woman's wailing
climbs and surmounts the crest of the high mountain;
she comes to the prophet, and presses the prophet with prayers and vows,
that he might call her son back to the upper air of heaven.
At once he sent his swift servant ahead to the house
of his hostess, and put the staff into his hand; and he ran
swifter than a javelin, and than an arrow that matches the winds;
then he laid the staff upon — so Elisha had ordered —
the lifeless boy; but he has no power to call the dead one back
to the threshold of life; nothing availed him,
neither the staff, nor his having outrun all delay; then straightway
the aged prophet, having returned from the top of the mountain,
stretched himself over the boy, and warmed him with close embraces,
Laying hands upon hands, and mouth upon mouth;
and he poured out prayers, and called Jehovah to [hear] his vows,
trying with his mouth to gather any breath that might still remain in the boy.
At last the longed-for warmth stole into his inmost bones;
and fresh strength returned to the boy, as it had been before.
So, after Satan had stripped Adam of life,
he lay lifeless for so many ages, until Jesus,
his servants having been sent ahead, but in vain, came [down] from heaven,
and flung himself upon his lifeless friend,
stretching out his arms, and clinging in our embrace,
and, bending down his face, bestowed kisses upon Adam;
and bade the dead man draw in the airs of life.
Then he carries the human race up with him to the heights of heaven.
The rod of your Law did not draw me back from Orcus,
nor did the prophetic seers who foretold all things,
O Christ, God—but rather the breath of your divine mouth,
and that love of yours, like a flame hidden in the marrow,
this soul to the pleasant light and breezes of heaven
brought back out of thick darkness and cruel death.
Now, as soon as Christ freed himself from that body,
he entered the homes below that have no sun, the regions of turmoil:
the pale shades of Erebus and its dread King
he terrified; the dead trembled at the light let in upon them;
and wherever he went, all around him the golden race of the vast heaven
went too, and with its light drives the dark night away.
And as God draws near — far off, oh far off be, you profane ones,
cry the winged attendants; there trembles Judas's unholy
shade, the Furies tremble, the huge gatekeeper of Orcus trembles,
and, bound with a hundred chains, he roars, terrible in countenance.
The empty superstition of the Greeks once believed
that Orpheus was able to summon up the shade of his wife,
relying on his Thracian lyre and his tuneful strings;
that Pollux redeemed his brother by taking turns with him in death;
and that Alcides too was unconquered in his strength,
who with his right hand set upon the Stygian guardian to chain him,
from the very throne of the king, and dragged him out trembling;
that those who undertook to lead the mistress of Dis from her chamber were
bold Pirithous, and mighty Theseus as well.
These are dreams that make sport of the sleeping senses;
for Christ alone, the child of almighty heaven,
by strength — and that his own — broke through the thresholds of death;
and, penetrating through the halls of Dis and deep Avernus,
seek these meetings with the Fathers, for impious
assemblies of the righteous and Elysium); in a great column, these
illustrious souls, destined to go to the light above,
he leads out, and bears [them] across the clear spheres of the upper air.
But for me, to lay open matters sunk deep in earth and darkness
is neither my intent nor permitted; yet it is worth believing
that Christ went down to the mournful shades of Erebus.
He is that mighty Samson who, robbed of his sight,
Toward the temple of the Philistines he was moving with his vast bulk;
and when he had entered in, beneath the mid roof-ridge, the po[st]
Bracing himself against it on the right, he shook it;
he tore it from its deepest roots; then destruction
he brings crashing down; and over the ranks of the Philistines the roof
falls, and by his signal death he destroyed his enemies;
And now Evening, glowing red, kindles his late lights.
At once Joseph is at hand, and as a suppliant Pilate
himself he entreats, and asked leave of him;
that he return the body and allow it to enter the earth in a tomb—
the lifeless body of the Lord. “Enough punishment,” he says, “this innocent man
has endured in life; now, to him bereft of the upper air,
I show mercy. Allow his mangled corpse to be covered by a tomb;
grant at last to the wretched one a quiet resting-place after death;
grant peace to the lifeless one, destroyed by a cruel death.
What race is so savage, or what land so barbarous
that it allows this custom, to bar from the hospitality of the tomb
the dead, and to bar them from resting in the bosom of their loving mother?
He had spoken; but when he asks for things not to be scorned, the Governor
grants him permission; whatever consolation burial affords,
whatever honor the grave affords, he grants to lifeless Jesus.
But when he saw the face of Christ, cold [in death], and his countenance,
that countenance pale in wondrous fashion, the man of Arimathea
groaned deeply in pity, and tears down his face
roll down: the image of [that] devotion stole upon his mind,
and the fate of his cruel death, and so many noble deeds,
And [his] face and the sound of his voice, and his memorable words:
No less did Nicodemus weep for the lifeless Je[sus],
when he sees him cut off by an undeserved and unworthy death,
now the eyes, now the hands, now the face he beho[lds],
the clotted hair, the uncombed beard upon the breast:
and he sees the wound driven deep between the ribs.
Then he was mingling incense and other sweet perfumes,
sighing, he washes and anoints the cold body;
he honoured the pale limbs with the last offerings,
and the ground is sprinkled with tears, and [their] faces are sprinkled too.
But the Virgin mother, when the pitiable body of her son
she saw, and the wound gaping in the smooth breast
made by the Ausonian spear-point, she sighs as the tears well up:
three and four times she struck her comely breast with her hand,
falling upon him, and clinging to him, and pressing kisses on him:
nor was a passage opened for her voice, so overwhelming was her grief:
and, clasping her lifeless son to her bosom, she cradled him
with groaning, and with her robe she dried the dark gore:
she dressed, as custom is, the hair befouled with blood,
weeping over him, and she closed his eyes, and washed his wounds:
Then the mothers lay Christ aloft upon a bed of straw:
like a flower cropped by a maiden's thumb:
whether of the soft violet or of the drooping hyacinth,
from which neither its brightness yet, nor its own beauty, has departed
No longer does mother earth nourish it or supply it with strength:
they pluck the thorns from his head, and press kisses
upon his wounds, and grip the nails with clinging pincers:
Soon a linen cloth is brought out; in it Nicodemus
with his companion wrap Christ, and lay him away in a tomb,
I see no funeral rites splendid with royal magnificence:
nor funeral torches, no emblems, nor any
mourning chariots; funereal cypresses in front
they do not set them up, nor adorn [the funeral structure] above with gleaming arms;
nor do they hang up any spoils [stripped] from slain enemies;
nor bridles, nor glowing wheels, nor handsome swords;
nor standards, nor shields, nor helmets or bloodstained weapons;
Nor did a warhorse walk with its trappings laid aside,
weeping, and wetting its face with great drops;
nor did the shout of men and the blare of trumpets
set the sky ablaze; our Lord had no such pomp;
he who scorned the luxury of the world, and the arrogance of the powerful
in life — does he care for luxury now, robbed of the light [of life]?
Joseph had a garden breathing with saffron flowers:
here, out of the living rock, beneath a hollowed crag, a tomb
he had cut out; this tomb had never before held any ashes
and no bones in its hollow; hither, with much groaning and with tears,
they were carrying Christ, laid upon a bier, under cover of night.
Alas, what land at last—what [lands] amid the sea—can
to receive me, or what now at last, wretched as I am, [remains] for me
from whom the sole hope of my life has been snatched by the violence of death,
and the world's highest salvation lies buried beneath a stone.
Now at last we know on what shores of the earth's globe
the space of heaven lies open no wider than three ells.
Behold, the Sun of righteousness has hidden his shining head in a cave,
the darkness thickens, and black night broods over the world,
which enfolds the minds of men with her dusky wings;
My husband, [my] solace in every care and misfortune,
deserts me, and hides himself behind the barrier of a vast stone;
He who first bound me to himself has taken away my love;
let him have it with him and preserve it in the tomb.
Never shall I pass you over in silence, Joseph, ever to be remembered,
if any age to come shall bring belief to so great a work.
you who [bury] the lifeless Lord, and [one] now [owing] nothing to any heavenly powers,
owing [nothing], exhausted by so many misfortunes, in want of all things,
you bury in the ground, and have laden [his] limbs with your own tomb,
with anxious care, [paying him] the only honour there is beneath deepest Acheron.
Indeed, with a linen shroud you covered your friend’s body, struck
and pierced through in five places;
O, if there is any justice in heaven that cares for such deeds,
may it pay you worthy thanks, and render the rewards
due — you who Christ's cruel wounds with a cloth
covered, and deemed his body worthy of the honors due the dead.
Woe is me, O Christ, I have robbed your body of light.
Behold, my guilt with a mighty blow pierces through the sacred
breast, and drives the monstrous spear through his ribs.
Alas, what am I to do, or what safety does life promise me?
Where am I to flee, or in what hiding-places shall I conceal myself,
conscious of the audacious deed and of my own crimes?
[crimes] which demand me, wretch that I am, for punishment for the slaying of Christ;
This one thing I beg — if there is any pardon for wretched enemies —
suffer my guilt to be covered with earth; let all our crimes
be committed to the earth with you; and you, best of rulers,
and you too, great Father of the gods, have mercy, and with your
word thrust down this guilt of mine beneath Tartarus:
And when the fates call, and release me from this body,
then grant me to share the tomb with your Son;
with whom I do not fear to go as companion through the sorrowful shades,
and without whom nothing at all of what is mine is sweet to me.
When the body of Jesus had entered the earthen tomb,
and when devoted Joseph had brought the funeral offerings to his friend:
behold, all the Priests, and the Governor Pilate,
assign guards to the tomb, to keep watch night and day,
sleepless, over the dead body, lest by chance anyone
should attempt to carry it off by stealth; presently, in a close-packed column,
armed with steel, their high heads flashing with crests,
they assemble and ring the whole sacred enclosure with guards.
They hurry to and fro, alternate their watches, and, sprawled upon the grass,
they give themselves to wine, and tip up the bronze mixing-bowls;
fires blaze all about; the watch draws out the night,
sleepless, in play.
O ignorant minds of the watchmen! O the frenzied [men's] blind
hearts! what good is it to give way to mad toil?
Relentless is this toil, empty this watching; for
the third day had scarcely removed the chill shadow from the sky,
when suddenly a young man, gliding down from the heavenly stars,
winged, and shining like the lamp of Phoebus,
parted the darkened air and scattered the shadows;
and he tore the stone away from the doors of the cave, and the world's
foundations he shakes; suddenly all things seemed to tremble —
the roof-ridges of the houses; cities sway along with the mountains.
For, retracing his step, he had escaped every misfortune —
Christ in triumph — and was coming once more to the upper air.
At once a chill shudder ran through the watchmen's hard
bones, and their blood congealed with sudden dread;
They fall prostrate to the ground, their voices caught in their throats.
The mothers return to the cave and behold two
winged nobles, clothed in white garments.
These tell the mothers that Christ has now risen.
No longer (they say) does the Lord lie low among the cruel shades,
but, as he promised, he has returned to the airs of heaven;
he has bound fast the king of Tartarus with brazen knots.
At him all the shades stood amazed, and death's innermost
depths, and, with dark-blue snakes entwined in their hair,
the Furies, and Cerberus held his three mouths agape.
He snatched himself from death, and broke the iron chains
of death, and overcame the pale realms of hell.
Go, then, and carry this joyful news back to the companions.
They at once fly off, and bring back what they have seen.
Peter in his joy flings his cries to the stars;
and out he darts, swifter than the winds and than the wings of the thunderbolt,
joyful John; Peter follows him at an unequal pace.
But he, having entered the tomb first, beheld it
empty; and now his companion treads close upon his heel;
who saw the tomb empty, and the linen cloths rolled back:
They, departing from there, go back to the mothers and their companions.
This is that day of light which, ever the greatest,
shall be [so] called by us, and shall ever be the greatest,
on which the cave appeared and the vast palace of Dis stood revealed,
and the shadowy caverns lay open to their depths;
on which Christ with the rays of his divine face scattered
a smoke-laden night, with darkness mingled with fire.
on which he alone overcame the monsters of the foul abyss,
and with [his] hand sought the ruler of Tartarus for chains,
on which Jonah, out of the foul darkness and the prison of its belly,
the fish vomited up, and left [him] on the tawny sand.
on which, renewed after shedding his old plumage and gleaming with youth,
the winged bird of Jove carried off his prey in hooked talons.
Now at last Daniel escaped the raging jaws of the lions.
And as once the boys escaped the flame of the furnace,
so Christ overcame the exultant flames of his Father’s wrath;
Christ, quenching those fires with fountains of blood.
Now Esther, radiant in face and in comely dress,
on behalf of the people whom savage Haman marks out for the altars,
implores her husband for peace with vows and prayers;
Relying on these, she neither employed envoys nor devised through guile
initial tests of her husband; she offered herself—her very self—and her own
head, and came as a suppliant to his threshold.
The mighty temple which lately fell from its high summit,
rising up today, hides its head among the clouds.
As the Phoenix, after it has kindled sweet spices,
soaring toward the Sun, is said to fan the fires with its wings
and to consume itself in the crackling flame;
but as soon as the ashes have sunk down and the flame has died,
a new offspring arises out of the parent's death;
which neither indulges in mating nor sluggishly gives its body
over to Venus, nor bears offspring in the pangs of labor;
but it begets an immortal race out of its own dust,
living by its own death, and born from a wondrous funeral.
So Christ, whom the flame of divine wrath burned up,
comes forth from the fragrant embers by his own power:
While the bones of the prophet Elisha rest softly
amid the settled ashes—wondrous to tell—
by their touch they called back to life [a man] bereft of the upper air.
Who would think that ash, or buried shades, could do this?
But Christ, as soon as he broke the merciless tyrant’s harsh
compact, from beyond the bank of the gulf from which before there was no return
of the gulf he emerged with many thousands; them
he bade lead an everlasting life in heaven.
Now the cavern of Dis lies open, now the joyful dove
claps her wings and, gliding through the clear air,
escapes, and, mounting steeply, flies above the high cloud.
Isaac, who once stood as a victim at the cruel altars,
and who on his shoulders—a pyre rich with pitch-pine and cleft oak—
chose to carry, and knowingly to receive the sword in his throat
and to meet death at his father's hands:
now he is snatched from death, for a ram caught fast in the briars
steeped the fated block with its innocent blood.
He who long before had been, in the breast, by a wound from hunters
stricken, and — a pitiable thing — mangled over his whole body,
now the lion of Judah stirs up arms, and rejoices,
shaking out the muscles on his mane-clad neck; and the robbers' planted
shaft he snaps undaunted, and roars with bloodied mouth.
Now Samson shook the gates of Gaza, and
he tore them loose from their deepest roots; then suddenly
he hurled them, and at their impact high heaven thundered.
The iron-shod bars and the door-posts wrenched from their hinge
he lifts up, and at a run makes for the heights of the towering mountain.
Not otherwise did Christ the iron thresholds of pale death
break through, and he wrenches the door-posts from their hinge.
These grim gates of death and of blackening Avernus
a hundred bars of bronze shut fast, and the everlasting
strength of iron; nor does the warder Satan quit the threshold,
sleepless, guarding the entrance-court night and day.
Moreover, the walls girt about with a triple rampart,
which a rushing river girds with scorching flames —
Tartarean Phlegethon — and whirls resounding rocks along.
Columns of solid adamant stand round about the gates;
so that no force of men—not even the heaven-dwellers themselves—could hew them down with steel;
an iron tower stands, rising into the air.
But as soon as Christ came down through the deep places of Avernus,
he himself struck the gates with his hand, and neither the bars nor the
guards themselves can withstand [him]; but with the hinge wrenched round
he broke through, by his divine power, the iron-bound doorposts of death.
From that time the honour has been celebrated, and joyful descendants
have preserved the day, which now from the name of the Sun
of Righteousness we call both the Sun's day and the Lord's.
Therefore, Christians, in the service of praises so great,
wreathe your hair with leafage, and hold out the cups in your right hands,
and call upon the God we share, and pour the wine willingly.
And you who burst the chains of cruel death,
and mastered the monsters of the pit over which you triumphed;
[may you will] this day [to be] joyful for us, and for all throughout the world,
may you wish [it] to be, and our descendants to remember it.
Be present, Christ, giver of all joy; and this day
descendants of Abraham, celebrate this sacred day with us in goodwill,
and grow accustomed now to the tables of Christ's people and of the brethren.
And me, Christ, as I breathe my last and groan out my final [moments],
take me up, your servant, and snatch me from the fates that press close.
Quickly, and lift this soul out of the dust of sin.
Arise, Morning Star, and, coming before the day, usher in the kindly day,
and at last, the night now spent, look again upon your companion.
But the trembling guards make straight for the lofty
houses of the priests, to whom they tell in order everything
that had happened about the tomb: then at once those men
bribe the guards with money and give them assurances,
that they should put it about that his companions had secretly carried off the body
in the dead of night, while their weary bodies were weighed down by
the first sleep, while slumber closed their drooping eyes.
From this the report is suddenly spread through the whole city.
Struck dumb and bewildered by the shifting appearance of events,
the governor stood silent, staring; a mighty shame seethes
deep in his heart, together with madness mingled with grief,
and his soul is driven by furies, knowing itself guilty.
And the priests rush, their minds maddened,
into the Temple and inflame the people’s anger against Christ
with false rumors, coupling fierce hatred with their words.
And he, out of his mind, and set ablaze by the bitter report,
threatens ruin and death to Christ's companions.
O unhappy nation! Do your impious deeds not trouble you?
Or are you not yet sated with Christ’s blood? Do not yet
so many limbs, doomed to die a cruel death, restrain you?
Why do you tear the guiltless Lord? now spare one [already] buried,
forbear to defile your hands with crime; Judah did not bear him as a stranger to you;
Judah bore him no stranger to you; this blood does not flow here from the branch
that you pluck, but slips out from the root itself.
Christ God, with a mighty hand you have snatched a trophy from the enemy,
and so many nations triumphed over from either shore
you hold down in servitude, and you lord it over the conquered abyss,
and with a word you send the king of hell down beneath Tartarus;
you have conquered the nations, and the sons of Abraham have seen them,
conquered, stretch out their hands; yet implacably there burns
against our Lord a race ever hard and harsh,
harrying with hatred the stock and the whole race to come
of Christians, nor yet, unbroken by the fates, does it rest.
See what peoples are joining forces, what city walls, behind closed
gates, sharpen steel against you and prepare the destruction of your people;
the dread Furies, and Phlegethon, and Erebus, and Chaos,
conspire together, and Bellona rages in trembling uproar.
In vain they attempt to overturn the kingdom of Jerusalem,
which has not deserved it; now they batter the walls with the ram's repeated stroke;
yet they stand unmoved, for these by no force
will they be able to overcome, nor tear [them] down with hard iron,
but they scorn the threats of the sea and the collapse of heaven:
just as a rock that juts out into the vast sea,
set against the fury of the winds and exposed to the deep,
endures all the violence and the threats of sky and sea
while itself remaining unmoved. Once, if one may believe it,
So the brothers, sworn together to tear heaven open,
made their attempt to thrust Jove down from the realms above.
But the Father cast down with his thunderbolt the mountains they had piled up;
So whoever dares to set himself against Christ's kingdom,
the almighty Father either drives him down to the shades with a thunderbolt,
or, as he breathes out flames from his pierced breast,
will snatch him up in a whirlwind and impale him on sharp rocks,
or, plunged in the deep, will overwhelm him with foaming waves.
And now the early [dawn] was sprinkling the lands with new light,
Aurora quitting the saffron couch of Tithonus;
when Magdalene stands beside the holy tomb,
deep in sorrow, her shining eyes brimming with tears,
because she found the rock-tomb empty, without Christ's body;
though the nobles of heaven [long] to soothe her in her grief
desire by consolation, and with words to turn aside [her] cares:
she nevertheless, pouring out tears between every word,
laments her lost Lord, and on the tomb now abandoned
she lies; though apart from him, she hears and sees him in his absence;
nor by any words — so great is the violence of love —
is she swayed; her love grows stronger still and is aggravated by attempts to cure it.
In just the same way my heart seeks you, Christ, my Master,
when morning has newly risen, and at night as the stars lead on;
and as often as night in her two-horse car crosses the mid-point of the sky,
behold, we pour out tears from the twin urns of our eyes,
And when the Cynthian [sun] kindles the midday heat,
when the grasses thirst, and shade is now more welcome to the flock,
a hidden flame burns me again within my blazing breast,
whereby my streaming eyes pour out warm waters,
while I lament the Lord whom I have lost, while I do not know
how I may find You, or in what region I am to seek You.
Nay more, although it now doubles the lengthening shadows —
the Sun now departing — and chill evening the air
tempers, and the dewy Moon now revives the glades;
yet love burns me; for what limit can there be to love?
and in the empty house of my heart my mind weeps alone.
You know how often I dared to fling my cries through the darkness,
[how] I filled the sky with shouting and, grieving, repeated “Master”
in vain; again and again I called.
Just as a stag which a viper has bitten with its fang,
drenched with gore, and terrified by the raging fever,
goes down to the clear waters and the streams he knows,
that he might ease his burning with the waters and the greening bank;
so my mind, steeped (alas) in the milk of black venom,
flees headlong to You through tears and through rivers.
Speak to me, and with Your face console my long travail;
and quench my thirst with the leaping stream of Your blood;
Christ, by Your skill relieve the serpent's bites,
You who were accustomed to drive diseases away by chant and by hand:
Ward off the midsummer heat of divine wrath with the shelter of your
with the covering of your wings, and [defend] the soul of the dying man in [your] shade.
But while these young men her burning and sorrowful
soul, were soothing with words, and were lightening her cares;
lo, of a sudden Christ transforms himself into the garden's
keeper, and Mary, as she tosses her cares within her breast,
he addresses: “Woman, why do you shed vain tears?”
Scarcely had he spoken these words, when with a groan she answers thus:
"Where the pitiable body of lifeless Christ has been laid,
tell me in what lands, or in what region he re[sts];
I will go, and try to place [him] upon my neck;
I myself will take [him] up on my shoulders, nor will that toil weigh me down."
“O woman, will you be able to bear this body?
Scarcely could twelve chosen men lift it upon their necks,
men with bodies such as the earth now produces;
but great is your faith." "Supply strength and spirit
to me, O Christ, that I may be able to carry you with a pure breast."
Then Christ addresses Mary by her own name,
and she, as soon as she had heard the familiar voice of Jesus,
runs up, and embracing his holy feet held them fast,
which he forbids Mary to touch with her hands, until
he should ascend to the Father; mothers from the city of Zion
are present, rejoicing, and worship his holy body.
And while Cleophas and Amaon are going back to Nicopolis,
sorrowful, they make their way burdened by like cares:
He joins them as a companion, his noble face uncovered:
just as a gem gleams that divides the tawny gold,
an ornament for the neck or for the head; or as, by craft,
set in boxwood or in Orician terebinth,
ivory shines; his milk-white neck receives his flowing locks,
receives, and his face was beaming with pure light.
Then with his voice he bends their feelings, and their faltering spirits
he drove onward, and then winds an unwonted fire through their bones;
and moreover, driving anxious cares from their hearts,
of his own accord he raises their spirits with his words, and of his own accord rebukes them.
He teaches them many things and lightened their journey with varied conversation.
Meanwhile the sun sinks, and the shadowy mountains are darkened.
Then Cleopas, beneath the gables of a little dwelling,
leads mighty Christ [within], and set him on the couch.
While they restore their strength with food, they begin to recognize Jesus—
they begin — so great a glory shines out from his noble face.
But suddenly he flees from their eyes like smoke into the air.
They soon return to Jerusalem and suddenly appear
unexpectedly before all their companions, and recount the matter in order:
they say that they have seen Christ, and that his holy words
they drank in with their ears, and that they reclined with him at table together.
Scarcely had they uttered this, when straightway the Master himself,
while they all linger indoors within the shut house,
stood still in their midst, and shone out in clear light;
in face and shoulders like God; for the Father himself had breathed comely
hair upon his Son — the Father — and the light of youth,
radiant, and he had breathed a joyful grace upon his eyes.
He wishes peace to all, and soon greets each one by name.
But these, their minds pressed hard by wavering dread,
are suddenly thrown into confusion, believing that a tenuous, bodiless life
flits about beneath the hollow semblance of a form;
Christ, seeing them doubt, threw off the cloak
sacred, from his shoulders, and shows his fresh wounds;
and soon he ate a honeycomb, and also a portion of broiled fish;
and from his holy breast breathed forth the holy Spirit.
You, whom the thresholds of the King of the underworld dread;
whom the Father raised from the Stygian realms to the heavens;
to whom he gave eternal life, from whom [the condition] of death was taken
the condition [of death], so that you may at last put an end to sorrows;
breathe into me a holy soul, and one that loves heavenly things;
and be kind and propitious to me, when on the last night
death shall have loosed my struggling soul and the limbs knit to it;
and when the earth clasps my bones in its lap;
the fallen ashes, and the bones weighed down by the tomb,
gather up, and send this soul back to the vaults above.
And when, the circle of time completed, you to us
the palace of starry heaven shall have given you back, then by [your] word
these very limbs of my body, these very bones and arms
call back from the infernal shades to the threshold of life;
and make [them] willing to return again into my limbs—
the ethereal sense, and the fire of pure air.
And now, for the forgiving of the sins committed by the world,
the Master granted authority to his companions, and bade them
to take away every stain, and the traces of deceits.
After this he showed himself to Thomas as he doubted, and in his deep
side the wound driven into it, and [the scars] of his hands and feet;
he shows the scars gleaming with light, and offers [them]
to be touched; Thomas touched them, and adores the body;
O fortunate Thomas, who the wounds of Christ
saw, and handled the vast opening in his side!
Grant, O Christ, that with the hands of faith I may touch your wounds,
that with my heart I may behold this wide-open window in [your] heart.
Happy—O exceedingly happy—if only I can believe
what Didymus touched or saw with his own eye.
Christ, [my] God, the hall of my breast is not yet shut against you;
night and day the door of the kindly heart stands open.
You unbar the gates of heaven to sick mortals,
calling everyone by your voice within the lofty halls; I beg you,
receive this soul, driven by so many errors of the world,
into the holy inner chambers of your breast, and its safe refuges;
that it may rest quietly with you for ever.
Do not regret having received your groaning servant into your bosom.
And do not disdain to lead the dove to the ark of the heart
and to sweet nests within [your] venerable breast;
and keep safe this ship, tossed upon the vast flood,
that it may come to rest in the safe harbour of the heart.
Meanwhile Peter and his companions make for the shore,
and mount the open water, and fly on over the foaming waves;
the breezes breathe fair on into the night, nor does the bright
moon deny them their course; the sea gleams beneath her trembling light.
After the boats had reached the deep, Peter lets down into the water
his nets; no fish appear in the flood.
That night they pass sleepless, and labour in vain.
And now the sea was reddening with the rays, and from high heaven
saffron Dawn was shining in her rosy two-horse car.
At the very edge of the shore Christ takes his stand, and in a loud
voice calls his companions, and bids the nets be sunk again
beneath the waters; the companions were making ready to obey the great
command, and, quicker than the word, Peter lowered into the waves
the dripping nets; soon the scaly race of the vast sea
rushes on, and, stirred up, cleaves the waters with quivering fins;
beneath the scaly throng the foaming wave murmurs,
while the shoal flies through the open sea, and the shallows whiten as the marble surface is churned;
then the fish, swifter than the wind or a winged arrow,
leap in, and have filled the nets with a joyful throng.
John recognized the Lord’s voice and face,
and all the more swiftly turns the boat about, and draws near the bank;
and he took [him] by the hand, and clasping his right hand clung to it,
but Peter flung himself with a plunge into the deep water,
and where he plunged, he sent the foaming wave whirling beneath his breast.
Then the joyful companions turn their prows toward the shore,
and make ready to roast fish; and stretched out on the grass
Christ with his companions feasts on a banquet unbought.
Through the night indeed toil had kept Peter busy, but all
the toil was spent in vain, without the divine power of Christ,
and as soon as access to him was granted, from the lowest depths
the fish leap forth; Christ’s presence drives them on.
They bear down upon the sea, and together strain toward the nets;
their breasts reared up among the waves, and their crests,
scaly, rise above the billows; the seething waters foam.
So once the prophets, beneath the dark night, through the shadows,
pressing hard at their work, sought to catch the nations
with the net of the son of Amram — he who first by laws the cities
of Judah founded; but indeed all that toil was empty,
while the world wandered through a long night without a star,
beneath the thick darkness of its crimes, and shadows that make men shudder:
But as soon as the shadow of night had withdrawn from the world,
and kindly light was given to wretched mortals, all
the nations came together, and stream toward the royal
dwellings down crowded streets, and the heights of Jerusalem are filled with people.
On this side and on that kings throng together from the sun's rising,
from the sun’s setting; fierce and unrestrained in anger rages
the people of Judaea, and at the same time burns implacably,
because for the world the dawn glows red, the darkness put to flight;
because Christ, when the night is spent, revisits his companions;
Because they see, approaching Jerusalem in a great throng,
mothers and men, boys and woodland maidens.
So, as they see the Sun's first light grow white,
the foul birds flee; the owl flees into the wilderness;
she who alone among tombs, or on deserted roof-tops,
sitting by night, ill-boding, sings her late song through the shadows.
Whom do you flee, ah madman? why do you spurn Christ who loves [you]?
What resentment, after all, against the nations’ settling on Jerusalem’s soil
is there? And for us too it is right to seek the kingdoms of heaven.
Or is your brow scarcely cheerful, your face and eyes downcast,
because your exiled brother has returned to his father’s home
after long exile, and through so many hazards?
See with how great love the father [received] his younger son
on his return home. He puts his arms about his neck,
and clings to him in embrace, and speaks to him with sweet love,
and pours tears down his cheeks, and touches him with kisses;
from [his] shoulders he lets hang a robe of glowing purple;
and encircles his fingers with gold, and his legs with buskins.
Then he cuts the calf's throat, and gladly sees to the feast;
May such a love hold you, Judah; imitate the father,
and from him learn true devotion, and faith

div.note: Here I do not mean the Nymphs of the poets, who were feigned to be born and to perish together with their oaks, and were for that reason called Hamadryads, but country maidens converted to the faith of Christ. Δρῦς signifies an oak, or a tree; and these women live among the trees. For this same reason the wise men of the Gauls were called Druids.

lg.l: Grant Christians to extend a right hand toward their brothers;
grant it, Judah, and do not withdraw yourself from our embrace.
Let the sons of Abraham receive our message and the rites of worship,
and customs, and let them confirm covenants of peace;
and let [our] fortunes be the same; let us make both Jerusalems
one in spirit; let that care abide with our descendants.
Christ, take pity at last on Judah's heavy toils;
you who guided the young man's stone missiles and hand
against the body of the Aetnaean brother; [the seas] encircling the lands
they have entered so many seas with you as guide, as well as the far-remote
nations of the Indians, and the fields that stretch before the Syrtes;
thus far had the fortune of Judaea followed [them].
From how great a flood, across how many vast seas they were borne!
What misfortunes befell the wretched, what dreadful wars followed them
ever since they stripped their master of the light of life —
Let both the European and Asian worlds know; and let those know
who live on the Libyan shore; whatever exists anywhere knows it,
of the human race, which lies scattered through the great world.
Now the same fortune pursues men driven by so many disasters;
what end to their toils do you grant, great King?
Spare a godly stock; it is right to spare the nation of Judah,
and thou wilt pity [their] crushed spirits and broken fortunes.
Let this be the last labour, and the goal of their long journeyings,
one destined to put an end to their ruin; grant that they receive fair
laws of the covenant together with us and build city walls.
May the Jewish race be mighty through the power of Christ.
Make them acknowledge their fault, and beg pardon of him
whom they have scorned, with so many years now slipping by,
and make them all Christians, we pray with one voice.
But when they receive the Lord, and gladly acknowledge [him],
make them return to Jerusalem; grant—I ask for no undeserved
kingdoms for your people—that they settle in their ancestral lands,
the wandering leaders too, and the harried bodies of the people.
Then to Christ and the Father temples of solid marble
they will establish, together with feast days named after Christ:
great sanctuaries in the realms of Judah await you too,
O Goddess, you who walk as queen of the gods, and of Jove
both daughter and mother, and an undefiled maiden.
Now, by the example of Judah, which, scattered over the whole world,
rages helpless in mind, and wanders on unknown shores,
because she spurned the terms of peace and the covenants offered,
learn, Christians, to settle your wars among yourselves,
alas, wars between those far too closely akin; let right hands join in covenant;
lest hereafter you pay for your offences with a like penalty.
Alas, how often have we seen the earth sweating with our blood,
and vast fields white with bones?
O Jerusalem! O golden home of the gods, renowned in fame,
O fatherland, to have fallen long ago into utter ashes
you have deserved, unless heaven’s loving care stands in the way.
Where are you rushing? Or what is this new discord that springs up?
Oh, hold back your anger, since the covenant has been struck, and
the laws of peace established in the blood of Christ.
For shame! O wretched men! Citizens, what is this great madness?
What undeserved fortune, O Latins, has entangled us in so great
a war? Or does it not yet move you to pity and shame to stain your
hands with the blood of your kinsmen?
Is there no love? and does your discord find no end?
Meanwhile the barbarian now looms on every side over your
ramparts; shall he deal such havoc unpunished throughout the world,
and send so many of the foremost youth down to the realm of the dead?
Does no regard for your unhappy homeland, and for your ancient forefathers,
touch your heart? If any dutiful concern gnaws at a man
for Christ’s words which he spoke at his final hour,
when he left us peace made firm by his blood;
If any regard for the dying Jesus clings to devout hearts,
do not, brothers, harry with war [nations] at rest;
nor overturn Jerusalem's tottering fortunes from their deepest foundation.
To press foreign fields beneath the yoke and carry off spoils,
and for us by battle to defend Europe [when she has been] carried off,
would be the better course, and to assail the Turk with just arms —
that barbarian who has so often laid waste your fields,
and often terrifies us with his arms, as though we were helpless sheep.
Against him do you, of one mind, close up your companies.
And Europe, and Asia, and Africa's shores once more
bring under the rule of Christ; tear apart with the sword
the enemy's battle-lines, and demand back your own cities.

div.p: Christ, about to ascend into heaven, gives various instructions to the Apostles, blesses them, and entrusts the care of his Church to Peter. God the Father, having summoned a council of the Angels, reveals his purpose concerning the elevation of Christ his Son into the heavens; to this all the Angels assented, and they rendered their service to Christ as he ascended. The glory of heaven is poetically described under the figure of a magnificent palace. While the Apostles, however, follow the ascending Christ rather too intently with their gaze, two Angels instruct them concerning his return. The Last Judgement and the glory of Christ's return are described. Meanwhile the Apostles return to Jerusalem, where, as they devote themselves with one accord to prayer in the upper room, the Holy Spirit descends upon them in the form of fiery tongues. Various mysteries and meditations are interwoven here. Christians are again exhorted to mutual peace and to wage war against the Turks.

lg.l: Now let us hasten to turn the prow toward land,
and to take in the sails at the very end of our labours.
That he was destined for heaven and was to be raised by the fates to the stars,
Jesus had long since shown by various signs.
So then, when forty suns had run their course since the time when
he left the infernal seats and the pale Realms behind,
to the Father, the relief of every care and mischance,
he set himself to make his way through the clear spheres of the upper air.
O if only [it] might now swim across the shining clouds with you —
my mind, which is so fastened to the mass of this body,
so that without you she cannot escape to the air above.
The cruel tyrant’s hard chains hold her,
so that in vain she tries to raise herself on balanced wings:
held back by the mass, and hemmed about by so great a weight:
as a winged dove clings to the wood on a cord passed across,
and, straining, tries in vain to lift herself on her wings,
and struggles to escape, beating the air with her pinions,
while the wooden mass holds her back, and the bonds confine her;
but if someone should break the knots and the linen bonds
by which, tied fast by the foot, she hangs; then on swift wings
she is borne flying into the fields and makes the sky resound with a mighty clapping of wings.
O, if only you would strike the fetters of sin with the drawn sword
of the thunderous word, with which I too can
to lift myself from the ground, and follow Christ through the clouds of heaven.
Strip me of the manacles and the clinging chains of this
prison; and me, a wretch enduring the worst for so many years,
guide through the homeland of storm-clouds to the threshold of the heavenly ones,
lead me into the chamber roofed with vaulted jasper.
No delay: Christ hastens, now that in due form have been completed
the divine observances; he sought the lofty ridges of the well-known
Mount of Olives; his companions attend him as he goes.
“Go,” he says, “straightway into the whole world,
and, mindful, carry my commands among the nations;
mothers and men, and little children, to the rivers
lead them there, and wash them all in fresh-flowing waters.
I shall never be far from you, and I shall set you safe on the threshold of heaven.
After adverse fortune has tossed you through many kinds of toil,
you will be granted a place in the Father’s kingdom.
Over heaven and earth eternal power is mine,
granted by the supreme ruler of gods and of men:
Thus [I have given] you peoples to be ruled in tranquil peace,
and I have given [you] to bridle the proud nations with justice.
Then he addresses Peter: “Am I loved with true love
by you, Peter?” Thus the hero gave his answer,
after God had set his kindled heart aflame with love:
“O Lord, by unmistakable signs you will be able to know
that you are dearer to me than the light, [you] whom with my whole heart
I receive and gladly acknowledge." Jesus answered
with a calmed breast: "Bar-Jona, if love of me has not yet
been driven from you, feed the lambs, feed the sheep.
When early youth clothed your cheeks with bloom,
you used to gather your tunic into a knot and tie it,
and make your way wherever you pleased.
But when the worn-out strength grows cold in your body,
and old age will lie white, scattered across your temples,
then, not of your own will, with iron and close-clamped bonds
they will shut you in, and drag you bound where you would not wish to go."
Saying this, in eagerness he stretched out both his hands
toward his companions, embraced them, and joyfully prays.
Meanwhile the house of all-open Olympus is thrown wide,
and the Father of the heavenly ones and King of men calls a council
into the starry seat, whence from on high he looks out upon all the lands
and the sail-bearing sea and the flying clouds he looks upon.
They gather in the halls open at either end; he himself begins:
"Great dwellers in heaven, Christ, my greatest care
and my offspring, has long since earned the honour
of immortal life, and to be set above the stars of heaven.
For willingly he underwent death, following my commands;
nor did he disdain to behold the realms of Dis, inaccessible to the living,
and, beneath dense night, to go through the shades
along the sorrowful road; therefore the devotion of the Son, awaited by his Father,
overcame the hard journey; for he unbarred black
Tartarus, and the unwilling Tyrant, by his mighty power,
he seized, and himself bound him in enormous coils.
Who forbids that the Son, carried through such great perils,
and triumphing over all his enemies, [be received] into the citadel
of the heavenly ones, and be set upon a starry throne;
and that his hair be wreathed with laurel, and axes be given
to his hands? For he alone has deserved to hold the sceptres
of the world, and to govern its people with everlasting reins.
To the shady grove of Paradise, and the soft meadows,
by an unknown road, Enoch was once carried up.
Afterwards a fiery chariot bore Elijah up into heaven;
but shall our own Son, born of Mary, whom the Spirit brought forth from a
virgin's womb, not climb the stars of heaven?
Go then, and escort our pledge into the hall.
When he had said this, the lofty house of the Thunderer trembled,
and the sea stood calm, free of winds, and the breeze sank away.
All the dwellers in heaven assented, and gave applause.
At once voices were heard, and a mighty harmony,
and the souls of the saints, standing on the threshold of heaven
about to welcome Christ, with harps and tuneful strings
soothed all things; within, the golden house gleams
with unceasing light, the panelled ceilings hang heavy with gems,
underfoot the ivory gleams white, a thousand columns stand in order
of pure silver; the windows, with the light of crystal,
scatter flashes through the temple; with diamond, with pyrope,
with jasper, beryl, sapphire, and red jacinth
the walls shine out, and with green emerald as well,
with chrysolite, and amethyst; here sardonyx, and topaz,
and chrysoprase glitter, and blaze with a thousand colours.
Here the fall of Satan and of his companions is portrayed, and here
the secret counsels, and the hidden decrees of the Thunderer,
and Nature’s hidden ways, and the concealed wonders of creation
are engraved; to know whose causes
is not permitted to us mortals here; likewise, carved
upon these walls shine the names of holy kings,
who will one day lay down their sceptres before Zion;
names then known to no mortal—for, indeed,
for the divine breath had not yet kindled the spark of life in their
bodies, or lit the heavenly fire.
Their devotion too toward Jerusalem, and all their good deeds,
are engraved, which no length of age can efface.
Here too are set fast the names of prophets and of teachers,
and of priests; and then of those by whose death to come
Christ shall be celebrated throughout the whole circle of the earth.
To these are assigned seats studded with pearls, in a long
row along the walls; purple is spread beneath their feet;
countless jewelled necklaces hang from the vault,
studded with pearls, and double crowns of gems and gold.
In the midst there spreads its boughs and gilded arms
a golden palm, with its shoots and leaves and trunk,
whose thin leaves of gold-foil rustled in the blast of the wind.
Around it winged youths and souls were flying,
plucking for Christ the golden-haired fruits from the tree.
For as often as the souls of the saints, sent forth from the body,
return to heaven, a winged company of the princes,
plucking branches of the palm, offers them to those arriving.
Nay more, when one is torn away, a like one — wondrous to tell —
comes forth, and the shoot puts out leaves of everlasting metal.
So this rich tree is never widowed of its leaves,
nor thirsts, nor droops in dying, nor fails with the years.
Then the souls, into the empty seats made from the beginning of the world,
are led, amid the thousands of winged
brethren; and, bidden to take their places on thrones, a robe
they receive snow-white, and upon their brows a twofold crown
let down from the vault, and they wear necklaces about the neck;
and in alternate song they resound the miracles of Christ.
But the temple rose by countless steps toward the east,
whose light, beyond our telling, the orb
of Phoebus it far surpasses with flashing brilliance.
Here the almighty Father sits, and will sit for ever,
upon a starry throne, surrounded by the Virtues; beside him
Justice was standing, her face veiled, and with her hand
holding up the twin scales with the balance made even.
Close by, smiling with serene countenance, kindly Peace
takes her stand, her hair bound with snow-white fillets;
treading weapons beneath her feet and holding out olive branches.
To her Plenty stretches out her right hand with a plaited horn.
Liberty, Chaste Love, Piety and Faith,
bare-breasted, Strength, Constancy, welcome Youth;
Gladness and Gentleness, then Holy Delight,
her gleaming hair let loose over her white neck;
glad Honour, Beauty of form, and joyful Victory;
kindly Wellbeing, untroubled Rest, Prudence bearing
as many watchful eyes beneath as she has feathers on her body,
Knowledge, Intelligence, Reason, Wisdom, the Muse,
and the Graces and the other handmaids, by night and by day
stand around the throne and carry out the divine commands.
Only thin shadows of these, and mere likenesses, does the Father
send down from heaven to wretched mortals; they themselves
never desert the throne, nor from the height of heaven
do they come down, except when the Spirit himself descends,
the Spirit of the Father, as when the dove's likeness settled upon Christ.
And now they pass and repass, this way and that, along the high stairs,
winged youths, following the commands of Jehovah;
like so many snow-white swans swimming across the rivers;
and as a silvery flock of doves goes flitting
about their nests that hang on the lofty rock.
Full in front there is a fountain of snow-white marble,
beside a fragrant grove of laurel; its water, purer than refined
silver, flows down with a gentle murmur;
and it embraces the grove all about with liquid arms:
These are the tears of the Saints, if it is worthy of belief,
drawn up above the heavens by hidden ways, without the Sun.
There, leaping from the pure spring, they wander through
the shadowy grove, and make the laurels fruitful with their stream;
and the unfading leaves of those laurels shall be worn upon the head by
those who swell this spring with the sorrowful welling of their tears.
There the winged ones, seated on the greening bank,
among pale violets beside the streams, make the groves
ring again with song, and they weave fresh garlands
for Christ, who is to ascend, and for all who follow him.
But it is not granted to enter this grove and these roofs
of gold, until by the sacred water of baptism and of blood
the saints’ minds have been washed clean while they were in the body.
Then God calls these forth to the grove in a great throng.
And here among the violets and among the rose-beds, with laurel
foliage the nurslings of the starry hall crown their locks.
So at last they are admitted into the longed-for citadel of heaven.
But between the grove and the temple there stretches a vast
a plain, fruitful without sun, growing green without cloud;
in the midst of which stands the venerable tree of life,
spreading out huge branches and everlasting fruit.
Reclining beneath the canopy of that spreading [tree], the fruits
the heavenly souls pluck, and robes the attendants,
the wing-bearing ones, fit out of leaves white as fine linen.
So at last, their gleaming temples wreathed with laurel,
and clothed in ankle-length tunics, the golden temples
they ascend, a great company of the wing-bearing ones going before.
But while Christ speaks his last words to his companions,
he left mortal sight in the midst of his speaking;
and, wrapped about in a mantle of shining cloud,
he is raised into heaven. An angelic harmony in the fields
is heard; far and wide the high groves send the sound back.
The mountains of the air flash with ruddy radiance,
and cast a quivering light up to the clouds; heaven
parts at its center, and the inner sanctuary of the heavenly ones opens.
The golden palace of the starry heaven blazes forth.
And as he ascends to his Father’s house and lofty realms,
radiant, he marvels at the unfamiliar threshold of heaven,
and beneath his feet Christ sees the clouds and the stars.
At the grove all the prophets and fathers run to meet him,
whom he had led out with him from the Elysian abodes; them
he sent on ahead, and bade them wait while he himself teaches his ministers
on earth, and leaves his last commands.
So at last, having traversed the grove and the open plain,
he bears the laurel on his head, and a snow-white robe upon his body.
The winged ones receive him with applause, and through the high temple
they escort him in full array to the Father's right hand.
He himself sits, wearing a threefold crown upon his brow;
in his left he bears a palm branch, and in his mighty right
he holds the sceptres, making serene the seas and lands and deep heaven,
and the storms as well, with his radiant face.
His eyes stand ablaze with flame, his golden face pours forth fires.
Souls stand about him on the right and on the left, singing,
and the countless princes of heaven; and the praises of the Thunderer
they redouble, and they sing of Christ: how the monsters of the pit
he terrified, and how, pinning down the ancient serpent, he crushed it;
how so many times he has preserved holy Zion from the enemy;
and how that same one destroyed the city of Babylon with a word,
how he made heaven and earth, and the liquid plains,
and the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars—
You made the kindly Sun shine out upon the world:
and [you made] the rains fall from higher up, with the clouds lifted;
you commanded that woodland rise from no seed;
and that birds cleave the air and fishes the sea,
and that living creatures roam over unknown mountains.
You rule both gods and men with everlasting sway;
you turn heaven and the lands and the seas by your divine will.
You are worthy to be extolled by the whole company of men and gods
with everlasting praises and celebrated in song.
Such deeds of the Thunderer they were celebrating in their songs,
and as they sing, the coffered ceilings of the Temple, struck [by their song], resound.
This is no Daedalus fleeing the realms of Minos,

div.note: Here, by "the Titanian stars," I do not understand the Sun, which is mentioned in the following verse, but the lesser stars; and this, I think, is how Virgil should be understood in Aeneid 6, when he says that the Spirit nourishes the Titanian stars—that is, that the Sun sustains the stars with its own light. For the Sun is the soul and mind of the world, as Macrobius shows from the poets and philosophers. The names of all the gods belong to the Sun. The Sun is also called Spirit by Solomon, Ecclesiastes 1.7. Virgil's commentators are therefore mistaken—unless I am mistaken myself—when they understand "the Titanian stars" to mean the Sun.

lg.l: Having dared to trust himself to the sky on swift-flying wings,
by an unaccustomed path, he swam out to the icy Bears of the north.
He calls no West Winds here, nor does he glide on wings through the upper air,
flitting on winged soles through the storm-tossed clouds
like Mercury, binding to his feet the sandals
of gold, which carry him aloft on wings, whether above the seas,
or over the land, keeping pace with the rushing blast.
These songs vain poets sang long ago.
But by his own power, not by wings, he parts the breezes,
and Christ, poising himself through the empty clouds,
skims his liquid path, and flies on high above the upper air.
Alas, my mind fails beneath the immense burden
of my bodily bulk, so that I cannot ascend to heaven with you,
O Christ, O God, nor glide beneath the stars in swift flight.
Alas for me! How shall I follow the Lord as he flies on high in a cloud,
And shall I cross the thresholds of highest heaven,
I, whom earthly limbs and dying members dull?
Supply me, I beg, with the oarage of faith's wings,
that I may have strength to fly back to heaven out of the blind prison
of the unclean body; where no rest from toils is
certain, but we are continually pressed within tight bonds,
where Grief and sorrowful Cares have made their beds,
and pale Diseases dwell, and gloomy Old Age,
and Fear dwells there, while the mercilessness of harsh death rages.
And when, at my final hour, life leaves me,
I commend this soul to you; then completely remove all
bodily corruptions, and lay her up pure
among the blessed nurslings of the starry heaven.
Grant that she, though now hindered by the wound of sin,
may be borne through the empty air and rise into the heavens,
so that she may settle with you in the longed-for seats above the ether.
But his companions raise their palms in vain toward the stars;
they strain their burning eyes to heaven in vain;
for two winged angels came flying from heaven
right before the men's very faces, and they pour these words from their mouths;
Why do you stand sorrowful, keeping your eyes raised toward the stars?
Him whom you saw flying above heaven’s
golden stars, you shall see returning, seated upon snowy
clouds, and shining in a red-gold mantle of light;
After saying this, they return to heaven on whirring wings.
The companions gaze up, breathless, and follow with their eyes
as far as their gaze can keep the winged angels in view,
as they leave the earth and direct their voices toward the stars.
See how Christ now, marked out with the spoils of victory,
advances, and as conqueror towers above all gods.
Now he brings the whole world completely beneath his yoke,
and masters the sea that lies above, and the sea that washes below.
Our Aaron, gleaming with gems and in comely vesture,
has at last taken his seat in the lofty inner sanctuary of heaven,
where on our behalf he has consecrated to the Father an undying offering,
And he makes heaven’s temple smoke with the incense of his merits.
This is that Elijah, carried in a chariot of flame
to a starry seat—his reins are fiery, and his team
flame-vomiting; he himself, all fire, blazes throughout,
yet without loss; for harmless in its soft touch
the flame licks his hair, and creeps about his temples.
And while on light wheels he glides across the highest spheres,
the mantle falls from his shoulders, which Elisha takes up.
So Christ, after he had handed over to his companions the reins
of the new-born kingdom, then, the sacred rites duly performed,
behold, he flies away toward the south winds and high into the clouds.
Fling wide, you dwellers in heaven, the gates of double-opening Olympus,
that this my Lord, now flashing with light and with gold,
may enter, and take his seat upon the Father's eastern throne.
and that, the world triumphed over, to the citadels of heaven
he may drive as victor his rosy chariot above the towering clouds;
his enemies slain, and distinguished by the spoils of honor.
and that, seated on the snow-white summit of the radiant heaven,
he may review the vows of the peoples, and, aloft, all

div.note: God is everywhere, yet his seat is placed in the East, and in the more honourable place. Therefore Christ, who is called the Dayspring from on high, Luke 1, is placed in the East; and from thence we hope that Christ will return. In the East the feet of Christ stood, Zach. 14 — namely, on the Mount of Olives. Out of the East, that is, out of Paradise, we were cast forth; toward the East we pray; our churches look toward the East. See Justin Martyr ad Orthodox. q. 118. Tertull. in Apolog. Origen Homil. 5. in Num. Athanas. de Necess. quaest. q. 14. Basil. de Spir. Sanct. cap. 27. &c. And the Seventy Interpreters, "toward the East," Psal. 68. 36. "As the lightning cometh out of the East, so shall the coming of the Son of man be," Matth. 24. 27.

lg.l: may look upon the earth and the conquered nations in long array,
as varied in their tongues as in the fashion of their dress and arms.
But although the Father has received him into the heavenly hall,
and has removed him far from mortal sight—from there,
from there nevertheless we hope for his return, terrible to all the nations of the world
that do not venerate Jesus.
Before him shall go a fire with crackling flames,
wrapping the trembling earth in pitch-black murk.
The whirling column shall surge up to heaven; the fire, with its reins
let slip, shall rage, and shed a grim light:
just as when, on a clear night, blood-red comets
glow ominously, or Sirius’s blaze,
bringing drought and disease to suffering mortals,
rises, and darkens the sky with its baleful light.
Besides, at his coming they shall see the stars
slip headlong from the sky, and through the shadows of night
long trails of flame whiten behind them.
The sun, glory of the stars, shall stain its face with dusky rust;
and the moon shall spread a maiden's blush over her face.
The heaven, parting asunder, shall melt like wax before the fire;
and the earth, shaken to its foundations, shall fall in vast ruin.
Then the huge groaning of the sea, and the battered rocks,
men shall hear, and the voices broken upon the shore;
and terrible trumpets bellowing through the upper air, and moreover
Arms amid the clouds, in a clear region of the sky,
they will see glowing crimson, and thundering as they are struck.
These signs will show that unseen upheavals are at hand,
as are crimes and deceptions, and that hidden wars are swelling.
Then, in fear, men everywhere along the shores
will scatter and stealthily make for the woods and, wherever they find them, hollow
rocks; and they will rue their own deceit and the light of day.
At last Christ will come forth, whom a thousand
souls will follow, on this side and on that, through the shining clouds of heaven.
Then the winged company of the princes, with the blare of trumpets
dread-sounding, will fill the whole world with terrors;
but Christ's coming will be sudden for mortals, and
unlooked-for; so once, in the time of Janus,
while in gladness they were busy with shared feasts among themselves,
and while they were celebrating marriages and the wedlock they had pledged,
washed the woods away, whirling them in its mad eddy,
Ocean, the fountain of rivers, and over all the plains
carried off the herds together with their stalls; and young men and old
the South Wind overwhelmed them with water and drowned them beneath the open sea.
Not otherwise will Christ, gliding down from heaven on high,
fall upon the unwary, just as a thief in the shadow of night
is wont to haul off his plunder, or to live by robbery;
or like an arrow that comes gliding in, whistling on its wings,
sped by a strong hand, and driven through the air in a whirl;
Or as when the whole sky roars with dread-sounding thunder,
lightning redoubles its fires from the riven clouds,
and suddenly races from east to west.
O how terrible for wretched mortals will that
day be, which will utterly shake the whole world with grief!
How great a wailing will then strike the heavens,
when God shall lay the smoking rooftops level with the ground?
when they see the world's luxury collapse in flames?
Such will be the appearance of Christ coming from heaven,
if it be permitted us to set great things beside small:
just as when, with the sky rent open, a storm cloud comes toward the lands
and through mid-sea (alas, foreknowing it far in advance,
the wretched farmers' hearts shudder: it will bring ruin
upon the trees, and havoc upon the crops, it will lay all things low far and wide;
the winds fly on ahead and will carry the sound to the shores)
But as soon as Christ shall come down from heaven on high,
behold, a shining rainbow will appear among the clouds,
drawing a thousand varied colors against the opposing sun.
Upon it, as on a throne, Jesus the Judge will take his seat,
towering, looking out on the seas on every side and on every side the lands;
and while he rolls his blazing eyes over each thing in turn
he will raise an immeasurable cry, at which the sea and every
wave will tremble, and the earth, terrified deep in its lowest
foundations, will unbar the pale realms of the shades.
Then at last [the gates] of death, grating on their dread-sounding hinge,
The gates shall be flung open; Christ will bid the lifeless
go forth from their tombs, and come out to the upper air.
Then those to whom their brothers were hateful while life remained,
or who struck a parent, and worked a fraud upon a dependant,
or who brooded alone over riches they had found,
and set no share aside for their own — which is the largest crowd of all;
and those slain for adultery, and those who followed arms
in an impious cause, and did not shrink from betraying their masters' trust;
they shall stand at the Judge's left hand, and all of them at once
a vast whirlpool will swallow, when Acheron has burst its way through,
and the wretches will suffer eternal punishment through all ages.
Savage fire will pant from devouring furnaces,
and the whole earth will thunder back with terrifying collapses.
From its jaws it will belch out a huge smoke — wondrous to tell —
and will wrap the day in blinding murk,
snatching the view from men's eyes; it will roll up within its cavern
a smoke-laden night, with darkness mingled with fire.
Girded by a whirlwind and by pitch-black, darkening ash,
the Stygian King; the wretched guilty ones, where the thickest smoke
where the smoke rolls on its billows thickest, and the vast cavern seethes with black mist,
he will drag them into the midst of the fires; and with a cruel lash
he will exult and trample upon them, and slay them with a lingering death.
But death will be immortal and rich in punishments,
nor will there be any respite from ever-renewed torments.
He, while [the other] resists, [seizes] him roaring with a dreadful cry,
that ruthless fury will snatch Judas away in its hooked talons:
and as when a tawny eagle, flying on high, carries off a serpent it has seized, and has twined its feet about it and clung fast with its talons;
but the wounded serpent twists its winding coils,
and bristles with scales upraised, and hisses with its mouth
as it rears upright; she presses no less hard with her hooked
beak the struggling [serpent], and at the same time beats the air with her wings:
just so will Satan carry his prey down to Orcus
and torment him with punishments; and for his former evils
the king begotten of night will exact just retribution.
From here roarings are heard, and there resound the savage
lashes, then weeping, laments, and the rage of souls
that refuse their chains, and groan beneath the long night.
Were the fates not against it, how gladly would they, in the air above,
endure base poverty and hard toils?
