Degenerate souls, you who violate every divine law,
you who despise the human race and mortal arms,
Take warning: learn justice and not to despise the divine Power,
and expect God to remember right and wrong.

div.note: Satan may be said to have been born of Night in that sense in which the wicked are called in Scripture the sons of darkness.

lg.l: You do indeed hope to conceal your crimes,
but the hiding-places of the soul and all the hearts of men are searched by
the Almighty, and the Father looks upon the world with impartial eyes;
nor is there any hope of flight, nor can you hide yourselves in darkness
from the fierce radiance of his countenance.
Do you believe you can take flight or conceal these crimes by stealth,
or do you hope that you can escape Christ’s mighty
hands? Once he has caught you,
will snatch you up, and crush you under his feet, and break you with his sceptre:
as easily as the hawk, that sacred bird, from a high crag
overtakes on the wing the dove high up in the cloud,
and holds it fast once seized, and disembowels it with hooked talons;
then blood, and feathers torn away, come drifting down from the sky.
Therefore the atonement for sins committed, until late death
do not defer it; for time flies irretrievably away,
nor will the power be granted hereafter to beg for pardon.
Now pray for peace, and stretch out your right hands to heaven
sorrowful and suppliant, beating your breasts with your palms.
At the right hand will stand those who suffered wounds for Christ,
and those who were chaste priests while life remained;
and those who were devout prophets, and spoke things worthy of Christ,
or who enriched life by the arts they discovered,
and those whose merit made others remember them,
All these shall have their brows encircled by a snow-white fillet.
And all shall bear palms, the prize for victors;
and they shall sing the paean forever, and utter songs,
here [is] the ancient race, Judah's fairest offspring,
great-hearted heroes born in better years,
and Janus, and Abraham, and Isaac, and holy Jacob,
and nations beyond number, and peoples shall follow Jesus,
shining now with a new light, and singing of the King,
while by his ascent he rises above the summits of highest heaven.
But among her sister nymphs the fairest maiden
shall shine among the stars like golden Phoebe;
Her hair is gleaming white, and gleaming white too her robe,
and, borne through the air by a choir of winged princes,
as Queen she shall enter the starry citadel of heaven;
This signal honour for her the high King of the upper air,
Jupiter, shall consecrate in return for her untouched virginity.

div.note: Of old, tombs, corpses, priests, sacrificial victims, women, brides, athletes, victors, princes and the like were adorned with the fillet. Here the fillet is taken for the diadem, for the diadem of the ancients was nothing else than a fillet, band or ribbon: I find these words used indifferently by the authors. Diadema from διαδέω, I bind about. Pompey bound up a wound with his diadem. "Wear the venerable bands laid upon thy head": Seneca in the Thyestes means the diadem. * The paean is a song of victory, as Servius teaches out of Aeschylus.

Jupiter, as it were "helping Father," or rather "Jova-Father," from the word Jehovah, as Adonis from Adonai. The wiser pagans acknowledged the same supreme God as we do; they named him Jove, "whose offspring we are," as St Paul proves from Aratus. Nor is it any less lawful for us to call him Jove than God (θεόν), mind (νοῦν), word (λόγον), or spirit (πνεῦμα), which are pagan words. "Zeus came into being first, Zeus last, ruler of the thunderbolt," and so forth. See Orpheus's poem on Jove.

lg.l: Christ God, than whom no one dearer to me lives,
be a lenient Judge to me and then, I beg, forget
the punishments and stain of my former sins.
Press no further with other [punishments]; have pity on my
errors, and remember my tears and my groans.
This last favour I beg; have pity on one who prays,
grant peace to me, lifeless and destroyed by the death that sin brings,
rescue me from death, and bid me hope for heaven.
So shall I sing of you, Christ, as you pity our afflictions,
and in my songs I shall praise [your] mighty deeds;
songs in which Thracian Orpheus shall not surpass me,
and no Muse shall celebrate your honours as well.
But the companions, their eyes cast down and their faces sorrowful,
descend together from the mountain, pondering various
outcomes within themselves, and determine to return to Jerusalem,
until the Spirit, having descended from heaven on high,
should send them throughout the whole world,
that they might found a Jerusalem to abide through all ages,
just as the Master at his departing had given his promises.
But while they all wait within closed doors,
praying, mindful of the promised gift; behold,
with a terrifying sound, from the highest clouds there come
blasts of wind, which filled the whole house with a whirlwind,
Whereupon the house, set trembling, sways with its roof shaken.
The leaders recognised God; as one, they felt the divine blasts
and the sound sent from heaven.
Moreover tongues of fire on the crown of the companions' heads
appear, and the lofty house gleams with a new light;
they recognise the fire, and the promises of their divine master,
namely that this was a sign of the Holy Spirit;
filled with this, they broke their silence in diverse tongues;
and with these [tongues] a new Jerusalem, far and wide throughout the world,
scattered abroad they build, and strive to raise [it] up to heaven.
Nor do they sound mortal, since they are breathed upon by the power
of God now nearer; but the holy oracles of the prophets,
and the praises of Christ, and his mighty deeds, they publish abroad;
and like a rushing flood of water, or a whirlwind, out into the world
they burst forth in swift course; the Stygian ranks, by a word,
they lay low; mighty Babylon has fallen in a vast collapse.
Pluto cannot hold out, nor strain against
so great a force, and such great blasts of the heavenly Spirit:
for in their rush they carry off with them all the kingdoms of the world
and drag the nations headlong, and lay the rebels low,
and overturn Satan's empire from its lowest foundations:
just as when the warring winds in the great sky
should tear up the heavy crop far and wide from its deepest roots,
and hurl it aloft; or, in a black whirlwind,
the storm would sweep away both the light stalk and the flying stubble;
Behold too the world subdued by cultivators to its farthest bounds,
and the eastern homes of the Arabs, and the painted Geloni.
Such was the Spirit, ranging over the whole circle of the earth
in twice six tongues burning with heavenly fire:
just as when the North Wind, thick [with storm], from Hyperborean shores
has swooped down, and scatters the winter storms of Scythia and the dry
clouds; then the tall crops and the waving plains
shiver under gentle gusts: and with a sound the topmost
woods give [answer], and the long waves press on toward the shores;
He flies on, sweeping both fields and seas at once in his course;
so now no chains hold them back, nor cruel lashes;
no crags nor hollow cliffs, nor do the rivers set in their way hold them back,
which with their flood whirl along mountains they have swept up.
The love of Christ carried [them] across Dindyma, and across the Garonne
and the Alpine snows, and the frosts of the sluggish Rhine;
nor yet does the rough ice cut the tender soles of these men,
Some of them went far away to the thirsty Africans:
others reached Scythia and Crete’s swift Oaxes,
and to the Britons, utterly sundered from the whole world.
Behold twice six swans rejoicing in their flock,
who bear the name of Christ on high to the stars:
now twice six doves are flying through the great void,
which in their beaks carry the boughs of the fruitful olive.
The twelve gates of Jerusalem are unbarred, and of the city
all its beauty appears, and the long halls lie open.
As soon as the golden Sun has set for the world, behold,
straightway twelve stars shine out for wretched mortals.
And now a rain bountiful for the sown fields is sent down from heaven,
From the deepest root a very dense forest springs up.
See, the earth is now opened for the crops by the hooked tooth.
Twice six husbandmen, the clods once broken, begin to turn over
the bristling field, and the bull at the plough
to groan, and the ploughshare to grow bright in the furrows of the word.
Christ God, sole tiller whom the fields obey,
do not suffer the sluggish field to harden in neglect,
of beloved Jerusalem, and break [it] up with sturdy bullocks,
and bring forth broad crops from the seed of the Word.
Do soften the wild fruits, and through constant cultivation
let the woodland wild-vine, pouring out its scattered clusters,
put off its rustic temper, and through the whole world
stretch out its branches, and spread itself wide toward the breezes—
the vine-shoot, let loose through the clear sky with slackened reins.
As a marching column of waters comes down from riven clouds, so descends
the Spirit, and drenches sorrowing minds with nectar.
Now the chief men, filled with the liquor of sweet new wine,
uttered oracles throughout the world in diverse tongues.
O with how great a sweetness does such wine gladden minds —
wine that drips down from the sky in generous drops!
Such wines are not laid up in Falernian cellars,
wines that would make men’s feet unsteady and bind their tongues.
But neither the Aminean vines, wines of the sturdiest sort,
nor the wines that Lesbos drinks from Methymna’s vine,
can vie with this new wine, last for as many years,
and banish such great cares from the heart.
This one alone is that Lyaeus, the giver of joy.
Orpheus in the woods, Arion among the dolphins,
and now the companions of Christ, among the rocks and the wild beasts,
sing sacred songs, at whose strain the lynxes, spellbound,
and the rivers, altered, stayed their own courses.
The stiff oaks begin to sway their tops,
and the sturdy ash-trees [begin] to come down from the mountain tops.
Stirred by this song, the shades from the abodes of Erebus
were struck with amazement; Pluto marvels at the unarmed flock
that soothes tigers and drives lions on with its voice.
A temple, august, vast, lofty with twice six columns,
is raised out of the living rock; breathing statues
stand in the vestibule; Christ stands in the midst of the sanctuary;
twice six gilded rays encircle his temples,
and to him the humble nations bring their solemn gifts.
Now twice six are accustomed to come beneath the Lord's chariot,
four-footed steeds, and to bear harmonious bridles under the yoke.

div.note: O wonderful twelve-horse team of good horses, whose bits are peace and whose reins are charity, bound fast to one another by the bonds of concord and set under the yoke of faith; who upon four wheels carry the mystery of the Gospel to the ends of the whole earth, bearing a good charioteer, the Word of God, by whose whip the enticements of the world are put to flight, &c. Ambros. in Psal. 118. serm. 5.

lg.l: He himself drives them on, and with his hands bends the streaming reins,
and while the axle flies blazing with speed, all
the realms he tramples beneath the hooves of his galloping horses.
Now they carry heavy clusters of grapes on their huge shoulders,
the twice six spies; and twelve stones
are lifted from the dry channel of the river Jordan;
Now the priests shoulder the uplifted ark of the covenant in due order
and carry it through the pathless places of the world;
twice six gems gleam upon the breast of the high
Priest, and with burning rays they light up all things.
And now, all unlooked for, there are hurled from the upper air thick
lightnings with thunder; the vast palace of heaven groans.
The high places of the earth tremble, while the flashing weapons
of the Word shatter the mountains and overturn the seas.
Lest, O Christ, the ship, with such waves rising against her,
should founder, stripped of her equipment and deprived of her helmsman,
behold, twelve sailors now begin to discharge the helmsman’s office
and to cleave the dark waves in the north wind.
So many chosen leaders were going in twice six ships
to the aid of Jerusalem, and were cutting the plains of salt with bronze.
This one spreads the wings of the sails, that one heaven's golden
stars surveys anew; one holds the tiller, and another
the iron-shod stakes and sharp-pointed poles
gets ready; that one fits the gangways and slackens the ropes:
and they slant the sails' bellies into the wind, and catch the air:

div.note: "By the lightnings he means the apostles, who showed forth to the whole world the light of the thunder." See Athanas. de Trinitat. Dial. 3.

lg.l: Others bend to the oars, and sweep the level waters;
one and the same fervour holds them all at once, a shout strikes the sky —
the sailors’ shout; the churned waters foam as their arms are drawn back,
together they cut their furrows, and the whole sea gapes open,
torn up by the oars and by the shrieking beaks:
Not so headlong across the course in a two-horse race
have chariots sped; they rush forth, streaming from the starting gate;
nor have charioteers so shaken the waving reins over the teams
let loose, and, leaning forward, hang over the lash.
Meanwhile a great thronging of the people gathers at the waters;
mothers and men, boys and unwedded girls
stood pleading to be the first to make the crossing,
and were stretching out their hands in longing for the farther shore,
that, admitted at last, they might look again upon the longed-for kingdom.
Christ, subduer of the sea, look upon this battered ship,
which the waves now hold, while winds toss her in the deep.
Do you not see her wandering adrift, with no helmsman aboard?
Do you not see the rudder, so often wrenched away by force,
to which you clung, appointed [its] guardian, and did govern the course?
Ah, the crime! see, a band of young men girt with firebrands
has filled the gangways with flames, and the hallowed pine
has foully burned; the fiery ardour of war rages
through the thwarts and oars and the painted sterns of fir.
O when will the fires lay down their unconquered strength?
Do the prayers of holy men avail nothing, nor the winds poured upon [them],
or the showers driven from the clouds of our eyes?
No one has power to drive the torches from the sacred vessels
the blazing torches of war? But still beneath the timber lives
tow, belching sluggish smoke; black all the way down to the keel
is the vapour, and the blight descends through the whole frame.
Almighty Father, if you do not yet hate, to the last man,
the Christians; if your ancient mercy has any regard for human toils,
of men, grant the fleet to escape the flame,
and now snatch the slender fortunes of Christ's offspring from death.
Let the half-burnt timbers now grow sodden with our tears,
until all the smoke of war is quenched, and all
the ships are saved from ruin, their enemies burnt up.
Dispel our fears, and allow your servant to accomplish this by his prayers:
lest, battered on any voyage or by the whirling wind,
they be overcome; may you hold the tiller, and watch the stars
again, and be yourself the ship's steersman in the rushing waves,
if ever, borne onward, she approaches the Sirens’ rocks,
so often perilous, and white with the bones of many;
none the less let the fleet run a safe course over the sea,
and, [relying] on your promises, kind Father, let her hold her course undaunted
through every mishap, with wave and tide favouring,
and be brought back at last to the longed-for shores of her homeland,
and, safe, reach the harbours of Olympus for which I long.
Christians, let us now seek the Lord with our whole mind,
who, when he was to send his companions to the world's furthest shores,
breathed upon them with the winds of his Spirit, and touched them with fire;
so that he may breathe into us the hidden flame of heavenly love
and kindle minds congealed with icy cold
may kindle [our minds], and burn up the abominable memorials of crimes,
that he may make firm an eternal peace among us, and [our] covenants.
O Father, O eternal power over men and over the gods,
(for who else could there be whom we might now implore)
your own nation of the Christians, with the blood of its own kin,
defiles itself, and never ceases to rise up in arms;
a nation which neither length of days nor any devotion softens,
nor, broken by Christ's command or by the fates, does it rest.
Alas, what battle-lines and what carnage they have stirred up against one another,
unsubdued as they are; the whole strength of the kingdom has been engaged in the struggle.
Meanwhile the barbarian enemy now looms over the walls
of languishing Jerusalem, nay, he terrifies heaven itself with his arms;
At last grant Jerusalem—grant her escape from the scourge of war,
holy Father, and take away the strife among your own,
and now, I pray, take pity upon such great sufferings;
and after the perils of sea and of vast land have been endured,
let harsh hearts now grow gentle, their weapons laid aside —
the hearts of the Christians — and may you make firm this peace by an eternal covenant,
rather, let us with our own hands deal cruel deaths upon the Turks.
Quickly, take up the sword and root out the accursed nation.
If there is any solid valour in [you]; and there will follow no small
glory: do we not have just as many lives and hands?
We scarcely have an enemy apiece, if we meet them man to man.
Do they not know how often we have stood against harsh weapons
and joined battle; how often he forced the enemy to flee,
and how many thousands in a single day the victorious
Hunyadi sent down to Tartarus? Or have you not heard that many fortifications
built by the hand of the Turks, sank down into the flames?
Why should I recount the fleets overthrown in the gulf of Naupactus,
barbarian fleets? and shall I sing of the straits churned by our prows,
and the fields of Neptune red with the blood of the Turks?
And why should I tell of the keels furrowing the deep seas
of the Christians, who now, where the Sun goes down into the waves,
and where the sun rises, throughout those regions, with the sea churned,
fly; you would think that, torn from their roots, there floated on the deep
the Cyclades, or that high mountains were clashing with mountains.
We do not lack, then, either strength or spirit.
We have resources too, and our young warriors are still unscathed;
at last, then, drive the enemy from our country’s borders;
arm yourselves in spirit, and in hope anticipate the war.
Arise, some avenger, out of the bones of our own people,
to hunt down the barbarian tyrants with firebrand and with sword,
now, hereafter, at whatever time the strength shall offer itself:
shores set against shores, waters against waves —
I invoke this curse: let arms clash with arms, and let their very descendants fight.
Therefore, as for the hated stock and every generation to come,
persecute them with hatred, and send these to our ashes as
offerings; let there be no love between the peoples and no treaties.
O You who filled the companions with the holy breath!
Breathe upon me too with the wafting breezes of the heavenly Zephyr,
breathe upon [it], so that, numb with the wintry cold of sins,
the field of my heart may bring forth for me, and be ever green.
Let it not irk [thee] to burn the barren fields of my breast,
and to burn up with flames the light stubble of my errors.
And us, tossed about by the world's wintry star,
steer through the swollen waves, through so many hidden shoals.
Grant that I may overcome Scylla's rage and the Cyclopean rocks;
with thee as guide, grant that I may escape the Syrtes and vast Charybdis;
and grant an easy course to the wind, and blow favorably;
let the longed-for breezes freshen, while over the great sea
alas, we follow a homeland that flees us, and are rolled by the waves.
Lest stormy Orion, rising suddenly with the swell,
carry [us] onto hidden shoals and, with violent south winds, utterly
dash [us] upon a rock, or fling [us] across the boundless seas.
As for what remains, I pray, may I be allowed to entrust safely across the waves
my sails to you, and may I be allowed to reach the heavenly harbor.
These verses I have been tuning on Virgil's reed,
while the hoarse trumpet gives the bloody signal for war
among kindred nations; and while, in trembling
uproar, all Latium bands together in oath, and the young men rage,
snatching up arms in madness, with too little reason in their arms.
Meanwhile Charles [restrains] the Britons, separated from the world,
after his father's example — for his father's very likeness is in him —
With justice he reins in [the Britons], and with iron and close-fastened bars
he has barred the gates of war, triumphing over arms
and over the Ocean too; whose broad waters gleam back
with sulphurous lightning, and the trembling wave bellows again with thunder;
whose crash is often heard in the pools of Avernus.
To him Neptune, tamer of the sea, yielded all authority,
the sovereignty of the deep, and his fierce trident.
No longer does Triton terrify the blue straits with his conch.
The Nymphs who watch over the sea and the rivers marvel;
Thetis and Melite marvel at men’s shields gleaming far
across the deep, and at such great ships afloat;
and away they flee in fear, the sea-beasts of monstrous body,
while our fleet glides over the waves of the Ocean,
and by leave of father Neptune is borne on undaunted.
At that season sweet [England] was nurturing me, Ross,
England, as I flourished in the pursuits of unglorious ease.
Pierian Muses, you shall dedicate this tribute to Christ—
to Christ, my love for whom grows so greatly from hour to hour,
as the green alder shoots up in the new spring:
O Christ, ornament of heaven, O Christ, glory of the earth,
keeper of a lovely flock, himself lovelier still,
let the flock give you no cause for shame, divine Master;
Be gracious—O, be propitious to your own—and do not forever withdraw
yourself from our sight; may it be granted us once more to behold your face,
O Christ, etc.
